Chromosomal Disorders — Down Syndrome, Turner & Mechanisms

Down syndrome (trisomy 21) — incidence ~1 in 700; risk rises with maternal age (but most affected babies are born to younger mothers).

Mechanisms: (1) nondisjunction in meiosis I (90–95%) — extra chromosome 21; recurrence risk ~1% (or maternal-age related). (2) Unbalanced Robertsonian translocation (4–5%; e.g. 14;21) — if a parent is a balanced carrier, recurrence risk is high (balanced mother → ~10%, balanced father → ~2%). (3) Mosaicism (1–2%) — milder phenotype. Recurrent trisomy 21 in siblings → test PARENTS with karyotype for a balanced translocation (not the child again).

Clinical features: hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, single palmar (simian) crease, sandal-gap toes, flat occiput/brachycephaly, small ears, protruding tongue, Brushfield spots; congenital heart (AVSD, VSD, PDA), duodenal atresia (double bubble), Hirschsprung, hypothyroidism, atlanto-axial instability, haematological malignancy (ALL/AML-M7), early Alzheimer-type dementia; global developmental delay; short stature.

Screening/management: confirm by karyotype (FISH for rapid confirmation if needed). At birth: echo + abdominal USS (duodenal atresia), hearing (OAE) and eye screen, TSH at birth/6 mo/yearly, full blood count; annual thyroid checks; early intervention. Counselling: recurrence risk; discuss prenatal diagnosis (CVS 11–14 wks, amniocentesis ≥15 wks, NIPT).

Trisomy 8 mosaicism — full trisomy 8 is embryonic lethal; surviving “trisomy 8” = mosaic (nondisjunction post-zygotically or trisomy rescue) → milder features (deep plantar creases, skeletal/urogenital).

Turner syndrome (45,X / X-monosomy) — girls: short stature, shield chest + widely spaced nipples, webbed neck, cubitus valgus, lymphedema at birth, streak ovaries → primary amenorrhoea/infertility + hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism, bicuspid aortic valve/coarctation, horseshoe kidney, normal IQ (may have visuospatial deficit), treat with growth hormone + oestrogen HRT; karyotype confirms; Y-material carrying → gonadectomy (gonadoblastoma risk).

Klinefelter (47,XXY) — tall, small firm testes, gynaecomastia, infertility (azoospermia), ↑FSH/LH.

Exam pearls
  • Recurrent Down in siblings → parental karyotype (translocation) — not “bad luck”.
  • Trisomy 8 survival = mosaicism.
  • Turner = coarctation + webbed neck + no puberty; confirm karyotype.
  • Down = AVSD + double-bubble + brushfield + simian crease.

#42MCQ edited2020-Genetics-MCQ-Medicine-1e976f2b
A child has features of Down syndrome. Which test would you perform?
  • A. Karyotype (chromosomal analysis)
  • B. FISH
  • C. Chromosomal microarray
  • D. DNA sequencing
  • E. Metabolic screening
Best answer
A. Karyotype (chromosomal analysis)
Down syndrome (trisomy 21) → karyotype is the first-line confirmatory test — it diagnoses regular trisomy, translocation and mosaicism and guides recurrence-risk counselling of the parents. FISH only confirms rapid aneuploidy (not the mechanism).
2020 · Genetics · 2 questions · MCQ

Fragile X Syndrome & Associated (FMR1) Disorders

Genetics: X-linked CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in FMR1 (Xq27.3). Normal <45 repeats; premutation 55–200; full mutation >200 → hypermethylation → silencing of FMRP (RNA-binding protein for synaptic development). Anticipation (repeats expand through generations, especially via mothers). Full mutations from fathers are rare (only daughters get his X). Premutations expand to full mutation when transmitted by a mother (not usually by a father).

Clinical features (males): intellectual disability (most common inherited cause of ID after Down syndrome), long face, large protruding ears, prominent jaw/forehead, macro-orchidism (post-puberty), large head circumference, joint hypermobility, autistic behaviour/gaze avoidance, mitral valve prolapse, seizures (~10–20%), behavioural problems (hand flapping, ADHD). Females (carriers) have milder/subtler features (learning difficulty, anxiety).

Premutation-associated conditions: Fragile X-associated primary ovarian insufficiency (FXPOI) — ~20% of female premutation carriers (premature ovarian failure/ovarian dysfunction — hence the ovarian-dysfunction question); FXTAS (fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome) — adult-onset intention tremor, cerebellar ataxia, parkinsonism, cognitive decline (older males, mean onset 60s).

Diagnosis: FMR1 DNA analysis (PCR ± Southern blot for methylation/repeat sizing). NOT detectable by karyotype/array/exome. Karyotype may show “fragile site” historical oddity only.

Genetic counselling: mother of affected son is an obligate premutation carrier → test her sisters/daughters; each daughter of a carrier has 50% chance of inheriting premutation (which expands in her offspring); discuss prenatal diagnosis (CVS/amniocentesis) for at-risk pregnancies.

Exam pearls
  • Intellectual disability + long face + large ears + macro-orchidism = fragile X → FMR1 testing.
  • Woman with ovarian insufficiency + intellectually disabled brothers = premutation → test her FMR1.
  • Testing fathers of young children with ID — daughters of an FMR1-premutation father are carriers too.

#39MCQ edited2020-Genetics-MCQ-Medicine-2a4f52e3
In a case of fragile X syndrome, which genetic test would you perform?
  • A. FMR1 CGG repeat (fragile X DNA) analysis
  • B. Karyotype
  • C. Chromosomal microarray
  • D. FISH
  • E. Whole exome sequencing
Best answer
A. FMR1 CGG repeat (fragile X DNA) analysis
Fragile X = CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in FMR1 (>200 repeats → methylation-silenced). Diagnosis by FMR1 methylation/repeat analysis — invisible to karyotype, CMA and exome. Most common inherited cause of intellectual disability.
#44MCQ edited2020-Genetics-MCQ-Medicine-ef979f35
A female has ovarian dysfunction and her brothers have intellectual disability. Which test would you perform?
  • A. Fragile X testing (FMR1 premutation analysis)
  • B. Karyotype
  • C. Mitochondrial DNA analysis
  • D. Hemoglobin electrophoresis
  • E. Thyroid function tests
Best answer
A. Fragile X testing (FMR1 premutation analysis)
Female FMR1 premutation carriers (55–200 CGG repeats) → premature ovarian insufficiency/POF; males with premutation → FXTAS (tremor-ataxia) in old age. Intellectual disability clusters in the family = fragile X — test the mother/sisters.
2020 · Genetics · 1 question · MCQ

Genetic Counselling

Definition: a communication process — help individuals/families understand the medical, psychological and familial implications of genetic disease: diagnosis, natural history, inheritance, risk to relatives, and options.

Non-directive counselling — the counsellor provides balanced, accurate, complete information without steering the client toward a particular decision (testing, termination, treatment). The couple decides. It respects autonomy, especially when no “right” medical answer exists (e.g. whether to have a prenatal diagnostic test). Counsellor should: assess understanding, explore values, offer all options (including doing nothing), support the decision, and never recommend for or against pregnancy termination.

Elements of a session: confirm diagnosis (medical records/tests), draw pedigree (≥3 generations), assess risk (calculation: e.g. 50% AD transmission, 25% AR if both carriers, X-linked 50% of sons), explain implications for family members, offer testing (predictive/carrier/prenatal), psychological support, written information, follow-up.

Confidentiality — genetic information affects relatives; the doctor may encourage family disclosure but cannot breach confidentiality without consent (except exceptional public-interest exceptions).

Common scenarios: couple with previous child with cystic fibrosis → 25% per pregnancy; discuss CVS/amniocentesis/NIPT, offer carrier testing to at-risk relatives; non-directive presentation of options. Balanced reproductive choices — allow time, repeat discussions.

Exam pearls
  • Non-directive = inform, support, don’t steer — the decision belongs to the family.
  • Always verify the diagnosis before quoting risks.
  • Testing of at-risk minors: generally defer predictive testing until adulthood unless it changes immediate management.

#41MCQ edited2020-Genetics-MCQ-Medicine-e6075838
A G2P1 woman and her husband attend a prenatal consultation. Their first child was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis and they are anxious about the current pregnancy. What does non-directive counseling mean?
  • A. Providing information without steering the couple's decision
  • B. Advising termination of pregnancy
  • C. Recommending prenatal testing
  • D. Referring the couple to social services
  • E. Offering only carrier screening
Best answer
A. Providing information without steering the couple's decision
Non-directive genetic counseling = educate on risks, options and implications; the couple decides — the counselor never recommends for or against testing/termination. Mandatory counselling before/after tests; confidential, balanced, informed choice.

Genetic Testing — Indications & Interpretation

Test selection by question:

QuestionBest test
Whole chromosome aneuploidy (Down, Turner, Klinefelter)Karyotype (or rapid FISH/QF-PCR for urgent confirmation)
Deletions/duplications below karyotype resolution (1–5 Mb), developmental delay + dysmorphismChromosomal microarray (CMA) — first-line for unexplained DD/ID
Submicroscopic/locus-specific (DiGeorge 22q11.2, Williams, Prader-Willi/Angelman imprinting)FISH / methylation analysis / MLPA
Single-gene sequence disorder with known gene (fragile X, achondroplasia, thalassaemia)Direct gene sequencing / repeat analysis
Unexplained Mendelian phenotype, multiple candidate genesWhole exome sequencing (WES) — covers 1–2% of genome (exons)
Mitochondrial diseaseMtDNA analysis / sequencing + muscle biopsy
Undiagnosed after WES / suspected non-codingWhole genome sequencing (WGS), RNA analysis, trio exome

Interpretation of a NEGATIVE WES: no pathogenic variant found in the coding regions tested — i.e. exon-sequencing was unrevealled; it does NOT exclude: non-coding/regulatory variants, intronic splice effects beyond standard analysis, large deletions/duplications (if CMA not done), chromosomal abnormalities, mitochondrial DNA changes, epigenetic/imprinting disorders, or non-genetic causes. It also cannot re-classify poorly characterized genes. Report as “no diagnosis reached” — consider WGS/trio analysis, re-phenotyping, research pathways.

VUS (variant of uncertain significance) — not diagnostic; do not use for predictive testing of relatives.

Exam pearls
  • Down → karyotype. Fragile X → FMR1 repeat analysis (invisible to everything else). DD + dysmorphic → CMA.
  • Negative WES ≠ nothing wrong — re-think the differential.
  • Confirm clinical diagnosis first; test to answer a specific question.

#43MCQ edited2020-Genetics-MCQ-Medicine-0ebf83bc
Whole exome sequencing (WES) was negative. What does this mean?
  • A. No pathogenic variant was found in the coding regions tested
  • B. The patient has a chromosomal abnormality
  • C. A mitochondrial disorder is excluded
  • D. A genetic cause is completely excluded
  • E. The test result is invalid
Best answer
A. No pathogenic variant was found in the coding regions tested
WES covers only ~1–2% of the genome (protein-coding exons). A negative WES means no diagnostic variant found in the tested coding regions — it does NOT exclude non-coding, structural, chromosomal, mitochondrial or epigenetic causes.

Inborn Errors of Metabolism

Classification (functional groups):

  1. Small-molecule intoxication syndromes — acute/recurrent encephalopathy, vomiting, acidosis after triggers (illness/fasting/protein load): amino acid disorders (PKU, MSUD, tyrosinaemia, homocystinuria), organic acidurias (propionic, methylmalonic, isovaleric — sweaty-feet odour), urea cycle defects (hyperammonaemia + respiratory alkalosis, NO acidosis — ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, X-linked).
  2. Energy-deficiency syndromes — hypoketotic hypoglycaemia during fasting: fatty-acid oxidation defects (medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase — MCAD; hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, encephalopathy), glycogen storage diseases (GSD I/von Gierke — fasting hypoglycaemia + lactic acidosis + hepatomegaly + hyperuricaemia; GSD V/McArdle — exercise cramps), mitochondrial disorders.
  3. Large-molecule (storage) disorders — progressive, static deficits, coarse features, organomegaly: lysosomal storage (Gaucher, Niemann-Pick, Tay-Sachs, mucopolysaccharidoses — Hurler/Hunter, Pompe/GSD II), peroxisomal (Zellweger).

Classic presentations (this exam’s EMQ):

  • Phenylketonuria (PKU) — normal at birth → developmental delay, seizures, eczema, fair hair/skin (↓tyrosine→↓melanin), “musty/mousy” odour; ↑phenylalanine on newborn screen (Guthrie test); treat low-Phe diet + sapropterin.
  • Galactosaemia — well at birth → days after milk feeds: poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, cataracts, E. coli sepsis, hypoglycaemia; GALT enzyme/1-phosphate-uridylyltransferase; treat lactose-free diet.
  • MSUD — 4–7 days: poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, maple-syrup urine odour, ↑BCAAs/ketoacids; treat BCAA-free diet.
  • Von Gierke (GSD I) — 3–4 months: fasting hypoglycaemia + lactic acidosis + hyperuricaemia + hepatomegaly; improves with frequent carbs.
  • Urea cycle defect — neonatal: hyperammonaemia (encephalopathy, seizures, coma) + respiratory alkalosis WITHOUT acidosis or hypoglycaemia.

Diagnosis: newborn screening (Guthrie/tandem mass spec), plasma amino acids, acylcarnitine profile, urine organic acids, ammonia, glucose, lactate, pH/anion gap, urinary ketones (absent in FAO defects), enzyme assays, genetic testing. Family history/consanguinity (first cousins — most are autosomal recessive).

Exam pearls
  • Healthy newborn → days later encephalopathy/vomiting/coma after feeds = IEM until proven otherwise (ammonia + VBG + glucose NOW).
  • Hyperammonaemia + alkalosis = urea cycle; acidosis + ketones/anion gap = organic aciduria; hypoketotic hypoglycaemia = FAO defect.
  • Musty urine + fair skin + eczema + ID = PKU.
  • Consanguinity + regression = storage disease — enzyme assay.

#45EMQ edited2020-Genetics-EMQ-Medicine-34a52f6a
Theme — Genetic (inborn errors of metabolism)
  • A. Phenylketonuria
  • B. Galactosemia
  • C. Maple syrup urine disease
  • D. Glycogen storage disease
  • E. Urea cycle defect
Scenario 1A newborn appears healthy at birth but develops developmental delay, seizures, and eczema during infancy. He has fair skin and hair compared with his parents. Newborn screening reveals markedly elevated phenylalanine levels. Without treatment, he is at risk of severe intellectual disability.
Which inherited metabolic disorder is the most likely diagnosis?
Scenario 2A 10-day-old infant develops poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice, and lethargy after breast milk or formula feeds are introduced. Examination reveals hepatomegaly and poor weight gain. Laboratory testing shows hypoglycemia and evidence of hepatic dysfunction. The infant's symptoms are associated with ingestion of lactose-containing feeds.
Which inherited metabolic disorder is the most likely diagnosis?
Scenario 3A 7-day-old infant develops poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, and abnormal muscle tone. His parents notice that his urine has a distinctive sweet, maple-syrup-like odor. Laboratory testing reveals markedly elevated branched-chain amino acids and their corresponding ketoacids.
Which inherited metabolic disorder is the most likely diagnosis?
Scenario 4A 4-month-old infant develops recurrent episodes of fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, and poor growth. Laboratory testing during an episode shows severe hypoglycemia with elevated lactate and uric acid levels. The child improves after frequent carbohydrate-containing feeds.
Which inherited metabolic disorder is the most likely diagnosis?
Best answer
1→A, 2→B, 3→C, 4→D
1: Phenylalanine ↑ + fair skin/eczema/seizures → PKU (PAH deficiency; treat low-Phe diet). 2: Lactose-feed intolerance + hepatomegaly + hypoglycaemia/liver dysfunction → galactosaemia ( GALT; switch to lactose-free). 3: Maple-syrup urine + BCAAs → MSUD (branched-chain ketoacid decarboxylase). 4: Fasting hypoglycaemia + lactate/uric acid↑ + GSD type I (von Gierke, glucose-6-phosphatase) — feeding dependent. (E — urea cycle: hyperammonaemia + respiratory alkalosis without acidosis.)
2020 · Genetics · 1 question · SAQ

Marfan Syndrome

Genetics: autosomal dominant, FBN1 mutation (15q21.1) — fibrillin-1 (extracellular matrix); ~25% de novo. Variable expressivity, complete penetrance.

Ghent criteria (2010): in the absence of family history, need aortic root dilatation (Z-score ≥2) or dissection PLUS one of: (1) FBN1 mutation, (2) ectopia lentis, (3) systemic score ≥7. With family history: need one of those three with the family history.

Clinical (systemic score): skeletal — tall, arachnodactyly (long slender fingers), arm span > height, pectus carinatum/excavatum, hindfoot valgus/pes planus, scoliosis, high arched palate, joint hypermobility, reduced elbow extension; ocular — ectopia lentis (upward lens dislocation — vs homocystinuria = downward), myopia, retinal detachment risk; cardiovascular — aortic root dilatation/dissection (commonest cause of death), mitral valve prolapse, aortic regurgitation; pulmonary — spontaneous pneumothorax; dural — dural ectasia (lumbosacral, MRI); striae; family history.

SAQ answer structure (this exam): (1) Diagnosis = Marfan syndrome. (2) Inheritance = autosomal dominant. (3) Investigations for comorbidities: echocardiography (aortic root diameter baseline, then annually) ± aortic imaging (CT/MRI) if dilated; slit-lamp/ophthalmology (ectopia lentis, myopia, retinal detachment); skeletal imaging (spine/chest X-ray — scoliosis/pectus); ECG; lung (pneumothorax awareness, PFTs); MRI lumbosacral spine (dural ectasia if back pain). Cascade: test first-degree relatives (echo + eye exam ± FBN1 testing if familial variant known).

Management: avoid isometric sport/contact sport/heavy lifting/competitive athletics; beta-blockers (or ARB losartan) to slow aortic root growth; serial echo 6–12 monthly; prophylactic aortic root replacement when root ≥50 mm (or ≥45 mm + risk factors/pregnancy planning); pregnancy = high risk if root >40–45 mm — counsel; dental endocarditis prophylaxis if valvular disease; annual surveillance; family counselling (50% transmission; reproductive options — PND/NIPT/PGD).

Exam pearls
  • Tall + arachnodactyly + pectus + ectopia lentis + aortic root dilatation = Marfan — autosomal dominant (FBN1).
  • The aorta kills — echo every year, beta-blockade, operate at 50 mm.
  • Ectopia lentis UP = Marfan; DOWN = homocystinuria.

Case 1: Marfan syndrome (patient with features of Marfan syndrome).
  1. What is the diagnosis? (1 pt)
  2. What is the mode of inheritance? (1 pt)
  3. What other investigations for comorbidities do you want to do for him? (2 pt)
Best answer
1) Marfan syndrome. 2) Autosomal dominant (FBN1, chromosome 15q21). 3) Investigations: echocardiography (aortic root diameter — annual), slit-lamp/ophthalmology (lens subluxation, myopia), skeletal survey/spine & chest X-ray (pectus, scoliosis), ECG, pulmonary function, MRI/CT aorta surveillance; family screening of first-degree relatives; counselling (50% transmission, 25% de novo).
Ghent criteria (2010): aortic root dilatation (Z≥2) or dissection + (FBN1 or ectopia lentis or systemic score) = diagnosis. Check the aorta — the killer lesion is aortic root aneurysm/dissection; also mitral valve prolapse. Offer regular echosurveillance and avoid isometric/heavy-lifting and contact sports; beta-blockers slow root growth.

Microdeletion & Imprinting Syndromes

Imprinting: genes expressed from only one parental allele; deletion/uniparental disomy → disease. 15q11-q13 region is THE exam locus:

Prader–Willi syndromeAngelman syndrome
Missing (expressed) parental contributionPaternal (paternal deletion, or maternal uniparental disomy, or imprinting defect)Maternal (maternal deletion, or paternal UPD, or UBE3A mutation)
FeaturesNeonatal hypotonia + poor feeding → later hyperphagia → morbid obesity, almond-shaped eyes + small hands/feet, short stature, hypogonadism (small genitalia), intellectual disability (IQ ~55–70), behaviour problems (skin picking, temper tantrums), small mouth/full lips, hypopigmentationSevere developmental delay/no speech, ataxic “puppet” gait, frequent inappropriate laughter/happy demeanour, microcephaly, seizures, prognathism, wide-spaced teeth, blond hair/blue eyes (hypopigmentation), fascination with water
TestMethylation analysis of 15q11-q13 (first-line); then FISH (deletion) / UPD study (UPD15) — methylation detects ~99% regardless of mechanismSame methylation MLPA/analysis; UBE3A sequencing if imprinting-normal

DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) — CATCH-22: Cardiac defects (TOF, truncus, interrupted aortic arch), Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia (—T-cell immunodeficiency, absent thymus on CXR, recurrent infections), Cleft palate, Hypocalcaemia (parathyroid hypoplasia → neonatal seizures). Most common microdeletion syndrome (1/4000); autosomal dominant; FISH/CMA diagnosis. Related: velocardiofacial (Shprintzen) & conotruncal anomaly face syndromes.

Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion) — “elfin” facies (full cheeks, wide mouth, stellate iris), supravalvular aortic stenosis, hypercalcaemia, cocktail-party personality (over-friendly), developmental delay with relatively strong language, visuospatial weakness.

Smith-Magenis (17p11.2), Cri-du-chat (5p deletion) (high-pitched cat-like cry, ID) — round out the group.

Exam pearls
  • Almond eyes + small hands/feet + neonatal hypotonia → later obesity = Prader–Willi.
  • Happy demeanour + ataxia + no speech + seizures = Angelman.
  • Absent thymus + cleft + cardiac + hypocalcaemia = DiGeorge (22q11).
  • Test with methylation analysis (PW/A) or FISH/microarray (DiGeorge/Williams).

Acute Kidney Injury — Pre-renal, Intrinsic (ATN), Post-renal

Definition (KDIGO): Creatinine ↑ ≥26.5 µmol/L within 48 h, or ≥1.5× baseline within 7 days, or UO <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h. Stage by creatinine rise / urine output.

Pre-renalIntrinsic — ATNPost-renal
Mechanism↓ renal perfusion (dehydration, sepsis, heart failure, ACEi/ARB + NSAIDs, renal artery)Ischaemic or nephrotoxic tubular damage (aminoglycosides, cisplatin, contrast, pigment, sepsis)Obstruction below collecting system (BPH, stones, tumour, blocked catheter)
FeNa<1%>2%Variable
Urine Na<20 mmol/L>40 mmol/LVariable
Urine microscopyBland / hyaline castsMuddy brown granular casts, renal tubular epithelial cellsBland; may see haematuria
Serum urea:Cr>20:1<10–15:1Variable
Urine osmolality>500<350Variable

Nephrotoxins to know: gentamicin/aminoglycosides → ATN (also causes hypomagnesaemia); cisplatin & carboplatin → ATN; amphotericin B → ATN + distal RTA/K⁺/Mg²⁺ wasting; ACE inhibitors/ARBs → functional (pre-renal) rise in Cr via efferent dilation, especially with bilateral renal artery stenosis; penicillins/cephalosporins/PPIs/NSAIDs → acute interstitial nephritis (fever, rash, eosinophilia, WBC casts); contrast → contrast-induced nephropathy (48–72 h); methotrexate/ethylene glycol.

Tumor lysis syndrome (leukaemia/lymphoma post-chemo): hyperkalaemia + hyperphosphataemia + hyperuricaemia + hypocalcaemia → AKI; prevent with allopurinol/rasburicase + IV fluids; life-threatening K⁺ → treat immediately.

Rhabdomyolysis (marathon, crush, statins): dark urine, myalgia, ↑↑ CK, hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia (early) → myoglobinuric ATN. Best test: serum CK (± urine myoglobin).

Obstructive (post-renal) clues: distended bladder, frequency/hesitancy/BPH, recent ACEi dose increase unmasking bilateral obstruction — small rise in creatinine with normal kidney size + palpable bladder → urethral catheter + ultrasound.

Management ATN: stop nephrotoxins, restore volume/perfusion, treat hyperkalaemia (calcium gluconate, insulin/dextrose, salbutamol, bicarbonate, K-binders, dialysis), treat acidosis & fluid overload. Indications for emergency dialysis (AEIOU): Acidosis refractory, Electrolyte (K⁺ >6.5 or symptomatic), Ingestions (toxins), Overload (pulmonary oedema refractory to diuretics), Uraemia (encephalopathy, pericarditis, seizures).

Exam pearls
  • FeNa <1% + history of poor intake/heart failure → pre-renal. FeNa >2% + muddy brown casts → ATN.
  • WBC casts → pyelonephritis/interstitial nephritis; RBC casts → glomerulonephritis; muddy brown granular casts → ATN.
  • Aminoglycosides: monitor levels; hypomagnesaemia + rising Cr = tubular toxicity — stop the drug.
  • Post-chemo leukaemia patient with high K, high PO₄, low Ca → tumour lysis → rasburicase + fluids.
  • After CABG/surgery → think ischaemic/pigment ATN ± cardiorenal.
Traps
  • In contrast nephropathy and rhabdomyolysis, FeNa can be <1% early — don’t exclude ATN solely on FeNa.
  • Creatinine can lag — the earliest sign of AKI is often rising K⁺ and oliguria.
  • Never give ACEi in bilateral renal artery stenosis — creatinine rises sharply.

Anaphylaxis — Recognition & Emergency Management

Definition: acute onset of illness with life-threatening airway, breathing or circulation problems usually with skin/mucosal changes (urticaria, flushing, angio-oedema), after exposure to a trigger (food — peanut/tree nut/shellfish, drugs — penicillin/NSAIDs/contrast, latex, hymenoptera stings). It is a clinical diagnosis — do not wait for tests.

Diagnosis criteria (any one): (1) acute illness with skin/mucosal involvement + respiratory compromise or hypotension; (2) acute illness with ≥2 of: skin/mucosal signs, respiratory compromise, hypotension, GI symptoms, after a likely allergen; (3) hypotension after a known allergen.

Immediate management — A→E approach:

  1. IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL, i.e. 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh — repeat every 5 minutes as needed. This is THE first-line, life-saving drug. (Not IV in a non-arrest patient in general wards; IV adrenaline only by experienced hands with monitoring.)
  2. Lie flat, legs elevate; call for help; high-flow O₂; rapid IV access; IV fluids (500–1000 mL bolus crystalloid) if hypotensive.
  3. Consider nebulised salbutamol (bronchospasm), nebulised adrenaline (upper airway obstruction), H₁ antihistamine (chlorphenamine/cetirizine) and corticosteroid (hydrocortisone/prednisolone) as ADJUNCTS — they do NOT reverse anaphylaxis and must never delay adrenaline.
  4. If cardiac arrest → standard ALS with early adrenaline, prolonged resuscitation may be needed.

After stabilisation: observe for biphasic reaction (typically ≥6–12 h, longer if severe/asthmatic/multiple doses/unknown trigger); check serum tryptase (baseline within 3 h of reaction + convalescent at ≥24 h) — supports mast-cell degranulation; identify and document the trigger; prescribe an adrenaline auto-injector (×2) and teach technique; refer to allergy services; written emergency plan; medic-alert; avoid trigger; counsel about future exposures and cross-reactivity; report to pharmacovigilance if drug.

Exam pearls
  • First drug in anaphylaxis = IM adrenaline — always. Antihistamines/steroids are adjuncts only.
  • Adrenaline goes IM into the thigh, repeatable at 5-min intervals.
  • Post-stabilisation: tryptase + allergen avoidance + auto-injector + allergy referral.
  • Risk factors for severity: asthma, beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, delay in adrenaline.

#51SAQ edited2020-InternalMedicine-SAQ-Medicine-5029e720
Case 2: Anaphylaxis.
  1. What is the diagnosis? (1 pt)
  2. What is the first medication to give? (1 pt)
  3. After stabilization, what will you do next? (1 pt)
Best answer
1) Anaphylaxis (acute severe multi-system allergic reaction — airway/breathing/circulation + skin). 2) IM adrenaline (epinephrine) 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL) into the anterolateral thigh; repeat every 5 min as needed + high-flow O₂ + IV fluids; antihistamines/steroids are adjuncts only. 3) After stabilisation: observe ≥6–12 h (biphasic reaction), serum tryptase (within 3 h + baseline at ≥24 h), identify/document trigger, adrenaline auto-injector ×2 with teaching, allergy clinic referral, written action plan, medic-alert.
ABCDE approach; adrenaline FIRST — never delay for antihistamines; treat refractory bronchospasm with nebulised salbutamol; IV adrenaline only with monitoring; counsel on trigger avoidance and cross-reactive drugs (NSAIDs/aspirin caution).
2020 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Aortic Dissection

Definition: tear in intima → blood tracks into media → false lumen separates layers; can propagate proximally (coronary ostia, aortic valve — AR, cardiac tamponade) or distally (branch occlusion — stroke, limb ischaemia, renal failure, mesenteric).

Stanford classification: Type A = any involvement of ascending aorta (surgical emergency — mortality rises ~1% per hour untreated); Type B = descending only (medical management first — IV beta-blockade, then vasodilators).

Risk factors: hypertension (most important — especially poorly controlled), connective tissue disease (Marfan, Ehlers–Danlos, Loeys–Dietz), bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, pregnancy (third trimester), cocaine, trauma, iatrogenic (catheterisation), vasculitis/infective aortitis.

Clinical picture: tearing/ripping chest pain radiating to the back, abrupt onset, maximal at onset; may migrate; hypertension (or hypotension if tamponade/rupture — ominous), pulse/BP differential between limbs, new diastolic murmur of AR, syncope, neuro deficits (stroke, paraplegia), abdominal pain (mesenteric), oliguria (renal).

Investigation: CT angiography (CTA) — the investigation of choice in haemodynamically stable patients: fast, defines entry tear, extent, branch vessels, perfusion, effusion. Transoesophageal echo for unstable patients or when CTA contraindicated. ECG to exclude MI (dissection can involve RCA ostium → inferior STEMI!). CXR: widened mediastinum (non-specific).

Management: Type A → immediate surgery; Type B (stable) → strict BP/HR control (target HR <60, SBP 100–120; IV labetalol/esmolol first, then nitroprusside/GTN), ICU care; surgery/EVAR if complicated (rupture, malperfusion, refractory pain, expansion). Lifelong anti-impulse therapy and imaging follow-up.

Exam pearls
  • Tearing pain radiating to back + hypertension + afebrile + no troponin story → dissection (not MI, not pericarditis — pericarditis is pleuritic, worse lying flat, better leaning forward).
  • CTA is the first-line test; TTE/TOoE if unstable.
  • Check bilateral BPs and pulses in every chest pain — inter-arm difference >20 mmHg is a red flag.
Traps
  • Do NOT give anticoagulants/fibrinolytics until dissection excluded in chest pain with back radiation — catastrophic if dissection.
  • Inferior STEMI + tearing pain = dissection involving RCA until proven otherwise.

Aphasia — Classification by Fluency, Comprehension, Repetition

Approach: test fluency (speech effort/quantity) → comprehension → repetition → naming. Lesion localisation follows.

TypeFluencyComprehensionRepetitionLesion
Broca’s (expressive/motor)Non-fluentIntactImpairedDominant frontal lobe — inferior frontal gyrus (postero-inferior), MCA territory
Wernicke’s (receptive/sensory)Fluent (but meaningless/jargon)ImpairedImpairedDominant superior temporal gyrus
GlobalNon-fluentImpairedImpairedDominant hemisphere — large MCA territory infarct
ConductionFluentIntactImpaired (disproportionately) ± namingArcuate fasciculus (dominant parietal/temporal)
Anomic (nominal)FluentIntactIntactVariable — dominant angular gyrus/temporoparietal; naming difficulty only
Transcortical motorNon-fluentIntactIntactDominant frontal, anterior/superior to Broca’s
Transcortical sensoryFluentImpairedIntactDominant temporo-occipital, posterior to Wernicke’s
Mixed transcorticalNon-fluentImpairedIntact (echolalia)Watershed zones both anterior/posterior

Classic discriminators in this exam: fluent + intact comprehension + impaired repetition/naming = conduction aphasia. Non-fluent + impaired comprehension + impaired repetition = global aphasia. Comprehension intact + repetition intact + poor naming = anomic.

Also distinguish from dysarthria (articulation problem — speech content normal, motor speech disorder: bulbar/pseudobulbar palsy, cerebellar, basal ganglia) and dysphonia (voice production — vocal cords/larynx). Aphasia is a disorder of language, not speech.

Exam pearls
  • Fluency first, comprehension second, repetition third — three questions, one box each.
  • Repetition spared → transcortical; repetition lost → Broca/Wernicke/conduction/global.
  • Conduction aphasia: intact fluent speech + intact understanding, but cannot repeat — "can speak and understand, cannot echo".
  • Global aphasia after massive MCA stroke — very poor prognosis.

Cardiac Arrhythmias — Recognition & Acute Management

Approach to any ECG rhythm: rate → regularity → P waves (present? each before a QRS?) → PR length → QRS width → ST/T. Then match to a rhythm and assess stability (ABCDE — shock, syncope/pre-syncope, ischaemia/chest pain, heart failure).

RhythmKey ECG featuresNotes / management
Sinus tachycardiaHR >100, normal P before each QRSPhysiological — treat the cause (pain, fever, hypovolaemia, PE, thyrotoxicosis, drugs)
AVNRT / AVRT (SVT, PSVT)Regular narrow-complex tachycardia ~150–250, P waves hidden/inverted/retrograde after QRSVagal manoeuvres → adenosine 6→12→12 mg rapid IV bolus; unstable → synchronized cardioversion; long-term: ablation
Atrial flutterSaw-tooth flutter waves ~300/min, typically 2:1/4:1 block (ventricular ~150), narrow QRSRate control (beta-blocker/verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin) or DC cardioversion; anticoagulation per CHA₂DS₂-VASc; CTI ablation is curative
Atrial fibrillationIrregularly irregular narrow complex, no distinct P wavesLoss of JVP “a” wave (no atrial contraction). Rate control first (BB/CCB/digoxin); anticoagulate per CHA₂DS₂-VASc; unstable → DC cardiovert; consider rhythm control/ablation if young/symptomatic
VTBroad complex regular tachycardia; concordance, AV dissociationStable → IV amiodarone/procainamide; unstable → immediate synchronized cardioversion; pulseless → defibrillation + ALS
Heart block1°: PR >200 ms constant. 2° Mobitz I (Wenckebach): progressive PR prolongation then dropped beat. 2° Mobitz II: sudden dropped beat, constant PR. 3° (complete): AV dissociation, regular escape rhythmMobitz II & CHB → admit, transcutaneous/transvenous pacing; atropine often ineffective; stop AV-nodal blockers
VF / pulseless VTChaotic or broad-complex without pulseImmediate defibrillation + CPR + adrenaline 1 mg every 3–5 min

CHA₂DS₂-VASc (stroke risk in AF): CHF (1), HTN (1), Age ≥75 (2), DM (1), Stroke/TIA (2), Vascular disease (1), Age 65–74 (1), Sex female (1). Score 0 (men) / 1 (women) → no anticoagulation; ≥1 (men)/≥2 (women) consider OAC; ≥2 → anticoagulate (DOAC preferred). HAS-BLED estimates bleeding risk — high score is NOT a reason to withhold anticoagulation; it flags need for closer review/modifiable factors.

JVP “a” wave is produced by atrial contraction → absent in AF (no organised atrial systole); giant “a” waves in tricuspid stenosis; cannon “a” waves in complete heart block/AV dissociation (atrium contracts against closed tricuspid valve).

Exam pearls
  • Irregularly irregular + absent “a” wave = AF. Narrow regular tachycardia in a young woman with normal baseline = AVNRT → vagal then adenosine.
  • Unstable tachycardia/bradycardia → electricity wins (synchronized shock for pulse present; defibrillation for pulseless).
  • High-grade AV block (Mobitz II, complete) → pacing, not atropine alone.
  • Antidromic AVRT/VT wide-complex doubt → treat as VT (procainamide/amiodarone; avoid AV-nodal blockers in pre-excited AF).
Traps
  • Do not use adenosine in pre-excited AF (irregular wide complex) — can precipitate VF.
  • Cardioversion in AF >48 h without anticoagulation/imaging → stroke risk; anticoagulate ≥3 weeks or do TOE, or cardiovert early (<48 h) with heparin.

#34MCQ edited2020-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-7611ba36
The JVP shows absence of the 'a' wave. What is the arrhythmia?
  • A. Atrial fibrillation
  • B. Atrial flutter
  • C. Complete heart block
  • D. Sinus tachycardia
  • E. Ventricular tachycardia

2020 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Asthma — Diagnosis & Acute Exacerbation

Diagnosis: variable respiratory symptoms (wheeze, cough, chest tightness, dyspnoea) + variable expiratory airflow limitation: FEV₁/FVC <0.7 with ≥12% and ≥200 mL improvement in FEV₁ after bronchodilator, or excessive diurnal peak-flow variability (>20%), or positive bronchial challenge (methacholine/histamine) if spirometry is normal. Normal spirometry does NOT exclude asthma in a symptomatic patient → methacholine challenge is the next step.

Obstructive defect pattern: low FEV₁, low FEV₁/FVC, normal/low-normal FVC, and (in asthma) normal DLCO (unlike emphysema where DLCO is low).

Acute severe asthma (admit): PEF 33–50% predicted/best, respiratory rate ≥25, HR ≥110, inability to complete sentences, or O₂ sat <92%. Life-threatening: PEF <33%, silent chest, exhaustion/altered consciousness, SpO₂ <92%, normal/high PaCO₂ (exhaustion — rising CO₂ is a red flag).

Management of acute exacerbation:

  1. High-flow O₂ to keep SpO₂ 94–98%.
  2. Nebulised salbutamol (5 mg) + ipratropium bromide (0.5 mg) driven by O₂, back-to-back/repeat.
  3. Oral prednisolone 40–50 mg (or IV hydrocortisone) — steroids early.
  4. Not responding/severe → IV magnesium sulfate 1.2–2 g over 20 min; call ICU; consider IV aminophylline; avoid sedation; intubation if failing (permissive hypercapnia).
  5. Discharge: when PEF >75%, stable ≥12–24 h off nebs; written asthma action plan, GP/asthma nurse follow-up, inhaler technique review, optimise preventer (ICS-containing), address triggers and adherence, safety-net re admission.

Chronic stepwise management (GINA): low-dose ICS-formoterol as reliever (or SABA + ICS) → add LABA → medium-dose ICS/LABA → refer. SABA-only is no longer recommended — every reliever should contain ICS to cut severe exacerbations.

Exam pearls
  • First-line in acute attack after O₂: nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium + early oral steroids.
  • Rising/normal PaCO₂ in acute asthma = life-threatening — call for help.
  • Normal spirometry + typical symptoms → methacholine challenge confirms.
  • Nasal flaring, intercostal recessions, tracheal tug in a child = severe exacerbation with respiratory distress.

Autoimmune Liver Disease — PBC vs PSC vs AIH

Three autoimmune cholestatic/hepatitic diseases — the exam loves the antibody table:

Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC)Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH)
WhoMiddle-aged womenYoung men, ulcerative colitis (70%)Young/middle-aged women
TargetSmall intrahepatic bile ductsIntra- and extrahepatic bile ducts (beading)Hepatocytes
AntibodyAnti-mitochondrial (AMA)p-ANCA (atypical); ANA/SMA sometimesType 1: ANA, anti-smooth muscle; Type 2: anti-LKM1
LFT patternCholestatic (↑ALP, ↑GGT), IgM↑Cholestatic (↑ALP/GGT), p-ANCA+Hepatocellular (↑↑ALT/AST), IgG↑
SymptomsFatigue, pruritus, dry eyes/mouth, xanthomata/osteoporosis (vitamin D malabsorption), progression to cirrhosisPruritus, fatigue, cholangitis; ↑ risk cholangiocarcinoma + colorectal cancerFatigue, jaundice, hepatomegaly, spider naevi; may be asymptomatic with high ALT
AssociationsSjögren’s, RA, thyroid disease, SSc, coeliacUC, cholangiocarcinomaOther autoimmune disease
TreatmentUrsodeoxycholic acid (slows progression); ± fibrates; later transplantUDCA (symptomatic), manage strictures (ERCP), surveill for cancers, liver transplant definitiveImmunosuppression: prednisolone ± azathioprine

Work-up in a cholestatic pattern: ultrasound first (exclude obstruction/dilated ducts) → if ducts not dilated → check AMA. PBC = AMA+ cholestasis with normal biliary imaging. PSC = AMA-negative cholestasis + MRCP showing biliary beading/stricturing. AIH = hepatitic pattern + autoantibodies + raised IgG ± biopsy. In a patient with SLE presenting with cholestasis and AMA positive, the answer is primary biliary cholangitis — despite SLE.

AMA (anti-mitochondrial antibody) is the characteristic — and most specific — antibody of PBC (present in ~95%). Anti-LKM1 = autoimmune hepatitis type 2 and chronic hepatitis C overlap; anti-smooth muscle + ANA = AIH type 1.

Exam pearls
  • Pruritus + fatigue + ↑ALP in a middle-aged woman + AMA → PBC → ursodeoxycholic acid.
  • PSC + UC → annual colonoscopy (CRC risk) and MRCP surveillance for cholangiocarcinoma.
  • Cholestatic picture with dilated ducts = obstruction — image before assuming autoimmune.

2020 · Internal Medicine · 2 questions · MCQ

Chronic Kidney Disease — Stages, Complications & Dialysis

Definition: GFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² for ≥3 months, or kidney damage (albuminuria, urine abnormalities, structural) ≥3 months. Stages (KDIGO, by GFR): G1 ≥90, G2 60–89, G3a 45–59, G3b 30–44, G4 15–29, G5 <15 (kidney failure). Albuminauria categories A1–A3. eGFR <45 = CKD G3b → significant CV risk.

Complications — the exam loves this:

  1. Anaemia of CKD — ↓erythropoietin (starts G3b). Normocytic; check iron first (iron deficiency common) → iron + ESAs (epoetin) when Hb <100 g/L; target 100–120 g/L.
  2. Mineral–bone disorder (renal osteodystrophy) — ↓1α-hydroxylase → low active vitamin D; phosphate retention (primary problem) → high phosphate, low calcium, secondary PTH↑; FGF23↑; high-PTH bone disease (osteitis fibrosa) or adynamic bone disease (low turnover, over-suppressed PTH). Management: phosphate binders (calcium acetate, sevelamer) + vitamin D analogues (calcitriol/alfacalcidol) ± cinacalcet; restrict dietary phosphate.
  3. Hyperkalaemia — ↓excretion; worse with ACEi/ARB/spiro/NSAIDs.
  4. Metabolic acidosis (anion gap normal-ish/high in late).
  5. Fluid overload / hypertension / uraemia — encephalopathy, pericarditis (rub!), frost, pruritus, platelet dysfunction (bleeding).
  6. CV disease — commonest cause of death in CKD (accelerated atherosclerosis); lipid-lowering, BP control.

Renal replacement therapy (RRT) — AEIOU: refractory Acidosis, Electrolytes (K >6.5/symptomatic), Ingestions (dialysable toxins — lithium, salicylates, methanol), Overload (pulmonary oedema failing diuretics), Uraemic symptoms (pericarditis, encephalopathy, seizures). Choice: haemodialysis vs peritoneal dialysis vs transplant (best outcomes). A pericardial rub or confusion in CKD = dialysis now, whatever the urea number.

ACEi/ARB in CKD: renoprotective in proteinuric CKD/diabetes — start with low dose, check Cr/K at 1–2 weeks; accept up to 30% Cr rise; avoid in bilateral renal artery stenosis & pregnancy.

Exam pearls
  • High phosphate + low Ca + high PTH in CKD = secondary hyperparathyroidism → treat phosphate first (binders + low-PO4 diet) + active vitamin D.
  • “When to start dialysis?” — never on a number alone; the answer is refractory symptoms/signs (overload despite diuretics, pericarditis, encephalopathy, K⁺).
  • eGFR 45 with no symptoms still has G3a disease → anaemia can already appear (ESA after iron).

#18MCQ edited2020-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-060b406f
A long-standing CKD patient is oriented and conscious with no pericardial rub and no flapping tremor. He has edema and bibasal crackles and furosemide did not work. Which finding is a stronger indicator for dialysis in this CKD patient?
  • A. Hyperkalemia
  • B. Creatinine 800
  • C. Urea ~30
  • D. Refractory hypervolemia
  • E. Pericardial effusion
Best answer
D. Refractory hypervolemia
AEIOU dialysis indications: Acidosis refractory, Electrolytes (K⁺>6.5/symptomatic), Intoxications, Overload (pulmonary oedema NOT responding to diuretics), Uraemia (encephalopathy/pericarditis/bleeding). Refractory fluid overload despite maximal furosemide is a strong, independent indication; creatinine/urea levels alone are never indications.
#25MCQ edited2020-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-7e7f8f8a
In a patient with CKD and lab findings of high phosphate, low calcium and high PTH, what is the primary cause of these findings?
  • A. Renal retention of phosphate
  • B. Excess vitamin D activation
  • C. High PTH
  • D. Decreased dietary calcium intake
  • E. Increased PTH breakdown
Best answer
A. Renal retention of phosphate
CKD: ↓GFR → phosphate retention → high phosphate. Phosphate binds calcium (low Ca) + ↓1α-hydroxylase → low active vitamin D → low Ca. Low Ca + low vit D → secondary PTH rise (renal osteodystrophy). The PRIMARY problem is phosphate retention.

Drug-Induced Movement Disorders

Dopamine-receptor blocking drugs (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) produce a timed syndrome:

SyndromeOnsetFeaturesManagement
Acute dystoniaHours–daysSustained muscle contraction — torticollis, oculogyric crisis (eyes deviate up), trismus, dysphagia, opisthotonos, laryngospasm (airway emergency)Stop the drug; IV/IM anticholinergic (benztropine 1–2 mg or procyclidine 5–10 mg) — dramatic response confirms; diazepam adjunct; maintain airway if laryngeal
ParkinsonismDays–weeksBradykinesia, rigidity, tremor, shuffling gaitReduce/switch drug; anticholinergic or amantadine
AkathisiaDays–weeksRestless urge to move, inner tensionReduce dose; propranolol, benzos
Tardive dyskinesiaMonths–years (late)Orofacial/buccal-lingual choreoathetoid movements, lip smackingStop/switch offending drug (may be irreversible); VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine/ tetrabenazine)
Neuroleptic malignant syndromeDays–weeksFever + rigidity (“lead-pipe”) + autonomic instability + altered consciousness + CK↑ — emergencyStop drug, ICU care, dantrolene/bromocriptine, cool, correct electrolytes/hydration

In this exam: antiemetic + unilateral neck twisting + oculogyric/abnormal eye movements in a young woman without confusion = acute dystonia — not epilepsy, not TIA, not pseudoseizure. Red flag: laryngospasm → call anaesthetics.

Exam pearls
  • Young patient + recent antiemetic + twisting neck/eyes = acute dystonia → anticholinergic.
  • NMS = fever + rigidity + autonomic chaos + CK↑ — stop drug, ICU.
  • Tardive = late; may be permanent — prevent rather than treat.

Electrolyte Disorders — Sodium & Potassium

Hyponatraemia — classify by volume status:

HypovolaemicEuvolaemicHypervolaemic
Urine NaLow <20 (extrarenal loss: GI, skin, third space) / High >20 (renal loss: diuretics, Addison’s, salt-wasting)>40 (SIADH); check TSH/cortisol (hypothyroid/adrenal = euvolaemic)Low <20 (HF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, CKD — effective arterial underfilling)
Treatment0.9% saline (restore volume) + treat causeFluid restrict (1 L/day) ± salt tablets/furosemide/vaptans (hypertonic 3% if seizures/severe neuro signs)Fluid + sodium restriction, loop diuretics, treat HF/cirrhosis; dialysis if renal failure

SIADH = hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia + inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osm >100, urine Na >40) + euvolaemia + normal renal/thyroid/adrenal + no diuretics. Causes: malignancy (small cell lung, pancreatic), CNS (stroke, tumour, meningitis), pulmonary (pneumonia, TB, PPV), drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, PPIs, chemotherapy, opioids, MDMA). Treat: fluid restriction ± hypertonic saline if symptomatic (Na <120 with seizures/coma — 3% saline, raise ≤8 mmol/L per 24 h to avoid central pontine myelinolysis).

Co-existing lung cancer + hyponatraemia = SIADH (ectopic ADH from small-cell carcinoma).

Hyperkalaemia: treat by severity/ECG. ECG progression: peaked (“tented”) T waves → PR prolongation → P flattening → QRS widening → sine wave → VF. K⁺ >6.5 or any ECG change = emergency: IV calcium gluconate (membrane stabilisation), insulin+dextrose, salbutamol nebulisers, sodium bicarbonate (if acidotic), K binders, dialysis if refractory. Stop K/ACEi/MRA/NSAIDs; check glucose (DKA?), renal function.

Hypokalaemia: causes — diuretics (loop/thiazide), vomiting/diarrhoea, hyperaldosteronism, hypokalaemic periodic paralysis (carbohydrate load in susceptible young men — e.g. “after a big carbohydrate meal”, resolves with K), Bartter/Gitelman, insulin, beta-agonists, RTA. Replace K orally if mild; IV if severe/symptomatic; check Mg (replace both). ECG: flattened T, U waves, ST depression, VT/VF.

Exam pearls
  • SIADH = low serum osm + urine Na>40 + euvolaemic → restrict fluid; symptomatic → 3% saline ≤8/24h.
  • Oedema + crackles + confusion + hyponatraemia = hypervolaemic dilutional (HF) — do NOT give saline.
  • Peaked T waves → calcium gluconate FIRST; insulin/dextrose second; dialysis if refractory.
  • Carbohydrate-feast weakness + low K in a young Asian male = hypokalaemic periodic paralysis.
Traps
  • Hypertonic saline for chronic asymptomatic hyponatraemia causes osmotic demyelination — correct slowly.
  • Pseudohyponatraemia (hypertriglyceridaemia/paraproteinaemia) — check osmolality/lab method if patient looks well.
  • Hypomagnesaemia → refractory hypokalaemia/hypocalcaemia — always co-check.

Gastrointestinal Bleeding

Upper GI bleed (above ligament of Treitz): haematemesis ± melaena ± coffee-ground vomitus ± shock. Common causes: peptic ulcer (commonest, ~40–50%), varices (cirrhosis — most lethal), erosive gastritis/duodenitis, Mallory–Weiss tear (binge/vomiting → mucosal tear at GOJ after forceful retching), oesophagitis, malignancy (gastric/oesophageal), Dieulafoy lesion.

Clinical assessment (A→E): IV access ×2 large-bore, crossmatch/G&S, FBC/U&E (urea↑ disproportionately in upper GI bleed — blood digestion), clotting, LFT; Blatchford score (pre-endoscopy risk), Rockall score (post-endoscopy); resuscitate first, then OGD within 24 h (urgent <12 h if unstable/varices).

Management: resuscitation (crystalloid/blood — target Hb 70–80 g/L or symptomatic; restrictive transfusion), PPI (pantoprazole 80 mg IV bolus then infusion 8 mg/h) for non-variceal bleeding, IV terlipressin + prophylactic antibiotics (ceftriaxone/quinolone) + urgent endoscopic band ligation/sclerotherapy for variceal bleeds,correct coagulopathy (vit K/FFP/PCC), stop NSAIDs/anticoagulants, H. pylori eradication after ulcer; surgery/IR embolisation if endoscopy fails.

Cirrhosis + upper GI bleed + hypotension = varices — terlipressin FIRST (reduces portal pressure), antibiotics (variceal bleeds are portal of bacterial infection), band ligation. Avoid beta-blockers in the acute phase (hypotension).

Lower GI bleed: diverticular disease (commonest cause of painless large-volume rectal bleeding in elderly), angiodysplasia, colitis (IBD, ischaemic, infectious), haemorrhoids (bright red on paper/dripping), malignancy (change of bowel habit, weight loss, iron deficiency), ischaemic colitis (elderly + AF + post-prandial pain + PR bleeding — “mesenteric angina”). Investigations: OGD (exclude upper) → colonoscopy/CT angiography.

Exam pearls
  • Haematemesis in cirrhosis = varices until proven otherwise → terlipressin + antibiotics + urgent OGD.
  • Raised urea:creatinine ratio with melaena = upper GI source.
  • Resuscitate BEFORE scoping; transfuse restrictively.
  • Post-prandial abdominal pain + AF + PR bleeding = chronic mesenteric ischaemia.

Heart Failure — HFrEF vs HFpEF, Acute & Chronic

Pathophysiology: inadequate cardiac output for metabolic needs (or only at high filling pressures). Classify by EF: HFrEF (EF ≤40%) — systolic failure (IHD/MI, dilated cardiomyopathy, hypertension long-standing, valvular); HFmrEF (41–49); HFpEF (≥50) — diastolic failure (hypertension, LVH, hypertrophic/restrictive CMP, constrictive pericarditis, ischaemia). Right-sided failure usually secondary to left-sided or lung disease (cor pulmonale).

Symptoms: dyspnoea (exertional), orthopnoea, PND, fatigue, ankle swelling, nocturia. Examination: raised JVP, S3 gallop (specific for volume overload/systolic failure), displaced apex, bibasal crackles, peripheral oedema, hepatojugular reflux, hepatomegaly.

Chronic HFrEF — the “four pillars” (all reduce mortality): (1) ACEi/ARB/ARNI (sacubitril–valsartan) — titrate to target; (2) beta-blocker (bisoprolol/carvedilol/metoprolol succinate) — start low, once stable; (3) MRA (spironolactone/eplerenone) — K & renal monitoring; (4) SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin/empagliflozin) — now regardless of diabetes. Plus: loop diuretic for congestion, ICD if EF ≤35% on optimal therapy, CRT if wide QRS (LBBB), iron for deficiency, treat sleep apnoea, vaccinate, cardiac rehab.

HFpEF: no drug reduces mortality — treat congestion with loop diuretics, aggressive BP/rate control, SGLT2i reduces hospitalisation; manage comorbidities (AF, IHD, obesity, diabetes).

Acute decompensated HF: ABCDE, sit up, high-flow O₂, IV furosemide (e.g. 40–80 mg or home dose ×2), stop beta-blocker if hypotensive/shocked (otherwise continue), CPAP if respiratory distress + acidosis; nitrates if hypertensive; treat precipitant (MI! infection, AF, NSAIDs, non-adherence); echocardiography for EF and valves; discharge plan + early follow-up.

ECG in severe LV dysfunction: reduced EF ± LBBB (CRT candidate if QRS ≥150 + LBBB + symptomatic on pillars).

Exam pearls
  • Four pillars for HFrEF: ACEi/ARB/ARNI + BB + MRA + SGLT2i. HFpEF = diuretics for symptoms.
  • S3 = failing ventricle — in volume overload.
  • Gradual weight gain + ankle swelling + breathlessness = fluid retention → furosemide.
  • New LBBB + EF 25% → CRT consideration after 3 months optimal pillars.

2020 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Hepatocellular Carcinoma

Risk factors: cirrhosis from any cause — chronic hepatitis B (even without cirrhosis; HBV DNA integration), chronic hepatitis C, alcoholic/NAFLD cirrhosis, aflatoxin exposure, hereditary haemochromatosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, Wilson disease.

Presentation: often asymptomatic on surveillance (6-monthly ultrasound ± AFP in cirrhotics); decompensation of previously stable cirrhosis, weight loss, RUQ pain, hepatomegaly with irregular/hard edge, bruit, paraneoplastic (polycythaemia, hypercalcaemia, hypoglycaemia, carcinoid-like).

Diagnosis: in a cirrhotic liver with a nodule >1 cm — multiphasic contrast CT or MRI (LI-RADS): arterial-phase hyperenhancement + venous/delayed washout is diagnostic (no biopsy needed). AFP supports (≥400 ng/mL with imaging is diagnostic; AFP-L3/DCP adjuncts). Biopsy only if imaging atypical.

Staging/treatment: BCLC staging — early (single ≤2 cm / ≤3 nodules ≤3 cm, preserved function): resection / ablation / transplant; intermediate: TACE; advanced: sorafenib/lenvatinib (TKIs), immunotherapy (atezolizumab+bevacizumab); terminal: best supportive care. Surveillance: 6-monthly USS + AFP every 6 months in cirrhosis/HBV (Asian males >40, females >50, Africans >20, family history).

Exam pearls
  • Cirrhosis + growing mass + weight loss → AFP + contrast CT/MRI (LI-RADS) — biopsy only if atypical.
  • HCC = arterial hyperenhancement + washout; hepatic haemangioma = peripheral nodular enhancement filling centripetally (don’t biopsy).
  • Screen cirrhotics every 6 months.

Liver Function Tests — Pattern Recognition

Three patterns — the single most useful LFT exercise:

PatternEnzyme profileThink of
HepatocellularALT/AST ≫ ALP (e.g., ALT 5–100× ULN)Viral hepatitis (AST:ALT <1 early), NAFLD/NASH (mild, ALT>AST), ischaemia, paracetamol (very high, >1000), autoimmune hepatitis, drug-induced (statins, isoniazid, methotrexate), Wilson, haemochromatosis, muscle (AST can rise with muscle injury — check CK)
CholestaticALP/GGT ≫ ALT/ASTObstruction — gallstones (dilated ducts on USS), PBC (AMA+), PSC (beading, UC), drugs (anabolic steroids, amox-clav), infiltration (TB, lymphoma), cholangiocarcinoma, pregnancy (ICP), bone ALP (check GGT! GGT confirms hepatic source)
MixedBoth ALT & ALP moderately raised (each ~2–5× ULN)Drug-induced liver injury (commonest pattern DILI), viral/DILI overlap, chronic cholestasis with hepatocellular injury
Isolated hyperbilirubinaemiaBilirubin ↑, enzymes normalGilbert’s syndrome (unconjugated, fasting/stress, young men, UGT1A1 — common, benign), haemolysis (↑LDH, retics, haptoglobin↓), inherited conjugated (Dubin–Johnson, Rotor)

Useful discriminators: GGT — confirms ALP is hepatic (bone ALP normal); R factor = (ALT/ULN) ÷ (ALP/ULN): >5 hepatocellular, <2 cholestatic, 2–5 mixed. Synthetic function — albumin, INR/PT, bilirubin (true markers of severity). Platelets/AST:ALT >2/indices for fibrosis; FIB-4 for NAFLD.

Approach: (1) is this hepatocellular or cholestatic? (2) acute (days–weeks) or chronic (>6 mo)? (3) severity — INR/albumin/encephalopathy? (4) cause — alcohol, drugs, viral serology, autoimmune (AMA/ASMA/ANA), metabolic (ferritin, caeruloplasmin, α1-AT, glucose/ lipids), USS (steatosis, ducts, mass) → further (CT/MRCP/biopsy) as needed.

Exam pearls
  • ALT/AST ≫ ALP + steatosis + diabetes = NAFLD. ALP/GGT ≫ ALT + dilated ducts = obstruction. AMA = PBC.
  • Isolated unconjugated bilirubin in a well young man, rises with fasting = Gilbert’s — reassure.
  • GGT confirms hepatic ALP source (not bone).

Theme — LFTs (liver function tests)
  • A. Hepatocellular pattern (raised ALT/AST)
  • B. Cholestatic pattern (raised ALP/GGT)
  • C. Mixed pattern
  • D. Isolated hyperbilirubinemia
  • E. Normal LFTs
Scenario 1A 46-year-old man presents with fatigue and right upper quadrant discomfort. He has obesity and type 2 diabetes. Liver function tests show ALT 320 U/L and AST 210 U/L, with only mild elevations of ALP and GGT. Bilirubin is normal. Viral hepatitis serology is negative, and ultrasound shows hepatic steatosis.
Which liver function test pattern is most appropriate for this patient?
Scenario 2A 62-year-old woman presents with progressive jaundice, generalized pruritus, dark urine, and pale stools. Laboratory tests show a markedly elevated ALP and GGT with only mild elevations of ALT and AST. Imaging demonstrates dilation of the common bile duct due to an obstructing gallstone.
Which liver function test pattern is most appropriate for this patient?
Scenario 3A 54-year-old man presents with fatigue and jaundice after starting a new medication. Laboratory testing shows ALT and AST approximately 5 times the upper limit of normal and ALP approximately 3 times the upper limit of normal. Bilirubin is also elevated. The pattern does not show a clear predominance of either aminotransferases or cholestatic enzymes.
Which liver function test pattern is most appropriate for this patient?
Scenario 4A 24-year-old man is found to have an elevated bilirubin level during a routine health examination. He is otherwise healthy, with normal ALT, AST, ALP, and GGT levels. The bilirubin is predominantly unconjugated, and he reports that similar episodes occur during periods of fasting or physical stress. He has no evidence of hemolysis or liver disease.
Which liver function test pattern is most appropriate for this patient?
Best answer
1→A, 2→B, 3→C, 4→D
1: Hepatocellular pattern — ALT/AST ≫ ALP, steatosis on USS (NAFLD/NASH). 2: Cholestatic pattern — ALP/GGT ≫ ALT/AST + dilated CBD + RUQ pain = obstructive cholestasis (gallstone). 3: Mixed — both ALT and ALP ~5×ULN → mixed DILI pattern. 4: Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in a well young man with normal enzymes, jaundice with fasting/stress = Gilbert’s syndrome (reduced UGT1A1 activity).

Meningitis — CSF, Causative Organisms & Meningococcaemia

CSF interpretation — the exam table:

NeutrophilsGlucoseProteinPressureClassic
Bacterial↑↑ (pleocytosis, often >1000)LOW (<½ plasma)↑↑Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae b (unimmunised), neonates Group B strep / E. coli / Listeria (add amoxicillin for listeria cover!)
Viral (aseptic)Lymphocytes (early can be neutrophils)NormalNormal–mild↑Normal–mild↑Enterovirus, HSV-2, VZV, mumps — self-limiting; treat supportive
TuberculousLymphocytesVERY LOW (<2.2 mmol/L)VERY HIGH (1–5 g/L)↑↑Insidious; cranial nerve palsies (VI), basal exudates, hydrocephalus (dilated ventricles); “cobweb” clot; ADA >10; AFB rare — treat with RHZE + dexamethasone
Fungal (Cryptococcus, TB-like)LymphocytesLowHigh↑↑Immunocompromised (HIV) — India ink/CR antigens; amphotericin + flucytosine
GBS (neonatal)AnyAnyAny↑E. coli, GBS — ampicillin + gentamicin

Clinical features: fever, headache, neck stiffness (meningism), photophobia, vomiting, altered consciousness, seizures, non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash (meningococcaemia), Kernig’s (pain on knee extension with hip flexed), Brudzinski’s (neck flexion → hip flexion), bulging fontanelle (infants). Meningococcaemia → septic shock, DIC, Waterhouse–Friderichsen (bilateral adrenal haemorrhage).

Management: do NOT delay antibiotics for imaging/LP if unwell — immediate IV ceftriaxone/cefotaxime (add amoxicillin if <3 months or listeria risk), dexamethasone with first dose (↓hearing loss in pneumococcal; continue if confirmed), ABCDE + fluids/vasopressors (shock), isolate (droplet), notify public health, contact prophylaxis (ciprofloxacin/rifampicin) for household contacts, hearing test after recovery, treat complications (seizures, hydrocephalus — neurosurgery/VP shunt, SIADH).

Neurological exam findings asked (this SAQ): neck stiffness, Kernig’s/Brudzinski’s signs positive, photophobia, altered GCS, focal deficits, bulging fontanelle; complications — sensorineural deafness, seizures, hydrocephalus, subdural effusion, learning difficulty, shock/amputation (meningococcaemia).

Exam pearls
  • LP first only if NO contraindication & child stable; otherwise antibiotics first — never delay.
  • Low glucose + high protein + lymphocytes = TB; high PMN + low glucose = bacteria.
  • Non-blanching purpuric rash + fever = ceftriaxone STAT + public health notification.

2020 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Neuromuscular Disorders — Myasthenia, GBS, Botulism

Myasthenia gravis — postsynaptic anti-AChR (or anti-MuSK) antibodies → fatigable weakness. Features: fatigable weakness WORSE with use/at the END of the day, improves with rest; starts with ocular (ptosis, diplopia — painless); bulbar (dysarthria, dysphagia, weak smile/head drop); generalised (neck/proximal/resp); spares reflexes and sensation; no autonomic signs. Associated: thymic hyperplasia/thymoma (15%) (check CT chest). Investigations: anti-AChR antibodies, anti-MuSK (if AChR-negative), repetitive nerve stimulation (decrement), ice-pack test (improves ptosis), CT chest (thymoma). Treatment: pyridostigmine (symptomatic), immunosuppression (prednisolone/azathioprine/mycophenolate), IVIG or plasma exchange for crises, thymectomy if thymoma or generalised AChR+ <65 y; avoid triggers (aminoglycosides!). Crisis = respiratory failure → NIV/intubation.

Guillain–Barré syndrome — post-infectious (Campylobacter jejuni (~40%), CMV, EBV, Zika, Mycoplasma, vaccination rare) autoimmune demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. Features: symmetric ASCENDING weakness + areflexia/hyporeflexia over days, sensory symptoms, minimal sensory loss, back/limb pain, autonomic instability; check FVC/NIF (respiratory failure in 20–30%); CSF: albuminocytologic dissociation (high protein, normal cell count) after week 1; EMG: demyelination (prolonged F waves, conduction block). Treatment: IVIG or plasma exchange (equal efficacy) — start ASAP; NO steroids; monitor respiratory function; VTE prophylaxis; most recover ~80% (mortality 3–5%).

Botulism — Clostridium botulinum preformed toxin (canned/preserved/smoked/honey in infants <12 mo) → blocks presynaptic ACh release. Features: descendING flaccid paralysis (cranial nerves FIRST — diplopia, ptosis, dysarthria, dysphagia, fixed dilated pupils, dry mouth) → arms → respiratory; deep tendon reflexes preserved; afebrile, clear mentation; autonomic signs (constipation). Infant botulism = “floppy baby” + constipation + poor suck. Diagnosis: clinical + toxin in serum/stool + EMG (incremental response on repetitive stimulation). Treatment: botulinum antitoxin ASAP (horse-derived; human BIG-IV for infants), supportive care, NO antibiotics in infant botulism (worsen toxin release), wound botulism → debridement + penicillin/metronidazole; recovery weeks–months (nerve terminal regrowth).

Peripheral nerve injury patterns: common peroneal (foot drop, dorsum sensory loss — fibular head), ulnar (claw hand, medial 1½ fingers — elbow groove), median (thenar wasting, “ape hand”, carpal tunnel — night numbness, Tinel/Phalen), radial (wrist drop), tibial (plantarflexion).

Exam pearls
  • Fatigable + evening + eyes first = MG (pyridostigmine; CT chest). Post-Campylobacter ascending areflexia = GBS (IVIG; watch FVC). Canned food + descendING = botulism (antitoxin).
  • MG fatigues; GBS ascends; botulism descends; both MG/GBS spare the pupils/bladder usually.

#36MCQ edited2020-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-f1fe3f99
A 40-year-old man ate canned food then developed blurred vision followed by body weakness. What is the natural history of this disease?
  • A. Descending paralysis
  • B. Ascending paralysis
  • C. Hemiplegia
  • D. Quadriparesis with preserved reflexes
  • E. Intermittent paralysis
Best answer
A. Descending paralysis
Botulism (canned/preserved food) → presynaptic block of acetylcholine release → cranial nerves first (diplopia, ptosis, dysarthria, dysphagia) then DESCENDING symmetric flaccid paralysis with autonomic signs (dry mouth, fixed pupils). GBS ascends.

Portal Hypertension

Definition: portal venous pressure > 10–12 mmHg (hepatic venous pressure gradient >5) — post-sinusoidal (this exam), pre-/intra-/post-hepatic.

Causes: cirrhosis (sinusoidal — commonest), portal vein thrombosis (pre-hepatic), schistosomiasis (pre-sinusoidal — outside Europe), Budd–Chiari (post-hepatic — hepatic vein thrombosis), right heart failure/constrictive pericarditis (post-hepatic), sarcoid/TB, massive splenomegaly.

Features: splenomegaly (± hypersplenism — pancytopenia), oesophageal/gastric varices (± haemorrhage — massive haematemesis), caput medusae, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, spider naevi, palmar erythema, fetor hepaticus, testicular atrophy, gynaecomastia.

THIS exam: “reverse (hepatofugal) flow in the portal vein on Doppler” indicates reduced/flow away portal circulation — a marker of severe portal hypertension (blood flowing away from liver via collaterals). Increased portal diameter occurs but is non-specific; splenomegaly/ascites are consequences not flow measures.

Investigations: USS Doppler (portal vein direction/velocity, splenomegaly, ascites, varices); LFTs, albumin, INR, platelets, hepatitis/causes screen; endoscopy (varices — screening when cirrhosis diagnosed); Fibroscan; CT/MRI; TIPSS for refractory varices/ascites.

Variceal bleed: ABCDE + 2 large-bore IV access + cross-match + terlipressin IV + prophylactic antibiotics (ceftriaxone) + restrictive transfusion + URGENT endoscopy ≤12 h → band ligation; if uncontrolled → TIPSS/stent; secondary prophylaxis: band + non-selective beta-blocker (propranolol) + treat cause (abstinence/decompensation care/lactulose for encephalopathy).

Exam pearls
  • Hepatofugal flow on Doppler = established portal hypertension with portosystemic shunting.
  • Variceal bleed: terlipressin + antibiotics + band in ≤12 h.
  • Cirrhosis + splenomegaly + varices = portal hypertension — screen at endoscopy.

#27MCQ edited2020-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-1d8c1352
Which of the following indicates reduced blood flow in the portal circulation?
  • A. Reversed (hepatofugal) portal flow on Doppler ultrasound
  • B. Increased portal vein diameter
  • C. Splenomegaly alone
  • D. Ascites alone
  • E. Dilated hepatic veins
Best answer
A. Reversed (hepatofugal) portal flow on Doppler ultrasound
Portal hypertension with decompensation reverses flow away from the liver (hepatofugal) on Doppler — evidence of established portal hypertension. Portal vein diameter >13 mm and splenomegaly/ascites are supportive but less specific signs of cirrhosis/portal HTN.

Stroke & Transient Ischaemic Attack — Localization

Hemisphere syndromes:

TerritoryDeficits
MCA (commonest)Contralateral face & arm > leg weakness, contralateral sensory loss, homonymous hemianopia, aphasia (dominant), neglect (non-dominant), gaze deviation toward lesion
ACAContralateral leg > arm weakness, urinary incontinence, grasp reflex, behavioural change
PCAContralateral homonymous hemianopia (macula-sparing), memory loss, Alexia without agraphia (dominant)

Brainstem/lacunar (cross findings = ipsilateral cranial nerve + contralateral body — the exam’s favourite):

SyndromeSiteFeatures
Weber’sParamedian midbrain (III fascicles + corticospinal)Ipsilateral CN III palsy (“down and out”, ptosis, dilated pupil) + contralateral UMN hemiparesis (face + limbs); ± altered sensorium if haemorrhage/large lesion
Millard–Gubler / FovillePons (VI + VII + corticospinal)Ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy (can’t look that way) + LMN facial palsy + contralateral hemiparesis
Wallenberg (lateral medullary)PICA (posterior inferior cerebellar a.)Ipsilateral: facial pain/temp loss (spinal trigeminal), Horner’s, limb ataxia, nystagmus, dysphagia/hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus), vertigo (vestibular nuclei); contralateral: body pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic); NO weakness — classic “crossed” sensory pattern
BenediktMidbrain (red nucleus + III)CN III palsy + contralateral involuntary movements/tremor
Lateral pontineAICALike Wallenberg + ipsilateral facial weakness & hearing loss (CN VII/VIII)

Pure sensory / pure motor / ataxic hemiparesis / clumsy-hand dysarthria = lacunar (thalamus = pure sensory; internal capsule/corona radiata = pure motor; base of pons = ataxic hemiparesis). Thalamus → isolated hemisensory loss (this exam).

Acute management: ABCDE, glucose, seizures controlled → non-contrast CT brain (exclude haemorrhage) → eligibility for thrombolysis (IV alteplase within 4.5 h) or thrombectomy (large vessel occlusion, up to 24 h in selected) → admit stroke unit; antiplatelet (aspirin 300 mg) if ischaemic and not thrombolysed; BP control (do NOT lower acutely unless >220/120 or thrombolysing); swallow assessment before feeding; DVT prophylaxis; secondary prevention (statin, antiplatelet/anticoagulant for AF, BP, diabetes, smoking); speech & language, PT/OT, MDT; carotid imaging/CT angiography for anterior circulation TIAs.

Exam pearls
  • Crossed signs (ipsilateral CN + contralateral body) = brainstem, NOT cortex.
  • Down-and-out eye + contralateral weakness = Weber’s (midbrain). Gaze palsy + facial weakness + weakness = Millard–Gubler (pons). PICA = Wallenberg.
  • Isolated hemisensory loss = thalamus.
  • Never sit on chest pain/stroke red flags — CT first, thrombolyse if eligible.

#28MCQ edited2020-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-434e649a
A patient presents with isolated loss of sensation in the right face and right body with dysarthria. Where is the lesion?
  • A. Left thalamus
  • B. Right thalamus
  • C. Left internal capsule
  • D. Left medulla
  • E. Right cerebral hemisphere
Best answer
A. Left thalamus
Isolated hemisensory loss of the contralateral face + body = pure sensory stroke = lacunar infarct of the contralateral thalamus (VPL/VPM). Internal capsule lesions give motor ± sensory but the face-body sensory dissociation localises to thalamus.
#52SAQ edited2020-InternalMedicine-SAQ-Medicine-7448077d
Case 3: A picture of a patient shows an oculomotor nerve abnormality on the left side. The patient has right-side weakness and drowsiness; a CT was provided — a scenario typical of Weber's syndrome.
  1. Which two neurological structures are involved? (2 pt)
  2. List 2 pathophysiological mechanisms for the altered sensorium in this patient. (2 pt)
  3. Describe the CT finding. (1 pt)
Best answer
1) Weber syndrome = midbrain stroke (oculomotor nerve palsy + contralateral hemiparesis) — involved structures: (a) oculomotor nerve fascicles (CN III, paramedian midbrain, ipsilateral ptosis/down-and-out eye/fixed mydriasis) and (b) crus cerebri/corticospinal tract (contralateral hemiparesis). 2) Causes of reduced GCS: (a) raised intracranial pressure — large hemispheric infarct with cerebral oedema ± uncal herniation; (b) brainstem (reticular activating system) ischaemia — basilar/PCA perforator territory involvement; also (c) haemorrhage into infarct, (d) seizures/post-ictal state, (e) hypoxia/metabolic. 3) CT: hypodense/A CT window showing midbrain lesion in paramedian perforator (PCA/basilar) territory — low attenuation in the ipsilateral midbrain ± oedema; exclude haemorrhage.
Crossed findings (ipsilateral CN palsy + contralateral weakness) localise to the brainstem. Weber = midbrain (III), Millard–Gubler = pons (VI/VII), Wallenberg = lateral medulla (IX/X/XI + spinothalamic + Horner). Always exclude haemorrhage before thrombolysis/antithrombotics.
2020 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Definition: multisystem autoimmune disease — antinuclear antibodies (ANA) + lupus-specific antibodies: anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith. Female >> male (9:1), childbearing age; HLA-DR2/DR3; complement-consuming immune-complex disease.

ACR-like criteria (≥4):

  • Malar “butterfly” rash — this exam (image): erythematous rash across cheeks & nasal bridge SPARING the nasolabial folds (photosensitive)
  • Discoid rash — raised, scaly, atrophic plaques (leaves scars)
  • Photosensitivity — rash after sun
  • Oral/nasal ulcers
  • Non-erosive arthritis (≥2 peripheral joints, tender/swollen)
  • Serositis — pleuritis/pericarditis ± effusion
  • Renal — persistent proteinuria or cellular casts (lupus nephritis) — 40% develop; check urine/PCR
  • Neuro — seizures or psychosis (other: headache, mood)
  • Haematological — haemolytic anaemia, leucopaenia, lymphopaenia, thrombocytopaenia
  • Immunological — anti-dsDNA or anti-Smith, ANA+, low complement (C3/C4 LOW), antiphospholipid (lupus anticoagulant/anticardiolipin/β2GPI → recurrent thrombosis + miscarriage + thrombocytopaenia)

Complications & overlap: ILD/pulmonary fibrosis (this exam: dry cough + exertional dyspnoea → SLE-ILD) — HRCT + PFTs; pulmonary hypertension; Libman–Sacks endocarditis (sterile vegetations); nephritis; premature atherosclerosis. Differentiating RA from SLE (this exam): SLE = non-erosive, reversible deformities (Jaccoud’s), malar rash, low complement, dsDNA+, multisystem (renal/CNS/haem), no nodules; RA = erosive symmetric small-joint arthritis with morning stiffness >1 h, RF/anti-CCP+, rheumatoid nodules, spares DIP.

Management: avoid sun/photoprotection; hydroxychloroquine (ALL patients — skin/joints, reduces flares/mortality); NSAIDs (arthralgia); corticosteroids (moderate–severe flares); immunosuppressants — mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide (nephritis/neuropsychiatric), azathioprine maintenance; biologics (belimumab, rituximab) refractory; ACEi/ARB (renal); aspirin/heparin for antiphospholipid (recurrent thrombosis → warfarin); vaccinate, monitor (BP, urine, FBC, complement, dsDNA).

Exam pearls
  • Malar rash spares nasolabial folds; discoid = scarring; both photosensitive.
  • dsDNA + low C3/C4 = active lupus; Smith = specific.
  • Hydroxychloroquine for everyone. Nephritis → mycophenolate; monitor urine.
  • Drug-induced lupus: hydralazine, isoniazid, procainamide, minocycline — anti-histone, milder, no renal.

2020 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · SAQ

Tuberculosis

Pathogenesis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (airborne) → primary Ghon focus → reactivation in apices (high O₂) when cell-mediated immunity falls (HIV, diabetes, steroids, malnutrition) — caseating granulomas (Langhans giant cells).

Forms (by site):

  • Pulmonary — fever, night sweats, weight loss, chronic cough (± haemoptysis), apical infiltrate/cavitation on CXR, homeless/overcrowding/immunosuppressed; miliary — diffuse millet-seed infiltrates.
  • Extrapulmonary — TB lymphadenitis (bilateral cervical nodes, “cold abscesses” with sinus tracts — scrofuloderma — this exam’s homeless man), TB meningitis (basilar, CN VI palsy, very low CSF glucose/very high protein, lymphocytes — treat + dexamethasone), Pott’s disease (spinal TB — gibbus deformity, PPD/MRI), pleural TB (unilateral lymphocytic exudate, high ADA), TB pericarditis/miliary.
  • TB in HIV — atypical CXR, disseminated disease, drug interactions (rifampicin with ART).

Diagnosis: CXR (apical cavities/infiltrates, miliary, effusion, hilar nodes); sputum smear + culture (gold standard) — AFB smear, culture (2–6 wks), GeneXpert MTB/RIF (PCR) — rapid, detects rifampicin resistance — first-line test; tuberculin skin test (Mantoux — latent), IGRA (latent TB; not for active); node biopsy (caseating granuloma + AFB) for TB lymphadenitis; FBC/CRP/ESR; HIV test.

Treatment (RIPE): 2 months HRZE + 4 months HR (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol → then INH + rifampicin ×4 months); isoniazid neuropathy → pyridoxine (vit B6); ethambutol → optic neuritis (check colour vision/acuity); rifampicin → orange fluids + drug interactions; monitor LFTs; drug-resistant TB (MDR — RIF + INH resistant) → specialist regimens (bedaquiline etc.). Latent TB: INH ×6–9 months or rifapentine-INH 3 months.

This exam: gibbus → Pott’s disease (A); sacroiliitis in a child → brucellosis (B). Homeless + cervical node discharge + fever + chronic cough → TB. Active TB CXR (Case 4): upper-lobe/apical infiltrate ± cavitation ± hilar lymphadenopathy; tests: sputum AFB smear/culture (or GeneXpert), tuberculin test/IGRA (but tests = sputum microbiology + imaging/biopsy).

Exam pearls
  • GeneXpert is the rapid first test; culture is gold standard.
  • Gibbus = Pott’s. Cervical “cold abscess” with sinus = scrofuloderma = TB.
  • RIPE × 2 months then RI × 4; B6 with INH; watch liver and eyes (EMB).

  1. What is the diagnosis? (1 pt)
  2. List 2 diagnostic tests. (2 pt)

Best answer
1) Active pulmonary tuberculosis. 2) Diagnostic tests: (a) sputum (or BAL/early-morning gastric lavage) ×3 for AFB smear + Mycobacterium tuberculosis culture and NAAT/GeneXpert MTB/RIF (rifampicin resistance); also (b) Mantoux/IGRA (exposure), pleural fluid ADA if effusion, HIV test. 3) X-ray findings: upper-lobe cavitary infiltrates, hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy, pleural effusion, miliary pattern, calcification/fibrosis of old disease.
Isolate (airborne precautions) if smear-positive; notify public health; 2HRZE/4HR regimen (6 months); contact tracing; check HIV and hepatitis; drug-susceptibility testing; ensure adherence (DOT); repeat CXR at 2 months.
