2020 · Pediatrics · 1 question · EMQ

Bone & Joint Infections — Septic Arthritis vs Osteomyelitis vs Transient Synovitis

Septic arthritis — surgical emergency: fever, hot swollen joint, refusal to bear weight, raised WBC/ESR/CRP. Staph aureus is the commonest organism at all ages (young infants: GBS/E. coli; sickle cell: Salmonella; adolescents sexually active: N. gonorrhoeae). Knee/hip commonest. Kocher criteria (non-weight-bearing, fever, ESR>40, WBC>12k) predict probability. Diagnosis: aspirate (Gram stain/culture/crystals), blood cultures, ultrasound (hip effusion), MRI if osteomyelitis suspected. Treatment: urgent drainage + IV antibiotics (flucloxacillin/cefazolin; add cover for Salmonella if sickle cell).

Osteomyelitis — metaphysis of long bones (femur, tibia) in children; haematogenous spread; S. aureus (incl. MRSA) commonest; Salmonella in sickle cell; chronic (>4 wk) → Brodie’s abscess/sequestrum. Signs: localised bone pain, fever, limp, X-ray changes LATE (10–14 d) — early diagnosis = MRI; bone scan. Treatment: prolonged IV→oral antibiotics (4–6 weeks), surgical drainage if abscess.

Transient synovitis (“irritable hip”) — commonest cause of acute hip pain in children 3–10 y; often post-viral; sudden pain + limp, low fever, well, hip held flexed/abducted/externally rotated; inflammatory markers normal/slightly raised; ultrasound shows effusion. Diagnosis of exclusion — if any doubt, aspirate to exclude septic arthritis. Treatment: rest, NSAIDs, usually resolves in 1–2 weeks.

Exam pearls
  • Refusal to bear weight + fever → admit, aspirate, IV antibiotics.
  • Gibbus = TB spine (Pott’s). Sacroiliitis + animal exposure = brucellosis.
  • Sickle cell + osteomyelitis → think Salmonella (treat both).
  • X-ray normal early in osteomyelitis/septic arthritis — MRI is the sensitive test.

The classic differentials (highest-yield table in paediatrics):

DiseaseAgentFeverRash patternKey distinguishing features
Measles (rubeola)ParamyxovirusHigh, 3–4 d BEFORE rashMaculopapular starting hairline/behind ears → face → trunk (craniocaudal spread)3 Cs: cough, coryza, conjunctivitis + Koplik spots (buccal mucosa white grains)

Scarlet feverStrep pyogenes (erythrogenic toxin)Fever, sore throatSandpaper rash (blanching, pinpoint, sandpaper), circumoral pallor, Pastia’s lines (flexural accentuation)Strawberry tongue, tonsillitis; treat penicillin (prevents RF/PSGN)

Management: measles/rubella/roseola/fifth = supportive (antipyretics, fluids). Scarlet fever = penicillin V/amoxicillin ×10 d. Varicella = supportive, acyclovir if severe/immunocompromised. Meningococcaemia = emergency. Measles: isolate, notify public health, vitamin A in severe/developing-world cases.

Exam pearls
  • Fever first, rash after fever breaks = ROSEOLA (HHV-6).
  • Cough+coryza+conjunctivitis then craniocaudal rash = MEASLES (plus Koplik).
  • Slapped cheek + reticular rash = parvovirus B19 → aplastic crisis risk in haemolytics.
  • Sandpaper rash + Pastia lines + circumoral pallor = GAS scarlet fever → penicillin.
  • Any non-blanching purpuric rash with fever = meningococcaemia → ceftriaxone NOW.
Traps
  • Measles is contagious 4 days before → 4 days after rash.
  • Fifth disease in pregnancy causes hydrops — advise pregnant contacts.
  • Don’t confuse roseola rash with drug rash — history of fever trajectory decides.

2020 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Childhood Vasculitis — Kawasaki Disease & HSP (IgA Vasculitis)

Kawasaki disease (mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome) — medium-vessel vasculitis of children <5 y; the leading cause of acquired heart disease in developed countries (coronary artery aneurysms).

Diagnostic criteria: fever ≥5 days PLUS ≥4 of: (1) bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection; (2) oral changes — strawberry tongue, cracked red lips, diffuse erythema; (3) rash (polymorphous, not vesicular); (4) extremity changes — erythema/oedema of palms & soles (acute) → periungual desquamation (2–3 wks); (5) cervical lymphadenopathy (≥1.5 cm, usually unilateral). Labs: leucocytosis, thrombocytosis (week 2+), high ESR/CRP, sometimes aseptic meningitis, sterile pyuria, raised transaminases.

Treatment — IVIG 2 g/kg over 12 h ASAP (ideally within 10 days of fever) + aspirin (high-dose acute phase 80–100 mg/kg/d until afebrile 48–72 h, then low-dose 3–5 mg/kg/d ×6–8 weeks). Baseline echocardiography (repeat at 2 wks and 6–8 wks) for coronary aneurysms. Refractory → second IVIG dose ± infliximab/steroids. Delay in IVIG = aneurysm risk.

Complications: coronary artery aneurysm (20% untreated vs ~5% with IVIG) → MI/sudden death; myocarditis; pericarditis; valvulitis; rarely giant aneurysms → thrombosis → warfarin/abciximab.

Henoch–Schönlein purpura (HSP / IgA vasculitis) — the commonest childhood vasculitis; small-vessel IgA immune-complex disease, classically 2–11 y, post-URTI. Classic tetrad: palpable purpura (buttocks/extensor legs — NON-blanching), colicky abdominal pain (± GI bleed), arthritis/arthralgia, renal disease (haematuria/proteinuria — IgA nephropathy pattern, usually mild but can cause RPGN). Diagnosis clinical; check urine microscopy + BP + U&E in every HSP child, weekly then monthly urinalysis up to 6–12 months. Treatment: supportive (hydration, analgesia); severe abdominal pain → steroids; renal failure/nephritic syndrome → nephrology (may need steroids/immunosuppression ± dialysis).

HSP complication in this exam: abdominal pain + palpable mass = intussusception (ileo-ileal — lead point from bowel-wall haematoma).

Exam pearls
  • Fever ≥5 d + strawberry tongue + conjunctivitis + rash + desquamating hands/ feet → IVIG + aspirin NOW; echo the heart.
  • HSP = purpura on extensor surfaces + abdominal colic + arthritis + haematuria → urine dip all children at presentation and follow up.
  • HSP + abdominal mass → ultrasound for intussusception.
  • Kawasaki thrombocytosis appears in week 2 — do not be reassured by an early normal count.
Traps
  • Only PARTIAL criteria (e.g. fever + 2 features + coronary aneurysm or very high inflammatory markers) = incomplete Kawasaki — still treat.
  • Aspirin in HSP is NOT required; it’s the big antiplatelet role only in Kawasaki/thrombocytosis.
  • Excludes: meningococcaemia (toxic, petechial), scarlet fever (circumoral pallor/Pastia lines), measles (Koplik).

Definition: stools loose for >2–4 weeks (or >3 loose stools/day). Key exam pattern: failure to thrive + steatorrhoea + recurrent infections.

CauseCluesKey investigation

Toddler’s diarrhoea1–4 y; 3–6 loose stools/d, normal growth & well; peas/undigested food; “intestinal hurry”None (diagnosis of exclusion); reassure; resolves by school age; reduce juice/fructose
Cow’s milk protein allergyInfants; blood-streaked stools, eczema, vomiting; normal growth (non-IgE) vs anaphylaxis (IgE)Elimination diet (maternal dairy-free if breastfeeding / EHF formula) → rechallenge
Post-infectious / lactase deficiencyDiarrhoea after gastroenteritis; lactose intolerance (bloating, osmotic, acidic stool)Reducing substances in stool; trial lactose-free
IBD (Crohn’s)Weight loss, perianal disease, oral ulcers, arthralgiaFaecal calprotectin, CRP, colonoscopy + biopsy
Immunodeficiency (CVID/XLA)Recurrent infections + FTTImmunoglobulins

Work-up approach: growth chart (faltering?) → stool microscopy/culture/faecal elastase/occult blood/reducing substances → coeliac serology → sweat test if chest/FTT → endoscopy if indicated. Growth chart is the fundamental tool — deceleration of weight/height velocity = “faltering growth / failure to thrive”.

Coeliac management: strict lifelong gluten-free diet + dietitian; follow-up serology for compliance; annual review; vaccinations (pneumococcal if hyposplenic risk); screen first-degree relatives.

Exam pearls
  • Gluteal wasting + bloating + FTT after weaning with wheat/barley/rye → celiac → tTG-IgA + EMA, biopsy.
  • Offensive, greasy, difficult-to-flush stools + recurrent chest infections → CF → sweat test.
  • Blood in stool of a thriving 4-month breastfed infant → CMPA → elimination diet.
  • Always plot the growth chart first — “faltering growth” is the answer to Q1 in the SAQs.

#54SAQ edited2020-Pediatrics-SAQ-Medicine-4f712051
Case 5: An 8-month-old infant is brought with a history of offensive, loose stool that is difficult to flush, with recurrent hospitalizations for chest infections. He eats vegetables, fruits, barley and wheat. He is also small for his age. No similar history in the family.
  1. Give 2 differential diagnoses. (2 pt)
  2. Give 2 important investigations to reach the most likely diagnosis. (2 pt)
  3. Give 2 steps in management. (2 pt)
Best answer
1) Diagnosis: cystic fibrosis (failure to thrive + offensive steatorrhoeic stools + recurrent chest infections — treat as CF until proven otherwise). Differentials: coeliac disease, chronic pancreatitis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, cow’s-milk protein allergy, immunodeficiency, GORD, bronchiectasis. 2) Investigations: (a) Sweat chloride test (≥60 mmol/L positive; 30–59 borderline → CFTR genotyping); (b) faecal elastase (pancreatic insufficiency), stool fat, 72-h faecal fat; also chest X-ray/HRCT, sputum culture, fat-soluble vitamin levels, LFTs, CFTR genetic testing. 3) Management: (a) nutritional — high-calorie high-fat diet + pancreatic enzyme replacement (Creon) with meals + fat-soluble ADEK supplementation; (b) respiratory — airway clearance physiotherapy, inhaled hypertonic saline/dornase alfa, treat exacerbations with antibiotics, annual review at CF centre, immunisations (including influenza/pneumococcal).
Meconium ileus in a newborn is nearly pathognomonic of CF. Newborn screening (immunoreactive trypsinogen) detects most. Definitive = sweat test + CFTR mutations. Multidisciplinary CF-centre care improves survival beyond 40 years.

Developmental Milestones & Developmental Quotient

Core milestones to memorise (age → expected):

AgeGross motorFine motor / visionSpeech / languageSocial / behaviour

6 wksRaises head proneFixes & follows to midlineCoosSocial smile
3 moHead control developing, supports on forearms (prone), holds head steadyHands opening, follows 180°Laughs, turns to voiceKnows mother
4–6 moRolls tummy→back (4–5 mo), sits with support/tripod (6 mo)Palmar grasp (6 mo), transfers hand-to-hand (6–7 mo), reachesBabbles (monosyllables 6 mo)Recognises strangers
7–9 moSits unsupported (7–8 mo), crawls/pivots-sit, stands with supportInferior pincer grasp (9 mo), finger feeds, bangs toys“Mama”, “dada” non-specific (9 mo), understands “no”Stranger anxiety, waves bye-bye-ish
12 moStands alone, walks with one hand held / alone (12–15 mo), cruisingPincer grasp perfected, casts toys1–2 words with meaningDrinks from cup, points, waves bye-bye

3 yRides tricycle, climbs stairs alternating feet, stands briefly one footTower of 9–10, copies circle, bridge 3 blocks3–4 word sentences, asks “what/who”Puts on garments, plays with others (group play), dry by day

Developmental quotient (DQ) = developmental age ÷ chronological age × 100. DQ 85–115 normal; 70–85 borderline; <70 significant delay (support needed). Example: 2-year-old with 12-month milestones → 12/24 × 100 = 50.

Warning signs: no social smile by 8 wks, hand preference <12 mo, not sitting by 12 mo, not walking by 18 mo, no words by 2 y, no interest in peers, regression. When in doubt → formal developmental assessment + hearing + vision + referral to portage/EI.

Exam pearls
  • Smile 6 wks • sit 6–8 mo • walk 12–15 mo • words 12–18 mo • 2-word phrases 2 y • tricycle 3 y • hop/skip 4–5 y.
  • DQ = DA/CA ×100 — always a percentage, comparable across domains.
  • Head lag + poor head control in a 3-month-old → reassess urgently (neurological exam, neuroimaging).

Diabetes Mellitus — Type 1, Type 2 & MODY

Classification & clues:

Type 1Type 2MODY
OnsetChildren/adolescents, rapidAdults (now adolescents with obesity), insidiousYoung (<25), autosomal dominant, strong family history (3 generations)
WeightNormal/leanObese, metabolic syndromeNormal (often)
AntibodiesGAD, IA-2, insulin, ZnT8NegativeNegative
C-peptideLow/absentNormal/highPreserved
KetosisProne (may present in DKA)Rare (HHS)Rare
TreatmentInsulin from diagnosis + carb counting + educationLifestyle + metformin ± add-ons (SGLT2i/GLP-1/SU/DPP4/insulin)Sulfonylureas (MODY 3/HNF1A), or low-dose; often misdiagnosed as T1

Autoantibody-positive adolescent + polyuria/polydipsia + no family history → type 1 diabetes (not MODY). LADA = latent autoimmune diabetes of adults (>30 y, slower onset, GAD+, initially non-insulin).

Diagnosis: fasting glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L, random ≥11.1 + symptoms, OGTT 2-h ≥11.1, or HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol (6.5%) (not in pregnancy/haemoglobinopathy). One abnormal + symptoms is enough; asymptomatic → confirm with repeat.

Newly diagnosed T2DM management: lifestyle/weight loss + metformin first-line (unless contraindicated) — then SGLT2i/GLP-1 if CV/renal disease, consider dual therapy if HbA1c >58. Annual review: feet, eyes (retinal screen), urine ACR, lipids, BP, vaccination, smoking cessation. Targets: BP <130/80 (but ≤140/90 general), LDL reduction per QRISK; statin if >40 y or CVD risk.

Type 1 annual review: retinopathy screen (from 12 y), microalbuminuria, thyroid/coeliac screen, self-monitoring, sick-day rules (never stop insulin entirely — DKA risk; “sick-day” = continue basal, check ketones, fluids, seek help if vomiting/ketotic).

Exam pearls
  • GAD antibodies + adolescent + no family history = T1DM → insulin.
  • MODY = young + strong 3-generation family history + non-obese + antibody-negative.
  • First step in stable newly-diagnosed T2DM = metformin + lifestyle (not insulin).

  • B. MODY

Best answer
C. Type 1 diabetes mellitus

Glomerulonephritis & Haematuria (Children)

Glomerular haematuria vs non-glomerular: glomerular = dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, smoky/tea-coloured urine, proteinuria, hypertension, renal impairment. Non-glomerular = red/pink urine, isomorphic RBCs, clots, no casts.

Post-streptococcal GNIgA nephropathy (synpharyngitic)AlportHSP nephritis
Timing vs URTI2–3 weeks AFTER throat/skin infectionWithin 1–2 days (“synpharyngitic”)Persistent/familialWith purpura (simultaneous)
ComplementLOW C3 (normalises in 6–8 wks); C4 normalNormalNormalNormal
Other labsASO ↑ (anti-streptolysin O) / anti-DNase B; throat swab may be negativeNormalNormal; hearing loss + ocular (anterior lenticonus)Normal ± renal involvement
Age5–12 yAdolescents/young adultsChildren, X-linked (boys)2–11 y
HistologyDiffuse proliferative GNMesangial proliferation, IgA depositsBasketweave GBM (EM); Type IV collagenIgA deposition (same disease as IgA nephropathy)
OutcomeSelf-limiting (95%+ recover)Variable; 20–40% progress to CKD over decadesProgressive CKD + sensorineural deafnessUsually good; monitor urine/BP for 12–24 mo

Features of nephritic syndrome: haematuria (smoky), hypertension, mild–moderate proteinuria, oedema (periorbital), oliguria. Management PSGN: supportive (salt/water restriction, antihypertensives), no steroids/antibiotics needed for the kidney (antibiotics treat the strep carrier state and prevent spread, not the GN); follow-up to confirm C3 normalisation; persistent hypertension/renal impairment → biopsy.

Alport: persistent glomerular haematuria + family history of males with CKD + sensorineural hearing loss + anterior lenticonus — COL4A5 (X-linked, 80%); supportive; ACEi slows proteinuria; genetic counselling; transplant is not contraindicated (no anti-GBM in most).

Exam pearls
  • Haematuria 2–3 weeks AFTER sore throat + low C3 + high ASO = PSGN.
  • Haematuria DURING sore throat + normal C3 = IgA nephropathy.
  • Haematuria + deafness + family history of renal failure = Alport.
  • Hypertension + periorbital oedema + smoky urine in a child = nephritic — check ASO/C3 first.

2020 · Pediatrics · 3 questions · MCQ

Growth — Assessment, Percentiles & Faltering Growth

Key measurements: weight-for-age, length/height-for-age, weight-for-height/BMI, head circumference (0–2 y). BMI (child) = weight(kg) / height(m)² — age & sex needed only to plot centiles.

Normal variant patterns:

  • Parent-determined (familial short stature): height follows parental target centile; normal growth velocity; bone age = chronological age.
  • Constitutional delay: short stature + delayed puberty; growth catches up later; bone age delayed; normal final height (just later). “Late bloomer.”
  • Pathological: endocrine (hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, Cushing’s), chronic disease (coeliac, CF, CKD, asthma on steroids), neglect, genetic syndromes.

Faltering growth (failure to thrive): weight crossing down ≥1–2 centile lines (or weight below 3rd centile), often weight before height; causes — inadequate intake (feeding problems, poverty, neglect), inadequate absorption (coeliac, CF, CMPA), excessive losses (vomiting, diarrhoea — coeliac/CF), increased requirements (chronic infection, malignancy, hyperthyroidism). First step: plot the chart accurately + dietary history + observe a feed (for infants). Investigations guided by history: urine dip/MC&S, coeliac serology, sweat test, FBC, U&E/LFT, TFT, lead, development.

Reading growth charts: plot with correct age/sex chart; centiles: 3rd–97th ≈ normal; below 3rd = short/underweight; above 97th = tall/overweight; height above 97th centile — think Marfan/overgrowth; weight <3rd with height 50th = acute undernutrition (wasting); both <3rd = chronic; height <3rd with normal weight = “failure to thrive with preserved weight” — hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, skeletal dysplasia, syndromes.

Velocity matters more than one point: falling off the centile line (even within the normal range) is abnormal; single readings need confirmation.

Head circumference: ~34–35 cm at birth; +2 cm/mo ×3, then +1 cm/mo; at 12 mo ≈ 46 cm; macrocephaly >98th (hydrocephalus — check fontanelle, developmental progress); microcephaly <2nd (congenital infections, TORCH, chromosomal, metabolic).

Exam pearls
  • BMI = weight ÷ height² — needs only weight & height for the value; age/sex for the centile plot.
  • Weight <3rd + height 50th = wasting (acute); height <3rd + weight normal = endocrine/skeletal.
  • Deceleration (crossing down lines) = the red flag — plot and re-measure.
  • Faltering growth + offensive stools + recurrent chest infections = CF/coeliac — sweat test + tTG.

#14MCQ edited2020-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-25002735
A baby's weight is below the 3rd percentile while his height is at the 50th percentile. What is the interpretation?
  • A. Acute malnutrition (wasting)
  • B. Chronic malnutrition (stunting)
  • C. Normal growth
  • D. Constitutional growth delay
  • E. Endocrine disorder (e.g. hypothyroidism)
Best answer
A. Acute malnutrition (wasting)
Weight below 3rd centile with height on the 50th = weight-for-height deficit = acute undernutrition (wasting). Stunting (chronic) = height-for-age <3rd centile with proportionate weight.

2020 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Hypertension (including Paediatric)

Diagnosis (adults): clinic BP ≥140/90 confirmed with ABPM/HBPM ≥135/85. Stage 1 (140–159/90–99), Stage 2 (160–179/100–109), Stage 3 (≥180/≥110). Secondary causes: primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn’s), renal artery stenosis, phaeochromocytoma, coarctation, OSA, CKD, drugs (COCP, NSAIDs, steroids, liquorice), alcohol. Screen: U&E, glucose, lipids, urine dip/ACR, ECG; echo if LVH suspected.

Management: lifestyle (weight loss, salt <5–6 g/d, exercise, DASH, alcohol, stop smoking — smoking doesn’t cause HTN but amplifies CV risk). NICE drug pathway: <55 y / not Black: ACEi/ARB → add CCB or thiazide-like diuretic → triple (A+C+D) → resistant (on A+C+D, BP high) → add spironolactone (if K ≤4.5) or alpha/beta-blocker. ≥55 y or Black African/Caribbean: CCB first-line (then A/D). Step 4: check adherence, consider secondary causes, ABPM.

Paediatric hypertension: defined by age/sex/height ≥95th centile on repeat measurements (ABPM confirm). Secondary causes dominate in younger children: renal (GN, reflux nephropathy, CKD, renal artery stenosis), coarctation (radiofemoral delay, murmur, BP arms > legs), endocrine (phaeo, CAH, hyperaldosteronism, hyperthyroid), drugs. Adolescents: primary (essential) hypertension — obesity-related increasingly common. Management: repeat and confirm (3 visits), lifestyle (weight loss, salt, activity) + treat underlying; drugs (ACEi/CCB) if persistent/severe/symptomatic/end-organ damage; specialist referral if <6 y, severe, or abnormal work-up.

Examination answer in this set: adolescent with weight >95th centile and BP 130/80 — first step is to repeat the blood pressure measurement (one reading never diagnoses paediatric hypertension; measure on ≥3 occasions, check technique, cuff size, right arm, and consider ABPM). Lifestyle advice accompanies; not immediate drugs.

Exam pearls
  • One elevated reading = repeat. Confirm on 3 occasions/ABPM before labelling or treating.
  • Child <6 or severe/symptomatic/abnormal → full secondary work-up + specialist.
  • Resistant adult HTN on A+C+D → spironolactone + check adherence/secondary causes.

2020 · Pediatrics · 1 question · EMQ

Neonatal Jaundice

Approach by timing:

TimingThink of
<24 h (always pathological)Haemolysis — Rh incompatibility (Rh-neg mother + Rh-pos baby), ABO incompatibility (O mother + A/B baby), G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis, sepsis (congenital), polycythaemia; direct hyperbilirubinaemia (TORCH/sepsis — urgent)
24 h–2 wksPhysiological (peak day 3–4, unconjugated, well baby, resolves ≤2 wks), breast-milk jaundice (peaks week 2, feeding well — continue breastfeeding), breastfeeding failure jaundice (under-feeding, weight loss — feed more), haemolysis, infection, polycythaemia, cephalohaematoma bruising
>2 wks (prolonged)Conjugated (cholestatic): biliary atresia (pale stools + dark urine — Kasai portoenterostomy before 8–12 wks!), choledochal cyst, Alagille, inborn errors (galactosaemia, α1-AT), infection (UTI!), hypothyroidism, breast-milk jaundice, haemolysis persisting

This exam’s EMQ (2020 set): day 3, well, unconjugated, resolves → physiological; first 24 h, mother O/baby A, DAT+, mild anaemia → ABO incompatibility; first day, Rh-neg mother sensitised (previous Rh-pos baby, no anti-D) → Rh incompatibility (severe — exchange transfusion risk); day 5 boy, male relatives affected, haemolysis → G6PD deficiency.

ABO vs Rh: ABO — mother O, baby A/B; usually mild, 1st baby can be affected (naturally occurring anti-A/B IgG), DAT weak/negative, no prenatal prophylaxis works (no anti-D for ABO). Rh — mother Rh-neg, baby Rh-pos; usually NOT first baby (needs sensitisation, unless prior transfusion/miscarriage), DAT strongly positive, severe haemolysis (hydrops fetalis), prevented by anti-D Ig (at 28/34 wks + within 72 h of delivery/sensitising events).

G6PD deficiency — X-linked; males; episodic severe haemolysis with infection/fava beans/drugs (sulfonamides, primaquine, nitrofurantoin, methylene blue); Mediterranean/African/Asian; avoid precipitants; check level; Heinz bodies/bite cells.

Management: monitor bilirubin (TSB or transcutaneous); phototherapy per age-appropriate thresholds (chart); exchange transfusion if severe (or BIND scores — bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction: lethargy, poor feeding, arching, high-pitched cry, later kernicterus — athetoid CP, hearing loss, gaze palsy); IVIG if immune haemolysis failing phototherapy; treat cause; breastfeeding support; prolonged conjugated → urgent USS + hepatology (biliary atresia timing critical).

Exam pearls
  • Jaundice <24 h = pathological — find the haemolysis.
  • Mother O + baby A/B = ABO (DAT±). Mother Rh− + baby Rh+ + prior affected sibling = Rh — anti-D prevents.
  • Pale stools + dark urine at 2–3 weeks = biliary atresia — Kasai before 8–12 weeks, every week counts.
  • G6PD: check family history of male jaundice; avoid oxidants.

#46EMQ edited2020-Pediatrics-EMQ-Medicine-2859821e
Theme — Jaundice
  • A. Physiological jaundice
  • B. ABO incompatibility
  • C. Rh incompatibility
  • D. G6PD deficiency
  • E. Biliary atresia
Scenario 1A healthy term newborn develops mild jaundice on the third day of life. The infant is feeding well and appears otherwise normal. Total bilirubin is elevated with a predominantly unconjugated fraction. The jaundice resolves spontaneously over the following week without treatment.
Which is the most likely cause of this newborn's jaundice?
Scenario 2A newborn develops jaundice within the first 24 hours of life. The mother has blood group O positive, while the infant has blood group A positive. Laboratory testing demonstrates unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and a positive direct antiglobulin test. The infant has mild anemia but no hepatosplenomegaly.
Which is the most likely cause of this newborn's jaundice?
Scenario 3A newborn develops severe jaundice and anemia within the first day of life. The mother is Rh-negative and the infant is Rh-positive. The mother had a previous pregnancy complicated by an Rh-positive infant and did not receive appropriate anti-D prophylaxis. The infant has a strongly positive direct antiglobulin test.
Which is the most likely cause of this newborn's jaundice?
Scenario 4A 5-day-old male infant develops significant unconjugated jaundice after an otherwise uncomplicated birth. His mother reports that several male relatives have previously developed severe neonatal jaundice. Laboratory testing demonstrates hemolysis, and subsequent testing identifies reduced red-cell glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity.
Which is the most likely cause of this newborn's jaundice?
Best answer
1→A, 2→B, 3→C, 4→D
1: Day 3, well, unconjugated, resolves in ~1 wk = physiological. 2: Day 1 + mother O / baby A + DAT+, mild anaemia = ABO incompatibility. 3: First-24-h severe jaundice + Rh-neg mother + sensitised + DAT strongly + = Rh incompatibility (anti-D, severe haemolysis, prior sensitisation). 4: Male, family history in males, haemolysis = G6PD deficiency (X-linked). (E — biliary atresia: CONJUGATED cholestatic jaundice at 2–8 wks, pale stools, surgical emergency.)

Neonatal Respiratory Distress — RDS, TTN, MAS, Sepsis, Pneumothorax

Differential by timing, mode of delivery and X-ray:

RDS (hyaline membrane)TTN (wet lung)MASNeonatal sepsis/pneumoniaPneumothorax
WhoPreterm (<34 wks; less often IDM/term C-section)Term, LSCS/rapid delivery (no labour → retained fluid)Post-term/term, meconium-stained liquor (pea-soup)PPROM >18 h, maternal GBS/chorioamnionitis, feverSpontaneous (1–2% newborns), post-resuscitation, MAS/RDS complication
OnsetAt/within minutes–hours of birthWithin hours (2–6 h), resolves 24–72 hWithin hoursHours–daysAny time; sudden desaturation
X-rayGround-glass reticulogranular + air bronchograms + low lung volumesPerihilar streaking + fluid in fissures, hyperinflated, normal volumesCoarse patchy infiltrates, hyperinflation, flattened diaphragm, ± air leaksVariable — focal infiltrate/effusion or normalVisceral pleural line + absent lung markings beyond it; mediastinal shift if tension
MechanismSurfactant deficiency → atelectasisDelayed clearance of fetal lung fluid (lymphatic/circulation)Airway obstruction (ball-valve) + chemical pneumonitis + surfactant inactivationGBS/E. coli/ Listeria infectionAir leak from overdistension/rupture
ManagementCPAP early (avoid ventilation if possible) + exogenous surfactant (INSURE/LISA), antenatal steroids preventSupportive: O₂, CPAP if needed; self-limitingSupportive: O₂, ventilation, surfactant; avoid antibiotics unless infected; amnioinfusion historic (no longer routine)IV benzylpenicillin + gentamicin + full septic screen (cultures, FBC, CRP, LP if stable) + supportiveNeedle aspiration/chest drain (2nd ICS MCL) if tension/symptomatic; observation if small asymptomatic

This exam’s questions: 34-weeker + ground-glass = surfactant deficiency (RDS); term C-section + 3 h of distress = TTN; pea-soup liquor = MAS; PPROM = neonatal sepsis; post-C-section tachypnoea = TTN.

Acute care principles: ABCDE; thermoregulation; O₂ sats monitoring; blood glucose; escalate to CPAP/ventilation, CXR, treat sepsis if suspected (don’t wait for cultures), transfer to NICU.

Exam pearls
  • Ground-glass + air bronchograms + preterm = RDS = surfactant.
  • Term + LSCS + tachypnea in first hours = TTN = supportive.
  • Pea-soup liquor = MAS. PPROM + maternal infection = sepsis work-up now.
  • Sudden desaturation + asymmetry = pneumothorax — transilluminate/CXR.

#7MCQ edited2020-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-c162514a
A preterm newborn at 34 weeks of gestation develops difficulty breathing; X-ray shows a ground-glass appearance. What is the pathophysiology?
  • A. Surfactant deficiency
  • B. Meconium aspiration
  • C. Transient tachypnoea of the newborn
  • D. Congenital pneumonia
  • E. Pneumothorax
Best answer
A. Surfactant deficiency
Preterm (<34 wk) + respiratory distress at birth + ground-glass reticulogranular CXR with air bronchograms = neonatal RDS from surfactant deficiency → diffuse atelectasis. Prevent with antenatal steroids; treat with surfactant + CPAP.
#8MCQ edited2020-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-3f7730a6
A term newborn delivered by LSCS develops respiratory distress after 3 hours. What is the diagnosis?
  • A. Transient tachypnoea of the newborn (TTN)
  • B. Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS)
  • C. Meconium aspiration syndrome
  • D. Congenital pneumonia
  • E. Pneumothorax
Best answer
A. Transient tachypnoea of the newborn (TTN)
Term infant delivered by LSCS (no labour → lung fluid not resorbed) + tachypnoea within hours, usually self-limiting by 48–72 h = TTN (“wet lung”). RDS is the preterm disease; MAS follows meconium-stained liquor.
2020 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Neonatal Resuscitation (NRP/ILCOR)

The golden questions at birth: term? breathing/crying? good tone? If YES to all → skin-to-skin, routine care. If NO → warm, dry, stimulate → reassess (30 s) → if apnoeic/gasping or HR <100 → positive-pressure ventilation (PPV) at 40–60 breaths/min, monitor heart rate (stethoscope/cord pulse/ECG — the best resuscitation monitor), pulse oximetry pre-ductal (right hand).

Algorithm: PPV → HR <100 after 30 s effective ventilation → ensure airway open (MR SOPA: Mask, Reposition, Suction, Open mouth, Pressure increase, Alternate airway — LMA/ETT) → if HR <60 after 30 s ventilation + chest compressions (3:1 compression:breath, 90 compressions + 30 breaths/min) + 100% O₂ + ETT + IV/IO adrenaline 10–30 microgram/kg (0.1–0.3 mL/kg of 1:10,000) → if HR remains <60 → repeat adrenaline every 3–5 min + consider volume (10 mL/kg 0.9% saline/O-negative blood if blood loss) → if no response ≥20 min: discuss stopping (poor prognosis), involve parents.

Meconium-stained liquor (this exam): vigorous + breathing/crying + good tone → routine care (no suction); NOT breathing or poor tone → open airway, clear secretions under direct vision, then PPV; if PPV ineffective or thick meconium obstructing → intubate and suction the trachea (only if trained/appropriate — not routine intubation of all meconium babies); do NOT routinely suction below the cords of vigorous infants; chest compressions only if HR <60 despite ventilation.

Apgar score (1 & 5 min; again at 10 if low): Appearance (colour), Pulse, Grimace (reflex irritability), Activity (tone), Respiration — 0–2 each. NOT used to guide resuscitation decisions — act on HR/breathing, not the score. Apgar 4 (this exam) = severe depression → immediate resuscitation.

Aftercare: prevent hypothermia (skin-to-skin, warm), monitor glucose, feeding, watch for complications (PPHN, hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy — consider therapeutic hypothermia if ≥36 wks, moderate/severe HIE within 6 h).

Exam pearls
  • First step for apnoeic baby after stimulation fails = PPV (not chest compressions, not O₂ mask).
  • Heart rate is THE monitor. Compressions only after effective ventilation.
  • Meconium + apnoeic/poor = clear airway under direct vision → PPV → intubate only if obstructed/failing.

#10MCQ edited2020-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-4bc627f6
A newborn is delivered with meconium-stained amniotic fluid, is apneic and cannot breathe. What is the next immediate resuscitation step?
  • A. Suctioning (tracheal suction under direct vision)
  • B. Oxygen by mask
  • C. Antibiotics
  • D. Intubation and ventilation
  • E. Chest compressions
Best answer
D. Intubation and ventilation
Meconium-stained, apnoeic/not breathing newborn: immediate airway management — under current NRP/ILCOR, clear the airway and provide positive-pressure ventilation; if apnoeic, PPV via mask first unless airway obstruction; if ineffective, intubate and suction the trachea (meconium aspiration). Of the listed options, establishing a definitive airway + ventilation (D) is the priority step for an apnoeic, non-vigorous infant; chest compressions only if HR remains <60 despite 30 s effective ventilation.
2020 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Nephrotic Syndrome & Proteinuria (Children)

Definition: (1) proteinuria — nephrotic range: urine PCR >200 mg/mmol (spot) or >40 mg/m²/h (24 h) or 3–4+ dipstick; (2) hypoalbuminaemia (<25 g/L typically); (3) oedema (periorbital, genital, dependent, ascites/pleural effusions); ± hyperlipidaemia.

Causes by age (critical age splits):

  • Congenital (<3 months): congenital nephrotic syndrome (Finnish type) — NPHS1 (nephrin) mutation; massive proteinuria from birth; needs albumin infusions + ACE-i + eventually bilateral nephrectomy + transplant. Also Denys–Drash, Pierson syndrome.
  • 1–12 years: MINIMAL CHANGE DISEASE (~90%) — steroid-SENSITIVE; insidious onset oedema over days; normal renal function, complement normal; NO haematuria (if present → biopsy). Diagnosis = clinical — empirical prednisolone 60 mg/m²/d (max 60–80 mg) ×4–6 weeks then taper; 85–90% respond (remission in 2–4 weeks). Biopsy ONLY if: age <1 or >12, steroid resistance (no response by 4–6 wks), haematuria, hypertension, low complement, renal impairment, atypical course.
  • Steroid-resistant/frequent relapsers/adults: FSGS, membranoproliferative GN, membranous nephropathy, IgA, lupus (renal biopsy to differentiate). FSGS commonest in steroid non-responders (and in older children).
  • Secondary: infections (post-strep, hepatitis B/C, HIV), SLE, HSP/IgA, drugs (NSAIDs — membranous), amyloid, malignancy.

Orthostatic (postural) proteinuria — benign; adolescent; proteinuria when upright, absent in first-morning urine; normal renal function/complement; confirm with split urine samples (early AM vs daytime) or first-void UPCR <20 mg/mmol; NO treatment, annual review.

Management of MCD: prednisolone course; relapses (proteinuria return) → re-treat; frequent relapsers → alternate-day low-dose steroids or second-line (levamisole, cyclophosphamide, cyclosporine, mycophenolate/tacrolimus; rituximab); oedema — salt restriction, fluid restriction if severe, loop diuretics (furosemide ± spironolactone) + IV albumin if severe symptomatic hypovolaemia (then furosemide); immunisations (pneumococcal + meningococcal + influenza — infection risk from immunosuppression + loss of complement/immunoglobulins); thrombosis risk (hypercoagulable — sparse activity restriction, avoid dehydration; consider aspirin/warfarin if albumin very low <20 g/L or thrombotic event); lipids — usually normalise with remission.

Investigations at presentation: urine dip/PCR, serum albumin, renal function, lipids, C3/C4, ASO (excludes PSGN), FBC (infection), urine microscopy; exclude secondary causes (ANA, HBV/HCV); biopsy only as above.

Exam pearls
  • Child >1 y + oedema + heavy proteinuria + normal renal function = MCD → steroids — biopsy only if atypical.
  • Proteinuria only when standing = orthostatic — split samples, benign.
  • <3 months onset = congenital (Finnish) — nephrin; very bad; genetic testing.
  • Steroid resistance → biopsy → FSGS.

2020 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Grunting & Work of Breathing in Children

Grunting = premature closure of the glottis during EXHALATION → generates positive end-expiratory pressure (auto-PEEP) → keeps alveoli open, increases functional residual capacity (FRC) and improves gas exchange. It is a sign of significant respiratory distress (like nasal flaring, chest recession, tachypnoea, head-bobbing in infants) — not a “harmless noise”.

Seen in: bronchiolitis (this exam — RSV), neonatal RDS, pneumonia, asthma exacerbation, pulmonary oedema/ARDS, neonatal sepsis.

This exam (two identical questions across 2017/2020): “Grunting → increases end-expiratory pressure” (A) / “Grunting physiology → keeps alveoli open (auto-PEEP)” — answer is the same concept; it increases FRC (does NOT decrease it) and does NOT reduce oxygen demand.

Assessment of work of breathing: rate + recession (subcostal/intercostal/sternal) + nasal flaring + grunting + head-bobbing (infants) + tracheal tug; red flags: apnoea, exhaustion, SpO₂ <90–92% despite O₂, altered consciousness, silent chest, hypoxaemia — immediate senior review/ITU.

Exam pearls
  • Grunting = auto-PEEP, keeps alveoli open.
  • All these signs (nasal flare, recession, grunt, head bob) = get help now.
  • Bronchiolitis: supportive + oxygen — no salbutamol/steroids routinely.

#3MCQ edited2020-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-fcb3bc3c
A patient with bronchiolitis worsened after admission and developed grunting. What is the physiological reason for grunting?
  • A. To increase end-expiratory pressure and keep alveoli open (auto-PEEP)
  • B. To decrease functional residual capacity
  • C. To increase inspiratory time
  • D. To reduce oxygen demand
  • E. To widen the airway diameter
Best answer
A. To increase end-expiratory pressure and keep alveoli open (auto-PEEP)
Grunting = expiration against a partially closed glottis, generating auto-PEEP. This keeps alveoli recruited (↑ FRC and gas exchange) in bronchiolitis/RDS — exactly what infants are trying to achieve physiologically.
2020 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Seizures & Epilepsy

Semiology first — type defines treatment:

TypeFeaturesDrug of choice
Absence (typical)Child 4–10 y; sudden staring/“in a daze”, eyelid flutter, 5–15 s, many per day, no post-ictal confusion; 3 Hz spike-waveEthosuximide (or valproate)
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME)Morning myoclonic jerks of limbs/shoulders + GTC seizures + absence; onset 12–18 y; sleep deprivation/alcohol trigger; 4–6 Hz polyspike-waveSodium valproate (females of childbearing age: levetiracetam/lamotrigine)
Temporal lobe (focal impaired awareness)Aura (epigastric rising / déjà vu / burning smell — “burning leather”), staring, lip-smacking/automatisms (chewing, picking), post-ictal confusionCarbamazepine / lamotrigine / levetiracetam
Generalized tonic-clonicSudden fall, tongue biting, incontinence, post-ictal drowsiness/confusionValproate / levetiracetam
Infantile spasms (West syndrome)3–12 months; salaam attacks — sudden flexion of head/trunk/limbs in clusters; hypsarrhythmia on EEG; developmental regression — treat with vigabatrin ± ACTH; think tuberous sclerosisVigabatrin ± steroids
Febrile seizure6 mo–5 y, fever, generalized, <15 min, single in 24 h = SIMPLE (benign, ~1% later epilepsy); complex: focal / >15 min / recurrence within 24 hReassurance + safety (side position, nothing in mouth); treat fever does NOT prevent recurrence; benzodiazepine if >5 min
Non-epileptic (psychogenic) seizureEyes closed, prolonged fluctuating jerks, pelvic thrusting, crying/emotional context (exam stress), NO incontinence/tongue bite/injury/post-ictal state; normal EEGCBT/psychology — NOT anti-epileptics

Management of acute seizure (this exam): ABCDE + position + O₂ → abortive drug if >5 min: midazolam (buccal/IM/IV) or lorazepam IV or diazepam IV/PR — repeat once → if still seizing (status): second-line levetiracetam / phenytoin / valproate (>15–20 min) → refractory (>40 min): phenobarbital or anaesthesia + ICU. Maintenance after abortion of prolonged convulsion: continue anti-seizure prophylaxis with sodium valproate (or leviteracetam), not single-agent benzodiazepines alone.

Risk factors for epilepsy after febrile convulsion: complex febrile seizure, family history of epilepsy, pre-existing neurodevelopmental delay, short interval from fever onset to seizure (<1 h). Simple febrile = near-population risk.

Exam pearls
  • “Smell burning leather + lip smacking + staring” = temporal lobe epilepsy. “Morning limb jerks” = JME. “Exam-time jerks, eyes closed, crying, no incontinence” = psychogenic.
  • Absence = ethosuximide. Status: midazolam → phenytoin/levetiracetam → phenobarbital.
  • Febrile seizure ≠ epilepsy; complex features are the risk.

2020 · Pediatrics · 1 question · EMQ

Tuberculosis

Pathogenesis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (airborne) → primary Ghon focus → reactivation in apices (high O₂) when cell-mediated immunity falls (HIV, diabetes, steroids, malnutrition) — caseating granulomas (Langhans giant cells).

Forms (by site):

  • Pulmonary — fever, night sweats, weight loss, chronic cough (± haemoptysis), apical infiltrate/cavitation on CXR, homeless/overcrowding/immunosuppressed; miliary — diffuse millet-seed infiltrates.
  • Extrapulmonary — TB lymphadenitis (bilateral cervical nodes, “cold abscesses” with sinus tracts — scrofuloderma — this exam’s homeless man), TB meningitis (basilar, CN VI palsy, very low CSF glucose/very high protein, lymphocytes — treat + dexamethasone), Pott’s disease (spinal TB — gibbus deformity, PPD/MRI), pleural TB (unilateral lymphocytic exudate, high ADA), TB pericarditis/miliary.
  • TB in HIV — atypical CXR, disseminated disease, drug interactions (rifampicin with ART).

Diagnosis: CXR (apical cavities/infiltrates, miliary, effusion, hilar nodes); sputum smear + culture (gold standard) — AFB smear, culture (2–6 wks), GeneXpert MTB/RIF (PCR) — rapid, detects rifampicin resistance — first-line test; tuberculin skin test (Mantoux — latent), IGRA (latent TB; not for active); node biopsy (caseating granuloma + AFB) for TB lymphadenitis; FBC/CRP/ESR; HIV test.

Treatment (RIPE): 2 months HRZE + 4 months HR (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol → then INH + rifampicin ×4 months); isoniazid neuropathy → pyridoxine (vit B6); ethambutol → optic neuritis (check colour vision/acuity); rifampicin → orange fluids + drug interactions; monitor LFTs; drug-resistant TB (MDR — RIF + INH resistant) → specialist regimens (bedaquiline etc.). Latent TB: INH ×6–9 months or rifapentine-INH 3 months.

This exam: gibbus → Pott’s disease (A); sacroiliitis in a child → brucellosis (B). Homeless + cervical node discharge + fever + chronic cough → TB. Active TB CXR (Case 4): upper-lobe/apical infiltrate ± cavitation ± hilar lymphadenopathy; tests: sputum AFB smear/culture (or GeneXpert), tuberculin test/IGRA (but tests = sputum microbiology + imaging/biopsy).

Exam pearls
  • GeneXpert is the rapid first test; culture is gold standard.
  • Gibbus = Pott’s. Cervical “cold abscess” with sinus = scrofuloderma = TB.
  • RIPE × 2 months then RI × 4; B6 with INH; watch liver and eyes (EMB).

2019 · Genetics · 1 question · MCQ

Chromosomal Disorders — Down Syndrome, Turner & Mechanisms

Down syndrome (trisomy 21) — incidence ~1 in 700; risk rises with maternal age (but most affected babies are born to younger mothers).

Mechanisms: (1) nondisjunction in meiosis I (90–95%) — extra chromosome 21; recurrence risk ~1% (or maternal-age related). (2) Unbalanced Robertsonian translocation (4–5%; e.g. 14;21) — if a parent is a balanced carrier, recurrence risk is high (balanced mother → ~10%, balanced father → ~2%). (3) Mosaicism (1–2%) — milder phenotype. Recurrent trisomy 21 in siblings → test PARENTS with karyotype for a balanced translocation (not the child again).

Clinical features: hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, single palmar (simian) crease, sandal-gap toes, flat occiput/brachycephaly, small ears, protruding tongue, Brushfield spots; congenital heart (AVSD, VSD, PDA), duodenal atresia (double bubble), Hirschsprung, hypothyroidism, atlanto-axial instability, haematological malignancy (ALL/AML-M7), early Alzheimer-type dementia; global developmental delay; short stature.

Screening/management: confirm by karyotype (FISH for rapid confirmation if needed). At birth: echo + abdominal USS (duodenal atresia), hearing (OAE) and eye screen, TSH at birth/6 mo/yearly, full blood count; annual thyroid checks; early intervention. Counselling: recurrence risk; discuss prenatal diagnosis (CVS 11–14 wks, amniocentesis ≥15 wks, NIPT).

Trisomy 8 mosaicism — full trisomy 8 is embryonic lethal; surviving “trisomy 8” = mosaic (nondisjunction post-zygotically or trisomy rescue) → milder features (deep plantar creases, skeletal/urogenital).

Turner syndrome (45,X / X-monosomy) — girls: short stature, shield chest + widely spaced nipples, webbed neck, cubitus valgus, lymphedema at birth, streak ovaries → primary amenorrhoea/infertility + hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism, bicuspid aortic valve/coarctation, horseshoe kidney, normal IQ (may have visuospatial deficit), treat with growth hormone + oestrogen HRT; karyotype confirms; Y-material carrying → gonadectomy (gonadoblastoma risk).

Klinefelter (47,XXY) — tall, small firm testes, gynaecomastia, infertility (azoospermia), ↑FSH/LH.

Exam pearls
  • Recurrent Down in siblings → parental karyotype (translocation) — not “bad luck”.
  • Trisomy 8 survival = mosaicism.
  • Turner = coarctation + webbed neck + no puberty; confirm karyotype.
  • Down = AVSD + double-bubble + brushfield + simian crease.

#149MCQ edited2019-Genetics-MCQ-Medicine-2ae391a9
A person with trisomy 8 survived. Why?
  • A. Mosaicism
  • B. Translocation
  • C. Deletion
  • D. Nondisjunction in meiosis
  • E. Uniparental disomy
Best answer
A. Mosaicism
Full trisomy 8 is incompatible with life — survivors carry mosaic trisomy 8 (nondisjunction post-zygotically) mixing normal and trisomic lines, attenuating the phenotype (Warkany syndrome 2; deep palmar/plantar furrows, skeletal/urogenital anomalies).
2019 · Genetics · 3 questions · MCQ

Inborn Errors of Metabolism

Classification (functional groups):

  1. Small-molecule intoxication syndromes — acute/recurrent encephalopathy, vomiting, acidosis after triggers (illness/fasting/protein load): amino acid disorders (PKU, MSUD, tyrosinaemia, homocystinuria), organic acidurias (propionic, methylmalonic, isovaleric — sweaty-feet odour), urea cycle defects (hyperammonaemia + respiratory alkalosis, NO acidosis — ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, X-linked).
  2. Energy-deficiency syndromes — hypoketotic hypoglycaemia during fasting: fatty-acid oxidation defects (medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase — MCAD; hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, encephalopathy), glycogen storage diseases (GSD I/von Gierke — fasting hypoglycaemia + lactic acidosis + hepatomegaly + hyperuricaemia; GSD V/McArdle — exercise cramps), mitochondrial disorders.
  3. Large-molecule (storage) disorders — progressive, static deficits, coarse features, organomegaly: lysosomal storage (Gaucher, Niemann-Pick, Tay-Sachs, mucopolysaccharidoses — Hurler/Hunter, Pompe/GSD II), peroxisomal (Zellweger).

Classic presentations (this exam’s EMQ):

  • Phenylketonuria (PKU) — normal at birth → developmental delay, seizures, eczema, fair hair/skin (↓tyrosine→↓melanin), “musty/mousy” odour; ↑phenylalanine on newborn screen (Guthrie test); treat low-Phe diet + sapropterin.
  • Galactosaemia — well at birth → days after milk feeds: poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, cataracts, E. coli sepsis, hypoglycaemia; GALT enzyme/1-phosphate-uridylyltransferase; treat lactose-free diet.
  • MSUD — 4–7 days: poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, maple-syrup urine odour, ↑BCAAs/ketoacids; treat BCAA-free diet.
  • Von Gierke (GSD I) — 3–4 months: fasting hypoglycaemia + lactic acidosis + hyperuricaemia + hepatomegaly; improves with frequent carbs.
  • Urea cycle defect — neonatal: hyperammonaemia (encephalopathy, seizures, coma) + respiratory alkalosis WITHOUT acidosis or hypoglycaemia.

Diagnosis: newborn screening (Guthrie/tandem mass spec), plasma amino acids, acylcarnitine profile, urine organic acids, ammonia, glucose, lactate, pH/anion gap, urinary ketones (absent in FAO defects), enzyme assays, genetic testing. Family history/consanguinity (first cousins — most are autosomal recessive).

Exam pearls
  • Healthy newborn → days later encephalopathy/vomiting/coma after feeds = IEM until proven otherwise (ammonia + VBG + glucose NOW).
  • Hyperammonaemia + alkalosis = urea cycle; acidosis + ketones/anion gap = organic aciduria; hypoketotic hypoglycaemia = FAO defect.
  • Musty urine + fair skin + eczema + ID = PKU.
  • Consanguinity + regression = storage disease — enzyme assay.

#104MCQ edited2019-Genetics-MCQ-Medicine-4cf81ed6
A case of inborn error of metabolism asks about the type. What type is it?
  • A. Lysosomal storage disorder
  • B. Fatty acid oxidation defect
  • C. Large molecule disorder
  • D. Amino acid metabolism defect
  • E. Organic acidemia
Best answer
D. Amino acid metabolism defect
The exemplar case in this set is an aminoacidopathy (e.g., PKU/MSUD-type — developmental delay ± seizures ± odd smell/urine after feeding). Amino-acid defects (PKU, MSUD, homocystinuria, tyrosinaemia) present with encephalopathy/developmental delay, often with normal glucose and NO acidosis.
#105MCQ edited2019-Genetics-MCQ-Medicine-a6cccbf4
What is the best indicator of an inborn error of metabolism?
  • A. Abnormal body smell
  • B. Metabolic acidosis with anion gap
  • C. Hypoglycemia
  • D. Hyperammonemia
  • E. Failure to thrive

B. Metabolic acidosis with anion gap
The signature lab clue to an inborn error (esp. organic acidurias/urea cycle/FAO) is high anion gap metabolic acidosis (± hyperammonaemia). Hypoglycaemia/FTT/smell are supportive but absent in many.
#106MCQ edited2019-Genetics-MCQ-Medicine-48065247
A child presents with encephalopathy. What is the likely mechanism?
  • A. Energy deficiency (e.g. hypoglycemia)
  • B. Lysosomal storage disease
  • C. Small molecule intoxication
  • D. Structural brain lesion
  • E. Mitochondrial cytopathy
Best answer
C. Small molecule intoxication
Encephalopathy from an IEM is typically from accumulation of toxic small molecules (organic acids, ammonia, leucine metabolites) overwhelming the brain — vs energy deficiency (FAO/glycogen) which usually also gives hypoglycaemia, or storage diseases which are slowly progressive.
2019 · Genetics · 1 question · MCQ

Mutation Types & Disease Mechanisms

Mutation (DNA-level) types:

TypeDefinitionExamples
MissenseSingle base change → different amino acidSickle cell (β6 Glu→Val); Arg185Leu (this exam); achondroplasia FGFR3 Gly380Arg; collagen in Marfan
Nonsense→ premature stop codonDuchenne (frame/stop); β-thalassaemia some; APC (FAP)
Silent→ same amino acid (wobble)Synonymous SNP (marker only)
FrameshiftInsertion/deletion NOT multiple of 3 → reading frame shiftsDuchenne (deletions), most severe CFTR loss-of-function
Trinucleotide repeat expansionRepeat grows beyond threshold (anticipation)Fragile X (CGG), Huntington’s (CAG), myotonic dystrophy (CTG), Friedreich’s (GAA)
Splice-siteDisrupts donor/acceptor sitesSome β-thalassaemia; Marfan some
Deletion (large)kb–Mb lossDiGeorge (22q11), Williams (7q11), Prader-Willi (15q), SMA (SMN1 exon 7)
DuplicationCopy gainCMT1A (PMP22 duplication), 17p11.2 duplication
Robertsonian translocationFusion at centromeres of acrocentrics (13,14,15,21,22)Down syndrome (14;21) — balanced parent
NondisjunctionChromosomes fail to separate in meiosisTrisomy 21/18/13; 45,X; 47,XXY; trisomy 8 (mosaic survival)
InversionSegment flips within chromosomeInv(9) benign; Inv(8)(p23q22)

From mutation to disease — mechanism levels: (1) Loss of function (null/hypomorphic) — enzyme deficiencies (PKU, lysosomal); (2) Gain of function — Huntington toxic protein; achondroplasia FGFR3 (constitutive activation); (3) Dominant-negative — Marfan (fibrillin multimers poisoned), collagen III (vascular EDS); (4) Haploinsufficiency — one normal copy insufficient (FBN1, SHOX in Turner); (5) Toxic metabolite accumulation — urea cycle, organic acidurias; (6) protein aggregation/misfolding — α1-antitrypsin Z; prions; (7) Nonsense-mediated decay; (8) Repeat expansion → methylation silencing — fragile X.

Exam pearls
  • Glu→Val = missense; stop codon = nonsense; shifts frame = frameshift.
  • Anticipation + maternal transmission = CGG repeat (fragile X).
  • Single amino-acid swap (Arg→Leu) = missense — always.

#108MCQ2019-Genetics-MCQ-Medicine-4a25725c
Arg185Leu — what is the type of mutation?
  • A. Missense
  • B. Frameshift
  • C. Translocation
  • D. Nonsense
  • E. Silent
Best answer
A. Missense
Arg185Leu = single amino-acid substitution (Arg→Leu at residue 185) caused by a single nucleotide change → missense (nonsynonymous). Frameshift = indel not divisible by 3; nonsense = premature stop (e.g. Arg→Ter); silent = same amino acid; translocation = chromosomal rearrangement.
2019 · Genetics · 1 question · MCQ

Neurocutaneous Syndromes (Phakomatoses)

Neurofibromatosis type 1 (von Recklinghausen): café-au-lait macules (≥6, >5 mm prepubertal/>15 mm post), axillary/inguinal freckling (Crowe sign), neurofibromas (cutaneous + plexiform — malignant transformation risk), Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), optic glioma, sphenoid dysplasia, learning difficulties, ↑phaeochromocytoma and juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia; autosomal dominant NF1 (17q11).

Neurofibromatosis type 2: bilateral vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuroma) → hearing loss, tinnitus, balance problems in young adulthood; meningiomas, ependymomas, juvenile posterior subcapsular cataracts; AD NF2 (22q12).

Tuberous sclerosis (TSC): renal angiomyolipomas (this exam: multiple benign tumours incl. renal/hepatic angiomyolipomas), cortical tubers/“ash-leaf” hypomelanotic macules, facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum — butterfly distribution), shagreen patch (lumbosacral, orange-peel), periungual fibromas (Koenen tumours), epilepsy (infantile spasms/West syndrome), intellectual disability, cardiac rhabdomyomas (prenatal/infancy), renal cysts/angiomyolipomas (haemorrhage risk); TSC1 (hamartin, 9q34) / TSC2 (tuberin, 16p13); AD. Management: MRI/EEG/skin/renal surveillance; vigabatrin for spasms; sirolimus for angiomyolipomas; specialist MDT.

Sturge–Weber syndrome: port-wine stain in ophthalmic trigeminal (V1) distribution + leptomeningeal angiomatosis + seizures (often refractory), contralateral hemiparesis, cortical calcification (“tram-track”), glaucoma (same side), developmental delay; sporadic (not inherited).

von Hippel–Lindau (VHL): retinal/cerebellar haemangioblastomas, clear-cell renal carcinoma, renal/pancreatic cysts, pheochromocytoma, epididymal cystadenomas; AD VHL (3p25); surveillance MRI/eyes/abdominal US; DNA testing.

Peutz–Jeghers: mucocutaneous hyperpigmented macules (lips/buccal) + hamartomatous GI polyps → intussusception risk, ↑colorectal/breast/pancreatic cancers; AD STK11.

Klippel–Trénaunay / Proteus — segmental overgrowth syndromes (rare).

Exam pearls
  • ≥6 café-au-lait + axillary freckling = NF1. Bilateral acoustic neuroma = NF2.
  • Ash-leaf spots + facial angiofibroma + angiomyolipomas + tubers = TSC.
  • V1 port-wine stain = Sturge–Weber → glaucoma + seizures surveillance.
  • Retinal/cerebellar haemangioblastoma + renal cancer = VHL.

#145MCQ edited2019-Genetics-MCQ-Medicine-830ecda3
A patient has an angiolipoma in the liver and pigmented skin lesions. What is the most likely diagnosis?
  • A. Neurofibromatosis
  • B. Tuberous sclerosis
  • C. von Hippel-Lindau disease
  • D. Sturge-Weber syndrome
  • E. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome
Best answer
B. Tuberous sclerosis
Multiple benign tumours everywhere: renal/hepatic angiomyolipomas, ash-leaf macules, shagreen patches, facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum), periungual fibromas, cortical tubers → seizures/ID = tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2). vHL = haemangioblastomas (retina/cerebellum) + renal cell carcinoma + phaeochromocytoma.
2019 · Genetics · 2 questions · MCQ

Patterns of Inheritance & Risk Calculation

Pedigree logic — the six patterns:

PatternHallmarksExamplesRisk to offspring
Autosomal dominantEvery generation; male-to-male; ~50% of children of affected parent; both sexesMarfan, HOCM, Huntington’s, neurofibromatosis, familial hypercholesterolaemia, achondroplasia50%
Autosomal recessiveSiblings only (one generation); consanguinity raises risk; 25% recurrence; silent carriers (2/3 of unaffected siblings are carriers)Cystic fibrosis, sickle cell, thalassaemia, PKU, congenital adrenal hyperplasia25% if both parents carriers
X-linked recessiveMales affected; female carriers usually unaffected (some manifesting); NO male-to-male; 50% sons of carrier mother affected; 50% daughters carriers; affected father → ALL daughters carriers, no sons affectedDMD, haemophilia A/B, G6PD, fragile X (X-linked with anticipation — CGG)Sons of carrier mother: 50%; daughters: 50% carriers (rarely symptomatic)
X-linked dominantBoth sexes; affected fathers → ALL daughters affected, no sons; 50% children of affected motherVitamin D–resistant rickets (XLH), Rett syndrome (female), Fragile X sometimes classified separately50%
MitochondrialMother → ALL children (both sexes) can inherit; father → NONE; highly variable (heteroplasmy); high energy tissues affected (MELAS, MERRF, LHON)MELAS, MERRF, Leber optic neuropathy, Kearns–SayreAll children of affected mother at risk (variable expression)
Y-linked (holandric)Only males; father → ALL sonsHairy ears (debated), some infertility (AZF deletions)100% of sons

Worked answers (this exam):

  • DMD in boy + 2 maternal uncles affected → mother obligate carrier → his sister: 50% carrier, 0% symptomatic.
  • HOCM: father, brother, paternal uncle — male-to-male = autosomal dominant.
  • Mitochondrial → maternal inheritance (all children of affected mother).
  • Marfan (father died suddenly, tall + pectus) = autosomal dominant.
  • DMD in family → daughter of affected? No — daughter of a carrier: 50% chance carrier; her sons: 50% affected. “Chance the daughters’ sons will be affected” = 50%.
Exam pearls
  • Father→son transmission = autosomal dominant (never X-linked).
  • Consanguinity = recessive; only one generation = recessive.
  • Mitochondrial = mothers transmit to all children; fathers transmit none.
  • DMD: sisters of affected boys — 50% carriers, ~0% symptomatic.

#143MCQ edited2019-Genetics-MCQ-Medicine-240c604a
A boy has Duchenne muscular dystrophy and his 2 maternal uncles also have Duchenne. What is the chance that his sister is symptomatic?
  • A. 0%
  • B. 25%
  • C. 50%
  • D. 75%
  • E. 100%
Best answer
A. 0%
DMD = X-linked. Sister of an affected boy: mother is an obligate carrier → sister has 50% chance of being a carrier, but symptomatic disease in females is rare (manifesting carriers ~10%, usually mild). Classic exam answer: 0% chance of being symptomatic (carrier yes, 50%).
#144MCQ edited2019-Genetics-MCQ-Medicine-2775dce8
A male patient has hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM). His father, his brother and his paternal uncle have it as well. What is the mode of inheritance?
  • A. Autosomal dominant
  • B. Autosomal recessive
  • C. X-linked dominant
  • D. X-linked recessive
  • E. Mitochondrial
Best answer
A. Autosomal dominant
HOCM: father → son and brother affected, male-to-male transmission = autosomal dominant (sarcomere proteins: β-myosin heavy chain, myosin-binding protein C). Not X-linked (father-to-son never passes X-linked), not mitochondrial (maternal only).
2019 · Genetics · 1 question · MCQ

Skeletal Dysplasias — Achondroplasia

Achondroplasia — commonest skeletal dysplasia (1/15,000 births); FGFR3 gain-of-function mutation (p.Gly380Arg, 4p16.3) — autosomal dominant — 80% DE NOVO (no family history; advancing paternal age is a risk factor).

Features: disproportionate (rhizomelic) short stature — short proximal limbs (humerus/femur) with relatively preserved trunk; large head with frontal bossing + midface hypoplasia (“coarse face”/small nose bridge), trident hands, genu varum, lumbar lordosis, thoracolumbar kyphosis, normal intelligence, normal sexual development and lifespan (mildly reduced related to cervicomedullary compression in infancy).

THIS exam: short stature + short extremities + coarse facies → confirmatory test = FGFR3 gene mutation analysis (C) — NOT karyotype (normal), NOT methylation test (that’s Prader–Willi/Angelman), NOT skeletal survey (supportive, shows “bullet” vertebrae/short pedicles/narrow interpedicular distance), NOT GH test (not GH-deficient — the receptor, not the hormone, is abnormal → GH is NOT the treatment; vosoritide — CNP analogue — is the new targeted drug).

Other skeletal dysplasias: hypochondroplasia (milder — p.Asn540Lys), thanatophoric dysplasia (lethal), osteogenesis imperfecta (COL1A1/2 — blue sclera, fractures, wormian bones, dentinogenesis imperfecta), mucopolysaccaridoses (Hurler — corneal clouding; Hunter — clear-eyed, X-linked), osteopetrosis (“marble bone” — dense, brittle).

Exam pearls
  • Disproportionate rhizomelic short limbs + big head/frontal bossing = achondroplasia → FGFR3.
  • AD, usually de novo; normal IQ; cervicomedullary monitoring in infancy.
  • Not a growth-hormone problem — GH ineffective; vosoritide is the new therapy.

A child with short stature, short extremities and a coarse face is diagnosed with achondroplasia. What is the confirmatory test?
  • A. Karyotyping
  • B. Methylation test
  • C. FGFR3 gene mutation analysis
  • D. Skeletal survey

Best answer
C. FGFR3 gene mutation analysis
Achondroplasia = activating mutation FGFR3 (4p16.3; p.Gly380Arg), autosomal dominant (80% de novo). Confirm with FGFR3 analysis. Skeletal survey shows features but isn’t “confirmatory”; methylation test is for imprinting disorders.
2019 · Genetics · 2 questions · MCQ

Treatment of Genetic Disorders — Levels of Intervention

The 2019/2017 exam questions test ONE concept — is this treatment acting at the level of the DNA/gene, the protein, or the phenotype/cell/organ?

LevelExamples
Gene/DNA levelCorrecting the mutation — gene therapy (viral vector with normal gene), CRISPR genome editing, spliced-oligo antisense (exon skipping — eteplirsen for DMD), transplantation IS NOT gene therapy per se but delivers normal cells
RNA levelmRNA therapy, antisense oligonucleotides, RNA interference (inclisiran for familial hypercholesterolaemia)
Protein level (this exam — TWICE)Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) — Pompe disease: recombinant acid α-glucosidase; ERT in Gaucher/Fabry/MPS; factor VIII/IX for haemophilia; insulin; growth hormone
Cellular level (this exam — TWICE)Stem cell (haematopoietic) transplantation — curative for SCID/thalassaemia major (matched sibling); bone-marrow transplant for lysosomal some; organ transplantation (liver for α1-antitrypsin)
Phenotype/organ levelSymptomatic: diet (low-Phe for PKU; galactose-free), drugs acting on pathways (sodium phenylbutyrate for urea cycle), surgery (appendicular... — e.g., coarctation repair), physiotherapy, chelation (iron overload in thalassaemia)

Worked answers: “Disease cured by giving a stem cell” → cellular level (D); “Pompe treated with ERT” → protein level (A/D depending on option letter in each year).

Family/familial level (prenatal): genetic counselling, PND (CVS/amniocentesis), NIPT, preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD for IVF — avoids transmission of cystic fibrosis etc.).

Exam pearls
  • ERT replaces the missing PROTEIN — answer “protein level”.
  • Stem cell transplant = cellular level (replaces the cell factory).
  • Gene therapy/CRISPR = gene/DNA level.

#107MCQ edited2019-Genetics-MCQ-Medicine-ebced6f8
A disease can be cured by giving a stem cell. At what level is this intervention?
  • A. Gene level
  • B. Phenotype level
  • C. Familial level
  • D. Protein level
  • E. Cellular level
Best answer
E. Cellular level
Levels of genetic intervention: gene (gene therapy/CRISPR), protein (enzyme replacement, e.g. Pompe), cellular (**stem-cell transplant**, e.g. HSCT in Hurler, CGD, SCID), organ (transplant), phenotype (symptomatic — diet, drugs). Stem-cell transplant corrects the cellular machinery → CELLULAR level.
#166MCQ edited2019-Genetics-MCQ-Medicine-c8c548ec
Pompe disease is treated with enzyme replacement therapy. At what level does this treatment act?
  • A. Protein level
  • B. DNA level
  • C. RNA level
  • D. Symptomatic level
  • E. Cellular level
Best answer
A. Protein level
Enzyme replacement therapy (alglucosidase-α in Pompe disease, alglucerase in Gaucher) bypasses the block by supplying the protein/enzyme product — Protein level. Gene therapy = DNA/RNA level; transplant = cellular; diet/surgery = symptomatic/organ level.
Internal Medicine
2019 · Internal Medicine · 4 questions · MCQ

Acid–Base Disorders

Every ABG question in this exam is solved the same way — do it mechanically, never by pattern-guessing:

  1. Look at pH. <7.35 = acidaemia, >7.45 = alkalaemia (7.35–7.45 can still hide a mixed disorder).
  2. Look at pCO₂ and HCO₃⁻. Whichever moves in the same direction as the pH is the primary process: pCO₂↑ → respiratory acidosis; HCO₃⁻↓ → metabolic acidosis; pCO₂↓ → respiratory alkalosis; HCO₃⁻↑ → metabolic alkalosis.
  3. Check compensation. Acute respiratory acidosis: HCO₃⁻ rises 1 per 10 mmHg pCO₂; chronic: rises 3.5–4 per 10 (max ~31). Metabolic acidosis: expected pCO₂ = (1.5 × HCO₃⁻) + 8 ± 2 (Winter’s formula). If compensation is not as expected → mixed disorder.
  4. Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO₃); normal 8–12 (without K). High gap → MUDPILES (methanol, uraemia, DKA, propylene glycol/paraldehyde, iron/isoniazid, lactic acidosis, ethylene glycol, salicylates). Normal gap (hyperchloraemic) → diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis, Addison’s, saline.
DisorderpHpCO₂HCO₃⁻Classic causes
Respiratory acidosis↓↑↑ (comp.)Opioids/sedatives, COPD, severe asthma, neuromuscular weakness, CNS depression
Respiratory alkalosis↑↓↓ (comp.)Pain, anxiety, early sepsis, salicylates (early), pregnancy, PE, hypoxia at altitude
Metabolic acidosis↓↓ (comp.)↓DKA/HHS, lactic acidosis (shock, metformin), diarrhoea, RTA, uraemia, toxins
Metabolic alkalosis↑↑ (comp.)↑Vomiting, NG suction, diuretics, Conn’s/Cushing’s, hypokalaemia, bicarbonate load

High CO₂ + low HCO₃⁻ + low pH (COPD patient) = mixed respiratory + metabolic acidosis — the low bicarbonate cannot be explained by compensation for a respiratory acidosis, so two primary processes are present. The same logic applies to the unconscious patient with an empty syringe and high lactate (respiratory depressant + lactic acidosis).

Exam pearls
  • Opioid/benzodiazepine overdose → acute respiratory acidosis (high pCO₂, normal/near-normal HCO₃⁻); ↓ respiratory rate (RR 6–8/min), pinpoint pupils.
  • Salicylates → mixed respiratory alkalosis + metabolic acidosis.
  • COPD chronic retainers live with high pCO₂ and high HCO₃⁻; give cautious O₂ (target 88–92%).
  • Lactate >2 = tissue hypoperfusion; treat the cause, not the number.
  • Toxic alcohols/methanol → high anion gap acidosis + high osmolar gap.
Traps
  • Normal pH does NOT mean normal ABG — mixed disorders can cancel out (e.g. mixed acidosis can sit near 7.35–7.40). Always compute the gap and check compensation.
  • "Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation" requires pCO₂ LOW; "respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation" requires HCO₃⁻ HIGH. High CO₂ + low HCO₃⁻ is always a mixed disorder.
  • Do not "treat" compensation — treat the primary process.
Questions covered in this review
#59MCQ2019-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-3a7b4e04
A COPD patient has high CO2, low HCO3- and low pH. What kind of acid-base imbalance does he have?
  • A. Respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
  • B. Metabolic alkalosis
  • C. Mixed acidosis
  • D. Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
  • E. Respiratory alkalosis
Best answer
C. Mixed acidosis
COPD + high CO₂ (respiratory acidosis) + LOW HCO₃⁻ (metabolic acidosis) + low pH: the low bicarbonate is far below what compensation allows → mixed respiratory + metabolic acidosis. Look for sepsis/renal failure/diarrhoea/lactic acidosis as the second hit.
#78MCQ edited2019-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-85b306cd
A patient was found on the street with an empty syringe. ABG: low pH 6.4, high CO2 55, low HCO3 11, lactate high. Which of the following is the correct diagnosis?
  • A. Respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
  • B. A respiratory acidosis
  • C. Mixed acidosis
  • D. Metabolic acidosis
  • E. Respiratory alkalosis with metabolic acidosis
Best answer
C. Mixed acidosis
pH 6.4 + pCO₂ 55 (high) + HCO₃⁻ 11 (very low) + lactate high: both high pCO₂ and low HCO₃⁻ = mixed respiratory + metabolic (high lactate) acidosis. Respiratory acidosis alone would have a higher HCO₃⁻; metabolic alone would have pCO₂ <40 (Winter’s formula ~24).
#116MCQ edited2019-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-f7e9665d
Another pH vignette — interpret the acid-base disorder.
  • A. Respiratory acidosis
  • B. Metabolic acidosis
  • C. Respiratory alkalosis
  • D. Metabolic alkalosis
  • E. Mixed disorder
Best answer
E. Mixed disorder
The stem as transcribed lacks the ABG numbers; in this question family the pattern is high pCO₂ (respiratory acidosis) with low/inappropriately-low HCO₃⁻ (metabolic component) → mixed acidosis. Use the 2-step rule every time: pH → pCO₂/HCO₃ direction → check compensation (Winter’s / 1+4) — anything outside compensation = mixed.
#163MCQ edited2019-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-bea0052a
A patient with no past medical history is found with an empty syringe and needle, with respiratory acidosis. What is the diagnosis?
  • A. Acute respiratory acidosis (opioid overdose)
  • B. Metabolic acidosis
  • C. Mixed acidosis
  • D. Respiratory alkalosis
  • E. Metabolic alkalosis
Best answer
A. Acute respiratory acidosis (opioid overdose)
Unwitnessed collapse + syringe + respiratory acidosis = acute opioid-induced respiratory depression (high CO₂, low pH, normal/high HCO₃). Give naloxone + supportive ventilation. (Mixed only if HCO₃ also disproportionately low — check the full panel.)
2019 · Internal Medicine · 2 questions · MCQ/SAQ

Acute Coronary Syndrome (STEMI / NSTEMI / Unstable Angina)

Definition spectrum of ACS — all from coronary plaque rupture/erosion with superimposed thrombosis:

Unstable anginaNSTEMISTEMI
Chest painAt rest / crescendoAt restSevere, prolonged >20–30 min
TroponinNormalElevatedElevated
ECGNormal / ST depression / T inversionST depression, T inversion, or normalST elevation ≥1 mm in ≥2 contiguous leads (or new LBBB)
ManagementAspirin + P2Y12 (clopidogrel/ticagrelor) + anticoagulant (heparin/enoxaparin) + high-risk features → early invasive angiography (≤24 h)Immediate reperfusion: primary PCI within 90–120 min of first medical contact, else fibrinolysis if PCI unavailable <120 min and pain <12 h (and no contraindications)

ECG localisation — memorise this cold:

  • Inferior (II, III, aVF) → RCA (80–90%, supplies RV + inferior wall); reciprocal ST depression in I, aVL. Think posterior MI if ST depression V1–V3 (check V7–V9), and right ventricular infarct (RV4R ST elevation) — avoid nitrates/preload reduction.
  • Anterior / anteroseptal (V1–V4) → LAD.
  • Lateral (I, aVL, V5–V6) → circumflex (LCx) / diagonal.
  • Extensive anterior (I, aVL, V1–V6) → proximal LAD; watch for pump failure.

Post-operative / post-PCI patients: chest pain with ECG changes after surgery — get a troponin (and repeat 3–6 h); troponin rise defines perioperative MI (usually Type 2 if supply–demand). After PCI + stenting, secondary prevention = DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel ~12 months) + high-intensity statin + ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker. Post-PCI with renal impairment: ACE inhibitors/ARBs both ↓GFR initially — monitor K⁺/Cr; the examinable "add-on" when ACEI/BB already in place and renal function is borderline is an ARB substitute or long-acting nitrate for angina.

NSTEMI management: dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin 300 mg loading then 75 mg + clopidogrel/ticagrelor), anticoagulation (LMWH/fondaparinux), beta-blocker if no heart failure, high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80), ACEi, risk-stratify (GRACE) → early coronary angiography if troponin-positive or ST changes.

Exam pearls
  • Pain + ST elevation + prior normal ECG = STEMI → activate cath lab, do not wait for troponin.
  • New LBBB + chest pain = treat as STEMI equivalent.
  • Inferior STEMI → check RV leads; give fluids if hypotensive, avoid nitrates/diuretics.
  • Troponin is the gatekeeper between unstable angina and NSTEMI — it changes management.
  • Post-MI discharge drugs: aspirin + P2Y12, statin, ACEi, beta-blocker ("ABAS").
  • Exertional chest pain with normal ECG → risk-stratify first (troponin if acute; stress test if stable).
Traps
  • ST depression in V1–V3 can be a posterior STEMI — upright tall R waves; don’t call it ischaemia only.
  • Do not give nitrates/ACEi to a hypotensive inferior/RV infarct.
  • "Troponin normal, pain settled, ECG flat" ≠ discharge without work-up — serial troponins and risk stratification.

#114MCQ edited2019-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-631ceed1
A patient has ST elevation, shortness of breath and angina symptoms. Previous ECGs showed no ST changes. What is the diagnosis?
  • A. Stable angina
  • B. Unstable angina
  • C. STEMI
  • D. NSTEMI
  • E. Pericarditis
Best answer
C. STEMI
New ST elevation in contiguous leads + symptoms + no prior ST changes = STEMI → emergent reperfusion (primary PCI). NSTEMI = ST depression/T-inversion + troponin↑ without STE; stable angina = exertional, relieved by rest/GTN.
#186SAQ edited2019-InternalMedicine-SAQ-Medicine-639036aa
A patient presents with central chest pain. ECG shows ST-segment elevation in all inferior leads with reciprocal ST-segment depression in the lateral leads.
  1. Mention the ECG findings. (1 pt)
  2. Which artery is involved? (1 pt)
Best answer
1) ST-segment ELEVATION in inferior leads II, III and aVF, with RECIPROCAL ST depression in lateral leads I and aVL (± right-ventricular ST elevation in V4R; posterior involvement may give ST depression V1–V3). 2) Culprit artery: RIGHT CORONARY ARTERY (RCA) — ostial/proximal occlusion before the RV marginal branch also gives RV infarct; check right-sided leads V4R and echo for inferior wall motion.
Inferior STEMI = RCA occlusion in ~80%; LCx (left-dominant) in the rest. Give antiplatelet/anticoagulation, reperfuse emergently (primary PCI), give fluids if hypotensive with clear lungs (RV infarct), AVOID nitrates/diuretics/ACEi in RV infarct.
2019 · Internal Medicine · 5 questions · MCQ

Acute Kidney Injury — Pre-renal, Intrinsic (ATN), Post-renal

Definition (KDIGO): Creatinine ↑ ≥26.5 µmol/L within 48 h, or ≥1.5× baseline within 7 days, or UO <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h. Stage by creatinine rise / urine output.

Pre-renalIntrinsic — ATNPost-renal
Mechanism↓ renal perfusion (dehydration, sepsis, heart failure, ACEi/ARB + NSAIDs, renal artery)Ischaemic or nephrotoxic tubular damage (aminoglycosides, cisplatin, contrast, pigment, sepsis)Obstruction below collecting system (BPH, stones, tumour, blocked catheter)
FeNa<1%>2%Variable
Urine Na<20 mmol/L>40 mmol/LVariable
Urine microscopyBland / hyaline castsMuddy brown granular casts, renal tubular epithelial cellsBland; may see haematuria
Serum urea:Cr>20:1<10–15:1Variable
Urine osmolality>500<350Variable

Nephrotoxins to know: gentamicin/aminoglycosides → ATN (also causes hypomagnesaemia); cisplatin & carboplatin → ATN; amphotericin B → ATN + distal RTA/K⁺/Mg²⁺ wasting; ACE inhibitors/ARBs → functional (pre-renal) rise in Cr via efferent dilation, especially with bilateral renal artery stenosis; penicillins/cephalosporins/PPIs/NSAIDs → acute interstitial nephritis (fever, rash, eosinophilia, WBC casts); contrast → contrast-induced nephropathy (48–72 h); methotrexate/ethylene glycol.

Tumor lysis syndrome (leukaemia/lymphoma post-chemo): hyperkalaemia + hyperphosphataemia + hyperuricaemia + hypocalcaemia → AKI; prevent with allopurinol/rasburicase + IV fluids; life-threatening K⁺ → treat immediately.

Rhabdomyolysis (marathon, crush, statins): dark urine, myalgia, ↑↑ CK, hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia (early) → myoglobinuric ATN. Best test: serum CK (± urine myoglobin).

Obstructive (post-renal) clues: distended bladder, frequency/hesitancy/BPH, recent ACEi dose increase unmasking bilateral obstruction — small rise in creatinine with normal kidney size + palpable bladder → urethral catheter + ultrasound.

Management ATN: stop nephrotoxins, restore volume/perfusion, treat hyperkalaemia (calcium gluconate, insulin/dextrose, salbutamol, bicarbonate, K-binders, dialysis), treat acidosis & fluid overload. Indications for emergency dialysis (AEIOU): Acidosis refractory, Electrolyte (K⁺ >6.5 or symptomatic), Ingestions (toxins), Overload (pulmonary oedema refractory to diuretics), Uraemia (encephalopathy, pericarditis, seizures).

Exam pearls
  • FeNa <1% + history of poor intake/heart failure → pre-renal. FeNa >2% + muddy brown casts → ATN.
  • WBC casts → pyelonephritis/interstitial nephritis; RBC casts → glomerulonephritis; muddy brown granular casts → ATN.
  • Aminoglycosides: monitor levels; hypomagnesaemia + rising Cr = tubular toxicity — stop the drug.
  • Post-chemo leukaemia patient with high K, high PO₄, low Ca → tumour lysis → rasburicase + fluids.
  • After CABG/surgery → think ischaemic/pigment ATN ± cardiorenal.
Traps
  • In contrast nephropathy and rhabdomyolysis, FeNa can be <1% early — don’t exclude ATN solely on FeNa.
  • Creatinine can lag — the earliest sign of AKI is often rising K⁺ and oliguria.
  • Never give ACEi in bilateral renal artery stenosis — creatinine rises sharply.
