#64MCQ2019-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-45f4bfe4
A marathon runner develops marked myalgia and notices darkening of his urine by the end of the day. Which is the best investigation to identify the cause of his AKI?
  • A. Fractional excretion of sodium
  • B. Creatine kinase (CK)
  • C. Urine myoglobin
  • D. Serum creatinine
  • E. 24-hour urine output
Best answer
B. Creatine kinase (CK)
Marathon + myalgia + dark urine → rhabdomyolysis → CK (usually >5× ULN, often >5000) is the best single test; also urine dipstick blood positive with no RBCs on microscopy (myoglobinuria) + K⁺/PO₄/uric acid rise.
#66MCQ2019-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-1c25a75a
A patient has been treated for leukemia. His chemotherapy includes cisplatin. Recent lab tests show high creatinine, indicating AKI. What is the likely cause of AKI?
  • A. Interstitial nephritis
  • B. Glomerulonephritis
  • C. Renal tubular necrosis (ATN)
  • D. Pre-renal AKI
  • E. Post-renal AKI
Best answer
C. Renal tubular necrosis (ATN)
Cisplatin is directly tubular-toxic → acute tubular necrosis. (The closely-related 2019 stem below with “high urine electrolytes after leukaemia treatment” is the same mechanism; classically FeNa>2% and muddy brown casts.) Hydrate aggressively and monitor Cr/K/Mg with cisplatin.
#79MCQ edited2019-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-18174dc6
A patient with leukemia was on treatment. Labs show high urine electrolytes and high creatinine, indicating AKI. What is the cause?
  • A. Interstitial nephritis
  • B. Glomerulonephritis
  • C. Renal tubular necrosis (ATN)
  • D. Pre-renal AKI
  • E. Post-renal AKI
Best answer
C. Renal tubular necrosis (ATN)
Leukaemia + treatment + high urine electrolytes + AKI → intrinsic tubular injury (ATN, e.g. cisplatin/tumour lysis). Pre-renal would show FeNa<1% and concentrated urine; post-renal needs obstruction.
#132MCQ edited2019-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-d1d83cfb
A patient taking gentamicin and penicillin develops AKI with low magnesium and all other electrolytes normal. What is the diagnosis?
  • A. Penicillin-induced interstitial nephritis
  • B. Gentamicin-induced tubular injury (ATN)
  • C. Pre-renal AKI
  • D. Post-renal AKI
  • E. Contrast nephropathy
Best answer
B. Gentamicin-induced tubular injury (ATN)
Aminoglycosides (gentamicin) → dose-related proximal tubular necrosis (ATN) + hypomagnesaemia (also hypocalcaemia/hypokalaemia). Penicillins → acute interstitial nephritis (fever/rash/eosinophils, WBC casts, normal magnesium).
#154MCQ edited2019-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-ba816228
Meropenem and gentamicin affect the kidneys. What type of AKI do they cause?
  • A. Acute tubular necrosis (ATN)
  • B. Acute interstitial nephritis
  • C. Pre-renal AKI
  • D. Post-renal AKI
  • E. Glomerulonephritis
Best answer
A. Acute tubular necrosis (ATN)
Aminoglycosides (gentamicin) + others (vancomycin, cisplatin, amphotericin) → direct tubular toxicity → ATN (muddy brown casts, FeNa>2%). Meropenem is comparatively safe but the combination with gentamicin is the classic ATN trap. Monitor drug levels — stop/adjust.
2019 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Acute Monoarthritis — Rule Out Septic Arthritis First

Acute monoarthritis is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. The single most important first step is joint aspiration (arthrocentesis) — synovial fluid analysis with Gram stain + culture + crystal microscopy — both diagnostic and therapeutic. Never treat empirically without aspirating if you can aspirate.

CauseCluesFluid
Septic arthritisFever, hot swollen joint, inability to bear weight; risk: diabetes, RA, prosthetic joint, prior joint disease, skin infection, immunosuppressionTurbid, WBC >50–100k, neutrophil predominant, glucose low, Gram+/culture+
GoutSudden severe pain, podagra (1st MTP), tophi, risk: alcohol, red meat, diuretics, renal impairment, post-op/fastingNeedle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals
Pseudogout (CPPD)Older patients, knee/wrist, chondrocalcinosis on X-rayRhomboid, positively birefringent crystals
Monoarticular flare of RA/PsAChronic history, morning stiffnessInflammatory, sterile
Reactive/Reiter’sPost-urethritis/dysentery, conjunctivitis, arthritis (can’t see, can’t pee, can’t climb a tree)Sterile inflammatory fluid
HaemarthrosisHaemophilia, anticoagulation, traumaBloody

Management: if septic — urgent IV antibiotics (flucloxacillin ± gentamicin, or vancomycin if MRSA risk) + joint washout/drainage; orthopaedic involvement. If gout — NSAIDs/colchicine/steroids; allopurinol only after the flare settles. Important exam point: serum uric acid can be normal during an acute gout attack — aspiration is definitive, not the uric acid level.

Exam pearl — In any acutely hot, swollen single joint: aspirate FIRST, interpret crystals, then Gram stain/culture before antibiotics are given whenever feasible. In a hospitalised, afebrile patient with knee swelling, gout is common, but septic arthritis must be excluded — hence aspiration is still the answer.

2019 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Aortic Dissection

Definition: tear in intima → blood tracks into media → false lumen separates layers; can propagate proximally (coronary ostia, aortic valve — AR, cardiac tamponade) or distally (branch occlusion — stroke, limb ischaemia, renal failure, mesenteric).

Stanford classification: Type A = any involvement of ascending aorta (surgical emergency — mortality rises ~1% per hour untreated); Type B = descending only (medical management first — IV beta-blockade, then vasodilators).

Risk factors: hypertension (most important — especially poorly controlled), connective tissue disease (Marfan, Ehlers–Danlos, Loeys–Dietz), bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, pregnancy (third trimester), cocaine, trauma, iatrogenic (catheterisation), vasculitis/infective aortitis.

Clinical picture: tearing/ripping chest pain radiating to the back, abrupt onset, maximal at onset; may migrate; hypertension (or hypotension if tamponade/rupture — ominous), pulse/BP differential between limbs, new diastolic murmur of AR, syncope, neuro deficits (stroke, paraplegia), abdominal pain (mesenteric), oliguria (renal).

Investigation: CT angiography (CTA) — the investigation of choice in haemodynamically stable patients: fast, defines entry tear, extent, branch vessels, perfusion, effusion. Transoesophageal echo for unstable patients or when CTA contraindicated. ECG to exclude MI (dissection can involve RCA ostium → inferior STEMI!). CXR: widened mediastinum (non-specific).

Management: Type A → immediate surgery; Type B (stable) → strict BP/HR control (target HR <60, SBP 100–120; IV labetalol/esmolol first, then nitroprusside/GTN), ICU care; surgery/EVAR if complicated (rupture, malperfusion, refractory pain, expansion). Lifelong anti-impulse therapy and imaging follow-up.

Exam pearls
  • Tearing pain radiating to back + hypertension + afebrile + no troponin story → dissection (not MI, not pericarditis — pericarditis is pleuritic, worse lying flat, better leaning forward).
  • CTA is the first-line test; TTE/TOoE if unstable.
  • Check bilateral BPs and pulses in every chest pain — inter-arm difference >20 mmHg is a red flag.
Traps
  • Do NOT give anticoagulants/fibrinolytics until dissection excluded in chest pain with back radiation — catastrophic if dissection.
  • Inferior STEMI + tearing pain = dissection involving RCA until proven otherwise.

Aphasia — Classification by Fluency, Comprehension, Repetition

Approach: test fluency (speech effort/quantity) → comprehension → repetition → naming. Lesion localisation follows.

TypeFluencyComprehensionRepetitionLesion
Broca’s (expressive/motor)Non-fluentIntactImpairedDominant frontal lobe — inferior frontal gyrus (postero-inferior), MCA territory
Wernicke’s (receptive/sensory)Fluent (but meaningless/jargon)ImpairedImpairedDominant superior temporal gyrus
GlobalNon-fluentImpairedImpairedDominant hemisphere — large MCA territory infarct
ConductionFluentIntactImpaired (disproportionately) ± namingArcuate fasciculus (dominant parietal/temporal)
Anomic (nominal)FluentIntactIntactVariable — dominant angular gyrus/temporoparietal; naming difficulty only
Transcortical motorNon-fluentIntactIntactDominant frontal, anterior/superior to Broca’s
Transcortical sensoryFluentImpairedIntactDominant temporo-occipital, posterior to Wernicke’s
Mixed transcorticalNon-fluentImpairedIntact (echolalia)Watershed zones both anterior/posterior

Classic discriminators in this exam: fluent + intact comprehension + impaired repetition/naming = conduction aphasia. Non-fluent + impaired comprehension + impaired repetition = global aphasia. Comprehension intact + repetition intact + poor naming = anomic.

Also distinguish from dysarthria (articulation problem — speech content normal, motor speech disorder: bulbar/pseudobulbar palsy, cerebellar, basal ganglia) and dysphonia (voice production — vocal cords/larynx). Aphasia is a disorder of language, not speech.

Exam pearls
  • Fluency first, comprehension second, repetition third — three questions, one box each.
  • Repetition spared → transcortical; repetition lost → Broca/Wernicke/conduction/global.
  • Conduction aphasia: intact fluent speech + intact understanding, but cannot repeat — "can speak and understand, cannot echo".
  • Global aphasia after massive MCA stroke — very poor prognosis.

Cardiac Arrhythmias — Recognition & Acute Management

Approach to any ECG rhythm: rate → regularity → P waves (present? each before a QRS?) → PR length → QRS width → ST/T. Then match to a rhythm and assess stability (ABCDE — shock, syncope/pre-syncope, ischaemia/chest pain, heart failure).

RhythmKey ECG featuresNotes / management
Sinus tachycardiaHR >100, normal P before each QRSPhysiological — treat the cause (pain, fever, hypovolaemia, PE, thyrotoxicosis, drugs)
AVNRT / AVRT (SVT, PSVT)Regular narrow-complex tachycardia ~150–250, P waves hidden/inverted/retrograde after QRSVagal manoeuvres → adenosine 6→12→12 mg rapid IV bolus; unstable → synchronized cardioversion; long-term: ablation
Atrial flutterSaw-tooth flutter waves ~300/min, typically 2:1/4:1 block (ventricular ~150), narrow QRSRate control (beta-blocker/verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin) or DC cardioversion; anticoagulation per CHA₂DS₂-VASc; CTI ablation is curative
Atrial fibrillationIrregularly irregular narrow complex, no distinct P wavesLoss of JVP “a” wave (no atrial contraction). Rate control first (BB/CCB/digoxin); anticoagulate per CHA₂DS₂-VASc; unstable → DC cardiovert; consider rhythm control/ablation if young/symptomatic
VTBroad complex regular tachycardia; concordance, AV dissociationStable → IV amiodarone/procainamide; unstable → immediate synchronized cardioversion; pulseless → defibrillation + ALS
Heart block1°: PR >200 ms constant. 2° Mobitz I (Wenckebach): progressive PR prolongation then dropped beat. 2° Mobitz II: sudden dropped beat, constant PR. 3° (complete): AV dissociation, regular escape rhythmMobitz II & CHB → admit, transcutaneous/transvenous pacing; atropine often ineffective; stop AV-nodal blockers
VF / pulseless VTChaotic or broad-complex without pulseImmediate defibrillation + CPR + adrenaline 1 mg every 3–5 min

CHA₂DS₂-VASc (stroke risk in AF): CHF (1), HTN (1), Age ≥75 (2), DM (1), Stroke/TIA (2), Vascular disease (1), Age 65–74 (1), Sex female (1). Score 0 (men) / 1 (women) → no anticoagulation; ≥1 (men)/≥2 (women) consider OAC; ≥2 → anticoagulate (DOAC preferred). HAS-BLED estimates bleeding risk — high score is NOT a reason to withhold anticoagulation; it flags need for closer review/modifiable factors.

JVP “a” wave is produced by atrial contraction → absent in AF (no organised atrial systole); giant “a” waves in tricuspid stenosis; cannon “a” waves in complete heart block/AV dissociation (atrium contracts against closed tricuspid valve).

Exam pearls
  • Irregularly irregular + absent “a” wave = AF. Narrow regular tachycardia in a young woman with normal baseline = AVNRT → vagal then adenosine.
  • Unstable tachycardia/bradycardia → electricity wins (synchronized shock for pulse present; defibrillation for pulseless).
  • High-grade AV block (Mobitz II, complete) → pacing, not atropine alone.
  • Antidromic AVRT/VT wide-complex doubt → treat as VT (procainamide/amiodarone; avoid AV-nodal blockers in pre-excited AF).
Traps
  • Do not use adenosine in pre-excited AF (irregular wide complex) — can precipitate VF.
  • Cardioversion in AF >48 h without anticoagulation/imaging → stroke risk; anticoagulate ≥3 weeks or do TOE, or cardiovert early (<48 h) with heparin.

#181SAQ edited2019-InternalMedicine-SAQ-Medicine-03de5151
A case with chest pain (ECG irregular) and unstable vital signs (hypotension).
  1. What is the most likely diagnosis? (1 pt)
  2. Mention 2 blood tests. (2 pt)
  3. How will you manage this patient? (1 pt)
Best answer
1) Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response — haemodynamically UNSTABLE (irregular rhythm + hypotension). 2) Blood tests: (a) troponin; (b) electrolytes/renal function (U&E — K⁺/Mg²⁺) + FBC + TSH + coagulation/INR (thyrotoxicosis, electrolytes, ischaemia trigger/consequence). 3) Management: immediate synchronised DC cardioversion (ABCDE, high-flow O₂, IV access, sedation) — unstable tachyarrhythmia = electricity. If it reverts: rate/rhythm control, anticoagulation per CHA₂DS₂-VASc, echo, treat trigger.
Unstable AF (shock/syncope/MI/HF) = synchronised cardioversion ± amiodarone. Stable AF = rate control (BB/CCB/digoxin) or rhythm control if young/symptomatic/first episode. Always anticoagulate per score; check for precipitants (PE, sepsis, hyperthyroid, alcohol).

Asthma — Diagnosis & Acute Exacerbation

Diagnosis: variable respiratory symptoms (wheeze, cough, chest tightness, dyspnoea) + variable expiratory airflow limitation: FEV₁/FVC <0.7 with ≥12% and ≥200 mL improvement in FEV₁ after bronchodilator, or excessive diurnal peak-flow variability (>20%), or positive bronchial challenge (methacholine/histamine) if spirometry is normal. Normal spirometry does NOT exclude asthma in a symptomatic patient → methacholine challenge is the next step.

Obstructive defect pattern: low FEV₁, low FEV₁/FVC, normal/low-normal FVC, and (in asthma) normal DLCO (unlike emphysema where DLCO is low).

Acute severe asthma (admit): PEF 33–50% predicted/best, respiratory rate ≥25, HR ≥110, inability to complete sentences, or O₂ sat <92%. Life-threatening: PEF <33%, silent chest, exhaustion/altered consciousness, SpO₂ <92%, normal/high PaCO₂ (exhaustion — rising CO₂ is a red flag).

Management of acute exacerbation:

  1. High-flow O₂ to keep SpO₂ 94–98%.
  2. Nebulised salbutamol (5 mg) + ipratropium bromide (0.5 mg) driven by O₂, back-to-back/repeat.
  3. Oral prednisolone 40–50 mg (or IV hydrocortisone) — steroids early.
  4. Not responding/severe → IV magnesium sulfate 1.2–2 g over 20 min; call ICU; consider IV aminophylline; avoid sedation; intubation if failing (permissive hypercapnia).
  5. Discharge: when PEF >75%, stable ≥12–24 h off nebs; written asthma action plan, GP/asthma nurse follow-up, inhaler technique review, optimise preventer (ICS-containing), address triggers and adherence, safety-net re admission.

Chronic stepwise management (GINA): low-dose ICS-formoterol as reliever (or SABA + ICS) → add LABA → medium-dose ICS/LABA → refer. SABA-only is no longer recommended — every reliever should contain ICS to cut severe exacerbations.

Exam pearls
  • First-line in acute attack after O₂: nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium + early oral steroids.
  • Rising/normal PaCO₂ in acute asthma = life-threatening — call for help.
  • Normal spirometry + typical symptoms → methacholine challenge confirms.
  • Nasal flaring, intercostal recessions, tracheal tug in a child = severe exacerbation with respiratory distress.

2019 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Brucellosis

“Undulant fever” — zoonosis from Brucella (abortus – cattle; melitensis – goats/sheep; suis – pigs) via unpasteurised dairy, direct contact with infected animals/placentas, or aerosols (lab/vets/abattoir). Common in the Mediterranean/Middle East/South Asia.

Clinical: gradual onset intermittent/relapsing fever (undulant), drenching sweats, malaise, weight loss, headache, migratory arthralgia, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy. Focal complications: sacroiliitis (very characteristic), spondylitis (vertebral osteomyelitis), epididymo-orchitis, hepatitis, neurobrucellosis, endocarditis (main cause of death).

Diagnosis: Serology (Rose Bengal screen; agglutination/Coombs/Brucellacapt; fourfold rise on paired sera or single high titre, e.g. >1:160) — first-line test. Blood culture is definitive but slow (keep 4–6 weeks). PCR; raised ESR mild; LFTs often deranged.

Treatment: combination therapy for ≥6 weeks — doxycycline + rifampicin (or doxycycline + streptomycin for severe/focal disease, e.g. spondylitis/endocarditis); children/pregnancy → TMP-SMX + rifampicin. Avoid drugs alone (relapse).

Exam pearls
  • Fever + night sweats + animal/dairy exposure → Brucella serology; sacroiliitis + that history = brucellosis till proven otherwise.
  • Spinal brucellosis: brucellar spondylitis — back pain + fever + raised inflammatory markers (TB gives gibbus; brucella gives sacroiliitis/vertebral osteomyelitis).
  • Endocarditis is the lethal complication — echo if murmur/emboli.

Calcium & Parathyroid Disorders

First, correct calcium for albumin (or use ionised calcium): corrected Ca (mmol/L) = measured + 0.02 × (40 − albumin g/L). Phosphate, PTH, vitamin D complete the picture.

Ca²⁺PO₄³⁻PTHThink of
Primary hyperparathyroidism↑↓↑/inappropriately normalAdenoma (80%); “stones, bones, groans, psychiatric moans”; check for MEN1/2A; management: parathyroidectomy if symptomatic/young/complications/eGFR low/osteoporosis/high stones risk
Secondary hyperparathyroidism↓ or N↑↑CKD / vitamin D deficiency — PTH elevated to compensate
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism↑↑/N↑↑Long-standing secondary disease → autonomous glands (post-transplant CKD) → parathyroidectomy
Hypoparathyroidism↓↑↓Post-surgery (thyroidectomy — commonest), autoimmune, DiGeorge, autoimmune polyglandular; symptoms: perioral numbness, carpopedal spasm, Trousseau’s, Chvostek’s, seizures, prolonged QT
Malignancy hypercalcaemia↑↓/NsuppressedPTHrP (squamous lung, breast, renal), bone mets, myeloma (high ALP/renal failure/anaemia + high Ig), 1,25-vit D (lymphoma)
Vitamin D deficiency↓/N↓↑Rickets/osteomalacia — secondary HPT normalises Ca; low phosphate (renal wasting under PTH)

Hypocalcaemia work-up: check Mg (low Mg causes/worsens hypocalcaemia and PTH resistance — correct it), phosphate, PTH, vitamin D, renal function. Acute severe: IV calcium gluconate 10–20 mL of 10% (cardiac monitoring). Chronic: oral calcium + calcitriol (1,25-OH vit D).

Tertiary HPT “next step”: confirm autonomy — raised Ca + raised/inappropriately normal PTH on background of CKD; localise with sestamibi scan/neck ultrasound then subtotal parathyroidectomy. Calcimimetics (cinacalcet) for those unfit for surgery.

Exam pearls
  • High Ca + low PO₄ + high PTH = primary HPT; high Ca + LOW PTH = malignancy/vitamin D excess/granulomas.
  • New numbness around mouth + carpopedal spasm after surgery = hypoparathyroidism → IV calcium gluconate.
  • CKD + high phosphate + low Ca + high PTH = secondary HPT → phosphate binders, vitamin D analogues; tertiary = autonomously high PTH + HYPERcalcaemia → surgery.
  • Back pain + high Ca + low phosphate + anaemia, normal WBC → check protein electrophoresis (myeloma) — NOT primary HPT alone.

2019 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

COPD — Diagnosis, PFT & Exacerbations

Definition: chronic respiratory symptoms + persistent airflow obstruction (post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC <0.7) usually from noxious exposure — smoking (commonest), biomass, occupational dusts, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Chronic bronchitis = productive cough ≥3 months in 2 consecutive years; emphysema = alveolar wall destruction.

Diagnosis & investigations: spirometry is mandatory — shows obstruction not fully reversible. CXR (hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms) often normal early; high-resolution CT if unclear; alpha-1 antitrypsin if young/basal emphysema/family history/non-smoker; sputum culture in exacerbations; ABG in severe disease (chronic CO₂ retention → target SpO₂ 88–92%). Reduced cricosternal distance (<3 cm) = hyperinflation.

PFT patterns (exam table): obstruction = ↓FEV₁, normal/↓FVC, ↓FEV₁/FVC, quiet DLCO only if emphysema; restriction = ↓FEV₁, ↓FVC, preserved/high FEV₁/FVC, ↓TLC, usually ↓DLCO.

Chronic management: stop smoking (only intervention that alters decline); vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID); pulmonary rehabilitation; SABA/SAMA as needed → LABA or LAMA → ICS/LABA or triple therapy if frequent exacerbations; LTOT (long-term oxygen) if PaO₂ ≤7.3 kPa (or ≤8 kPa with cor pulmonale/polycythaemia).

Exacerbation (Anthonisen criteria): increased dyspnoea + increased sputum volume + increased sputum purulence. Treatment: controlled oxygen (target 88–92%), nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium, oral prednisolone 30 mg × 5 days, antibiotics (amoxicillin/doxycycline) if purulent sputum, NIV if respiratory acidosis persists despite therapy. Identify triggers (infection most common; PE and pneumothorax are mimics — CXR).

Exam pearls
  • Smoker + chronic cough + reduced cricosternal distance + obstruction on spirometry = COPD; asthma shows REVERSIBILITY.
  • COPD O₂ target = 88–92% (hypoxic drive considerations) — controlled, not non-rebreather-titrate-to-100%.
  • Spirometry confirms — peak flow/X-ray do not diagnose COPD.

Diabetes Insipidus & Polyuria Work-up

Definition: passing >3 L (or >40–50 mL/kg) of dilute urine per day (or nocturnal polyuria). First split by urine osmolality: if concentrated (>750 mOsm/kg) → osmotic diuresis (DM, mannitol); if dilute → DI vs primary polydipsia.

Central DINephrogenic DIPrimary polydipsia
Cause↓ADH secretion — pituitary/hypothalamic surgery or tumour, trauma, infection (TB/meningitis), infiltration, Sheehan’s, idiopathicRenal resistance to ADH — lithium, demeclocycline, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, CKD, congenital (AVPR2/AQP2)Psychogenic (schizophrenia, anxiety), dipsogenic
Serum Na↑ (unless drinking keeps up)↑↓ or low-normal
Water deprivation testUrine stays dilute, plasma osm rises (>300)Urine stays dilute, plasma osm risesUrine concentrates normally (>750)
Desmopressin (DDAVP) responseConcentrates urine (+>50% osm)No responseConcentrates (normal)

Key exam scenario: post–pituitary/sellar surgery + hypernatraemia + normal other electrolytes + high-normal glucose → central DI (damaged posterior pituitary/stalk). Treat: desmopressin (DDAVP — intranasal/oral/IV), free water access; monitor Na.

Lithium-induced NDI: stop/reduce lithium; amiloride or thiazide + salt restriction (induces mild volume depletion → ↑proximal Na/water reabsorption); NSAID (indomethacin) adjunct if needed.

Always rule out: hyperglycaemia (DM), hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, diuretics before the water-deprivation test (only after stopping confounders, under supervision — stop when >3% body weight lost or plasma osm >305/Na >150).

Exam pearls
  • Polyuria + hypernatraemia after pituitary surgery = central DI → DDAVP.
  • Lithium + polyuria + normal glucose = nephrogenic DI → stop lithium ± amiloride/thiazide.
  • Hypernatraemia post-op also = lost insensible losses without replacement — check.

Diabetes Mellitus — Type 1, Type 2 & MODY

Classification & clues:

Type 1Type 2MODY
OnsetChildren/adolescents, rapidAdults (now adolescents with obesity), insidiousYoung (<25), autosomal dominant, strong family history (3 generations)
WeightNormal/leanObese, metabolic syndromeNormal (often)
AntibodiesGAD, IA-2, insulin, ZnT8NegativeNegative
C-peptideLow/absentNormal/highPreserved
KetosisProne (may present in DKA)Rare (HHS)Rare
TreatmentInsulin from diagnosis + carb counting + educationLifestyle + metformin ± add-ons (SGLT2i/GLP-1/SU/DPP4/insulin)Sulfonylureas (MODY 3/HNF1A), or low-dose; often misdiagnosed as T1

Autoantibody-positive adolescent + polyuria/polydipsia + no family history → type 1 diabetes (not MODY). LADA = latent autoimmune diabetes of adults (>30 y, slower onset, GAD+, initially non-insulin).

Diagnosis: fasting glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L, random ≥11.1 + symptoms, OGTT 2-h ≥11.1, or HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol (6.5%) (not in pregnancy/haemoglobinopathy). One abnormal + symptoms is enough; asymptomatic → confirm with repeat.

Newly diagnosed T2DM management: lifestyle/weight loss + metformin first-line (unless contraindicated) — then SGLT2i/GLP-1 if CV/renal disease, consider dual therapy if HbA1c >58. Annual review: feet, eyes (retinal screen), urine ACR, lipids, BP, vaccination, smoking cessation. Targets: BP <130/80 (but ≤140/90 general), LDL reduction per QRISK; statin if >40 y or CVD risk.

Type 1 annual review: retinopathy screen (from 12 y), microalbuminuria, thyroid/coeliac screen, self-monitoring, sick-day rules (never stop insulin entirely — DKA risk; “sick-day” = continue basal, check ketones, fluids, seek help if vomiting/ketotic).

Exam pearls
  • GAD antibodies + adolescent + no family history = T1DM → insulin.
  • MODY = young + strong 3-generation family history + non-obese + antibody-negative.
  • First step in stable newly-diagnosed T2DM = metformin + lifestyle (not insulin).

Electrolyte Disorders — Sodium & Potassium

Hyponatraemia — classify by volume status:

HypovolaemicEuvolaemicHypervolaemic
Urine NaLow <20 (extrarenal loss: GI, skin, third space) / High >20 (renal loss: diuretics, Addison’s, salt-wasting)>40 (SIADH); check TSH/cortisol (hypothyroid/adrenal = euvolaemic)Low <20 (HF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, CKD — effective arterial underfilling)
Treatment0.9% saline (restore volume) + treat causeFluid restrict (1 L/day) ± salt tablets/furosemide/vaptans (hypertonic 3% if seizures/severe neuro signs)Fluid + sodium restriction, loop diuretics, treat HF/cirrhosis; dialysis if renal failure

SIADH = hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia + inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osm >100, urine Na >40) + euvolaemia + normal renal/thyroid/adrenal + no diuretics. Causes: malignancy (small cell lung, pancreatic), CNS (stroke, tumour, meningitis), pulmonary (pneumonia, TB, PPV), drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, PPIs, chemotherapy, opioids, MDMA). Treat: fluid restriction ± hypertonic saline if symptomatic (Na <120 with seizures/coma — 3% saline, raise ≤8 mmol/L per 24 h to avoid central pontine myelinolysis).

Co-existing lung cancer + hyponatraemia = SIADH (ectopic ADH from small-cell carcinoma).

Hyperkalaemia: treat by severity/ECG. ECG progression: peaked (“tented”) T waves → PR prolongation → P flattening → QRS widening → sine wave → VF. K⁺ >6.5 or any ECG change = emergency: IV calcium gluconate (membrane stabilisation), insulin+dextrose, salbutamol nebulisers, sodium bicarbonate (if acidotic), K binders, dialysis if refractory. Stop K/ACEi/MRA/NSAIDs; check glucose (DKA?), renal function.

Hypokalaemia: causes — diuretics (loop/thiazide), vomiting/diarrhoea, hyperaldosteronism, hypokalaemic periodic paralysis (carbohydrate load in susceptible young men — e.g. “after a big carbohydrate meal”, resolves with K), Bartter/Gitelman, insulin, beta-agonists, RTA. Replace K orally if mild; IV if severe/symptomatic; check Mg (replace both). ECG: flattened T, U waves, ST depression, VT/VF.

Exam pearls
  • SIADH = low serum osm + urine Na>40 + euvolaemic → restrict fluid; symptomatic → 3% saline ≤8/24h.
  • Oedema + crackles + confusion + hyponatraemia = hypervolaemic dilutional (HF) — do NOT give saline.
  • Peaked T waves → calcium gluconate FIRST; insulin/dextrose second; dialysis if refractory.
  • Carbohydrate-feast weakness + low K in a young Asian male = hypokalaemic periodic paralysis.
Traps
  • Hypertonic saline for chronic asymptomatic hyponatraemia causes osmotic demyelination — correct slowly.
  • Pseudohyponatraemia (hypertriglyceridaemia/paraproteinaemia) — check osmolality/lab method if patient looks well.
  • Hypomagnesaemia → refractory hypokalaemia/hypocalcaemia — always co-check.

2019 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Oesophageal Disorders — Webs, Strictures & Cancer

Plummer–Vinson (Paterson–Brown–Kelly) syndrome — classic triad: iron-deficiency anaemia + postcricoid/upper oesophageal web + dysphagia. Middle-aged women; koilonychia (spoon nails) and angular stomatitis accompany the iron deficiency. Risk: squamous cell carcinoma of the upper oesophagus/pharynx (premalignant). Treatment: iron replacement ± endoscopic dilatation of web; surveillance if severe.

Dysphagia triage: progressive (solids → liquids) over weeks + weight loss + age >50 = oesophageal cancer until proven otherwise → urgent endoscopy. Dysphagia to solids only from the start suggests mechanical obstruction (web/ring/stricture). Dysphagia to liquids + solids from onset + regurgitation of undigested food + halitosis = achalasia (bird’s-beak on barium; manometry; treat dilation/myotomy). Episodic dysphagia with solids/liquids + chest pain = spasm. Odynophagia = ulcer/infection (Candida in immunosuppression).

Oesophageal cancer types: squamous (upper/mid — smoking/alcohol/Plummer–Vinson/hot drinks) vs adenocarcinoma (lower — Barrett’s/GORD/obesity). Staging CT + EUS; treatment depends on stage (surgery/chemoradiation/palliation).

Exam pearls
  • Dysphagia + koilonychia + IDA = Plummer–Vinson — treat iron, screen for web (and consider SCC surveillance).
  • Progressive dysphagia + weight loss = cancer → OGD.
  • Achalasia: regurgitation + bird’s beak + failure of LES relaxation.

Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD / MASLD)

Definition: hepatic steatosis ≥5% of hepatocytes on imaging/histology without significant alcohol (<20–30 g/day) and without another cause. Now renamed MASLD (metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease); with inflammation/ballooning = MASH (NASH) → fibrosis → cirrhosis (~20–25% of NASH) → HCC.

Risk factors: obesity (central), T2DM/insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, metabolic syndrome (the reason this question’s hypertensive, hyperlipidaemic, diabetic patient is the classic vignette), PCOS, hypothyroidism, drugs (amiodarone, methotrexate, tamoxifen, steroids).

Diagnosis: often incidental — deranged LFTs (ALT/AST usually <5× ULN, ALT>AST until cirrhosis develops) or steatosis on ultrasound. Then EXCLUDE other causes: viral serology (B/C), autoimmune screen (AMA/ANA/ASMA), ferritin/transferrin saturation (haemochromatosis), caeruloplasmin (Wilson if young), α1-antitrypsin, TFTs, alcohol history. Fibrosis assessment: NAFLD fibrosis score/FIB-4 → if high risk: FibroScan (transient elastography) or ELF blood test → biopsy if unclear.

Management: weight loss (7–10% body weight) is the only proven therapy; control diabetes (metformin; pioglitazone/GLP-1 agonists benefit MASH), statins (safe), exercise, avoid alcohol; vaccinate hepatitis A/B; HCC surveillance (6-monthly USS) once cirrhotic; treat complications.

Exam pearls
  • Metabolic syndrome + asymptomatic deranged LFTs + steatosis on USS → NAFLD/MASLD — diagnosis of exclusion.
  • ALT>AST early; AST>ALT ratio reversal signals progression to cirrhosis (like alcohol but milder).
  • #1 treatment: weight loss & metabolic control.

Fibromyalgia

Definition: chronic (≥3 months) widespread pain (both sides, above/below waist, axial) + fatigue + non-restorative sleep + cognitive difficulty (“fibro fog”) + point tenderness, in the ABSENCE of inflammation or tissue damage. Commoner in women 30–55.

Diagnosis (WPI + SSS, ACR 2010): Widespread Pain Index ≥7 + Symptom Severity Score ≥5 (or WPI 3–6 + SSS ≥9), symptoms ≥3 months, no other disorder explaining the pain. 2016 criteria added regional pain + somatic symptoms. Investigations should be NORMAL — ESR/CRP/RF/CK/TFT — do tests to exclude mimics, not to confirm.

Differential: hypothyroidism (check TFT), vitamin D deficiency, polymyalgia rheumatica (>50 y, shoulder/hip girdle + raised ESR — responds to steroids), inflammatory arthritis (swollen joints, raised CRP), SLE (rashes, arthritis, ANA), myositis (CK↑), depression/somatiform, malignancy, sleep apnoea, hypermobility syndrome.

Management — non-drug first: aerobic graded exercise + CBT + patient education (explain the pain amplification model — normal tests are reassuring news, not “imagining”); treat sleep (amitriptyline low-dose at night / sleep hygiene), psychological care; avoid chronic opioids. Pharmacological if needed: duloxetine, pregabalin, amitriptyline; tramadol occasionally. No role for NSAIDs/steroids/strong opioids or surgery.

Exam pearls
  • Widespread pain + fatigue + poor sleep + normal tests + point tenderness = fibromyalgia.
  • PMR = age >50 + girdle pain + ESR↑ — different treatment entirely.
  • Validation + exercise + CBT is the treatment; chasing more tests re-enforces illness behaviour.

Gastroenteritis & Food Poisoning — Organism Recognition

Key differentiators: incubation period, vomiting vs diarrhoea predominance, watery vs bloody, food type, setting (outbreak).

OrganismIncubationCluesNotes
Norovirus12–48 hExplosive vomiting + watery diarrhoea; cruise ships/hospitals/institutions/outbreaks; very contagiousSelf-limiting 1–3 d; isolate; hydration; soap & water
Rotavirus1–3 dInfants/young children, watery diarrhoea + vomiting + feverVaccine available; winter peaks
Staphylococcus aureus1–6 hVomiting predominant after custard, cream, mayo, reheated rice/chicken (picnic/party food); toxin-mediatedNo fever; self-limiting <24 h; no antibiotics
Bacillus cereus1–6 h (emetic) / 8–16 h (diarrheal)Reheated fried rice (Chinese takeaway) — vomiting; or meat/veg — diarrhoeaPreformed toxin; self-limiting
Clostridium perfringens8–16 hLarge institutional beef/poultry/gravies → watery diarrhoeaSelf-limiting
Salmonella (non-typhi)6–48 hUndercooked poultry/eggs → watery → bloody diarrhoea, feverUsually self-limiting; antibiotics only if severe/immunosuppressed; Sickle cell → osteomyelitis risk

Entamoeba histolytica2–4 wksBloody diarrhoea, liver abscessMetronidazole + luminal agent
C. difficileVariableAntibiotic-associated diarrhoea/pseudomembranous colitisOral vancomycin; see separate review

Management of acute diarrhoea: oral rehydration (ORS) is the cornerstone — IV fluids only if severe dehydration/unable to tolerate. Antibiotics NOT indicated for most (NOT for EHEC — precipitates HUS). Test stool only if bloody/severe/prolonged/immunocompromised.

Exam pearls
  • Cruise ship + everyone vomiting = norovirus. Reheated rice = B. cereus. Custard/cream 2 h later = S. aureus.
  • Bloody diarrhoea after beef + HUS risk = EHEC — NO antibiotics.
  • Bloody diarrhoea + travel = Shigella/Campylobacter; persistent after travel = Giardia.
  • Fluids first; antibiotics rarely.

Gastro-oesophageal Reflux Disease (GORD/GERD)

Symptomatic / complicated reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus. Common mechanisms: transient LOS relaxation (commonest), hiatus hernia, impaired oesophageal clearance, gastroparesis. Risk factors: obesity, pregnancy, smoking, alcohol, caffeine, large/fatty meals, lying flat, drugs (NSAIDs, nitrates, calcium-channel blockers, anticholinergics, theophylline), connective tissue disease (scleroderma).

Typical symptoms: heartburn, regurgitation, waterbrash (hypersalivation), retrosternal chest pain worsened by lying flat/bending, relieved by antacids, nocturnal symptoms. Extra-oesophageal: chronic cough, hoarseness (laryngitis), asthma exacerbation, dental erosion, Globus sensation.

Children: GORD = frequent regurgitation + distress/faltering growth/apnoea/posturing; “silent” reflux (arching, feed refusal); usually self-limiting by 12–18 months; treat with feed thickening, frequent small feeds, positioning; PPI only for distressing/complicated cases; consider CMPA in infants.

Diagnosis: clinical in typical cases — start empirical PPI trial (4–8 weeks). Endoscopy (OGD) if: age >55, alarm features (weight loss, dysphagia, odynophagia, GI bleeding/anaemia, persistent vomiting), or atypical symptoms. pH/impedance monitoring if symptoms persist despite PPI and endoscopy normal (non-erosive reflux/hypersensitive oesophagus).

Complications: erosive oesophagitis → peptic stricture, Barrett’s oesophagus (intestinal metaplasia — 0.5–1%/yr → adenocarcinoma) → surveillance endoscopy every 3–5 years; aspiration pneumonia; dental erosion.

Management: lifestyle (weight loss, elevate head of bed, avoid late meals/trigger foods, stop smoking/alcohol) + PPI (omeprazole 20–40 mg OD 30 min before breakfast, 4–8 wks); H₂-blockers second line; antacids/alginate for breakthrough. Refractory → escalate PPI, re-evaluate diagnosis, fundoplication for severe cases.

Exam pearls
  • Retrosternal pain worse lying/bending + waterbrash + relieved by antacids = GORD.
  • Alarm symptoms → endoscopy FIRST, not PPI.
  • Barrett’s → endoscopic surveillance.
  • Child “chest pain at night + vomiting” = GORD; if alarm (dysphagia, weight loss, anaemia) → scope.

Heart Failure — HFrEF vs HFpEF, Acute & Chronic

Pathophysiology: inadequate cardiac output for metabolic needs (or only at high filling pressures). Classify by EF: HFrEF (EF ≤40%) — systolic failure (IHD/MI, dilated cardiomyopathy, hypertension long-standing, valvular); HFmrEF (41–49); HFpEF (≥50) — diastolic failure (hypertension, LVH, hypertrophic/restrictive CMP, constrictive pericarditis, ischaemia). Right-sided failure usually secondary to left-sided or lung disease (cor pulmonale).

Symptoms: dyspnoea (exertional), orthopnoea, PND, fatigue, ankle swelling, nocturia. Examination: raised JVP, S3 gallop (specific for volume overload/systolic failure), displaced apex, bibasal crackles, peripheral oedema, hepatojugular reflux, hepatomegaly.

Chronic HFrEF — the “four pillars” (all reduce mortality): (1) ACEi/ARB/ARNI (sacubitril–valsartan) — titrate to target; (2) beta-blocker (bisoprolol/carvedilol/metoprolol succinate) — start low, once stable; (3) MRA (spironolactone/eplerenone) — K & renal monitoring; (4) SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin/empagliflozin) — now regardless of diabetes. Plus: loop diuretic for congestion, ICD if EF ≤35% on optimal therapy, CRT if wide QRS (LBBB), iron for deficiency, treat sleep apnoea, vaccinate, cardiac rehab.

HFpEF: no drug reduces mortality — treat congestion with loop diuretics, aggressive BP/rate control, SGLT2i reduces hospitalisation; manage comorbidities (AF, IHD, obesity, diabetes).

Acute decompensated HF: ABCDE, sit up, high-flow O₂, IV furosemide (e.g. 40–80 mg or home dose ×2), stop beta-blocker if hypotensive/shocked (otherwise continue), CPAP if respiratory distress + acidosis; nitrates if hypertensive; treat precipitant (MI! infection, AF, NSAIDs, non-adherence); echocardiography for EF and valves; discharge plan + early follow-up.

ECG in severe LV dysfunction: reduced EF ± LBBB (CRT candidate if QRS ≥150 + LBBB + symptomatic on pillars).

Exam pearls
  • Four pillars for HFrEF: ACEi/ARB/ARNI + BB + MRA + SGLT2i. HFpEF = diuretics for symptoms.
  • S3 = failing ventricle — in volume overload.
  • Gradual weight gain + ankle swelling + breathlessness = fluid retention → furosemide.
  • New LBBB + EF 25% → CRT consideration after 3 months optimal pillars.

Haemolytic Anaemia — Intravascular vs Extravascular

Haemolysis = premature RBC destruction (lifespan <120 d). Both types: ↑reticulocytes, ↑LDH, ↑unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin, ↓haptoglobin.

IntravascularExtravascular
SiteInside vesselsSpleen/liver macrophages
PlasmaHaemoglobinaemia → haemoglobinuria (dark/red urine), methaemalbuminaemiaBilirubin↑ (gallstones), haptoglobin↓ (mild)
LDH/haptoglobin↑↑ / ↓↓↑ / ↓
CausesG6PD deficiency (oxidant stress — fava beans, sulfa drugs, antimalarials, infection), mechanical (prosthetic valve, microangiopathic — DIC/TTP/HUS/HELLP/malignant HTN, “march” haemoglobinuria), transfusion reactions (ABO incompatibility), PNH, cold agglutinin (occasionally)Hereditary spherocytosis, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (warm — IgG; cold — IgM/EBV/Mycoplasma), sickle cell disease, thalassaemia, hypersplenism, clostridial sepsis

G6PD deficiency (X-linked): episodic haemolysis triggered by oxidant stress — fava beans, drugs (primaquine, sulfa, nitrofurantoin), infections; severe intravascular episodes with haemoglobinuria (classically asked: “what type of haemolysis?” → intravascular — many exams key it so; there is also an extravascular component via splenic removal of Heinz-body cells); neonatal jaundice risk; Heinz bodies and bite cells on film during crisis; enzyme level may be falsely normal during acute haemolysis (young RBCs) — retest later. Management: avoid triggers; transfusion if severe.

Hereditary spherocytosis: autosomal dominant; spherocytes, ↑MCHC, osmotic fragility/EMA binding, splenomegaly, gallstones (pigment) — splenectomy if symptomatic/severe (lifelong infection risk — vaccinate).

Exam pearls
  • Dark urine + jaundice + recent fava/sulfa/infection in a Mediterranean/African male = G6PD → intravascular haemolysis.
  • Fragmented cells (schistocytes) = mechanical/MAHA — check platelets/coagulation/BP.
  • Spherocytes + Coombs+ = autoimmune (warm IgG); Coombs− = hereditary spherocytosis.
  • Before splenectomy: vaccines (pneumo, HiB, meningococcal).

Immunisation — Live Vaccines, Household Contacts & Contraindications

Live (attenuated) vaccines: BCG, MMR, varicella, oral polio (OPV), rotavirus, live intranasal influenza, live zoster (Zostavax), yellow fever, oral typhoid, Japanese encephalitis (live SA14). These are replication-competent — dangerous in severe immunosuppression (chemotherapy, transplant, high-dose steroids, biologics, primary immunodeficiency, HIV with low CD4) and can infect household contacts (OPV shed in stool).

Inactivated/killed/subunit/toxoid: hepatitis B, HiB, pneumococcal (conjugate/polysaccharide), DTP/Tdap, injectable polio (IPV), hepatitis A, HPV, injectable influenza, meningococcal — safe in immunosuppression.

Absolute contraindications: anaphylaxis to a previous dose or vaccine component; live vaccines in severe immunosuppression/pregnancy (MMR, varicella, BCG, OPV, yellow fever). NOT contraindications: mild febrile illness, recent exposure, prematurity (vaccinate by chronological age), breastfeeding, family history of seizures/adverse events, stable neurological conditions, antibiotic therapy, recovery from recent illness, local reaction/low-grade fever after dose.

Household contact rule (tested twice here): a severely immunocompromised child (chemotherapy for leukaemia) living with a sibling — the sibling must NOT receive live vaccines, especially OPV (viral shedding can paralyse the immunocompromised child) and BCG/varicella/MMR where applicable; use inactivated alternatives (IPV instead of OPV). Close contacts of transplant patients: avoid live vaccines except MMR/VZV per guidance (risk-benefit).

Tetanus prophylaxis for wounds: fully immunised + booster within 5 years → nothing; booster 5–10 y (clean wound) / any high-risk wound with booster >5 y → booster; incomplete/uncertain + high-risk wound → tetanus toxoid + tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG); dirty wounds: check.

Special situations: egg allergy → influenza/MMR/yellow fever generally safe with observation (severe egg anaphylaxis → specialist); HIV (CD4 >200): give MMR/varicella; pregnancy: no live vaccines (give MMR postpartum; Tdap from 16 weeks each pregnancy for pertussis; influenza any trimester); premature infants: vaccinate by chronological age.

Exam pearls
  • Chemo child at home → sibling gets IPV, NOT OPV; no live vaccines.
  • Immunosuppressed transplant patient → no live vaccines, ever (varicella!).
  • Only true general contraindication = anaphylaxis to prior dose. Mild illness ≠ contraindication.

Infective Endocarditis

Definition: microbial infection of the endocardial surface (valves, congenital lesions, prosthetic material, device leads) with vegetations (platelet-fibrin-microbe). Modified Duke criteria: 2 major (typical organism in ≥2 sets of blood cultures; echo positive — vegetation/abscess/new regurgitation) OR 1 major + 3 minor OR 5 minor (fever, predisposition, vascular phenomena — emboli/Janeway/conjunctival haemorrhage, immunological — Osler nodes/Roth spots/RF, positive culture not typical, positive echo not major).

Organisms by setting:

SettingLikely organism
Native valve, dental diseaseViridans streptococci
Native valve, skin/soft-tissue, IVDUStaphylococcus aureus (commonest overall; tricuspid in IVDU)
Prosthetic valve (early <60 d)Coagulase-negative staphylococci
Prosthetic valve (late) / healthcareCoagulase-negative staphylococci, S. aureus, enterococci
GU/GI instrumentation, catheter (this exam!)Enterococcus faecalis
Dental + colon cancerStreptococcus gallolyticus (bovis) — check colonoscopy
Q fever settingCoxiella burnetii
HACEK group (culture-negative)Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella

Clinical: fever + malaise + new/changing murmur + emboli (stroke, limb ischaemia, splenic/renal infarcts, mycotic aneurysm) + peripheral stigmata: Osler’s nodes (tender, finger pulps — immune), Janeway lesions (painless palmar macules — septic emboli), splinter haemorrhages, Roth spots (retinal haemorrhages with pale centres), clubbing, splenomegaly.

Diagnosis steps: ≥3 blood culture sets from separate sites BEFORE antibiotics → echocardiography (TTE first; TOE if prosthetic/high suspicion/TTE negative — vegetation, abscess, perforation, new dehiscence).

Treatment: prolonged IV antibiotics (4–6 weeks; native valve Viridans → benzylpenicillin ± gentamicin; S. aureus → nafcillin/flucloxacillin ± gentamicin; MRSA → vancomycin; enterococcal → ampicillin + gentamicin/ceftriaxone); surgery (urgent) for heart failure, valve abscess/fistula, uncontrolled infection, large >10 mm vegetations with emboli, prosthetic dehiscence. Prophylaxis (high-risk: prosthetic valves, previous IE, cyanotic congenital): amoxicillin before dental procedures.

Exam pearls
  • Fever + new murmur + embolic/immune stigmata → blood cultures ×3 then echo.
  • Catheter/UTI → enterococci; IVDU → S. aureus tricuspid; dental → viridans; prosthetic early → coag-neg staph; colon cancer → S. bovis.
  • Osler = ow (painful); Janeway = just a mark (painless).

Best answer
1) Name the sign: Osler’s node (tender, raised, erythematous lesion on finger pulp) — vs Janeway lesion (painless macule on palm/thenar eminence); image consistent with Osler’s node / Janeway-type peripheral stigmata. 2) Clinical diagnosis: infective endocarditis. 3) Best confirmatory test: multiple sets of blood cultures (before antibiotics) ± transthoracic/transoesophageal echocardiography — Modified Duke criteria: positive cultures + echo (vegetation/abscess/new regurgitation).
Peripheral stigmata: Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots (fundi), splinter haemorrhages, clubbing, splenomegaly, emboli. Always take ≥3 blood culture sets from separate sites before antibiotics; echo for complications (abscess, surgery if refractory/valve failure).

Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Crohn’s vs Ulcerative Colitis

Crohn’s disease — transmural, discontinuous (“skip”) inflammation anywhere from mouth to anus (terminal ileum commonest). Features: crampy abdominal pain (often RLQ), weight loss, chronic diarrhoea (may be non-bloody), fever, oral ulcers, perianal disease (fistulae, fissures, abscesses), extra-intestinal (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, uveitis, iritis, episcleritis, arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, gallstones (↓bile salt absorption), renal stones (oxalate), B₁₂ deficiency). Histology: transmural lymphoid aggregates, non-caseating granulomas. Complications: strictures, fistulae, abscess, malabsorption/anaemia.

Ulcerative colitis — mucosal, continuous inflammation starting at the rectum extending proximally (always involves rectum). Features: bloody diarrhoea with mucus, urgency, tenesmus, lower abdominal pain, fever in flares; extra-intestinal (primary sclerosing cholangitis!, uveitis, arthritis, erythema nodosum); colon cancer risk (surveillance colonoscopy from ~8–10 y). Histology: continuous cryptitis, crypt abscesses, goblet cell depletion, no granulomas.

Crohn’sUlcerative colitis
DistributionMouth→anus, skip lesions, terminal ileumRectum→ proximally, continuous, colon only
DepthTransmuralMucosa/submucosa
Blood in stoolVariableAlways (hallmark)
PerianalCommon (fistulae)Rare
GranulomasNon-caseating (30–50%)Absent
SurgeryNot curative (recurs)Curative (proctocolectomy)
Cancer riskModestSignificant (esp. PSC overlap)

Diagnosis: colonoscopy + biopsy (gold standard), faecal calprotectin (raised in IBD; normal in IBS — great separator), CRP/ESR, FBC (anaemia), albumin, iron/B₁₂, stool cultures (exclude infection), barium/MRI enterography for Crohn’s, ASCA+ (Crohn) vs p-ANCA+ (UC). IBD vs IBS: IBD = blood, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, raised CRP/calprotectin; IBS = normal tests, no blood, never nocturnal.

Management flares: UC mild–moderate → 5-ASA (mesalazine) oral/topical; moderate–severe → oral prednisolone → steroid-refractory/dependent → azathioprine/mercaptopurine, anti-TNF (infliximab/adalimumab), vedolizumab; acute severe colitis → IV hydrocortisone + DVT prophylaxis → rescue ciclosporin or colectomy if failing. Crohn’s: induction steroids; maintenance azathioprine/antimetabolite ± anti-TNF; surgery for strictures/fistulae/refractory disease (resection, not curative); nutritional therapy (exclusive enteral) in children; stop smoking (worsens Crohn’s).

Exam pearls
  • Oral ulcers + RLQ pain + weight loss + aphthous ulcers = Crohn’s. Bloody diarrhoea from rectum upward = UC.
  • Calprotectin separates IBD from IBS — cheap and non-invasive.
  • UC + PSC = highest colon cancer risk — colonoscopy surveillance.

Meningitis — CSF, Causative Organisms & Meningococcaemia

CSF interpretation — the exam table:

NeutrophilsGlucoseProteinPressureClassic
Bacterial↑↑ (pleocytosis, often >1000)LOW (<½ plasma)↑↑Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae b (unimmunised), neonates Group B strep / E. coli / Listeria (add amoxicillin for listeria cover!)
Viral (aseptic)Lymphocytes (early can be neutrophils)NormalNormal–mild↑Normal–mild↑Enterovirus, HSV-2, VZV, mumps — self-limiting; treat supportive
TuberculousLymphocytesVERY LOW (<2.2 mmol/L)VERY HIGH (1–5 g/L)↑↑Insidious; cranial nerve palsies (VI), basal exudates, hydrocephalus (dilated ventricles); “cobweb” clot; ADA >10; AFB rare — treat with RHZE + dexamethasone
Fungal (Cryptococcus, TB-like)LymphocytesLowHigh↑↑Immunocompromised (HIV) — India ink/CR antigens; amphotericin + flucytosine
GBS (neonatal)AnyAnyAny↑E. coli, GBS — ampicillin + gentamicin

Clinical features: fever, headache, neck stiffness (meningism), photophobia, vomiting, altered consciousness, seizures, non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash (meningococcaemia), Kernig’s (pain on knee extension with hip flexed), Brudzinski’s (neck flexion → hip flexion), bulging fontanelle (infants). Meningococcaemia → septic shock, DIC, Waterhouse–Friderichsen (bilateral adrenal haemorrhage).

Management: do NOT delay antibiotics for imaging/LP if unwell — immediate IV ceftriaxone/cefotaxime (add amoxicillin if <3 months or listeria risk), dexamethasone with first dose (↓hearing loss in pneumococcal; continue if confirmed), ABCDE + fluids/vasopressors (shock), isolate (droplet), notify public health, contact prophylaxis (ciprofloxacin/rifampicin) for household contacts, hearing test after recovery, treat complications (seizures, hydrocephalus — neurosurgery/VP shunt, SIADH).

Neurological exam findings asked (this SAQ): neck stiffness, Kernig’s/Brudzinski’s signs positive, photophobia, altered GCS, focal deficits, bulging fontanelle; complications — sensorineural deafness, seizures, hydrocephalus, subdural effusion, learning difficulty, shock/amputation (meningococcaemia).

Exam pearls
  • LP first only if NO contraindication & child stable; otherwise antibiotics first — never delay.
  • Low glucose + high protein + lymphocytes = TB; high PMN + low glucose = bacteria.
  • Non-blanching purpuric rash + fever = ceftriaxone STAT + public health notification.

A patient has matted lymphadenopathy, multiple neurological deficits and acute neck stiffness with fever. Brain MRI shows no mass lesion and no midline shift but dilated ventricles; CXR shows calcifications (possibly TB).
  1. What will you find in the CSF? (1 pt)
  2. What is the best test to confirm the diagnosis? (1 pt)
Best answer
1) CSF in tuberculous meningitis: lymphocytic pleocytosis (10–500/µL), VERY high protein (1–5 g/L), LOW glucose (<2.2 mmol/L), high opening pressure (cobweb clot) ± AFB on smear (rarely) — basilar exudates with hydrocephalus on MRI. 2) Best confirmatory test: CSF GeneXpert MTB/RIF (NAAT) ± AFB smear and culture, plus checking HIV; (adenosine deaminase >10 U/L supportive).
TB meningitis: insidious, cranial nerve palsies (VI/III/V/VII), hydrocephalus, hypodense basal exudates; high mortality — treat on suspicion with RHZE + adjuvant dexamethasone; treat 12 months; notify; contact trace; check HIV.

Pericardial Disease — Acute Pericarditis & Pericardial Effusion/Tamponade

Acute pericarditis — inflammation of the pericardium; commonest cause: viral (Coxsackie B, Echovirus, adenovirus); also post-MI (early peri-infarction/Dressler’s 2–6 wks), post-cardiac surgery, TB, uremia, autoimmune (SLE, RA), malignancy, radiotherapy, drugs, uraemia.

Features: central chest pain — sharp, pleuritic, WORSE LYING FLAT, BETTER SITTING FORWARD; pericardial friction rub (scratchy, best left sternal edge, leaning forward, breath held); fever, dyspnoea; ECG: widespread CONCAVE (“saddle-shaped”) ST elevation across multiple leads + PR depression (vs STEMI: regional, convex, reciprocal changes); raised troponin sometimes (myopericarditis); CRP/ESR↑.

Treatment: NSAIDs (ibuprofen/indomethacin) + colchicine (3 months) — first-line; avoid anticoagulants (haemorrhagic effusion risk); restrict exercise; steroids if refractory/contraindication (avoid in infective cases) or autoimmune; treat cause.

Pericardial effusion — fluid in pericardial sac; causes mirror pericarditis (+ uraemia, malignancy — lung/breast, hypothyroidism). Large/atypical (>3 cm) or any effusion → echocardiography (diagnostic). “Water-bottle” globular cardiac silhouette on CXR (this exam’s image).

Cardiac tamponade — life-threatening compression of the heart: Beck’s triad — hypotension + raised JVP + muffled heart sounds; pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg inspiratory SBP drop); tachycardia, dyspnoea, anxiety, cool periphery, electrical alternans (alternating QRS amplitude) on ECG, low-voltage QRS; echo = collapse of right atrium/ventricle, respiratory variation in flows. Emergency: urgent pericardiocentesis (echo-guided) — do NOT delay for imaging if obstructive shock.

Constrictive pericarditis (chronic) — RHF signs + Kussmaul’s sign (JVP rises with inspiration) + pericardial knock; TB commonest worldwide; treat: surgical pericardiectomy.

Exam pearls
  • Pain better sitting forward + friction rub + diffuse concave STE = pericarditis → NSAID + colchicine.
  • Globular water-bottle heart on CXR + SOB + raised JVP = pericardial effusion → echo.
  • Tamponade = Beck’s triad + pulsus paradoxus → urgent pericardiocentesis NOW.

Pituitary Disorders

Pituitary adenomas — benign; functioning (prolactinoma, GH — acromegaly, ACTH — Cushing’s, TSH rare) vs non-functioning. Mass effects (any macroadenoma >10 mm): bitemporal hemianopia (optic chiasm compression — starts superiorly, respects vertical meridian), headache, hypopituitarism (hormone deficits — order: GH → gonadotrophins → TSH → ACTH last), cavernous sinus invasion (CN III/IV/VI palsies).

Prolactinoma — commonest functioning adenoma. Women: oligomenorrhoea/amenorrhoea + galactorrhoea ± infertility; men: hypogonadism, low libido, erectile dysfunction, gynaecomastia (earlier macro), bitemporal hemianopia. Prolactin very high (>5000 mIU/L usually macroadenoma; >10,000 = macroprolactinoma likely); check TSH (primary hypothyroidism → TRH → prolactin↑ — “pseudoprolactinoma”) and drugs (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, SSRIs, verapamil, opiates). Treatment: dopamine agonists — cabergoline/bromocriptine (first-line — shrinks tumour & normalises PRL); surgery (trans-sphenoidal) if intolerant/failed.

Acromegaly — GH excess (usually pituitary somatotroph adenoma): frontal bossing, prognathism, macroglossia, interdental spacing, coarse facies, large spade-like hands/feet, thick skin, sweating, carpal tunnel, sleep apnoea, diabetes, hypertension, colonic polyps, cardiomyopathy. Diagnosis: IGF-1 ↑; OGTT — GH fails to suppress (<1 mU/L); pituitary MRI. Treatment: trans-sphenoidal surgery (first-line); octreotide/lanreotide (somatostatin analogues), pegvisomant (GH-receptor antagonist), cabergoline; radiotherapy if refractory. Screen: colonoscopy, echo, glucose, sleep study.

Cushing’s disease — ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma: central obesity, moon facies, striae, proximal myopathy, diabetes, osteoporosis; diagnose: 24-h urinary free cortisol / low-dose dexamethasone suppression test; IPSS for localization; TS surgery.

Sheehan’s syndrome — postpartum pituitary necrosis after severe postpartum haemorrhage → panhypopituitarism: failure of lactation (first sign) + amenorrhoea + fatigue + loss of pubic/axillary hair + hypothyroidism/hypoadrenalism; treat with hormone replacement (thyroxine, hydrocortisone, oestrogen/progesterone, GH, fertility — gonadotrophins).

Pituitary apoplexy — sudden haemorrhage/infarction (this exam): sudden severe headache + visual loss (bitemporal) + acute ophthalmoplegia (CN III palsy) + meningism ± shock — emergency: IV hydrocortisone, urgent MRI, neurosurgery/ophthalmology; treat as adrenal crisis.

Visual fields: bitemporal hemianopia (chiasmal), homonymous hemianopia (retro-chiasmal — optic tract/radiations), tunnel vision (psychogenic).

Exam pearls
  • High prolactin + menstrual/galactorrhoea → cabergoline — but FIRST exclude pregnancy (β-HCG) and hypothyroidism/drugs.
  • Postpartum haemorrhage + lactation failure + amenorrhoea = Sheehan.
  • Big hands + jaw + field defect = acromegaly → IGF-1 + OGTT.
  • Sudden headache + chiasmal signs = apoplexy — hydrocortisone + urgent imaging/surgery.

Pleural Effusion — Light’s Criteria & Causes

Light’s criteria (exudate if ANY one): (1) pleural fluid/serum protein > 0.5; (2) pleural fluid/serum LDH > 0.6; (3) pleural LDH > 2/3 upper normal serum LDH. Otherwise transudate.

TransudateExudate
Mechanism↑ hydrostatic / ↓ oncotic pressure↑ capillary permeability / ↓ lymphatic drainage
CausesHeart failure (commonest), cirrhosis (hepatic hydrothorax — right), nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminaemia, peritoneal dialysis, constrictive pericarditis, SVC obstructionParapneumonic/empyema, malignancy (lung, breast, mesothelioma — this exam), TB, PE, pancreatitis (left), RA/SLE, trauma/haemothorax, chylothorax, post-CABG
Fluid appearanceClear, strawCloudy/turbid/bloody/chylous

Approach: CXR (blunting of costophrenic angle; >200–300 mL visible; meniscus sign; massive → mediastinal shift away) + ultrasound-guided diagnostic aspiration (thoracentesis) — pH, protein, LDH, glucose, cell count (neutrophils = parapneumonic; lymphocytes = TB/malignancy), cytology, Gram stain/culture, AFB/ADA (TB), triglycerides (chylothorax >1.2 mmol/L), amylase (pancreatitis).

Parapneumonic effusion — uncomplicated: antibiotics; drain if: pH <7.2, glucose <3.3, LDH >1000, loculations on USS/CT, positive Gram stain, or large (>half hemithorax)/sepsis (chest drain ± fibrinolytics ± surgery/VATS).

Malignant effusion: cytology (sensitivity ~60%); repeat aspiration; indwelling pleural catheter or talc pleurodesis for symptom control.

This exam (2017 smoker, massive left effusion, weight loss, night sweats): X-ray findings: massive left pleural effusion with opacification of lower hemithorax, blunting costophrenic angle/obscured left hemidiaphragm, mediastinal shift to the right. Investigations: diagnostic thoracentesis (cytology, ADA/AFB/Gram/culture, Light’s), CT chest (mass, pleural thickening), bronchoscopy/biopsy, US. Top 2 diagnoses: malignant pleural effusion (bronchogenic carcinoma) and TB effusion.

Exam pearls
  • Light’s: protein >0.5, LDH >0.6, LDH >2/3 ULN — any ONE → exudate.
  • Fever + effusion + low pH/glucose = empyema — drain.
  • Lymphocytic exudate + high ADA = TB — treat as TB effusion (anti-TB + steroids sometimes).

Pneumonia — Consolidation

Consolidation vs effusion vs pneumothorax — the bedside table:

Vocal fremitusPercussionBreath soundsAdded
Consolidation (pneumonia)IncreasedDullBronchial (harsh, expiratory component)Crackles, ± pleural rub; dullness definite
Pleural effusionDecreased/absentStony dullDecreasedBronchial above fluid; meniscus on CXR
PneumothoraxDecreasedHyperresonantAbsentSurgical emphysema; tracheal shift if tension
Collapse/atelectasisDecreasedDullDecreased/absentTracheal deviation TOWARD side; hyperinflation elsewhere

Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) — CURB-65 (confusion, urea >7, RR ≥30, SBP <90 or DBP ≤60, age ≥65; 1 point each): 0–1 home oral amoxicillin; 2 admit (IV benzylpenicillin + clarithromycin); ≥3 severe (IV co-amoxiclav + clarithromycin ± ICU). Common organisms: S. pneumoniae (commonest), H. influenzae (COPD), Mycoplasma (young, dry cough, extrapulmonary — cold agglutinins), Legionella (air-con/water systems, hyponatraemia, GI upset — urinary antigen), Klebsiella (alcoholics — red-currant sputum), S. aureus (post-influenza — cavitation).

This exam: increased fremitus + dullness + bronchial breathing = lobar consolidation. 4-year-old with bronchial breathing + image of opacification = lobar pneumonia — most common organism in a child = S. pneumoniae (pneumococcus).

Exam pearls
  • Increased fremitus + dull + bronchial = consolidation.
  • Child’s lobar pneumonia = pneumococcus; adults CAP = pneumococcus; atypicals in the young.
  • Pleural effusion = decreased fremitus + stony dull; pneumothorax = hyperresonant.

Poisoning & Overdose — Toxidromes

This exam: homeless + unconscious + respiratory acidosis (high CO₂) + RR 30 (opioid typically depresses — note the inconsistency; some written stems pair “respiratory acidosis + RR 30” with salicylate overdose (mixed respiratory alkalosis → high anion gap metabolic acidosis with compensation — but the pH in chronic salicylate intoxication can be acidemia). Empty syringe + RR 6 = opioid intoxication (respiratory depression → low minute ventilation → CO₂ retention → respiratory acidosis) — the classic pairing.

ToxidromeKey featuresTreatment
Opioids (heroin, morphine)CNS + respiratory depression (low RR!), miosis (pinpoint pupils), comaNaloxone IV (0.4–2 mg, repeat), ventilation support
SalicylatesTinnitus, vomiting, hyperventilation (early respiratory alkalosis) → metabolic acidosis (mixed), sweating, fever, confusionABCs, activated charcoal (<1–2 h), urinary alkalisation (sodium bicarbonate), dialysis if severe (>700 mg/L / renal failure / altered conscious / refractory acidosis)
ParacetamolOften delayed: days 1–2 asymptomatic (± nausea), day 3–5 fulminant hepatic failure (AST/ALT in thousands, INR↑)N-acetylcysteine (best <8 h; effective up to 24 h); check level at 4 h & plot nomogram
Methanol/ethylene glycol (toxic alcohols)Visual loss (methanol) / flank pain & hypocalcaemia (ethylene glycol), high anion gap + osmolar gap + acidosisFomepizole (alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor) or ethanol; sodium bicarbonate; haemodialysis
BenzodiazepinesSedation, ataxia, respiratory depression (mild), normal pupilsSupportive; flumazenil rarely (seizure risk)
Stimulants (cocaine/amphetamine)Hypertension, tachycardia, mydriasis, hyperthermia, agitation, seizures; cocaine → chest pain (ACS)Benzodiazepines; avoid pure beta-blockers (unopposed α); cooling
Anticholinergic“Mad as a hatter, blind as a bat, red as a beet, dry as a bone, hot as a hare” — dilated pupils, tachycardia, urinary retention, hyperthermiaSupportive; physostigmine (rare, specialist)

General: ABCDE first; call poison control/National Poisons Information Service; activated charcoal within 1–2 h (protected airway only!); avoid inducing vomiting; check glucose, ECG (QRS/QTc), U&E/osmolality/lactate; whole-bowel irrigation (iron/lithium); MDAC (multiple-dose charcoal) for carbamazepine/theophylline; specific antidotes per above.

Exam pearls
  • Empty syringe + RR 6 = opioid → naloxone.
  • Tinnitus + acidosis + hyperventilation = salicylate → bicarbonate.
  • Paracetamol day 3–5 liver failure — N-acetylcysteine works even late.
  • Methanol (blind) / ethylene (renal) — both high anion gap: fomepizole.

Pulmonary Function Tests — Reading the Pattern

The 6-number framework:

FEV₁FVCFEV₁/FVCDLCOFRC/TLCPattern
Obstructive↓↓N or ↓<0.7N or ↓ (emphysema ↓)↑ (hyperinflation)Asthma (+reversibility ≥12%/200 mL), COPD, bronchiectasis
Restrictive↓↓↓↓N or ↑ (≥0.7)↓ (parenchymal) or N (chest wall/ neuromuscular)↓↓ILD/fibrosis, scoliosis, obesity hypoventilation, neuromuscular, pleural effusion
Mixed↓↓↓↓<0.7↓variableSevere COPD + restriction, cf bronchiectasis + effusion

Which numbers change (exam question): in restriction, FEV₁/FVC is NOT reduced (both fall proportionally); FEV₁, FVC, PEF, TLC, VC, FRC all fall; DLCO falls when the lung parenchyma is stiff (ILD, emphysema) and stays normal in extraparenchymal restriction (obesity, chest wall, diaphragmatic weakness).

RA lung involvement (this exam): progressive dyspnoea + RA → restrictive defect + LOW DLCO (RA-ILD — usual interstitial pneumonia pattern); check HRCT, PFTs; treat: stop smoking, steroids/immunosuppressants per MDT; pirfenidone/nintedanib for fibrotic ILD.

Exam pearls
  • Obstruction: FEV₁/FVC <0.7; restriction: ratio normal/high + ↓TLC; mixed: ratio low + ↓TLC.
  • DLCO low = ILD (or emphysema/pulmonary vascular disease).
  • Asthma = obstruction WITH reversibility.

Acute Rheumatic Fever

Definition: systemic autoimmune disease after Group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes) pharyngitis (never skin); 2–4 weeks after infection; type II hypersensitivity (molecular mimicry) — antibodies cross-react with valve/joint/brain antigens. Peak 5–15 y.

Jones criteria (2015): need evidence of preceding GAS infection (↑ASO titre or anti-DNase B, positive throat swab, or recent scarlet fever) + 2 major OR 1 major + 2 minor:

MAJOR (JONES)MINOR
Joints — migratory polyarthritis (knees/ankles/wrists/elbows — “moves from joint to joint”)
O — carditis (new murmur — mitral regurgitation (apical pansystolic → axilla), tachycardia, pericarditis/pleuritic pain, or echo valve regurgitation)
N — subcutaneous nodules (extensor surfaces, painless)
E — erythema marginatum (pink, ringed, non-pruritic rash on trunk)
S — Sydenham’s chorea (involuntary movements, emotional lability — may appear months later)		Fever; arthralgia; raised ESR/CRP; prolonged PR interval; previous RF/rheumatic heart disease

This exam: migratory polyarthritis + ASO+ + ESR/CRP↑ + new apical pansystolic murmur radiating to axilla = rheumatic fever with carditis (mitral regurgitation).

Management: eradicate strep — penicillin V/benzathine penicillin IM (or erythromycin); NSAIDs (naproxen/ibuprofen) for arthritis (avoid aspirin in children — Reye’s); severe carditis → prednisolone; bed rest while active; SECONDARY PROPHYLAXIS (the most important): penicillin V 250 mg BD (or benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU IM every 3–4 weeks) for 10 years or until age 21–25 (longer — life / to 40 y — if carditis); echo/serial follow-up for valvular disease; echo every 1–5 years; dental prophylaxis if prosthetic valve; avoid NSAIDs if renal issues.

Exam pearls
  • Migratory polyarthritis + post-strep + new MR murmur = RF with carditis.
  • Jones: 2 major or 1 major + 2 minor + evidence of GAS (ASO).
  • MS mid-diastolic murmur comes years later — acute RF gives MR (pansystolic).
  • Secondary prophylaxis benzathine penicillin every 3–4 weeks ×10 years — stops progression to chronic rheumatic heart disease.

Seizures & Epilepsy

Semiology first — type defines treatment:

TypeFeaturesDrug of choice
Absence (typical)Child 4–10 y; sudden staring/“in a daze”, eyelid flutter, 5–15 s, many per day, no post-ictal confusion; 3 Hz spike-waveEthosuximide (or valproate)
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME)Morning myoclonic jerks of limbs/shoulders + GTC seizures + absence; onset 12–18 y; sleep deprivation/alcohol trigger; 4–6 Hz polyspike-waveSodium valproate (females of childbearing age: levetiracetam/lamotrigine)
Temporal lobe (focal impaired awareness)Aura (epigastric rising / déjà vu / burning smell — “burning leather”), staring, lip-smacking/automatisms (chewing, picking), post-ictal confusionCarbamazepine / lamotrigine / levetiracetam
Generalized tonic-clonicSudden fall, tongue biting, incontinence, post-ictal drowsiness/confusionValproate / levetiracetam
Infantile spasms (West syndrome)3–12 months; salaam attacks — sudden flexion of head/trunk/limbs in clusters; hypsarrhythmia on EEG; developmental regression — treat with vigabatrin ± ACTH; think tuberous sclerosisVigabatrin ± steroids
Febrile seizure6 mo–5 y, fever, generalized, <15 min, single in 24 h = SIMPLE (benign, ~1% later epilepsy); complex: focal / >15 min / recurrence within 24 hReassurance + safety (side position, nothing in mouth); treat fever does NOT prevent recurrence; benzodiazepine if >5 min
Non-epileptic (psychogenic) seizureEyes closed, prolonged fluctuating jerks, pelvic thrusting, crying/emotional context (exam stress), NO incontinence/tongue bite/injury/post-ictal state; normal EEGCBT/psychology — NOT anti-epileptics

Management of acute seizure (this exam): ABCDE + position + O₂ → abortive drug if >5 min: midazolam (buccal/IM/IV) or lorazepam IV or diazepam IV/PR — repeat once → if still seizing (status): second-line levetiracetam / phenytoin / valproate (>15–20 min) → refractory (>40 min): phenobarbital or anaesthesia + ICU. Maintenance after abortion of prolonged convulsion: continue anti-seizure prophylaxis with sodium valproate (or leviteracetam), not single-agent benzodiazepines alone.

Risk factors for epilepsy after febrile convulsion: complex febrile seizure, family history of epilepsy, pre-existing neurodevelopmental delay, short interval from fever onset to seizure (<1 h). Simple febrile = near-population risk.

Exam pearls
  • “Smell burning leather + lip smacking + staring” = temporal lobe epilepsy. “Morning limb jerks” = JME. “Exam-time jerks, eyes closed, crying, no incontinence” = psychogenic.
  • Absence = ethosuximide. Status: midazolam → phenytoin/levetiracetam → phenobarbital.
  • Febrile seizure ≠ epilepsy; complex features are the risk.

Spinal Cord & Brainstem Crossings — Brown-Séquard & Others

Key anatomy: Corticospinal tract & dorsal columns (vibration/proprioception) decussate HIGH (medullary pyramids) → lesions below cause ipsilateral weakness/proprioception loss. Spinothalamic tract (pain/temperature) decussates 1–2 levels BELOW its entry → lesions cause contralateral pain/temperature loss below the lesion.

Brown-Séquard syndrome (cord hemisection): ipsilateral spastic weakness + ipsilateral proprioception/vibration loss + contralateral pain/temperature loss (starting ~2 levels below) + ipsilateral LMN signs at the level + Horner’s if cervical (sympathetics at T1). Causes: trauma (penetrating), tumour, transverse myelitis, MS, disc herniation, cervical spondylotic myelopathy.

Cervical myelopathy: progressive UMN signs (spastic paraparesis, hyperreflexia, upgoing plantars) + hand wasting/weakness (LMN at level) + gait change + neck pain/stiffness; MRI is diagnostic; decompression for progressive/symptomatic disease.

This exam’s SAQ (right-sided ptosis + miosis + arm/leg numbness over days): lesion = lower cervical cord (T1-level — intramedullary) with ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome (T1 sympathetic outflow) + bilateral sensory level + UMN legs. Causes: intramedullary tumour (glioma/ependymoma), transverse myelitis (inflammatory — idiopathic/MS/NMO/post-infectious), syrinx, metastasis/compression (extrinsic); (disc disease less typical with Brown-Séquard pattern at C7-T1). Investigations: MRI whole cervical cord with gadolinium (first-line) + CSF analysis (cells, protein, oligoclonal bands, IgG index, viral PCR) ± visual evoked potentials, neuro-immunology (AQP4, MOG), work-up for infection (TB).

Central cord syndrome (syringomyelia): cape-like loss of pain/temperature in arms with preserved touch; anterior spinal artery syndrome: bilateral motor + pain/temp loss, preserved proprioception; cauda equina: saddle anaesthesia + urinary retention + bilateral LMN leg weakness (emergency).

Exam pearls
  • Hemisection: ipsilateral weakness + proprioception loss, contralateral pain/temp loss.
  • Horner’s + cord signs = T1 level — look there (MRI).
  • Myelopathy = MRI first, always.
  • Sphincter/saddle loss = cauda equina = emergency surgery.

#137MCQ edited2019-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-bdb39ef7
A patient has spastic paralysis with wasting (possibly a long-standing UMN lesion) and weakness in the arms and hands. What is the diagnosis?

  • B. Motor neuron disease
  • C. Stroke
  • D. Brachial plexopathy

Best answer
B. Motor neuron disease
UMN signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia) in the legs + LMN signs (wasting, fasciculations, weakness) in the hands/arms, no sensory loss = motor neuron disease (ALS). Cervical myelopathy would have sensory level/pathological hand signs only at the level; MS = episodic, younger.
#138MCQ edited2019-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-344d5111
A patient has loss of pain and temperature on the right side and weakness on the left side. Where is the lesion?

  • B. Right spinal cord
  • C. Left brainstem
  • D. Right brainstem
  • E. Right cerebral hemisphere
Best answer
A. Left spinal cord (hemisection / Brown-Sequard)
Ipsilateral weakness + ipsilateral loss of vibration/proprioception + contralateral pain/temperature loss (below the lesion) = Brown-Séquard (cord hemisection). Pain/T crosses within 1–2 segments (spinothalamic) — so contralateral loss starts ~2 levels BELOW the lesion; weakness/proprioception ipsilateral and below. Side = side of weakness.

Stroke & Transient Ischaemic Attack — Localization

Hemisphere syndromes:

TerritoryDeficits
MCA (commonest)Contralateral face & arm > leg weakness, contralateral sensory loss, homonymous hemianopia, aphasia (dominant), neglect (non-dominant), gaze deviation toward lesion
ACAContralateral leg > arm weakness, urinary incontinence, grasp reflex, behavioural change
PCAContralateral homonymous hemianopia (macula-sparing), memory loss, Alexia without agraphia (dominant)

Brainstem/lacunar (cross findings = ipsilateral cranial nerve + contralateral body — the exam’s favourite):

SyndromeSiteFeatures
Weber’sParamedian midbrain (III fascicles + corticospinal)Ipsilateral CN III palsy (“down and out”, ptosis, dilated pupil) + contralateral UMN hemiparesis (face + limbs); ± altered sensorium if haemorrhage/large lesion
Millard–Gubler / FovillePons (VI + VII + corticospinal)Ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy (can’t look that way) + LMN facial palsy + contralateral hemiparesis
Wallenberg (lateral medullary)PICA (posterior inferior cerebellar a.)Ipsilateral: facial pain/temp loss (spinal trigeminal), Horner’s, limb ataxia, nystagmus, dysphagia/hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus), vertigo (vestibular nuclei); contralateral: body pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic); NO weakness — classic “crossed” sensory pattern
BenediktMidbrain (red nucleus + III)CN III palsy + contralateral involuntary movements/tremor
Lateral pontineAICALike Wallenberg + ipsilateral facial weakness & hearing loss (CN VII/VIII)

Pure sensory / pure motor / ataxic hemiparesis / clumsy-hand dysarthria = lacunar (thalamus = pure sensory; internal capsule/corona radiata = pure motor; base of pons = ataxic hemiparesis). Thalamus → isolated hemisensory loss (this exam).

Acute management: ABCDE, glucose, seizures controlled → non-contrast CT brain (exclude haemorrhage) → eligibility for thrombolysis (IV alteplase within 4.5 h) or thrombectomy (large vessel occlusion, up to 24 h in selected) → admit stroke unit; antiplatelet (aspirin 300 mg) if ischaemic and not thrombolysed; BP control (do NOT lower acutely unless >220/120 or thrombolysing); swallow assessment before feeding; DVT prophylaxis; secondary prevention (statin, antiplatelet/anticoagulant for AF, BP, diabetes, smoking); speech & language, PT/OT, MDT; carotid imaging/CT angiography for anterior circulation TIAs.

Exam pearls
  • Crossed signs (ipsilateral CN + contralateral body) = brainstem, NOT cortex.
  • Down-and-out eye + contralateral weakness = Weber’s (midbrain). Gaze palsy + facial weakness + weakness = Millard–Gubler (pons). PICA = Wallenberg.
  • Isolated hemisensory loss = thalamus.
  • Never sit on chest pain/stroke red flags — CT first, thrombolyse if eligible.

#67MCQ2019-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-ec86bc2d

Syncope & Loss of Consciousness

Classify first:

FeaturesExamples
Vasovagal (neural reflex)Prodrome (hot, sweaty, nauseated, pallor, tunnel vision, situational — standing in queue/supermarket, heat, pain, emotion), rapid recovery, normal exam & vitalsMost common (this exam: collapse in supermarket, vitals normal → vasovagal syncope)
CardiogenicNo prodrome — sudden, exertional, or supine; family history of sudden death; structural heart disease/murmur; abnormal ECG; dangerousArrhythmia (VT/SVT — ECG), HOCM, long-QT, severe aortic stenosis, PE, dissection, MI — ALL need echo + ECG + troponin
Orthostatic (postural)On standing — drop SBP ≥20 or DBP ≥10; elderly, volume depletion, drugs (antihypertensives, diuretics, α-blockers, nitrates), autonomic dysfunction (diabetes/Parkinson’s)Tilt-table if unclear
NeurologicalConvulsive jerks → EPILEPSY until proven otherwise; tongue biting, incontinence, post-ictal confusionIncontinence excludes syncope (mostly) — but see “convulsive syncope” (myoclonic jerks)
Psychiatric/metabolicPanic attack; hypoglycaemia (sweating, tremor, confusion — check glucose); anaemiaPsychogenic non-epileptic attack — eyes closed, no injury

This exam: supermarket collapse, normal vitals, no jerks/incontinence → vasovagal syncope (A).

Red flags (cardiogenic until proven otherwise): syncope ON exertion; supine syncope; chest pain; palpitation before syncope; family history of sudden death <40 y; abnormal ECG (WPW/long QT/Brugada/complete heart block); murmur; structural disease — → admit, continuous telemetry, troponin, echo, electrophysiology.

Exam pearls
  • Supermarket + prodrome + normal vitals = vasovagal. Exertional + no prodrome = cardiac — never miss.
  • Check glucose in every unexplained collapse.
  • ECG is the minimum for every syncope admission.
