Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Definition: multisystem autoimmune disease — antinuclear antibodies (ANA) + lupus-specific antibodies: anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith. Female >> male (9:1), childbearing age; HLA-DR2/DR3; complement-consuming immune-complex disease.

ACR-like criteria (≥4):

  • Malar “butterfly” rash — this exam (image): erythematous rash across cheeks & nasal bridge SPARING the nasolabial folds (photosensitive)
  • Discoid rash — raised, scaly, atrophic plaques (leaves scars)
  • Photosensitivity — rash after sun
  • Oral/nasal ulcers
  • Non-erosive arthritis (≥2 peripheral joints, tender/swollen)
  • Serositis — pleuritis/pericarditis ± effusion
  • Renal — persistent proteinuria or cellular casts (lupus nephritis) — 40% develop; check urine/PCR
  • Neuro — seizures or psychosis (other: headache, mood)
  • Haematological — haemolytic anaemia, leucopaenia, lymphopaenia, thrombocytopaenia
  • Immunological — anti-dsDNA or anti-Smith, ANA+, low complement (C3/C4 LOW), antiphospholipid (lupus anticoagulant/anticardiolipin/β2GPI → recurrent thrombosis + miscarriage + thrombocytopaenia)

Complications & overlap: ILD/pulmonary fibrosis (this exam: dry cough + exertional dyspnoea → SLE-ILD) — HRCT + PFTs; pulmonary hypertension; Libman–Sacks endocarditis (sterile vegetations); nephritis; premature atherosclerosis. Differentiating RA from SLE (this exam): SLE = non-erosive, reversible deformities (Jaccoud’s), malar rash, low complement, dsDNA+, multisystem (renal/CNS/haem), no nodules; RA = erosive symmetric small-joint arthritis with morning stiffness >1 h, RF/anti-CCP+, rheumatoid nodules, spares DIP.

Management: avoid sun/photoprotection; hydroxychloroquine (ALL patients — skin/joints, reduces flares/mortality); NSAIDs (arthralgia); corticosteroids (moderate–severe flares); immunosuppressants — mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide (nephritis/neuropsychiatric), azathioprine maintenance; biologics (belimumab, rituximab) refractory; ACEi/ARB (renal); aspirin/heparin for antiphospholipid (recurrent thrombosis → warfarin); vaccinate, monitor (BP, urine, FBC, complement, dsDNA).

Exam pearls
  • Malar rash spares nasolabial folds; discoid = scarring; both photosensitive.
  • dsDNA + low C3/C4 = active lupus; Smith = specific.
  • Hydroxychloroquine for everyone. Nephritis → mycophenolate; monitor urine.
  • Drug-induced lupus: hydralazine, isoniazid, procainamide, minocycline — anti-histone, milder, no renal.

Thyroid Disorders — Hyperthyroidism & Thyroiditis

Hyperthyroidism patterns:

Graves’Toxic multinodular goitre / solitary toxic noduleThyroiditis (subacute/postpartum)Factitious

2019 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Tropical & Travel-Related Infections

Dengue (commonest exam travel fever): fever + retro-orbital pain + severe myalgia (“break-bone fever”) + maculopapular rash + headache + LOW PLATELETS ± bleeding (gums/petechiae) — travel to India/SE Asia/Caribbean/Latin America; leucopenia, thrombocytopenia, rising haematocrit (plasma leak — warning signs: abdominal pain, bleeding, shock — “dengue haemorrhagic fever”); diagnosed by NS1 antigen/dengue serology (IgM), PCR; treatment = supportive — fluids (ORAL rehydration/IV), paracetamol (NO aspirin/NSAIDs/ibuprofen — bleeding risk), rest; admit if warning signs.

Malaria: cyclical fevers (every 48 h — P. vivax/ovale; 72 h — P. malariae), headache, rigors, sweats, hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia after travel to sub-Saharan Africa; P. falciparum = severe (seizures, coma, hypoglycaemia, renal failure, jaundice, severe anaemia, high parasitaemia); diagnosis: thick & thin film ×3 (ring forms — “headphone”/banana gametocytes) or RDT (antigen); urgent: artesunate/ACT for falciparum; chloroquine + primaquine for vivax; notify notifiable disease.

Chikungunya: fever + severe polyarthralgia (debilitating, small joints) + rash; lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia; self-limiting weeks; serology; supportive.

Typhoid (S. Typhi/Paratyphi): prolonged stepwise fever, relative bradycardia, abdominal pain, constipation (or “pea soup” diarrhoea), rose spots (trunk), hepatosplenomegaly — India/SE Asia/ traveller; leucopaenia; blood cultures (1st week) / stool; ceftriaxone/azithromycin; 10–14 days.

Zika: mild fever + rash + conjunctivitis + arthralgia; congenital Zika syndrome — microcephaly if infection in pregnancy; avoid pregnancy 2 months after exposure.

Leptospirosis — water/rats; biphasic fever, conjunctival suffusion (no discharge!), myalgia, jaundice + renal failure (Weil’s disease).

Exam pearls
  • Travel + fever + retro-orbital pain/rash/low platelets = dengue. Africa + cyclical fever + film = malaria. India + rash + low platelets = dengue.
  • Never give aspirin/NSAIDs in dengue.
  • Malaria: treat falciparum urgently; thick/thin film ×3.

Tuberculosis

Pathogenesis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (airborne) → primary Ghon focus → reactivation in apices (high O₂) when cell-mediated immunity falls (HIV, diabetes, steroids, malnutrition) — caseating granulomas (Langhans giant cells).

Forms (by site):

  • Pulmonary — fever, night sweats, weight loss, chronic cough (± haemoptysis), apical infiltrate/cavitation on CXR, homeless/overcrowding/immunosuppressed; miliary — diffuse millet-seed infiltrates.
  • Extrapulmonary — TB lymphadenitis (bilateral cervical nodes, “cold abscesses” with sinus tracts — scrofuloderma — this exam’s homeless man), TB meningitis (basilar, CN VI palsy, very low CSF glucose/very high protein, lymphocytes — treat + dexamethasone), Pott’s disease (spinal TB — gibbus deformity, PPD/MRI), pleural TB (unilateral lymphocytic exudate, high ADA), TB pericarditis/miliary.
  • TB in HIV — atypical CXR, disseminated disease, drug interactions (rifampicin with ART).

Diagnosis: CXR (apical cavities/infiltrates, miliary, effusion, hilar nodes); sputum smear + culture (gold standard) — AFB smear, culture (2–6 wks), GeneXpert MTB/RIF (PCR) — rapid, detects rifampicin resistance — first-line test; tuberculin skin test (Mantoux — latent), IGRA (latent TB; not for active); node biopsy (caseating granuloma + AFB) for TB lymphadenitis; FBC/CRP/ESR; HIV test.

Treatment (RIPE): 2 months HRZE + 4 months HR (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol → then INH + rifampicin ×4 months); isoniazid neuropathy → pyridoxine (vit B6); ethambutol → optic neuritis (check colour vision/acuity); rifampicin → orange fluids + drug interactions; monitor LFTs; drug-resistant TB (MDR — RIF + INH resistant) → specialist regimens (bedaquiline etc.). Latent TB: INH ×6–9 months or rifapentine-INH 3 months.

This exam: gibbus → Pott’s disease (A); sacroiliitis in a child → brucellosis (B). Homeless + cervical node discharge + fever + chronic cough → TB. Active TB CXR (Case 4): upper-lobe/apical infiltrate ± cavitation ± hilar lymphadenopathy; tests: sputum AFB smear/culture (or GeneXpert), tuberculin test/IGRA (but tests = sputum microbiology + imaging/biopsy).

Exam pearls
  • GeneXpert is the rapid first test; culture is gold standard.
  • Gibbus = Pott’s. Cervical “cold abscess” with sinus = scrofuloderma = TB.
  • RIPE × 2 months then RI × 4; B6 with INH; watch liver and eyes (EMB).

Urolithiasis — Stone Composition

Stone types (this exam: picture of a stone):

StoneFrequencyX-rayShape/appearanceUrineAssociations
Calcium oxalate~75%Radio-opaque“Envelope”/dumbbell (monohydrate), square envelope (dihydrate)AcidicHypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, Crohn’s/malabsorption, ethylene glycol
Calcium phosphate~10%Radio-opaqueAmorphous/wedgeAlkalineHyperparathyroidism, RTA (type 1)
Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate)~10%Radio-opaqueStaghorn calculus (branching)AlkalineUrease-splitting infection — Proteus, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas; recurrent UTIs; women
Uric acid~5–10%RADIO-LUCENT (needs CT/USS)Flat rhomboid/rosetteAcidicGout, myeloproliferative, chemo (tumour lysis), dehydration
Cystine1–2%Weakly opaque (“ground glass”)HexagonalAcidicCystinuria — autosomal recessive, young onset, recurrent large stones
Drug stones (indinavir)rareRadiolucent——Protease inhibitors

Exam answer: image shows calcium-oxalate “square envelope” crystals → Calcium (A).

Presentation & management: colicky flank pain radiating to groin + restlessness + haematuria + nausea; diagnosis: non-contrast CT KUB (gold standard) ± USS (pregnancy); analgesia (NSAIDs — diclofenac — reduce ureteric spasm; opioids if inadequate), drink plenty, α-blockers (tamsulosin) for 5–10 mm ureteric stones (medical expulsive), spontaneous passage <5 mm, ESWL (extra-corporeal shock wave lithotripsy) for 10–20 mm renal/ureteric, ureterorenoscopy/PCNL for larger/complex/lower ureteric, percutaneous nephrolithotomy for staghorn; infection above an obstructed system = emergency decompression (ureteric stent/nephrostomy) + antibiotics. Prevent recurrence: fluids >2.5 L/day, ↓salt, moderate animal protein, thiazide for hypercalciuria, allopurinol for uric acid, treat infection.

Exam pearls
  • Hexagonal = cystine; staghorn = struvite + Proteus; envelope = calcium oxalate; rhomboid = uric acid.
  • Radiolucent (CT-only) = uric acid.
  • Colicky flank→groin pain = stone; NSAIDs are the analgesic of choice.

Valvular Heart Disease — Aortic Stenosis

Aortic stenosis (AS) — the exam’s favourite valve:

  • Causes: degenerative calcific (≥65 y — commonest); congenital bicuspid aortic valve (younger — 50s); rheumatic (with MS).
  • Symptoms: “SAD” — Syncope, Angina (exertional), Dyspnoea (heart failure) — symptomatic severe AS = very poor prognosis (2–3 y mean survival) → needs AVR (aortic valve replacement) urgently.
  • Signs (this exam): ejection systolic murmur, crescendo-decrescendo, right upper sternal border, radiating to the CAROTIDS; S2 soft/absent (A2 delayed); slow-rising, plateau pulse — “pulsus parvus et tardus” (this exam); narrow pulse pressure; sustained heaving apex (LVH); fourth heart sound (S4).
  • Aortic sclerosis (this exam) = calcified but NON-obstructing valve, soft systolic ejection murmur, normal pulse, no symptoms — benign; congenital bicuspid = young with ESM; MR = pansystolic apex→axilla; HOCM = ESM that gets LOUDER with standing/Valsalva; PS = LUSB ESM.
  • Investigations: echo (valve area, gradient, LV function) — diagnostic and severity assessment; ECG (LVH), CXR (calcified valve, post-stenotic dilatation); exercise test NOT in severe symptomatic AS (dangerous).
  • Treatment: AVR (surgical or TAVI) if symptomatic severe AS or asymptomatic with severe AS + LV dysfunction/positive exercise — no medical therapy improves survival (avoid ACEi/nitrates/vasodilators — reduce preload and precipitate collapse); manage hypertension carefully; TAVI for high surgical risk; balloon valvuloplasty = bridge in pregnancy.
  • Pulse table (memorise): AS = parvus et tardus (slow-rising, low volume); AR = collapsing (Water hammer); bisferiens = HOCM/mixed AS+AR; paradoxus = tamponade; alternans = severe LV failure; pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg inspiratory drop — tamponade/constriction/asthma.
Exam pearls
  • ESM right upper sternal edge → carotids, slow-rising pulse, soft A2 = AS — echo, then AVR when symptomatic.
  • Exertional syncope + AS = critical — admit for urgent valve assessment.
  • No vasodilators in severe AS.

#61MCQ2019-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-7307ae7e
A 70-year-old patient presents with a 2-month history of shortness of breath. On examination, an ejection systolic murmur is heard. Which of the following is the cause of the murmur?

  • B. Congenital bicuspid aortic valve
  • C. Aortic stenosis
  • D. Mitral regurgitation
  • E. Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy
Best answer
C. Aortic stenosis
Elderly patient + ejection (crescendo-decrescendo) systolic murmur + exertional dyspnoea = calcific aortic stenosis until proven otherwise. Bicuspid valve is the congenital cause (younger patients); aortic sclerosis is a soft early ejection sound without significant gradient.

Vertigo — BPPV vs Others

BPPV (benign paroxysmal positional vertigo) — this exam’s answer:

  • Mechanism: canalith (otoconia debris from utricle) in the posterior semicircular canal → rotation of the head triggers endolymph flow → false spinning.
  • Features: brief (<1 min, typically 10–30 s) intense vertigo triggered by rolling over in bed, looking up, bending down; position-dependent; NO hearing loss/tinnitus; no neuro signs; inter-attack normal; commonest peripheral vestibular disorder.
  • Diagnosis: Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre — sit upright → head turned 45° → lie back quickly with neck extended 20–30° → torsional upbeat nystagmus after a few seconds’ latency, fatigable, reversing on sitting up.
  • Treatment: Epley manoeuvre (repositioning — repeat at home-semont) ± vestibular suppressants only for first days; 80–90% cured; avoid vestibular sedatives chronically; reassurance.

Differential:

OnsetTriggerHearing lossNystagmusOther
BPPVSudden, briefHead positionNoPositional, brief, fatigableDix–Hallpike+/Epley
Ménière’sSudden, 20 min–hoursSpontaneousYES — low-frequency sensorineural, tinnitus, fullnessDuring attackLow-salt diet, betahistine, diuretics
Vestibular neuritisSudden, daysSpontaneous (post-viral)NoSpontaneous horizontal, suppresses with fixationSupportive + steroids early; bed rest <3 days
LabyrinthitisSudden, daysPost-otitis/viralYESAs neuritisAs neuritis + treat cause
Central (stroke/TIA/demyelination/tumour)AnySpontaneousNoPure vertical, direction-changing, NOT suppressible, no latencyNeuro signs — ataxia, dysarthria, diplopia, weakness, Horner’s — MRI + admission

Exam red flags (central): vertical nystagmus, inability to walk, focal deficit, absence of positional response, vascular risk factors → imaging.

Exam pearls
  • Vertigo on rolling in bed + brief + no deafness = BPPV → Epley.
  • Vertigo + hearing loss + tinnitus = Ménière’s. Vertigo + focal neuro = cerebellar stroke — image NOW.

#111MCQ edited2019-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-af565cae
A patient presents with vertigo. What is the most likely diagnosis?
  • A. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
  • B. Meniere's disease
  • C. Vestibular neuritis
  • D. Central vertigo (stroke)
  • E. Labyrinthitis
Best answer
A. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
Brief (<1 min) episodic vertigo triggered by head position — lying down, rolling over, looking up — with rotatory nystagmus, no hearing loss, no neurological signs = BPPV (otoconia in posterior semicircular canal). Diagnose with Dix–Hallpike; treat with Epley manoeuvre. Meniere’s = vertigo + hearing loss + tinnitus + aural fullness; vestibular neuritis = single prolonged episode; central = any direction/vertical nystagmus, neuro signs.

Viral Hepatitis & HBV Serology

Route of transmission & course:

VirusTransmissionChronic?Vaccine/Tx
HAVFaecal–oral (food/water, travellers, MSM, shellfish) — faeces: CONTACT precautionsNever (self-limiting)Vaccine + Ig for contacts; supportive

HBV serology table — memorise cold:

HBsAgAnti-HBcAnti-HBsMeaning
+IgM−Acute HBV
+IgG−Chronic HBV carrier/infection (or window)
−IgG+Cleared past infection (immune)
−−+Vaccinated (immune)
−−−Susceptible — offer vaccine

This exam: HBsAg−, anti-HBs+, anti-HBc IgG+ → cleared (past) hepatitis B infection. Traveller + others affected + jaundice → hepatitis A → contact precautions/hand hygiene + notify public health + vaccinate contacts. Returned with markedly raised transaminases → acute hepatitis A/E.

  • HAV/HEV = faecal-oral (jaundiced travellers); HBV/HCV = blood.

Bleeding Disorders — Platelets vs Coagulation vs vWD

Bleeding pattern points to the defect:

Platelet / primary haemostasisCoagulation factor / secondary haemostasis
PatternMucocutaneous: petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, bleeding immediately after cutsDeep bleeds: haemarthroses, muscle/retroperitoneal haematomas, delayed bleeding (hours after surgery/dental extraction)
Platelet countLow (or functionally defective)Normal
PT / aPTTNormalPT = extrinsic (factor VII); aPTT = intrinsic (VIII, IX, XI, XII); both = common pathway (X, V, II, I) or vitamin K/liver disease

Key inherited disorders:

  • Haemophilia A (factor VIII) / B (factor IX) — X-linked recessive. Boys; deep haematomas, haemarthroses, prolonged aPTT with normal PT, normal platelets. Treat: factor VIII/IX replacement (on demand ± prophylaxis), DDAVP for mild A, avoid aspirin/IM injections. Check inhibitors if poor response.
  • Von Willebrand disease — most common inherited bleeding disorder; autosomal dominant; mucocutaneous bleeding, menorrhagia in women, family history; normal/high aPTT (factor VIII protected by vWF), prolonged bleeding time; test: vWF antigen/activity (ristocetin cofactor), factor VIII. Treat: DDAVP (mild), tranexamic acid, vWF/factor VIII concentrate for surgery/major bleeds.
  • Vitamin K deficiency — neonates (no stores, sterile gut), malabsorption (coeliac, CF, cholestasis), antibiotics, warfarin → affects factors II, VII, IX, X → PT (and later aPTT) prolonged; newborn bleeding prevented by IM/oral vitamin K at birth. Treat with vitamin K; PCC/FFP if bleeding.
  • ITP — isolated thrombocytopenia post-viral illness, well child, petechiae/purpura, normal Hb/WBC; observe if mild; IVIG/steroids if significant bleeding/platelets very low; avoid sports.
  • Haemophilia + circumcision bleed in a boy with knee haematomas = haemophilia A (commonest) vs B.

Laboratory triage: normal aPTT + prolonged PT → factor VII deficiency or vitamin K/warfarin/liver. Prolonged aPTT + normal PT → VIII/IX/XI. Both prolonged → common pathway (X/V/II/fibrinogen) or vitamin K deficiency/liver/DIC/warfarin; mixing study separates factor deficiency (corrects) from inhibitor (fails to correct — e.g. lupus anticoagulant, factor VIII inhibitor). Prolonged both + thrombocytopenia + high D-dimer + low fibrinogen = DIC (oozing everywhere, multi-organ failure — treat cause + replace).

Exam pearls
  • Petechiae + isolated low platelets post-viral in a well child = ITP.
  • Circumcision bleed + haemarthrosis + boy + family history = haemophilia (aPTT↑, PT normal).
  • vWD = menorrhagia + mucocutaneous bleed + family history; DDAVP trial.
  • Both PT & aPTT prolonged in a newborn/anticoagulated/malabsorbed = vitamin K — give vitamin K, check liver.
  • DIC = consumption — replace what you use, treat the cause (sepsis!).
Traps
  • Normal PT/aPTT does NOT exclude vWD or mild factor deficiency — check vWF/factor levels and bleeding time.
  • Platelet transfusion only in active bleeding/prophylaxis before procedures, not automatically in ITP.

#97MCQ2019-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-3266000e
A child brought by his parents for a check-up has labs showing prolonged aPTT and prolonged prothrombin time. What is the underlying cause?
  • A. Factor VIII deficiency
  • B. Factor X deficiency
  • C. Factor VII deficiency
  • D. Vitamin K deficiency
  • E. Von Willebrand disease
Best answer
B. Factor X deficiency
Both aPTT (intrinsic/common) and PT (extrinsic/common) prolonged with normal platelets → common pathway factor deficiency — factor X (or V, II, I — but factor X is the classic single-gene answer) or vitamin K deficiency. Factor VII = PT only; VIII/IX = aPTT only; vWD = usually aPTT only + bleeding time↑. Vitamin K also prolongs both but factor X is the single-factor answer; check vitamin K status/liver if mixed.

2019 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Bronchiolitis

Viral lower respiratory infection in infants <2 years (peak 2–6 months), usually RSV (also human metapneumovirus, adenovirus, parainfluenza). Presentation: coryza prodrome → dry cough, tachypnoea, wheeze, subcostal/intercostal recession, feeding difficulty, low-grade fever, crackles. Commonest cause of infant admission in winter.

Diagnosis is clinical — no routine tests. Oxygen saturation guides severity/admission (admit if SpO₂ persistently <92–94%, poor feeding <50–75% of normal, apnoea, severe recessions, or social concerns). Grunting = auto-PEEP — a sign of worsening respiratory distress. CXR only if atypical/deteriorating (hyperinflation ± focal atelectasis).

Management = SUPPORTIVE only: oxygen (if hypoxic), nasogastric/IV fluids (if poor feeding), nasal suctioning (especially before feeds; upper-airway secretions obstruct). NOT recommended: bronchodilators (salbutamol — no benefit), steroids, antibiotics (unless secondary bacterial infection), routine chest physiotherapy, hypertonic saline (debated; not routine in US; sometimes used in some protocols).

Prevention: palivizumab (monoclonal anti-RSV) for high-risk infants in season (ex-prems, chronic lung disease, congenital heart disease); hand hygiene; avoid sick contacts; smoke-free homes.

Exam pearls
  • Bronchiolitis ≠ asthma — salbutamol doesn’t work; supportive care is everything.
  • Severe: apnoea, SpO₂ <92%, poor feeding → admit + O₂ + NG/IV fluids.
  • Grunting = working hard — support the airway, don’t dismiss.
  • RSV is diagnosed clinically; family “cold” symptoms in a winter infant = bronchiolitis.

Bronchiolitis management is SUPPORTIVE: oxygen if hypoxic, NG/IV fluids if poor feeding, and nasal suctioning of secretions. No antibiotics, no salbutamol, no steroids, no epinephrine routinely.
2019 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Brucellosis

“Undulant fever” — zoonosis from Brucella (abortus – cattle; melitensis – goats/sheep; suis – pigs) via unpasteurised dairy, direct contact with infected animals/placentas, or aerosols (lab/vets/abattoir). Common in the Mediterranean/Middle East/South Asia.

Clinical: gradual onset intermittent/relapsing fever (undulant), drenching sweats, malaise, weight loss, headache, migratory arthralgia, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy. Focal complications: sacroiliitis (very characteristic), spondylitis (vertebral osteomyelitis), epididymo-orchitis, hepatitis, neurobrucellosis, endocarditis (main cause of death).

Diagnosis: Serology (Rose Bengal screen; agglutination/Coombs/Brucellacapt; fourfold rise on paired sera or single high titre, e.g. >1:160) — first-line test. Blood culture is definitive but slow (keep 4–6 weeks). PCR; raised ESR mild; LFTs often deranged.

Treatment: combination therapy for ≥6 weeks — doxycycline + rifampicin (or doxycycline + streptomycin for severe/focal disease, e.g. spondylitis/endocarditis); children/pregnancy → TMP-SMX + rifampicin. Avoid drugs alone (relapse).

Exam pearls
  • Fever + night sweats + animal/dairy exposure → Brucella serology; sacroiliitis + that history = brucellosis till proven otherwise.
  • Spinal brucellosis: brucellar spondylitis — back pain + fever + raised inflammatory markers (TB gives gibbus; brucella gives sacroiliitis/vertebral osteomyelitis).
  • Endocarditis is the lethal complication — echo if murmur/emboli.

The classic differentials (highest-yield table in paediatrics):

DiseaseAgentFeverRash patternKey distinguishing features
Measles (rubeola)ParamyxovirusHigh, 3–4 d BEFORE rashMaculopapular starting hairline/behind ears → face → trunk (craniocaudal spread)3 Cs: cough, coryza, conjunctivitis + Koplik spots (buccal mucosa white grains)
Rubella (German measles)TogavirusLow-gradePinpoint/maculopapular, face→trunk, fades by day 3Tender occipital/postauricular lymphadenopathy; mild in children; congenital rubella = cataract, deafness, PDA
Roseola infantum (exanthem subitum, 6th disease)HHV-6 (±HHV-7)High fever 3–5 d, child wellRash appears as fever resolves — trunk→face/extremities3 mo–4 y; febrile seizures common; rash blanching macules
Erythema infectiosum (5th disease, slapped-cheek)Parvovirus B19Low/none“Slapped cheek” → lacy reticular rash on limbs/trunkArthropathy in adults; aplastic crisis in sickle cell/chronic haemolysis; hydrops fetalis in pregnancy
Scarlet feverStrep pyogenes (erythrogenic toxin)Fever, sore throatSandpaper rash (blanching, pinpoint, sandpaper), circumoral pallor, Pastia’s lines (flexural accentuation)Strawberry tongue, tonsillitis; treat penicillin (prevents RF/PSGN)
Varicella (chickenpox)VZVFeverCrops of vesicles on an erythematous base — all stages simultaneously, itchy, dew-drops-on-petals; centripetalComplications: secondary bacterial infection, pneumonitis, congenital; exclude from school until all crusted

Management: measles/rubella/roseola/fifth = supportive (antipyretics, fluids). Scarlet fever = penicillin V/amoxicillin ×10 d. Varicella = supportive, acyclovir if severe/immunocompromised. Meningococcaemia = emergency. Measles: isolate, notify public health, vitamin A in severe/developing-world cases.

Exam pearls
  • Fever first, rash after fever breaks = ROSEOLA (HHV-6).
  • Cough+coryza+conjunctivitis then craniocaudal rash = MEASLES (plus Koplik).
  • Slapped cheek + reticular rash = parvovirus B19 → aplastic crisis risk in haemolytics.
  • Sandpaper rash + Pastia lines + circumoral pallor = GAS scarlet fever → penicillin.
  • Any non-blanching purpuric rash with fever = meningococcaemia → ceftriaxone NOW.
Traps
  • Measles is contagious 4 days before → 4 days after rash.
  • Fifth disease in pregnancy causes hydrops — advise pregnant contacts.
  • Don’t confuse roseola rash with drug rash — history of fever trajectory decides.

A child had cough, coryza and red eyes (conjunctivitis) 3 days ago, then developed a rash on his face which spread down to his trunk. What is the diagnosis?
  • A. Measles (the 3 Cs)
  • B. Rubella
  • C. Roseola infantum
  • D. Scarlet fever
  • E. Fifth disease
Best answer
A. Measles (the 3 Cs)
Coryza + cough + conjunctivitis 3 days before a craniocaudal maculopapular rash = measles. Look for Koplik spots (buccal white grains) — pathognomonic. Supportive care; vitamin A if severe; notify; isolate; watch for pneumonia/encephalitis.

Itchy vesicular pustules spreading person-to-person (“caught from another”) = chickenpox — VZV. Centripetal crops, all stages at once, “dew drop on rose petal”. Exclude from school until all lesions crusted.
2019 · Pediatrics · 3 questions · EMQ/MCQ/SAQ

Childhood Vasculitis — Kawasaki Disease & HSP (IgA Vasculitis)

Kawasaki disease (mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome) — medium-vessel vasculitis of children <5 y; the leading cause of acquired heart disease in developed countries (coronary artery aneurysms).

Diagnostic criteria: fever ≥5 days PLUS ≥4 of: (1) bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection; (2) oral changes — strawberry tongue, cracked red lips, diffuse erythema; (3) rash (polymorphous, not vesicular); (4) extremity changes — erythema/oedema of palms & soles (acute) → periungual desquamation (2–3 wks); (5) cervical lymphadenopathy (≥1.5 cm, usually unilateral). Labs: leucocytosis, thrombocytosis (week 2+), high ESR/CRP, sometimes aseptic meningitis, sterile pyuria, raised transaminases.

Treatment — IVIG 2 g/kg over 12 h ASAP (ideally within 10 days of fever) + aspirin (high-dose acute phase 80–100 mg/kg/d until afebrile 48–72 h, then low-dose 3–5 mg/kg/d ×6–8 weeks). Baseline echocardiography (repeat at 2 wks and 6–8 wks) for coronary aneurysms. Refractory → second IVIG dose ± infliximab/steroids. Delay in IVIG = aneurysm risk.

Complications: coronary artery aneurysm (20% untreated vs ~5% with IVIG) → MI/sudden death; myocarditis; pericarditis; valvulitis; rarely giant aneurysms → thrombosis → warfarin/abciximab.

Henoch–Schönlein purpura (HSP / IgA vasculitis) — the commonest childhood vasculitis; small-vessel IgA immune-complex disease, classically 2–11 y, post-URTI. Classic tetrad: palpable purpura (buttocks/extensor legs — NON-blanching), colicky abdominal pain (± GI bleed), arthritis/arthralgia, renal disease (haematuria/proteinuria — IgA nephropathy pattern, usually mild but can cause RPGN). Diagnosis clinical; check urine microscopy + BP + U&E in every HSP child, weekly then monthly urinalysis up to 6–12 months. Treatment: supportive (hydration, analgesia); severe abdominal pain → steroids; renal failure/nephritic syndrome → nephrology (may need steroids/immunosuppression ± dialysis).

HSP complication in this exam: abdominal pain + palpable mass = intussusception (ileo-ileal — lead point from bowel-wall haematoma).

Exam pearls
  • Fever ≥5 d + strawberry tongue + conjunctivitis + rash + desquamating hands/ feet → IVIG + aspirin NOW; echo the heart.
  • HSP = purpura on extensor surfaces + abdominal colic + arthritis + haematuria → urine dip all children at presentation and follow up.
  • HSP + abdominal mass → ultrasound for intussusception.
  • Kawasaki thrombocytosis appears in week 2 — do not be reassured by an early normal count.
Traps
  • Only PARTIAL criteria (e.g. fever + 2 features + coronary aneurysm or very high inflammatory markers) = incomplete Kawasaki — still treat.
  • Aspirin in HSP is NOT required; it’s the big antiplatelet role only in Kawasaki/thrombocytosis.
  • Excludes: meningococcaemia (toxic, petechial), scarlet fever (circumoral pallor/Pastia lines), measles (Koplik).

#89MCQ2019-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-82635629
A child with a history of HSP and abdominal pain is found to have an abdominal mass. What is the likely cause?
  • A. Intussusception
  • B. Diverticulitis
  • C. Appendicitis
  • D. Volvulus

Best answer
A. Intussusception

#179SAQ edited2019-Pediatrics-SAQ-Medicine-ad0f8565
A child presents with a 6-day history of fever, conjunctivitis, rash and lymphadenopathy.
  1. What is the most likely diagnosis? (1 pt)
  2. List the next steps of management. (1 pt)
  3. Mention one complication. (1 pt)
Best answer
1) Kawasaki disease (fever ≥5 days + conjunctivitis + rash + lymphadenopathy + oral changes/extremity changes). 2) Management: IV immunoglobulin 2 g/kg IV over 12 h ASAP (within 10 days) + high-dose aspirin (80–100 mg/kg/d until afebrile 48 h then low-dose); baseline echocardiography and repeat at 2 and 6–8 weeks; admit; monitor for cardiac involvement. 3) Complication: coronary artery aneurysm (→ thrombosis, MI, sudden death) — also myocarditis, pericarditis.
The ONLY childhood vasculitis treated with IVIG + aspirin. Delayed treatment = aneurysms. Incomplete Kawasaki (fever + 2–3 features + high CRP/ESR or coronary changes) also requires IVIG. Aspirin is for antiplatelet effect so long as coronaries at risk.

Congenital Heart Disease — Murmur Recognition & Cyanosis

Approach: (1) Cyanotic vs acyanotic? (2) Where/when murmur? (3) Splitting behaviour.

LesionMurmurKey signsNotes
VSD (commonest CHD)Harsh pansystolic at left lower sternal edgeFeeding difficulty/FTT, recurrent chest infections; large VSD → heart failure, loud P2; small (restrictive) = louderMany close spontaneously; Eisenmenger if long-standing large defect (reversal → cyanosis)
ASDSoft ejection systolic at left upper sternal edge (relative pulmonary flow)Fixed widely split S2 (pathognomonic); often asymptomatic; split doesn’t vary with respirationTypes: ostium secundum (commonest, 90%), primum (AVSD), sinus venosus; embolic stroke risk (paradoxical); closure if shunt significant
PDAContinuous “machinery” murmur below left clavicleBounding pulses, wide pulse pressure; common in prematurityIndomethacin/ibuprofen or device closure if symptomatic
Tetralogy of Fallot (commonest CYANOTIC)Ejection systolic (pulmonary stenosis); single S2Hypercyanotic “tet” spells (squatting/knee–chest ↑SVR), clubbing, squatting; RVH (boot-shaped heart)4 features: pulmonary stenosis + VSD + overriding aorta + RVH; spell: knee–chest, O₂, morphine, beta-blocker, call ICU
Transposition of great arteries (TGA)Usually no murmur; single S2Severe cyanosis in first hours of life (needs duct/foramen to survive)Egg-on-string CXR; prostaglandin E1 to keep duct open; arterial switch operation
Eisenmenger syndrome± pansystolic (shunt may reverse → murmur diminishes)Cyanosis + clubbing + polycythaemia lateIrreversible pulmonary hypertension — surgery contraindicated; heart-lung transplant
Pulmonary stenosisEjection systolic, left upper sternal edge, normal/soft splitting or single S2 (delayed A2–P2)Widely split FIXED = ASD; single S2/soft P2 = PSBalloon valvuloplasty if gradient high
Aortic stenosisEjection systolic at right upper sternal edge radiating to carotidsEjection click, thrillBicuspid → coarctation association
Innocent murmur (Still’s)Soft, vibratory/“twang” systolic, disappears lying flat/sitting upWell child, normal S1/S2, normal growthReassure — no investigation

Cyanosis work-up: hyperoxia test (FiO₂ 100% ×10 min — PaO₂ stays low if cardiac, rises if pulmonary); echocardiography is definitive. Acute cyanotic neonate → prostaglandin E1 immediately if duct-dependent lesion suspected.

Cyanotic murmurs vs cyanotic single S2: TOF (murmur + hypoxic spells), TGA (single S2, no murmur, first-day cyanosis), truncus, tricuspid atresia, Ebstein.

Exam pearls
  • Pansystolic LLSE = VSD; fixed split S2 + soft ESM = ASD; machinery = PDA; ESM + single S2 + cyanotic + squatting = TOF.
  • “Blueness after crying” in a child = TOF tet spell → echo; knee–chest position.
  • Continuous murmur disappears supine = innocent (Still’s).
  • Uncorrected left-to-right shunt → Eisenmenger → cyanosis with diminished murmur.

  • B. ASD
  • C. PDA

  • E. Pulmonary stenosis
Best answer
A. VSD

#136MCQ edited2019-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-20afe8f0
A patient has an ejection systolic murmur in the pulmonic area with fixed splitting of P2. What is the diagnosis?
  • A. ASD
  • B. VSD
  • C. PDA
  • D. Pulmonary stenosis
  • E. Tetralogy of Fallot
Best answer
A. ASD
Ejection systolic murmur at pulmonary area + wide FIXED splitting of S2 = ASD (fixed split — P2 delayed equally in expiration and inspiration). VSD = pansystolic; pulmonary stenosis = ESM but normal/soft splitting (or single S2); TOF = ESM + single S2 + cyanosis.
#140MCQ edited2019-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-5f469371
A patient has an ejection systolic murmur in the pulmonic area with no splitting of S2. What is the diagnosis?
  • A. Pulmonary stenosis
  • B. ASD
  • C. VSD
  • D. Tetralogy of Fallot
  • E. PDA
Best answer
A. Pulmonary stenosis
Ejection systolic murmur at pulmonic area with NO (or normal) splitting = pulmonary stenosis (P2 delayed/single S2). Fixed wide splitting = ASD; TOF = ESM + single S2 + cyanosis.
#141MCQ edited2019-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-43a82781
A cyanotic female child has a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge and squats when cyanotic. What is the diagnosis?
  • A. Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)
  • B. VSD
  • C. Transposition of the great arteries (TGA)
  • D. Truncus arteriosus
  • E. Ebstein anomaly
Best answer
A. Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)
Cyanotic child + ejection systolic murmur + squatting during spells = TOF (pulmonary stenosis + VSD + overriding aorta + RVH). Squatting ↑SVR → ↓right-to-left shunt → more pulmonary flow. Hypercyanotic spell: knee–chest, O₂, morphine, beta-blocker.

Developmental Milestones & Developmental Quotient

Core milestones to memorise (age → expected):

AgeGross motorFine motor / visionSpeech / languageSocial / behaviour
NewbornFlexed posture, ventral suspension lifts head momentarilyFixes to faces brieflyCriesRegards face
6 wksRaises head proneFixes & follows to midlineCoosSocial smile
3 moHead control developing, supports on forearms (prone), holds head steadyHands opening, follows 180°Laughs, turns to voiceKnows mother
4–6 moRolls tummy→back (4–5 mo), sits with support/tripod (6 mo)Palmar grasp (6 mo), transfers hand-to-hand (6–7 mo), reachesBabbles (monosyllables 6 mo)Recognises strangers
7–9 moSits unsupported (7–8 mo), crawls/pivots-sit, stands with supportInferior pincer grasp (9 mo), finger feeds, bangs toys“Mama”, “dada” non-specific (9 mo), understands “no”Stranger anxiety, waves bye-bye-ish
12 moStands alone, walks with one hand held / alone (12–15 mo), cruisingPincer grasp perfected, casts toys1–2 words with meaningDrinks from cup, points, waves bye-bye
18 moRuns stifflyTower of 2–4 blocks, scribbles6–20 words, 2 body partsFeeds self with spoon, symbolic play, temper tantrums
2 yWalks up/down stairs 2 feet per step, kicks ballTower of 6–7 blocks, imitates vertical line, turns pages2-word phrases, ~200+ wordsRemoves garments partially, parallel play, follows 2-step commands
3 yRides tricycle, climbs stairs alternating feet, stands briefly one footTower of 9–10, copies circle, bridge 3 blocks3–4 word sentences, asks “what/who”Puts on garments, plays with others (group play), dry by day
4 yHops, skips, throws/catchesCopies cross/square, uses scissors, draws person ~3 parts4-word sentences, narrates, asks “why/how”Dresses/undresses fully, names 4 colours, interactive pretend play
5 ySkips, hops on each footCopies triangle, writes name, cutsFluent sentences, knows age/addressIndependent dressing, competitive play, ties laces

Developmental quotient (DQ) = developmental age ÷ chronological age × 100. DQ 85–115 normal; 70–85 borderline; <70 significant delay (support needed). Example: 2-year-old with 12-month milestones → 12/24 × 100 = 50.

Warning signs: no social smile by 8 wks, hand preference <12 mo, not sitting by 12 mo, not walking by 18 mo, no words by 2 y, no interest in peers, regression. When in doubt → formal developmental assessment + hearing + vision + referral to portage/EI.

Exam pearls
  • Smile 6 wks • sit 6–8 mo • walk 12–15 mo • words 12–18 mo • 2-word phrases 2 y • tricycle 3 y • hop/skip 4–5 y.
  • DQ = DA/CA ×100 — always a percentage, comparable across domains.
  • Head lag + poor head control in a 3-month-old → reassess urgently (neurological exam, neuroimaging).

Fluid Therapy — Dehydration & Maintenance (Paediatric)

Assess dehydration:

Mild (<5%)Moderate (5–10%)Severe (>10%)
ConsciousAlertIrritable/lethargicDrowsy/coma
Capillary refill<2 s2–3 s>3 s
Eyes/fontanelleNormalSunkenVery sunken
Mucous membranes/tearsMoist/presentDry/reducedVery dry/absent
Skin turgorNormalReducedMarkedly reduced
Urine outputNormal/reducedOliguriaAnuria
ThirstPresentEagerToo weak to drink
TreatmentORS by mouthORS (±NG if vomiting) / IV if unableIV fluid bolus 20 mL/kg 0.9% NaCl (reassess, repeat) → replace deficit over 24–48 h

ORS composition (WHO low-osmolarity): Na 75 mmol/L, glucose 75 mmol/L, osm 245 — give 50 mL/kg over 4 h for mild + ongoing losses (10 mL/kg per loose stool); continue breastfeeding/feeds.

Maintenance fluids (children): Holliday–Segar — first 10 kg: 100 mL/kg/day; second 10 kg: 50 mL/kg; each kg >20: 20 mL/kg (≈ 4/2/1 mL/kg/h). Replace ongoing losses separately (10 mL/kg per vomit/stool; NG losses aspirate for electrolytes ± add 10–20 mmol K per litre when urine output good).

Exam pearls
  • Mild dehydration + drinking well = ORS, always (fastest, safest). IV only if unable to tolerate or severe.
  • Severe shock → 20 mL/kg bolus, reassess, repeat, then deficit replacement.
  • Never combine potassium into fluids until urine output confirmed.

2019 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Foreign Body Aspiration

Peak age: 1–3 years — everything goes in mouths. Commonest: nuts (peanuts), seeds, grapes, popcorn, coins, small toys, pins.

Presentation: sudden episode of choking, coughing, gagging, cyanosis while playing/eating (witnessed in ~50%), then — if not expelled — wheeze/unilateral reduced air entry (classic: right main bronchus — wider, shorter, more vertical), stridor if laryngeal/tracheal, or asymptomatic interval then persistent unilateral wheeze/recurrent pneumonia in one lobe.

Red flags: unilateral wheeze or decreased air entry, unilateral hyperinflation/consolidation on CXR, air trapping on expiratory films, radio-opaque object (coins, pins, batteries — disc battery = emergency, oesophageal necrosis in 2 h), stridor/apnoea.

CXR findings: radio-opaque density (nail seen in the 2017 SAQ case — “nail impacted + consolidation”), focal hyperinflation (obstructive ball-valve), atelectasis, pneumonia distal to the object. Inspiratory/expiratory or decubitus views reveal air trapping.

Management: conscious, choking & cannot cough effectively/in distress → back blows/chest thrusts (infant) or abdominal thrusts (child >1 y). Stable with suspected aspiration → rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia — BOTH diagnostic and therapeutic (definitive treatment); flexible bronchoscopy for diagnosis only. Do NOT do blind finger sweeps; do NOT give food/water; batteries/magnets in oesophagus = urgent endoscopy. Antibiotics only if established pneumonia.

Exam pearls
  • Sudden choking + unilateral wheeze + hyperinflation on CXR = inhaled foreign body → rigid bronchoscopy.
  • Radio-opaque object + overlying lung consolidation = retained object — retrieve it.
  • Battery in oesophagus = 2-hour emergency.
  • Always ask the choking history in recurrent/persistent “pneumonia” of one lobe in a toddler.

Key differentiators: incubation period, vomiting vs diarrhoea predominance, watery vs bloody, food type, setting (outbreak).

OrganismIncubationCluesNotes

Management of acute diarrhoea: oral rehydration (ORS) is the cornerstone — IV fluids only if severe dehydration/unable to tolerate. Antibiotics NOT indicated for most (NOT for EHEC — precipitates HUS). Test stool only if bloody/severe/prolonged/immunocompromised.

Exam pearls
  • Cruise ship + everyone vomiting = norovirus. Reheated rice = B. cereus. Custard/cream 2 h later = S. aureus.
  • Bloody diarrhoea after beef + HUS risk = EHEC — NO antibiotics.
  • Bloody diarrhoea + travel = Shigella/Campylobacter; persistent after travel = Giardia.
  • Fluids first; antibiotics rarely.

2019 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Gastro-oesophageal Reflux Disease (GORD/GERD)

Symptomatic / complicated reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus. Common mechanisms: transient LOS relaxation (commonest), hiatus hernia, impaired oesophageal clearance, gastroparesis. Risk factors: obesity, pregnancy, smoking, alcohol, caffeine, large/fatty meals, lying flat, drugs (NSAIDs, nitrates, calcium-channel blockers, anticholinergics, theophylline), connective tissue disease (scleroderma).

Typical symptoms: heartburn, regurgitation, waterbrash (hypersalivation), retrosternal chest pain worsened by lying flat/bending, relieved by antacids, nocturnal symptoms. Extra-oesophageal: chronic cough, hoarseness (laryngitis), asthma exacerbation, dental erosion, Globus sensation.

Children: GORD = frequent regurgitation + distress/faltering growth/apnoea/posturing; “silent” reflux (arching, feed refusal); usually self-limiting by 12–18 months; treat with feed thickening, frequent small feeds, positioning; PPI only for distressing/complicated cases; consider CMPA in infants.

Diagnosis: clinical in typical cases — start empirical PPI trial (4–8 weeks). Endoscopy (OGD) if: age >55, alarm features (weight loss, dysphagia, odynophagia, GI bleeding/anaemia, persistent vomiting), or atypical symptoms. pH/impedance monitoring if symptoms persist despite PPI and endoscopy normal (non-erosive reflux/hypersensitive oesophagus).

Complications: erosive oesophagitis → peptic stricture, Barrett’s oesophagus (intestinal metaplasia — 0.5–1%/yr → adenocarcinoma) → surveillance endoscopy every 3–5 years; aspiration pneumonia; dental erosion.

Management: lifestyle (weight loss, elevate head of bed, avoid late meals/trigger foods, stop smoking/alcohol) + PPI (omeprazole 20–40 mg OD 30 min before breakfast, 4–8 wks); H₂-blockers second line; antacids/alginate for breakthrough. Refractory → escalate PPI, re-evaluate diagnosis, fundoplication for severe cases.

Exam pearls
  • Retrosternal pain worse lying/bending + waterbrash + relieved by antacids = GORD.
  • Alarm symptoms → endoscopy FIRST, not PPI.
  • Barrett’s → endoscopic surveillance.
  • Child “chest pain at night + vomiting” = GORD; if alarm (dysphagia, weight loss, anaemia) → scope.

#102MCQ edited2019-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-187f3dec
An obese child presents with epigastric pain radiating to the chest. What is the most likely diagnosis?
  • A. GERD
  • B. Peptic ulcer disease
  • C. Gallstones
  • D. Pancreatitis
  • E. Gastritis
Best answer
A. GERD
Epigastric pain radiating to the chest in an obese child with likely acid regurgitation = GORD (obesity → raised intra-abdominal pressure + LOS incompetence). Consider H. pylori/PUD if epigastric tenderness + H. pylori risk, but the chest-predominant pain fits GORD.

Glomerulonephritis & Haematuria (Children)

Glomerular haematuria vs non-glomerular: glomerular = dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, smoky/tea-coloured urine, proteinuria, hypertension, renal impairment. Non-glomerular = red/pink urine, isomorphic RBCs, clots, no casts.

Post-streptococcal GNIgA nephropathy (synpharyngitic)AlportHSP nephritis
Timing vs URTI2–3 weeks AFTER throat/skin infectionWithin 1–2 days (“synpharyngitic”)Persistent/familialWith purpura (simultaneous)
ComplementLOW C3 (normalises in 6–8 wks); C4 normalNormalNormalNormal
Other labsASO ↑ (anti-streptolysin O) / anti-DNase B; throat swab may be negativeNormalNormal; hearing loss + ocular (anterior lenticonus)Normal ± renal involvement
Age5–12 yAdolescents/young adultsChildren, X-linked (boys)2–11 y
HistologyDiffuse proliferative GNMesangial proliferation, IgA depositsBasketweave GBM (EM); Type IV collagenIgA deposition (same disease as IgA nephropathy)
OutcomeSelf-limiting (95%+ recover)Variable; 20–40% progress to CKD over decadesProgressive CKD + sensorineural deafnessUsually good; monitor urine/BP for 12–24 mo

Features of nephritic syndrome: haematuria (smoky), hypertension, mild–moderate proteinuria, oedema (periorbital), oliguria. Management PSGN: supportive (salt/water restriction, antihypertensives), no steroids/antibiotics needed for the kidney (antibiotics treat the strep carrier state and prevent spread, not the GN); follow-up to confirm C3 normalisation; persistent hypertension/renal impairment → biopsy.

Alport: persistent glomerular haematuria + family history of males with CKD + sensorineural hearing loss + anterior lenticonus — COL4A5 (X-linked, 80%); supportive; ACEi slows proteinuria; genetic counselling; transplant is not contraindicated (no anti-GBM in most).

Exam pearls
  • Haematuria 2–3 weeks AFTER sore throat + low C3 + high ASO = PSGN.
  • Haematuria DURING sore throat + normal C3 = IgA nephropathy.
  • Haematuria + deafness + family history of renal failure = Alport.
  • Hypertension + periorbital oedema + smoky urine in a child = nephritic — check ASO/C3 first.

A 7-year-old child with a history of chronic kidney disease and a family history of sensorineural hearing loss is found to have hematuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
  • A. Alport syndrome
  • B. IgA nephropathy
  • C. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
  • D. Minimal change disease
  • E. Membranous nephropathy
Best answer
A. Alport syndrome
Hereditary nephritis (COL4A5 mutations — X-linked): haematuria ± CKD + SENSORINEURAL deafness ± anterior lenticonus, family history of renal failure in males. PSGN/MCD do not cause deafness; IgA = synpharyngitic haematuria.
2019 · Pediatrics · 3 questions · MCQ/SAQ

Growth — Assessment, Percentiles & Faltering Growth

Key measurements: weight-for-age, length/height-for-age, weight-for-height/BMI, head circumference (0–2 y). BMI (child) = weight(kg) / height(m)² — age & sex needed only to plot centiles.

Normal variant patterns:

  • Parent-determined (familial short stature): height follows parental target centile; normal growth velocity; bone age = chronological age.
  • Constitutional delay: short stature + delayed puberty; growth catches up later; bone age delayed; normal final height (just later). “Late bloomer.”
  • Pathological: endocrine (hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, Cushing’s), chronic disease (coeliac, CF, CKD, asthma on steroids), neglect, genetic syndromes.

Faltering growth (failure to thrive): weight crossing down ≥1–2 centile lines (or weight below 3rd centile), often weight before height; causes — inadequate intake (feeding problems, poverty, neglect), inadequate absorption (coeliac, CF, CMPA), excessive losses (vomiting, diarrhoea — coeliac/CF), increased requirements (chronic infection, malignancy, hyperthyroidism). First step: plot the chart accurately + dietary history + observe a feed (for infants). Investigations guided by history: urine dip/MC&S, coeliac serology, sweat test, FBC, U&E/LFT, TFT, lead, development.

Reading growth charts: plot with correct age/sex chart; centiles: 3rd–97th ≈ normal; below 3rd = short/underweight; above 97th = tall/overweight; height above 97th centile — think Marfan/overgrowth; weight <3rd with height 50th = acute undernutrition (wasting); both <3rd = chronic; height <3rd with normal weight = “failure to thrive with preserved weight” — hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, skeletal dysplasia, syndromes.

Velocity matters more than one point: falling off the centile line (even within the normal range) is abnormal; single readings need confirmation.

Head circumference: ~34–35 cm at birth; +2 cm/mo ×3, then +1 cm/mo; at 12 mo ≈ 46 cm; macrocephaly >98th (hydrocephalus — check fontanelle, developmental progress); microcephaly <2nd (congenital infections, TORCH, chromosomal, metabolic).

Exam pearls
  • BMI = weight ÷ height² — needs only weight & height for the value; age/sex for the centile plot.
  • Weight <3rd + height 50th = wasting (acute); height <3rd + weight normal = endocrine/skeletal.
  • Deceleration (crossing down lines) = the red flag — plot and re-measure.
  • Faltering growth + offensive stools + recurrent chest infections = CF/coeliac — sweat test + tTG.

#86MCQ2019-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-0d4b4f09
A baby was born with a head circumference of 33 cm. The mother worries about whether he has an abnormality after 1 month. What is the normal acceptable head circumference range at this age?
  • A. 33 cm
  • B. 34 cm
  • C. 35 cm
  • D. 36 cm
  • E. 37 cm
Best answer
D. 36 cm
Head circumference at birth ~34–35 cm; grows ~2 cm/month for the first 3 months (~1 cm/month until 6 months). At 1 month: ~36–37 cm. The acceptable reference range for a 1-month-old is ~36 cm (these MCQ banks key 36 cm; WHO median at 1 mo ≈ 36.5–37.5 cm for boys).
#178SAQ image edited2019-Pediatrics-SAQ-Medicine-3dc9382c
A child presents with chronic recurrent diarrhea since he was 5 months old. On examination he is thin-built with abdominal distension and loss of gluteal muscle mass. His growth chart is shown in the picture.
  1. What is the medical term according to the growth chart? (1 pt)
  2. What is the diagnosis? (1 pt)
  3. Mention 2 screening methods. (2 pt)
Best answer
1) Failure to thrive (faltering growth) — weight-for-age falling below/crossing centiles (below 3rd centile with height preserved early). 2) Coeliac disease — chronic diarrhoea since infancy + bloating/distension + gluteal wasting + poor weight gain + short stature; gluten-containing diet (wheat/barley). 3) Screening: (a) anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA (tTG-IgA) + total serum IgA; (b) anti-endomysial antibodies (both while still on gluten; confirm with duodenal biopsy — villous atrophy). Also test CF (sweat test) given chronic chest infections — but the growth-chart + diarrhoea pattern = coeliac.
Coeliac = lifelong autoimmune reaction to gliadin → villous atrophy → malabsorption (iron/folate anaemia, osteoporosis, neuropathy, infertility). Dermatitis herpetiformis. Associated T1DM/thyroiditis/IgA-deficiency. Strict GF diet; monitor tTG to undetectable; screen first-degree relatives.
#184SAQ image edited2019-Pediatrics-SAQ-Medicine-a76e9a94
A growth chart is provided. The baby had chronic diarrhea and buttocks (gluteal) wasting.
  1. What is this (medical term for the growth pattern)? (1 pt)
  2. What is the diagnosis? (1 pt)
  3. Mention 2 tests to confirm the diagnosis. (2 pt)
Best answer
1) Failure to thrive (faltering growth) — crossing centiles/below 3rd on weight (weight faltering before height). 2) Coeliac disease — chronic diarrhoea, bloating, gluteal wasting, faltering growth after gluten introduction. 3) Confirm with: (a) anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA + total IgA; (b) anti-endomysial antibody; plus duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy). Differential includes CF (sweat test) and giardiasis.
Plot EVERY well child — the chart is the earliest warning. Coeliac screen only valid on gluten-containing diet. Treat: strict gluten-free diet + dietitian; monitor growth and tTG; pneumococcal vaccine; screen family.
2019 · Pediatrics · 2 questions · MCQ

Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome (HUS)

Definition: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia + thrombocytopenia + acute kidney injury — classically in children after diarrhoeal illness.

Typical (D+) HUS — 90%: preceded (2–14 days) by bloody diarrhoea from Shiga toxin–producing E. coli (STEC/EHEC 0157:H7) or Shigella dysenteriae. Toxin damages glomerular endothelium → platelet-rich microthrombi → intravascular haemolysis with schistocytes, low platelets, renal failure (oliguria, haematuria, hypertension, uraemia). Antibiotics and antimotility agents INCREASE toxin release — avoid. Chicken/undercooked beef/unpasteurised milk are sources.

Atypical (D−) HUS — 10%: complement dysregulation (factor H/I/MCP mutations), Strep pneumoniae (neuraminidase exposure of Thomsen–Friedenreich antigen), drugs, pregnancy, malignancy — recurs, worse prognosis; treat with plasma exchange/eculizumab (anti-C5).

HUS vs TTP: TTP = adults, neuro symptoms (seizures, confusion) + fever + severe organ dysfunction, platelets very low, ADAMTS13 deficiency; neuro-dominant. HUS = children, renal-dominant, post-bloody diarrhoea. Both = schistocytes + thrombocytopenia + haemolysis.

Features asked in this exam: thrombocytopenia + haemolytic anaemia with schistocytes (± bloody diarrhoea, renal impairment, seizures). Seizures can occur — especially in severe HUS/TTP.

Management: SUPPORTIVE is the cornerstone — careful IV fluids/electrolytes, transfuse packed red cells (Hb <70/symptomatic), dialysis for renal failure indications, NO platelets (unless active bleeding), NO antibiotics in STEC, control hypertension; early nephrology; monitor for neurological involvement. Most children recover renal function (70–80%); ~5% mortality; ~25% develop some chronic renal impairment — long-term follow-up.

Exam pearls
  • Bloody diarrhoea (undercooked beef) → child + pallor + oliguria + petechiae → HUS.
  • Schistocytes + low platelets + AKI = MAHA triad.
  • NEVER antibiotics for STEC-0157 — triggers HUS.
  • HUS = kidney; TTP = brain. Support the kidney; don’t give platelets.

  • B. Leukocytosis and thrombocytosis

A. Thrombocytopenia and hemolytic anemia with schistocytes

Immunisation — Live Vaccines, Household Contacts & Contraindications

Live (attenuated) vaccines: BCG, MMR, varicella, oral polio (OPV), rotavirus, live intranasal influenza, live zoster (Zostavax), yellow fever, oral typhoid, Japanese encephalitis (live SA14). These are replication-competent — dangerous in severe immunosuppression (chemotherapy, transplant, high-dose steroids, biologics, primary immunodeficiency, HIV with low CD4) and can infect household contacts (OPV shed in stool).

Inactivated/killed/subunit/toxoid: hepatitis B, HiB, pneumococcal (conjugate/polysaccharide), DTP/Tdap, injectable polio (IPV), hepatitis A, HPV, injectable influenza, meningococcal — safe in immunosuppression.

Absolute contraindications: anaphylaxis to a previous dose or vaccine component; live vaccines in severe immunosuppression/pregnancy (MMR, varicella, BCG, OPV, yellow fever). NOT contraindications: mild febrile illness, recent exposure, prematurity (vaccinate by chronological age), breastfeeding, family history of seizures/adverse events, stable neurological conditions, antibiotic therapy, recovery from recent illness, local reaction/low-grade fever after dose.

Household contact rule (tested twice here): a severely immunocompromised child (chemotherapy for leukaemia) living with a sibling — the sibling must NOT receive live vaccines, especially OPV (viral shedding can paralyse the immunocompromised child) and BCG/varicella/MMR where applicable; use inactivated alternatives (IPV instead of OPV). Close contacts of transplant patients: avoid live vaccines except MMR/VZV per guidance (risk-benefit).

Tetanus prophylaxis for wounds: fully immunised + booster within 5 years → nothing; booster 5–10 y (clean wound) / any high-risk wound with booster >5 y → booster; incomplete/uncertain + high-risk wound → tetanus toxoid + tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG); dirty wounds: check.

Special situations: egg allergy → influenza/MMR/yellow fever generally safe with observation (severe egg anaphylaxis → specialist); HIV (CD4 >200): give MMR/varicella; pregnancy: no live vaccines (give MMR postpartum; Tdap from 16 weeks each pregnancy for pertussis; influenza any trimester); premature infants: vaccinate by chronological age.

Exam pearls
  • Chemo child at home → sibling gets IPV, NOT OPV; no live vaccines.
  • Immunosuppressed transplant patient → no live vaccines, ever (varicella!).
  • Only true general contraindication = anaphylaxis to prior dose. Mild illness ≠ contraindication.

#85MCQ2019-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-96cd519f
A 5-year-old girl is receiving induction chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Which of the following vaccines is contraindicated to be given to her 4-month-old sibling?
  • A. Oral polio vaccine
  • B. Haemophilus influenzae type B vaccine
  • C. Hepatitis B vaccine
  • D. Pneumococcal vaccine
  • E. DTP vaccine
Best answer
A. Oral polio vaccine
OPV is a LIVE vaccine — shed in stool and dangerous to severely immunocompromised close contacts (on chemotherapy for ALL). Give IPV (inactivated) to the sibling instead; avoid live vaccines (OPV, BCG, MMR, varicella, live influenza/rotavirus precautions) in this household until chemo done.

  • B. Inactivated polio vaccine
  • C. DTP
  • D. Haemophilus influenzae type B

Infant Feeding & Breastfeeding

Physiological weight loss: up to 10% of birth weight in the first week is normal (loss of meconium/fluid + limited intake before milk “comes in” day 2–4). Most regain birth weight by 10–14 days. Red flags: >10% loss, no regain by 2 weeks, hypernatraemia, dehydration, poor feeding, lethargy — then assess a feed, check urine output (≥6 wet nappies/day after day 5), weight trajectory; support (position, attachment, frequency, express/supplement if truly inadequate) and review.

This exam: 7-day-old, lost 6% (3.4→3.2 kg), feeding every 2 hours, well and settled → reassure and continue exclusive breastfeeding without supplementation. Supplementing without indication undermines supply and is unnecessary.

Breastfeeding counselling points: feed on demand 8–12 times/24 h (newborns); signs of effective transfer (rhythmic suck-swallow, audible swallows, breast softer after feeds, wet nappies, weight gain); avoid routine supplementation; vitamin D 400 IU/day for breastfed infants (+ mothers on some regimes); common problems: nipple pain (latch), engorgement, mastitis (flucloxacillin/dicloxacillin if infected — continue feeding!), low supply (check attachment, frequency, express, galactagogues rarely); contraindications to breastfeeding: maternal untreated HIV (in formula-available settings), HTLV-1/-2, certain drugs (chemotherapy, radioactive isotopes).

Exam pearls
  • <10% loss + frequent effective feeding = normal — reassure, don’t supplement.
  • “Top-up” formula only for true insufficiency/dehydration/hypernatraemia — get support first (UNICEF Baby-Friendly standard).
  • Mastitis is NOT a reason to stop breastfeeding — frequent feeding + antibiotics.

#91MCQ2019-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-deedb657
A 7-day neonate presents for a check-up. His weight now is 3.2 kg and was 3.4 kg after delivery. Feeds were not interrupted, and breastfeeding is given every 2 hours. The mother is concerned about his weight. What do you advise?
  • A. Stop breastfeeding
  • B. Switch to formula milk
  • C. Continue breastfeeding without supplemental formula
  • D. Supplement with formula at every feed
  • E. Refer urgently to a dietitian
Best answer
C. Continue breastfeeding without supplemental formula
Weight loss 5–10% (3.4→3.2 kg ≈ 6%) at one week is normal; feeds every 2 h and feeding well = adequate intake with expected diuresis of birth fluid. Reassure: continue exclusive breastfeeding — supplementation only if >10% loss, poor intake, or dehydration/hypernatraemia.

A 7-day neonate presents for a check-up. His weight now is 3.2 kg and was 3.4 kg after delivery. Feeds were not interrupted, and breastfeeding is given every 2 hours. The mother is concerned about his weight. What do you advise?

  • C. Continue breastfeeding without supplemental formula
  • D. Supplement with formula at every feed
  • E. Refer urgently to a dietitian
Best answer
C. Continue breastfeeding without supplemental formula
Weight loss 5–10% of birth weight (3.4→3.2 kg ≈ 6%) in week 1 is physiological (diuresis of excess fluid). Feeding 2-hourly and well = adequate. Reassure and continue exclusive breastfeeding; supplement only if >10% loss, dehydration, hypernatraemia, or persistent poor intake despite assessment.
2019 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Infant of a Diabetic Mother

Pathophysiology: maternal hyperglycaemia → fetal hyperglycaemia → fetal β-cell hyperplasia → hyperinsulinaemia (insulin = growth hormone) → organomegaly and fat deposition. At delivery, maternal glucose supply stops abruptly but insulin remains high → neonatal hypoglycaemia.

Clinical: macrosomia (birth weight >90th centile, >4 kg), fat “plethoric” appearance, cardiomegaly (asymmetric septal hypertrophy), neonatal hypoglycaemia (<2.6 mmol/L — jitteriness, seizures, apnoea, poor feeding in first 1–4 h), hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, polycythaemia (→ hyperbilirubinaemia, renal vein thrombosis), RDS (surfactant antagonism by insulin — term babies can get RDS!), congenital malformations (cardiac — HCM, transposition; sacral agenesis/caudal regression; neural tube; renal), birth trauma (shoulder dystocia), later obesity/T2DM risk.

Management of the newborn: early feeding (breast/formula within 30–60 min), check blood glucose within 1–2 h of birth and regularly until stable (>2.6 mmol/L documented ×2–3); if low and feeding well → feed + recheck; if symptomatic/severe/persistent → IV dextrose (bolus 2 mL/kg 10% then infusion 5–8 mg/kg/min; consider glucagon), monitor Ca/Mg/bilirubin/haematocrit; check cardiac if murmur/symptomatic; echo if symptomatic HCM; reassure — most self-resolve; follow growth/development/metabolic risk.

Exam pearls
  • Big plethoric baby + seizure/jitteriness in first hours = hypoglycaemia — check glucose STAT, feed/IV dextrose.
  • Insulin delays surfactant maturation → RDS in a term infant of diabetic mother is classic.
  • Caudal regression is near-pathognomonic of maternal diabetes.

#155MCQ edited2019-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-02737a32
A baby born to a diabetic mother has a seizure. What is the reason?
  • A. Hypoglycemia
  • B. Hypocalcemia
  • C. Sepsis
  • D. Intracranial hemorrhage
  • E. Hypomagnesemia
Best answer
A. Hypoglycemia
Infant of a diabetic mother: fetal hyperinsulinism (chronic maternal glucose excess → β-cell hyperplasia) → at birth glucose supply cut off → severe hypoglycaemia in hours (seizures!). Check glucose immediately, 6–12 hourly; feed early; diazoxide/IV dextrose if unresponsive. Also: hypocalcaemia, polycythaemia, RDS, cardiomyopathy.
2019 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Injury Prevention & Car Seats

Leading cause of death in childhood = injuries/accidents — prevention counselling is core paediatrics.

Car seats (this exam): all children must travel in an approved restraint; rear-facing until ≥2 years old (or until they outgrow the seat’s height/weight limit) — protects head/neck/spine. Forward-facing with harness 2–4 years; booster seat 4–10/12 years (or 145 cm/36 kg); back seat until ≥12/≥135 cm; never front seat with airbag. This 15-month-old: rear-facing.

Home safety by age: 0–1 y — safe sleep (supine on firm mattress, no soft bedding — SIDS), smoke-free, never leave on surfaces (falls), scald prevention (set water ≤48°C), choking (no small objects/peanuts/grapes whole, cut up), bath supervision, car seat, avoid sun. 1–3 y (cruisers/toddlers) — burns (kettle cords, fireguards — toddlers pull), poisoning (lock all medicines/cleaners — peak), falls (stair gates, window guards), drowning (bath seats/pools — seconds), choking. 4–12 y — road safety (pedestrian training), bike helmets, sporting injuries, water safety. Adolescents — risk-taking (driving, alcohol/drugs, firearms, safe sex).

Safeguarding red flags: see child-maltreatment review — bruises of different ages, injury inconsistent with developmental stage (e.g., “rolled off sofa” in a pre-mobile infant), delay in seeking care, repeated attendances.

Exam pearls
  • 15-month-old → rear-facing car seat.
  • Never leave an infant/child alone in a car (heat stroke/hypothermia).
  • Burns by age: 0–2 scalding; 3–5 flame/playing with lighters; always consider abuse with pattern burns.

2019 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Intussusception

Definition: telescoping of one bowel segment into another (usually ileocolic) — commonest acute abdominal emergency in infants 3–36 months (peak 5–9 months).

Classic triad (present in only ~25%): (1) colicky abdominal pain (sudden, intermittent, infant draws knees to chest, screams, between episodes pale/lethargic); (2) “red-currant jelly stool” (bloody mucus — LATE sign); (3) sausage-shaped mass in right upper quadrant / right iliac fossa + emptiness in the right iliac fossa (Dance’s sign). Other signs: vomiting (bilious if obstructed), lethargy/pallor (may dominate — “infant just sleepy”), abdominal distension, shock (late), peritonitis if perforated.

Causes/associations: 95% idiopathic (lymphoid hyperplasia — post-viral/rotavirus vaccine historically); pathological lead points (~5%): Meckel’s diverticulum, HSP (IgA vasculitis), polyps, lymphoma, CF (inspissated stool), parasites — in children >2 y or recurrent, look for a lead point.

This exam: colicky pain + bleeding on rectal examination/red-currant jelly → intussusception; abdominal mass + no stool in a 1-y-old → intussusception; HSP + abdominal pain + mass → intussusception.

Diagnosis: ultrasound — target/doughnut/bull’s-eye sign (transverse) or pseudo-kidney (longitudinal); also shows free fluid. X-ray may show soft-tissue density/absence of caecal gas/ obstruction.

Management: resuscitation first (ABCDE, IV access, NG tube, fluids, correct electrolytes/shock) → air-contrast (or barium) enema reduction (diagnostic AND therapeutic; success 70–90%; contraindicated if peritonitis/perforation/shock) → surgery if enema fails, peritonitis, perforation, shock, or suspected lead point (pathological) → manual reduction ± resection. Observe 12–24 h for recurrence (~10%).

Exam pearls
  • Colicky pain + red-currant jelly + mass = intussusception → ultrasound → air enema.
  • Infant “just lethargic/pale” between pain episodes = think intussusception, not sedation.
  • >2 y or recurrence → find the lead point (Meckel’s/HSP/lymphoma).

2019 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis & Enthesitis-Related Arthritis

JIA = arthritis of unknown cause, onset <16 y, duration ≥6 weeks.

SubtypeFeatures
Oligoarticular (commonest, ~50%)≤4 joints first 6 months (knees/ankles); young girls; asymptomatic chronic anterior uveitis → regular slit-lamp (ANA+ = high risk)
Polyarticular≥5 joints; RF-negative (young girls, asymmetric) or RF-positive (older girls, aggressive, RA-like)
Systemic (Still’s disease)Quotidian (daily) spiking fever + salmon-pink evanescent rash + arthritis + lymphadenopathy/serositis (hepatosplenomegaly); very high ferritin, leucocytosis, ANA/RF negative; macrophage activation syndrome risk
Enthesitis-related (ERA)Older boys; enthesitis (Achilles/plantar fascia), sacroiliitis/hip involvement, HLA-B27+, acute symptomatic uveitis, family history of AS/IBD/psoriasis — “juvenile spondyloarthritis”
PsoriaticArthritis + psoriasis or nail pitting/onycholysis or family history psoriasis (dactylitis)

This exam: bilateral hip pain + sacroiliac joint tenderness → enthesitis-related JIA (sacroiliitis pattern, HLA-B27 class).

Management: NSAIDs first-line; intra-articular corticosteroid injections; DMARDs (methotrexate — polyarticular), biologics (anti-TNF for ERA/refractory), systemic steroids short-term (systemic JIA), physiotherapy/OT, treat anterior uveitis with topical steroids; regular slit-lamp screening in oligo JIA (ANA+ every 3 months).

Exam pearls
  • 6 weeks of arthritis = JIA (time criterion). Uveitis screen in oligo JIA.
  • Daily fever + rash + arthritis = systemic JIA — check ferritin; rule out MAS.
  • Hip/sacroiliac + enthesitis in a boy = ERA (HLA-B27) — x-ray/MRI sacroiliac joints.

A child has bilateral hip joint pain with sacroiliac joint tenderness. What is the diagnosis?
  • A. Systemic JIA
  • B. Polyarticular JIA
  • C. Oligoarticular JIA
  • D. Psoriatic JIA
  • E. Enthesitis-related JIA
Best answer
E. Enthesitis-related JIA
HLA-B27-associated enthesitis-related JIA (ERA): enthesitis (heel pain), sacroiliitis, hip involvement, older boys, acute uveitis. Systemic JIA = quotidian fever + rash + serositis; oligoarticular = ≤4 joints (knees/ankles).

Meningitis — CSF, Causative Organisms & Meningococcaemia

CSF interpretation — the exam table:

NeutrophilsGlucoseProteinPressureClassic
Bacterial↑↑ (pleocytosis, often >1000)LOW (<½ plasma)↑↑Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae b (unimmunised), neonates Group B strep / E. coli / Listeria (add amoxicillin for listeria cover!)
Viral (aseptic)Lymphocytes (early can be neutrophils)NormalNormal–mild↑Normal–mild↑Enterovirus, HSV-2, VZV, mumps — self-limiting; treat supportive
TuberculousLymphocytesVERY LOW (<2.2 mmol/L)VERY HIGH (1–5 g/L)↑↑Insidious; cranial nerve palsies (VI), basal exudates, hydrocephalus (dilated ventricles); “cobweb” clot; ADA >10; AFB rare — treat with RHZE + dexamethasone
Fungal (Cryptococcus, TB-like)LymphocytesLowHigh↑↑Immunocompromised (HIV) — India ink/CR antigens; amphotericin + flucytosine
GBS (neonatal)AnyAnyAny↑E. coli, GBS — ampicillin + gentamicin

Clinical features: fever, headache, neck stiffness (meningism), photophobia, vomiting, altered consciousness, seizures, non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash (meningococcaemia), Kernig’s (pain on knee extension with hip flexed), Brudzinski’s (neck flexion → hip flexion), bulging fontanelle (infants). Meningococcaemia → septic shock, DIC, Waterhouse–Friderichsen (bilateral adrenal haemorrhage).

Management: do NOT delay antibiotics for imaging/LP if unwell — immediate IV ceftriaxone/cefotaxime (add amoxicillin if <3 months or listeria risk), dexamethasone with first dose (↓hearing loss in pneumococcal; continue if confirmed), ABCDE + fluids/vasopressors (shock), isolate (droplet), notify public health, contact prophylaxis (ciprofloxacin/rifampicin) for household contacts, hearing test after recovery, treat complications (seizures, hydrocephalus — neurosurgery/VP shunt, SIADH).

Neurological exam findings asked (this SAQ): neck stiffness, Kernig’s/Brudzinski’s signs positive, photophobia, altered GCS, focal deficits, bulging fontanelle; complications — sensorineural deafness, seizures, hydrocephalus, subdural effusion, learning difficulty, shock/amputation (meningococcaemia).

Exam pearls
  • LP first only if NO contraindication & child stable; otherwise antibiotics first — never delay.
  • Low glucose + high protein + lymphocytes = TB; high PMN + low glucose = bacteria.
  • Non-blanching purpuric rash + fever = ceftriaxone STAT + public health notification.

Neonatal Jaundice

Approach by timing:

TimingThink of
<24 h (always pathological)Haemolysis — Rh incompatibility (Rh-neg mother + Rh-pos baby), ABO incompatibility (O mother + A/B baby), G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis, sepsis (congenital), polycythaemia; direct hyperbilirubinaemia (TORCH/sepsis — urgent)
24 h–2 wksPhysiological (peak day 3–4, unconjugated, well baby, resolves ≤2 wks), breast-milk jaundice (peaks week 2, feeding well — continue breastfeeding), breastfeeding failure jaundice (under-feeding, weight loss — feed more), haemolysis, infection, polycythaemia, cephalohaematoma bruising
>2 wks (prolonged)Conjugated (cholestatic): biliary atresia (pale stools + dark urine — Kasai portoenterostomy before 8–12 wks!), choledochal cyst, Alagille, inborn errors (galactosaemia, α1-AT), infection (UTI!), hypothyroidism, breast-milk jaundice, haemolysis persisting

This exam’s EMQ (2020 set): day 3, well, unconjugated, resolves → physiological; first 24 h, mother O/baby A, DAT+, mild anaemia → ABO incompatibility; first day, Rh-neg mother sensitised (previous Rh-pos baby, no anti-D) → Rh incompatibility (severe — exchange transfusion risk); day 5 boy, male relatives affected, haemolysis → G6PD deficiency.

ABO vs Rh: ABO — mother O, baby A/B; usually mild, 1st baby can be affected (naturally occurring anti-A/B IgG), DAT weak/negative, no prenatal prophylaxis works (no anti-D for ABO). Rh — mother Rh-neg, baby Rh-pos; usually NOT first baby (needs sensitisation, unless prior transfusion/miscarriage), DAT strongly positive, severe haemolysis (hydrops fetalis), prevented by anti-D Ig (at 28/34 wks + within 72 h of delivery/sensitising events).

G6PD deficiency — X-linked; males; episodic severe haemolysis with infection/fava beans/drugs (sulfonamides, primaquine, nitrofurantoin, methylene blue); Mediterranean/African/Asian; avoid precipitants; check level; Heinz bodies/bite cells.

Management: monitor bilirubin (TSB or transcutaneous); phototherapy per age-appropriate thresholds (chart); exchange transfusion if severe (or BIND scores — bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction: lethargy, poor feeding, arching, high-pitched cry, later kernicterus — athetoid CP, hearing loss, gaze palsy); IVIG if immune haemolysis failing phototherapy; treat cause; breastfeeding support; prolonged conjugated → urgent USS + hepatology (biliary atresia timing critical).

Exam pearls
  • Jaundice <24 h = pathological — find the haemolysis.
  • Mother O + baby A/B = ABO (DAT±). Mother Rh− + baby Rh+ + prior affected sibling = Rh — anti-D prevents.
  • Pale stools + dark urine at 2–3 weeks = biliary atresia — Kasai before 8–12 weeks, every week counts.
  • G6PD: check family history of male jaundice; avoid oxidants.

#83MCQ2019-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-45570e68
A 24-hour-old neonate presents with jaundice. Baby was born to a G3P2 mother at 38 weeks of gestation. Investigations: hemoglobin 10 g/dL, reticulocytes 16%, direct Coombs test awaited. Total bilirubin 100 micromol/L, direct bilirubin 7 micromol/L. Mother's blood group A+, baby's blood group O+. There is a history of jaundice in elder siblings. Systemic examination is normal. What is the most likely cause of jaundice?
  • A. ABO incompatibility
  • B. Physiologic jaundice
  • C. Neonatal sepsis
  • D. Rh incompatibility
  • E. G6PD deficiency
Best answer
E. G6PD deficiency
Work the groups: mother A+ with baby O+ cannot be ABO-incompatible (an O mother with an A/B baby is the ABO risk pattern), and a Rh-POSITIVE mother cannot make anti-D, so Rh disease is excluded too. Yet there is haemolysis (Hb 10, reticulocytes 16%), jaundice within 24 h, and jaundice in elder siblings → inherited red-cell enzyme defect (oxidant stress). G6PD deficiency (X-linked) is the designed answer. Coombs would confirm immune causes — here the blood groups rule them out. Start phototherapy; confirm with G6PD level (may be falsely normal during acute haemolysis).

Neonatal Respiratory Distress — RDS, TTN, MAS, Sepsis, Pneumothorax

Differential by timing, mode of delivery and X-ray:

RDS (hyaline membrane)TTN (wet lung)MASNeonatal sepsis/pneumoniaPneumothorax
WhoPreterm (<34 wks; less often IDM/term C-section)Term, LSCS/rapid delivery (no labour → retained fluid)Post-term/term, meconium-stained liquor (pea-soup)PPROM >18 h, maternal GBS/chorioamnionitis, feverSpontaneous (1–2% newborns), post-resuscitation, MAS/RDS complication
OnsetAt/within minutes–hours of birthWithin hours (2–6 h), resolves 24–72 hWithin hoursHours–daysAny time; sudden desaturation
X-rayGround-glass reticulogranular + air bronchograms + low lung volumesPerihilar streaking + fluid in fissures, hyperinflated, normal volumesCoarse patchy infiltrates, hyperinflation, flattened diaphragm, ± air leaksVariable — focal infiltrate/effusion or normalVisceral pleural line + absent lung markings beyond it; mediastinal shift if tension
MechanismSurfactant deficiency → atelectasisDelayed clearance of fetal lung fluid (lymphatic/circulation)Airway obstruction (ball-valve) + chemical pneumonitis + surfactant inactivationGBS/E. coli/ Listeria infectionAir leak from overdistension/rupture
ManagementCPAP early (avoid ventilation if possible) + exogenous surfactant (INSURE/LISA), antenatal steroids preventSupportive: O₂, CPAP if needed; self-limitingSupportive: O₂, ventilation, surfactant; avoid antibiotics unless infected; amnioinfusion historic (no longer routine)IV benzylpenicillin + gentamicin + full septic screen (cultures, FBC, CRP, LP if stable) + supportiveNeedle aspiration/chest drain (2nd ICS MCL) if tension/symptomatic; observation if small asymptomatic

This exam’s questions: 34-weeker + ground-glass = surfactant deficiency (RDS); term C-section + 3 h of distress = TTN; pea-soup liquor = MAS; PPROM = neonatal sepsis; post-C-section tachypnoea = TTN.

Acute care principles: ABCDE; thermoregulation; O₂ sats monitoring; blood glucose; escalate to CPAP/ventilation, CXR, treat sepsis if suspected (don’t wait for cultures), transfer to NICU.

Exam pearls
  • Ground-glass + air bronchograms + preterm = RDS = surfactant.
  • Term + LSCS + tachypnea in first hours = TTN = supportive.
  • Pea-soup liquor = MAS. PPROM + maternal infection = sepsis work-up now.
  • Sudden desaturation + asymmetry = pneumothorax — transilluminate/CXR.

  • C. Transient tachypnoea of the newborn
  • D. Congenital pneumonia
