2019 · Pediatrics · 4 questions · MCQ

Nephrotic Syndrome & Proteinuria (Children)

Definition: (1) proteinuria — nephrotic range: urine PCR >200 mg/mmol (spot) or >40 mg/m²/h (24 h) or 3–4+ dipstick; (2) hypoalbuminaemia (<25 g/L typically); (3) oedema (periorbital, genital, dependent, ascites/pleural effusions); ± hyperlipidaemia.

Causes by age (critical age splits):

  • Congenital (<3 months): congenital nephrotic syndrome (Finnish type) — NPHS1 (nephrin) mutation; massive proteinuria from birth; needs albumin infusions + ACE-i + eventually bilateral nephrectomy + transplant. Also Denys–Drash, Pierson syndrome.
  • 1–12 years: MINIMAL CHANGE DISEASE (~90%) — steroid-SENSITIVE; insidious onset oedema over days; normal renal function, complement normal; NO haematuria (if present → biopsy). Diagnosis = clinical — empirical prednisolone 60 mg/m²/d (max 60–80 mg) ×4–6 weeks then taper; 85–90% respond (remission in 2–4 weeks). Biopsy ONLY if: age <1 or >12, steroid resistance (no response by 4–6 wks), haematuria, hypertension, low complement, renal impairment, atypical course.
  • Steroid-resistant/frequent relapsers/adults: FSGS, membranoproliferative GN, membranous nephropathy, IgA, lupus (renal biopsy to differentiate). FSGS commonest in steroid non-responders (and in older children).
  • Secondary: infections (post-strep, hepatitis B/C, HIV), SLE, HSP/IgA, drugs (NSAIDs — membranous), amyloid, malignancy.

Orthostatic (postural) proteinuria — benign; adolescent; proteinuria when upright, absent in first-morning urine; normal renal function/complement; confirm with split urine samples (early AM vs daytime) or first-void UPCR <20 mg/mmol; NO treatment, annual review.

Management of MCD: prednisolone course; relapses (proteinuria return) → re-treat; frequent relapsers → alternate-day low-dose steroids or second-line (levamisole, cyclophosphamide, cyclosporine, mycophenolate/tacrolimus; rituximab); oedema — salt restriction, fluid restriction if severe, loop diuretics (furosemide ± spironolactone) + IV albumin if severe symptomatic hypovolaemia (then furosemide); immunisations (pneumococcal + meningococcal + influenza — infection risk from immunosuppression + loss of complement/immunoglobulins); thrombosis risk (hypercoagulable — sparse activity restriction, avoid dehydration; consider aspirin/warfarin if albumin very low <20 g/L or thrombotic event); lipids — usually normalise with remission.

Investigations at presentation: urine dip/PCR, serum albumin, renal function, lipids, C3/C4, ASO (excludes PSGN), FBC (infection), urine microscopy; exclude secondary causes (ANA, HBV/HCV); biopsy only as above.

Exam pearls
  • Child >1 y + oedema + heavy proteinuria + normal renal function = MCD → steroids — biopsy only if atypical.
  • Proteinuria only when standing = orthostatic — split samples, benign.
  • <3 months onset = congenital (Finnish) — nephrin; very bad; genetic testing.
  • Steroid resistance → biopsy → FSGS.

#101MCQ edited2019-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-f6d9397d
A 7-year-old child presents with facial puffiness and 4+ protein in urine. He was given a 4-week course of prednisolone with no response. What is the most likely diagnosis?
  • A. Minimal change disease (MCD)
  • B. IgA nephropathy
  • C. FSGS (focal segmental glomerulosclerosis)
  • D. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN)
  • E. Membranous nephropathy
Best answer
C. FSGS (focal segmental glomerulosclerosis)
Nephrotic syndrome + steroid resistance (no response after 4–6 weeks prednisolone) = steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome — FSGS is the commonest cause (also consider C1q nephropathy, minimal change variants, genetic (nephrin/podocin mutations)). Renal biopsy indicated. MCD is steroid-SENSITIVE.

  • B. When it is steroid-resistant
  • C. When there is macroscopic hematuria
  • D. When complement is low
  • E. When it occurs in adults

A. When it responds to steroids
Minimal change disease accounts for ~90% of steroid-SENSITIVE nephrotic syndrome in children — diagnosis is clinical (no biopsy needed). Failure to respond → FSGS/other → biopsy. Steroid sensitivity IS the clue.

2019 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Neurodevelopmental Disorders — ADHD & ASD

ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder): persistent (≥6 months), onset <12 y, in ≥2 settings (home + school): inattention (careless mistakes, can’t sustain attention, doesn’t listen, fails to finish tasks — “does he leave tasks uncompleted?”), hyperactivity (fidgets, leaves seat, “driven by a motor”, talks excessively), impulsivity (blurts out, can’t wait turn, interrupts). Prevalence ~5%; boys > girls; strong genetic component (74%); co-morbid: ASD, conduct disorder, learning difficulties, anxiety, tics.

Diagnosis: clinical — interview parents + child + teacher rating scales (Conners, SNAP-IV); exclude mimics (hearing/vision, sleep apnoea, thyroid, absence seizures, iron deficiency, lead, psychosocial); DSM-5/ICD-11 criteria (≥6 inattentive and/or ≥6 hyperactive-impulsive symptoms).

Management: psychoeducation (parents, child, school — seat front, chunked tasks, movement breaks, immediate rewards); environmental interventions first for preschoolers; medication for ≥6 y (or moderate–severe): methylphenidate (first-line — immediate/modified release), lisdexamfetamine, atomoxetine (non-stimulant — if stimulants contraindicated), guanfacine; monitor growth, appetite, BP/HR, sleep; review every 6 months.

Autism spectrum disorder: impaired social communication/interaction (poor eye contact, no joint attention, not pointing by 18 mo, not sharing enjoyment, no pretend play, difficulty reading social cues) + restricted, repetitive behaviours (hand-flapping, lining up toys, rigid routines, sensory hyper/hyposensitivity, intense narrow interests). Recognised by 12–24 months; red flags: not responding to name, no babble, no pointing, no words by 18 mo, regression of language/social skills.

Screening: M-CHAT-R/F at 16–30 months (universal at 18 months) → positive → referral for formal developmental assessment (ADOS, MDT).

Management: early intervention (EI) programmes, behavioural therapy (ABA/ESDM), speech & language therapy (PECS if non-verbal), occupational therapy (sensory/integration), educational support, family counselling; treat comorbidities (sleep, anxiety, GI); NO medication for core symptoms (only for associated ADHD/irritability — risperidone short-term for severe aggression).

Exam pearls
  • M-CHAT at 16–30 months. 18-month universal screen.
  • ADHD: methylphenidate first-line ≥6 y; psychoeducation + behavioural always.
  • Language delay → HEARING TEST first — then M-CHAT/ASD screen.
  • Regression = urgent evaluation (metabolic, neuroimaging, genetics).

2019 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Otitis Media & Otitis Externa

Acute otitis media (AOM) — middle-ear infection, commonest in 6–24 months; usually follows URTI (eustachian tube dysfunction — short/horizontal in infants). Organisms: S. pneumoniae (commonest), non-typable H. influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis; in neonates/IC: Gram-negatives; GBS; post-influenza → S. aureus/GBS.

Presentation (this exam): rhinorrhoea prodrome → fever, earache (otalgia), irritability, pulling at ear, hearing loss, poor feeding; otoscopy: bulging, erythematous, immobile tympanic membrane, loss of light reflex, effusion (± pus behind TM) — image typically shows a bulging red TM with loss of landmarks/light reflex.

Diagnosis = clinical (pneumatic otoscopy — impaired mobility). Management: analgesia + antipyretic; most viral and self-limiting — watchful waiting 24–48 h if mild >2 y; antibiotics (oral amoxicillin 5–7 d) if: <2 y (esp. bilateral/otorrhoea), severe symptoms, high fever, otorrhoea, unwell, no improvement; alternatives — amoxicillin-clavulanate (recent antibiotics/treatment failure); allergy → macrolide. Complications: mastoiditis (post-auricular swelling/erythema, pinna pushed forward — urgent IV antibiotics + CT + mastoidectomy), facial nerve palsy, meningitis, intracranial abscess, persistent effusion (glue ear → hearing loss — grommets).

Otitis externa — canal inflammation (swimming, trauma): pain with tragal movement/pinna pull, itchy, discharge, canal swelling; organisms S. aureus/Pseudomonas; treat: topical ciprofloxacin/ofloxacin drops (± steroid), keep dry, aural toilet; avoid aminoglycoside drops if perforated TM.

Exam pearls
  • Bulging erythematous TM after URTI = AOM → amoxicillin if severe/<2 y/otorrhoea; analgesia always.
  • Mastoiditis (boggy swelling behind ear) = emergency.
  • Ear pain + tragal tenderness + swimming = otitis externa — drops, not oral antibiotics.

Pneumonia — Consolidation

Consolidation vs effusion vs pneumothorax — the bedside table:

Vocal fremitusPercussionBreath soundsAdded
Consolidation (pneumonia)IncreasedDullBronchial (harsh, expiratory component)Crackles, ± pleural rub; dullness definite
Pleural effusionDecreased/absentStony dullDecreasedBronchial above fluid; meniscus on CXR
PneumothoraxDecreasedHyperresonantAbsentSurgical emphysema; tracheal shift if tension
Collapse/atelectasisDecreasedDullDecreased/absentTracheal deviation TOWARD side; hyperinflation elsewhere

Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) — CURB-65 (confusion, urea >7, RR ≥30, SBP <90 or DBP ≤60, age ≥65; 1 point each): 0–1 home oral amoxicillin; 2 admit (IV benzylpenicillin + clarithromycin); ≥3 severe (IV co-amoxiclav + clarithromycin ± ICU). Common organisms: S. pneumoniae (commonest), H. influenzae (COPD), Mycoplasma (young, dry cough, extrapulmonary — cold agglutinins), Legionella (air-con/water systems, hyponatraemia, GI upset — urinary antigen), Klebsiella (alcoholics — red-currant sputum), S. aureus (post-influenza — cavitation).

This exam: increased fremitus + dullness + bronchial breathing = lobar consolidation. 4-year-old with bronchial breathing + image of opacification = lobar pneumonia — most common organism in a child = S. pneumoniae (pneumococcus).

Exam pearls
  • Increased fremitus + dull + bronchial = consolidation.
  • Child’s lobar pneumonia = pneumococcus; adults CAP = pneumococcus; atypicals in the young.
  • Pleural effusion = decreased fremitus + stony dull; pneumothorax = hyperresonant.

  1. Describe the lesion. (1 pt)

  3. What is the most common organism? (1 pt)

Bacterial pneumonia: fever, toxicity, lobar consolidation, ↑WCC/CRP — high-dose amoxicillin 5–7 d; complications (parapneumonic effusion/empyema — drain if pH<7.2 or large), follow-up CXR if slow resolution; vaccinate.
2019 · Pediatrics · 1 question · SAQ

Acute Rheumatic Fever

Definition: systemic autoimmune disease after Group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes) pharyngitis (never skin); 2–4 weeks after infection; type II hypersensitivity (molecular mimicry) — antibodies cross-react with valve/joint/brain antigens. Peak 5–15 y.

Jones criteria (2015): need evidence of preceding GAS infection (↑ASO titre or anti-DNase B, positive throat swab, or recent scarlet fever) + 2 major OR 1 major + 2 minor:

MAJOR (JONES)MINOR
Joints — migratory polyarthritis (knees/ankles/wrists/elbows — “moves from joint to joint”)
O — carditis (new murmur — mitral regurgitation (apical pansystolic → axilla), tachycardia, pericarditis/pleuritic pain, or echo valve regurgitation)
N — subcutaneous nodules (extensor surfaces, painless)
E — erythema marginatum (pink, ringed, non-pruritic rash on trunk)
S — Sydenham’s chorea (involuntary movements, emotional lability — may appear months later)		Fever; arthralgia; raised ESR/CRP; prolonged PR interval; previous RF/rheumatic heart disease

This exam: migratory polyarthritis + ASO+ + ESR/CRP↑ + new apical pansystolic murmur radiating to axilla = rheumatic fever with carditis (mitral regurgitation).

Management: eradicate strep — penicillin V/benzathine penicillin IM (or erythromycin); NSAIDs (naproxen/ibuprofen) for arthritis (avoid aspirin in children — Reye’s); severe carditis → prednisolone; bed rest while active; SECONDARY PROPHYLAXIS (the most important): penicillin V 250 mg BD (or benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU IM every 3–4 weeks) for 10 years or until age 21–25 (longer — life / to 40 y — if carditis); echo/serial follow-up for valvular disease; echo every 1–5 years; dental prophylaxis if prosthetic valve; avoid NSAIDs if renal issues.

Exam pearls
  • Migratory polyarthritis + post-strep + new MR murmur = RF with carditis.
  • Jones: 2 major or 1 major + 2 minor + evidence of GAS (ASO).
  • MS mid-diastolic murmur comes years later — acute RF gives MR (pansystolic).
  • Secondary prophylaxis benzathine penicillin every 3–4 weeks ×10 years — stops progression to chronic rheumatic heart disease.

#187SAQ edited2019-Pediatrics-SAQ-Medicine-3256a992
Rheumatic fever with arthritis/arthralgia.
  1. Mention 2 minor criteria of rheumatic fever. (2 pt)
  2. Mention 2 major criteria of rheumatic fever. (2 pt)
Best answer
Minor criteria: fever; arthralgia; elevated ESR/CRP; prolonged PR interval; previous RF/rheumatic heart disease. Major criteria (JONES): Joints — migratory polyarthritis; carditis (pancarditis: new murmur, heart failure, pericarditis); subcutaneous Nodules; Erythema marginatum (ring-like rash, non-pruritic, trunk); Sydenham chorea (St Vitus dance — purposeless movements, emotional lability).
Diagnosis (Jones): 2 major OR 1 major + 2 minor + evidence of preceding GAS infection (ASO/anti-DNase B/throat culture/rapid antigen). Treat: penicillin eradication + salicylates/naproxen for arthritis, steroids if severe carditis; secondary prophylaxis (IM benzathine penicillin every 3–4 weeks for years).
2019 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Rickets

Definition: defective mineralisation of growing bone/cartilage in children (osteomalacia = the adult equivalent) — vitamin D deficiency (commonest), calcium deficiency, phosphate deficiency / renal phosphate wasting, renal failure (↓1-α hydroxylase).

THIS exam: child with rickets but normal serum calcium — secondary hyperparathyroidism (B) keeps calcium normal — low vitamin D → ↓gut Ca absorption → ↓Ca → PTH↑ → renal Ca reabsorption + bone resorption restores normocalcaemia at the cost of ↓phosphate and bone turnover; ALP elevated; PTH high; 25-OH vitamin D low; Ca normal–low; phosphate normal–low.

Features: craniotabes (soft skull), frontal bossing, delayed fontanelle closure, rickety rosary (costochondral beading), Harrison’s sulcus, pigeon chest, widened wrists/ankles, bow legs (genu varum) / knock-knees, delayed dentition, hypotonia (“floppy baby”), irritability, delayed walking, hypocalcaemic seizures/tetany (if severe), fractures, delayed growth.

Diagnosis: X-ray wrists/knees — fraying, cupping, widening of the metaphysis; ↑ALP; ↓25-OH-D; normal/low Ca; high PTH; often ↓phosphate.

Management: vitamin D (colecalciferol / ergocalciferol) high-dose + adequate calcium (Ca-fortified feeds/supplements); breast-fed infants need vitamin D supplement (400 IU/day); fortification of milk; correct clothing/sun exposure; treat renal causes with alfacalcidol + phosphate binders; surgery only for severe deformity after healing; dental care.

Exam pearls
  • Normal Ca in rickets = secondary hyperparathyroidism.
  • Metaphyseal cupping/fraying on X-ray; ALP high; 25-OH-D low.
  • Give vitamin D + calcium — not calcium alone.

#139MCQ edited2019-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-584a5d14
A child has rickets symptoms but serum calcium is normal. What keeps the calcium normal?
  • A. Primary hyperparathyroidism
  • B. Secondary hyperparathyroidism
  • C. Vitamin D deficiency
  • D. Hypoparathyroidism
  • E. Renal failure
Best answer
B. Secondary hyperparathyroidism
Vitamin D deficiency (rickets): Ca falls → PTH rises (secondary hyperparathyroidism) → normalises serum Ca (at cost of bone resorption). Hence rickets with normal calcium — low phosphate + high ALP + high PTH. Primary HPT gives HIGH Ca; hypoparathyroidism gives LOW Ca.

Seizures & Epilepsy

Semiology first — type defines treatment:

TypeFeaturesDrug of choice
Absence (typical)Child 4–10 y; sudden staring/“in a daze”, eyelid flutter, 5–15 s, many per day, no post-ictal confusion; 3 Hz spike-waveEthosuximide (or valproate)
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME)Morning myoclonic jerks of limbs/shoulders + GTC seizures + absence; onset 12–18 y; sleep deprivation/alcohol trigger; 4–6 Hz polyspike-waveSodium valproate (females of childbearing age: levetiracetam/lamotrigine)
Temporal lobe (focal impaired awareness)Aura (epigastric rising / déjà vu / burning smell — “burning leather”), staring, lip-smacking/automatisms (chewing, picking), post-ictal confusionCarbamazepine / lamotrigine / levetiracetam
Generalized tonic-clonicSudden fall, tongue biting, incontinence, post-ictal drowsiness/confusionValproate / levetiracetam
Infantile spasms (West syndrome)3–12 months; salaam attacks — sudden flexion of head/trunk/limbs in clusters; hypsarrhythmia on EEG; developmental regression — treat with vigabatrin ± ACTH; think tuberous sclerosisVigabatrin ± steroids
Febrile seizure6 mo–5 y, fever, generalized, <15 min, single in 24 h = SIMPLE (benign, ~1% later epilepsy); complex: focal / >15 min / recurrence within 24 hReassurance + safety (side position, nothing in mouth); treat fever does NOT prevent recurrence; benzodiazepine if >5 min
Non-epileptic (psychogenic) seizureEyes closed, prolonged fluctuating jerks, pelvic thrusting, crying/emotional context (exam stress), NO incontinence/tongue bite/injury/post-ictal state; normal EEGCBT/psychology — NOT anti-epileptics

Management of acute seizure (this exam): ABCDE + position + O₂ → abortive drug if >5 min: midazolam (buccal/IM/IV) or lorazepam IV or diazepam IV/PR — repeat once → if still seizing (status): second-line levetiracetam / phenytoin / valproate (>15–20 min) → refractory (>40 min): phenobarbital or anaesthesia + ICU. Maintenance after abortion of prolonged convulsion: continue anti-seizure prophylaxis with sodium valproate (or leviteracetam), not single-agent benzodiazepines alone.

Risk factors for epilepsy after febrile convulsion: complex febrile seizure, family history of epilepsy, pre-existing neurodevelopmental delay, short interval from fever onset to seizure (<1 h). Simple febrile = near-population risk.

Exam pearls
  • “Smell burning leather + lip smacking + staring” = temporal lobe epilepsy. “Morning limb jerks” = JME. “Exam-time jerks, eyes closed, crying, no incontinence” = psychogenic.
  • Absence = ethosuximide. Status: midazolam → phenytoin/levetiracetam → phenobarbital.
  • Febrile seizure ≠ epilepsy; complex features are the risk.

A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency room after having tonic-clonic convulsions for 2 minutes. What is the most appropriate drug to abort the seizure?

  • B. IV acetaminophen

#148MCQ edited2019-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-a58948f5
Which of the following is a risk factor for a febrile convulsion becoming epilepsy?
  • A. Family history of epilepsy
  • B. Age less than 2 years
  • C. Simple febrile seizure
  • D. Female gender
  • E. High-grade fever
Best answer
A. Family history of epilepsy
Risk factors for febrile seizure → epilepsy: family history of epilepsy, complex febrile seizure (focal/prolonged >15 min/recurrent in 24 h), neurodevelopmental abnormality, short duration of fever before seizure. Simple febrile seizure in a normal child = ~1–2% risk (close to general population).
2019 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Sickle Cell Disease — Parvovirus Aplastic Crisis

Pathophysiology: β6 Glu→Val point mutation → HbS polymerises when deoxygenated → RBC sickling → haemolysis (compensated-reticulocytosis normally) + vaso-occlusion (ischaemic pain, acute chest syndrome, stroke, splenic infarction/sequestration, priapism, osteonecrosis).

This exam’s key teaching set (two 2019/2017 items):

  • SCD + sudden fall in haemoglobin with LOW reticulocytes (and pancytopenia ±) → parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis — the virus infects erythroid precursors → marrow arrest — confirm with reticulocyte count (LOW — the answer, B) + parvovirus IgM/PCR. Management: supportive — transfusion if symptomatic; self-limiting ~1–2 weeks; isolate (teratogenic — pregnant contacts at risk of hydrops).
  • SCD + acute chest syndrome (fever, hypoxia, new infiltrate on CXR) + low Hb/platelets/WCC = parvovirus aplastic crisis (the answer A) — but in real life acute chest has an infectious trigger (Mycoplasma/chlamydia/virus/fat embolism) and needs: O₂, incentive spirometry, broad-spectrum antibiotics (cover atypicals), bronchodilators, analgesia, and urgent transfusion/exchange transfusion if severe (PaO₂ falling, multilobar).

SCD core: newborn screen; hydroxycarbamide (raises HbF — fewer crises); penicillin V + PCV vaccine (functional asplenia — S. pneumoniae/H. flu/Neisseria risk); folic acid; transcranial Doppler annually (stroke — transfuse if abnormal); avoid dehydration/cold/hypoxia/altitude; immunisations including meningococcal vaccine.

Exam pearls
  • SCD + low Hb + LOW reticulocytes = parvovirus aplastic crisis.
  • Sickle test distinguishes SCD from thalassaemia; Hb electrophoresis confirms.
  • Functional asplenia → pneumococcal/meningococcal vaccination + daily penicillin.

#131MCQ edited2019-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-2200d402
A patient with sickle cell disease (SCD) has low Hb and low platelets with normal/low-normal WBC. Parvovirus B19 is suspected. How would you confirm it?
  • A. Reticulocyte count will be low
  • B. Positive blood culture
  • C. Raised CRP
  • D. Positive direct Coombs test
  • E. Low haptoglobin
Best answer
A. Reticulocyte count will be low
Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid progenitors → transient aplastic crisis — Hb falls but RETICULOCYTE COUNT IS LOW/absent (marrow not producing). Confirm with parvovirus IgM/DNA; supportive transfusion if symptomatic; usually self-resolving in 1–2 weeks.

Skin & Soft-Tissue Infections — Cellulitis, Abscess

IDSA classification:

TypeFeaturesOrganismTreatment
Non-purulent cellulitisDiffuse, spreading erythema, warmth, swelling, pain, poorly demarcated, ± fever/streaking (lymphangitis)β-haemolytic streptococci (Group A — S. pyogenes)Oral/IV flucloxacillin/penicillin (+ clindamycin if severe)
Purulent (abscess/furuncle)Localized, fluctuant, tender, indurated red area ± central point/“head”Staphylococcus aureus (incl. MRSA — commonest purulent cause)Incision & drainage (main treatment) ± antibiotics if surrounding cellulitis/fever/immunocompromised

Paediatric SAQ (this exam): fever + leg pain + red image in a child → cellulitis — Group A (or S. aureus); treatment beyond antibiotics/fluids: supportive — elevate the limb, analgesia/antipyretic, mark the border, admit if unwell/rapidly spreading (measure & monitor spread; escalate to surgery if necrotising).

Exam pearls
  • Diffuse spreading (adults) = Group A strep → penicillin/flucloxacillin.
  • Localised fluctuant/child’s calf = S. aureus → drainage ± anti-staph antibiotics.
  • Pain out of proportion + dusky skin = necrotising fasciitis → operate NOW.

#180SAQ image edited2019-Pediatrics-SAQ-Medicine-e20ec1dd
A patient presents with fever and leg pain (image shown).
  1. What is the most likely diagnosis? (1 pt)
  2. Which organism causes this condition? (1 pt)
  3. Mention treatment other than fluids and antibiotics. (1 pt)
Best answer
1) Cellulitis with possible necrotising fasciitis — fever + rapidly spreading painful leg erythema (image: gram-positive cocci in chains). 2) Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A β-haemolytic streptococcus). 3) Other than fluids + IV antibiotics: urgent surgical exploration/debridement of necrotic tissue (necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency — “source control”), plus early plastic/orthopaedic involvement.
GAS cellulitis: painful spreading erythema, non-purulent, lymphangitis ± bacteraemia. Necrosis signs — pain out of proportion, bullous, crepitus, skin necrosis, rapid spread — mandate immediate debridement; mortality high if delayed; add clindamycin (toxin suppression) to penicillin.

  • Rheumatic fever = erythema marginatum.
  • HSV + target lesions = erythema multiforme.
  • Newborn blotches day 2 = erythema toxicum (benign).

2019 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Urinary Tract Infection in Children

Why nitrites can be NEGATIVE in a UTI (this exam):

  • Non-nitrate-reducing organism — enterococci, Klebsiella? no (nitrate+), Staphylococcus saprophyticus, Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas — the classic negatives: enterococci & S. saprophyticus; early sample (insufficient bladder incubation time — <4 h)
  • Frequent voiding/dilute urine (no time for nitrate reductase to work)
  • Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) in urine — blocks the nitrite reaction
  • Technical — expired strip, contamination, reading too early
  • High-grade fever/dehydration = DILUTE urine? — no: these reduce sensitivity; the pure “reason” options are the organism or inadequate retention

The exam answer: infection with a non-nitrate-reducing organism (D).

Paediatric UTI core: suspect sepsis pathway — young infant + fever = urine MUST be checked (clean catch/MSU/suprapubic aspirate/catheter — bag urine only for screening, never for diagnosis); leucocyte esterase + nitrite + pyuria/bacteriuria + culture; treat oral cefalexin/nitrofurantoin (lower tract) / co-amoxiclav or cefalosporin (pyelonephritis) 7–10 days; infants <3 months or septic → IV antibiotics + admission; imaging: USS all <6 months or atypical/recurrent; DMSA for scarring; MCUG if reflux suspected; vesicoureteric reflux = commonest underlying abnormality — check siblings; treat with prophylactic antibiotics if severe (grades IV–V) / surgery.

Exam pearls
  • Negative nitrite ≠ no UTI — non-reducers (enterococci) or inadequate bladder dwell.
  • Young infants: check urine in ALL unexplained fevers; treat with cephalosporin.
  • Recurrent/atypical → imaging (USS, DMSA, MCUG).

#96MCQ2019-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-d256cd88
A neonate with fever is suspected to have a UTI. The urine dipstick shows a negative nitrate result. What is a possible reason for this result?
  • A. High-grade fever
  • B. Dehydration
  • C. Klebsiella infection
  • D. Infection with a non-nitrate-reducing organism
  • E. Contaminated sample
Best answer
D. Infection with a non-nitrate-reducing organism
Urine dipstick nitrites need nitrate reductase enzymes (Enterobacterales — E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus). Gram-positives (Enterococcus, Staph saprophyticus, GBS) and Pseudomonas do NOT reduce nitrate → nitrite negative despite true UTI. In neonates always send culture anyway — treat on culture, not dipstick.

2018 · Genetics · 1 question · MCQ

Chromosomal Disorders — Down Syndrome, Turner & Mechanisms

Down syndrome (trisomy 21) — incidence ~1 in 700; risk rises with maternal age (but most affected babies are born to younger mothers).

Mechanisms: (1) nondisjunction in meiosis I (90–95%) — extra chromosome 21; recurrence risk ~1% (or maternal-age related). (2) Unbalanced Robertsonian translocation (4–5%; e.g. 14;21) — if a parent is a balanced carrier, recurrence risk is high (balanced mother → ~10%, balanced father → ~2%). (3) Mosaicism (1–2%) — milder phenotype. Recurrent trisomy 21 in siblings → test PARENTS with karyotype for a balanced translocation (not the child again).

Clinical features: hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, single palmar (simian) crease, sandal-gap toes, flat occiput/brachycephaly, small ears, protruding tongue, Brushfield spots; congenital heart (AVSD, VSD, PDA), duodenal atresia (double bubble), Hirschsprung, hypothyroidism, atlanto-axial instability, haematological malignancy (ALL/AML-M7), early Alzheimer-type dementia; global developmental delay; short stature.

Screening/management: confirm by karyotype (FISH for rapid confirmation if needed). At birth: echo + abdominal USS (duodenal atresia), hearing (OAE) and eye screen, TSH at birth/6 mo/yearly, full blood count; annual thyroid checks; early intervention. Counselling: recurrence risk; discuss prenatal diagnosis (CVS 11–14 wks, amniocentesis ≥15 wks, NIPT).

Trisomy 8 mosaicism — full trisomy 8 is embryonic lethal; surviving “trisomy 8” = mosaic (nondisjunction post-zygotically or trisomy rescue) → milder features (deep plantar creases, skeletal/urogenital).

Turner syndrome (45,X / X-monosomy) — girls: short stature, shield chest + widely spaced nipples, webbed neck, cubitus valgus, lymphedema at birth, streak ovaries → primary amenorrhoea/infertility + hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism, bicuspid aortic valve/coarctation, horseshoe kidney, normal IQ (may have visuospatial deficit), treat with growth hormone + oestrogen HRT; karyotype confirms; Y-material carrying → gonadectomy (gonadoblastoma risk).

Klinefelter (47,XXY) — tall, small firm testes, gynaecomastia, infertility (azoospermia), ↑FSH/LH.

Exam pearls
  • Recurrent Down in siblings → parental karyotype (translocation) — not “bad luck”.
  • Trisomy 8 survival = mosaicism.
  • Turner = coarctation + webbed neck + no puberty; confirm karyotype.
  • Down = AVSD + double-bubble + brushfield + simian crease.

#249MCQ2018-Genetics-MCQ-Medicine-e265a3b3
The mother of a 4-year-old Down syndrome child came to the genetics clinic; she previously had two other children with the same problem. What is the likely cause of this?
  • A. Nondisjunction
  • B. Unbalanced translocation
  • C. Balanced translocation
  • D. Mosaicism
  • E. Robertsonian translocation
Best answer
C. Balanced translocation
Recurrent Down syndrome in siblings → one parent is a BALANCED translocation carrier (usually 14;21 Robertsonian) with no phenotype themselves — their gametes produce unbalanced translocations. Karyotype the PARENTS — recurrence risk then quantifiable (mother balanced → ~10–15%; father → ~1–3%).
2018 · Genetics · 2 questions · MCQ/SAQ

Inborn Errors of Metabolism

Classification (functional groups):

  1. Small-molecule intoxication syndromes — acute/recurrent encephalopathy, vomiting, acidosis after triggers (illness/fasting/protein load): amino acid disorders (PKU, MSUD, tyrosinaemia, homocystinuria), organic acidurias (propionic, methylmalonic, isovaleric — sweaty-feet odour), urea cycle defects (hyperammonaemia + respiratory alkalosis, NO acidosis — ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, X-linked).
  2. Energy-deficiency syndromes — hypoketotic hypoglycaemia during fasting: fatty-acid oxidation defects (medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase — MCAD; hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, encephalopathy), glycogen storage diseases (GSD I/von Gierke — fasting hypoglycaemia + lactic acidosis + hepatomegaly + hyperuricaemia; GSD V/McArdle — exercise cramps), mitochondrial disorders.
  3. Large-molecule (storage) disorders — progressive, static deficits, coarse features, organomegaly: lysosomal storage (Gaucher, Niemann-Pick, Tay-Sachs, mucopolysaccharidoses — Hurler/Hunter, Pompe/GSD II), peroxisomal (Zellweger).

Classic presentations (this exam’s EMQ):

  • Phenylketonuria (PKU) — normal at birth → developmental delay, seizures, eczema, fair hair/skin (↓tyrosine→↓melanin), “musty/mousy” odour; ↑phenylalanine on newborn screen (Guthrie test); treat low-Phe diet + sapropterin.
  • Galactosaemia — well at birth → days after milk feeds: poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, cataracts, E. coli sepsis, hypoglycaemia; GALT enzyme/1-phosphate-uridylyltransferase; treat lactose-free diet.
  • MSUD — 4–7 days: poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, maple-syrup urine odour, ↑BCAAs/ketoacids; treat BCAA-free diet.
  • Von Gierke (GSD I) — 3–4 months: fasting hypoglycaemia + lactic acidosis + hyperuricaemia + hepatomegaly; improves with frequent carbs.
  • Urea cycle defect — neonatal: hyperammonaemia (encephalopathy, seizures, coma) + respiratory alkalosis WITHOUT acidosis or hypoglycaemia.

Diagnosis: newborn screening (Guthrie/tandem mass spec), plasma amino acids, acylcarnitine profile, urine organic acids, ammonia, glucose, lactate, pH/anion gap, urinary ketones (absent in FAO defects), enzyme assays, genetic testing. Family history/consanguinity (first cousins — most are autosomal recessive).

Exam pearls
  • Healthy newborn → days later encephalopathy/vomiting/coma after feeds = IEM until proven otherwise (ammonia + VBG + glucose NOW).
  • Hyperammonaemia + alkalosis = urea cycle; acidosis + ketones/anion gap = organic aciduria; hypoketotic hypoglycaemia = FAO defect.
  • Musty urine + fair skin + eczema + ID = PKU.
  • Consanguinity + regression = storage disease — enzyme assay.

#263SAQ edited2018-Genetics-SAQ-Medicine-4904a08d
A child came with progressive weakness and repeated fractures. Parents are first-degree cousins (case of a metabolism defect).
  1. What is the likely mechanism of disease? (1 pt)
  2. What is the mode of inheritance? (1 pt)
  3. If the maternal uncle decides to marry the paternal aunt, what is the chance that each carries the same defect? (2 pt)
Best answer
1) Likely mechanism: enzyme deficiency causing inborn error of metabolism with lysosomal storage — most consistent here with a lysosomal/metabolic disorder (progressive weakness + fractures); in the classic case of this stem (consanguinity), the mechanism = autosomal recessive single-gene metabolic defect — accumulation of toxic metabolites or energy failure/storage. 2) Mode of inheritance: autosomal recessive (consanguinity = first-cousin marriage strongly supports AR). 3) If the maternal uncle marries the paternal aunt: each is an obligate/near-obligate carrier in an AR pedigree where both sides carry the same allele; each has ~2/3 chance of being a carrier (if they are unaffected siblings of an affected individual), and the chance BOTH carry the same recessive allele ≈ 2/3 × 2/3 = 4/9 (per the pedigree probabilities; if known obligate carriers = 100%). State assumptions: for offspring of an affected person it is 100%; for siblings of affected = 2/3.
Consanguinity multiplies the probability of homozygosity for rare recessive alleles. In this scenario the answer typically: both cousins marry — each has a 2/3 prior risk of carrier status → each child 1/4 affected if both carriers. Confirm with targeted gene testing rather than relying on risk alone.
2018 · Genetics · 1 question · EMQ

Mutation Types & Disease Mechanisms

Mutation (DNA-level) types:

TypeDefinitionExamples
MissenseSingle base change → different amino acidSickle cell (β6 Glu→Val); Arg185Leu (this exam); achondroplasia FGFR3 Gly380Arg; collagen in Marfan
Nonsense→ premature stop codonDuchenne (frame/stop); β-thalassaemia some; APC (FAP)
Silent→ same amino acid (wobble)Synonymous SNP (marker only)
FrameshiftInsertion/deletion NOT multiple of 3 → reading frame shiftsDuchenne (deletions), most severe CFTR loss-of-function
Trinucleotide repeat expansionRepeat grows beyond threshold (anticipation)Fragile X (CGG), Huntington’s (CAG), myotonic dystrophy (CTG), Friedreich’s (GAA)
Splice-siteDisrupts donor/acceptor sitesSome β-thalassaemia; Marfan some
Deletion (large)kb–Mb lossDiGeorge (22q11), Williams (7q11), Prader-Willi (15q), SMA (SMN1 exon 7)
DuplicationCopy gainCMT1A (PMP22 duplication), 17p11.2 duplication
Robertsonian translocationFusion at centromeres of acrocentrics (13,14,15,21,22)Down syndrome (14;21) — balanced parent
NondisjunctionChromosomes fail to separate in meiosisTrisomy 21/18/13; 45,X; 47,XXY; trisomy 8 (mosaic survival)
InversionSegment flips within chromosomeInv(9) benign; Inv(8)(p23q22)

From mutation to disease — mechanism levels: (1) Loss of function (null/hypomorphic) — enzyme deficiencies (PKU, lysosomal); (2) Gain of function — Huntington toxic protein; achondroplasia FGFR3 (constitutive activation); (3) Dominant-negative — Marfan (fibrillin multimers poisoned), collagen III (vascular EDS); (4) Haploinsufficiency — one normal copy insufficient (FBN1, SHOX in Turner); (5) Toxic metabolite accumulation — urea cycle, organic acidurias; (6) protein aggregation/misfolding — α1-antitrypsin Z; prions; (7) Nonsense-mediated decay; (8) Repeat expansion → methylation silencing — fragile X.

Exam pearls
  • Glu→Val = missense; stop codon = nonsense; shifts frame = frameshift.
  • Anticipation + maternal transmission = CGG repeat (fragile X).
  • Single amino-acid swap (Arg→Leu) = missense — always.

2018 · Genetics · 1 question · MCQ

Patterns of Inheritance & Risk Calculation

Pedigree logic — the six patterns:

PatternHallmarksExamplesRisk to offspring
Autosomal dominantEvery generation; male-to-male; ~50% of children of affected parent; both sexesMarfan, HOCM, Huntington’s, neurofibromatosis, familial hypercholesterolaemia, achondroplasia50%
Autosomal recessiveSiblings only (one generation); consanguinity raises risk; 25% recurrence; silent carriers (2/3 of unaffected siblings are carriers)Cystic fibrosis, sickle cell, thalassaemia, PKU, congenital adrenal hyperplasia25% if both parents carriers
X-linked recessiveMales affected; female carriers usually unaffected (some manifesting); NO male-to-male; 50% sons of carrier mother affected; 50% daughters carriers; affected father → ALL daughters carriers, no sons affectedDMD, haemophilia A/B, G6PD, fragile X (X-linked with anticipation — CGG)Sons of carrier mother: 50%; daughters: 50% carriers (rarely symptomatic)
X-linked dominantBoth sexes; affected fathers → ALL daughters affected, no sons; 50% children of affected motherVitamin D–resistant rickets (XLH), Rett syndrome (female), Fragile X sometimes classified separately50%
MitochondrialMother → ALL children (both sexes) can inherit; father → NONE; highly variable (heteroplasmy); high energy tissues affected (MELAS, MERRF, LHON)MELAS, MERRF, Leber optic neuropathy, Kearns–SayreAll children of affected mother at risk (variable expression)
Y-linked (holandric)Only males; father → ALL sonsHairy ears (debated), some infertility (AZF deletions)100% of sons

Worked answers (this exam):

  • DMD in boy + 2 maternal uncles affected → mother obligate carrier → his sister: 50% carrier, 0% symptomatic.
  • HOCM: father, brother, paternal uncle — male-to-male = autosomal dominant.
  • Mitochondrial → maternal inheritance (all children of affected mother).
  • Marfan (father died suddenly, tall + pectus) = autosomal dominant.
  • DMD in family → daughter of affected? No — daughter of a carrier: 50% chance carrier; her sons: 50% affected. “Chance the daughters’ sons will be affected” = 50%.
Exam pearls
  • Father→son transmission = autosomal dominant (never X-linked).
  • Consanguinity = recessive; only one generation = recessive.
  • Mitochondrial = mothers transmit to all children; fathers transmit none.
  • DMD: sisters of affected boys — 50% carriers, ~0% symptomatic.

The mother of a male child with progressive weakness on walking (case of DMD) came to you concerned about the chance of her daughter having the disease. What is the percentage that her daughter will have the disease?
  • A. 25%
  • B. 100%
  • C. 0%
  • D. 50%
  • E. 75%
Best answer
C. 0%
Mother is the obligate carrier of DMD (one of her sons affected). Her daughters each have 50% chance of being carriers — chance of a DAUGHTER being AFFECTED (symptomatic) ≈ 0% (manifesting carriers mild, rare; full manifestation only with skewed X-inactivation). (Exam key: 0%.)

Primary Immunodeficiency

The clinical rule: pattern of infection tells you the defect:

ArmTypical infectionsDiseases
B-cell (antibody)Recurrent bacterial — sinopulmonary (pneumonia, sinusitis, otitis), encapsulated organisms (S. pneumo, H. flu), enteroviruses, Giardia; present after 6 months (maternal IgG gone)X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (Bruton — BTK) — ABSENT TONSILS/LYMPH NODES (this exam), absent B cells/Ig; common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) — low IgG, later onset; IgA deficiency (commonest — recurrent sinopulmonary/GI, anaphylaxis to blood products)
T-cellViral, fungal, protozoal, mycobacteria, opportunisticSevere combined immunodeficiency (SCID) — absent T (± B/NK) cells — absent thymic shadow on CXR (this exam!), chronic diarrhoea, failure to thrive, opportunistic infections from birth; DiGeorge (22q11) — thymic hypoplasia + hypocalcaemia + cardiac + cleft
PhagocyteCatalase-positive organisms — S. aureus, Serratia, Burkholderia, Aspergillus; deep abscesses, osteomyelitis; granulomasChronic granulomatous disease (CGD) — NADPH oxidase defect; leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD) — delayed umbilical stump separation, no pus, neutrophilia — treat: HSCT
ComplementRecurrent Neisseria (C5–9 MAC deficiency), SLE-like picture (C1q/C4)Complement deficiencies

This exam: repeated infections from birth + absent thymus on CXR = DiGeorge syndrome (absent/hypoplastic thymus — T-cell deficiency); recurrent infections + no tonsils + maternal uncle = X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (Bruton’s) — haemoglobin and lymphocytes may be normal; immunoglobulins very low; check CD19 B cells absent; treatment = lifelong replacement immunoglobulin therapy (IVIG/SCIG) + antibiotics.

Exam pearls
  • Absent tonsils/nodes + boys + bacterial infections = XLA.
  • Absent thymus on CXR = DiGeorge (22q11) — check Ca, echo, FISH.
  • SCID = no T cells — urgent HSCT before infection/vaccination.

  • D. HIV

Best answer
E. DiGeorge syndrome
Absent thymus (CXR) + recurrent infections since birth = DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) — also cleft palate, cardiac defects (TOF/truncus), hypocalcaemia (absent parathyroids), T-cell deficiency. “No thymus shadow on CXR in an infant + infections” is the classic stem.

2018 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Acid–Base Disorders

Every ABG question in this exam is solved the same way — do it mechanically, never by pattern-guessing:

  1. Look at pH. <7.35 = acidaemia, >7.45 = alkalaemia (7.35–7.45 can still hide a mixed disorder).
  2. Look at pCO₂ and HCO₃⁻. Whichever moves in the same direction as the pH is the primary process: pCO₂↑ → respiratory acidosis; HCO₃⁻↓ → metabolic acidosis; pCO₂↓ → respiratory alkalosis; HCO₃⁻↑ → metabolic alkalosis.
  3. Check compensation. Acute respiratory acidosis: HCO₃⁻ rises 1 per 10 mmHg pCO₂; chronic: rises 3.5–4 per 10 (max ~31). Metabolic acidosis: expected pCO₂ = (1.5 × HCO₃⁻) + 8 ± 2 (Winter’s formula). If compensation is not as expected → mixed disorder.
  4. Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO₃); normal 8–12 (without K). High gap → MUDPILES (methanol, uraemia, DKA, propylene glycol/paraldehyde, iron/isoniazid, lactic acidosis, ethylene glycol, salicylates). Normal gap (hyperchloraemic) → diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis, Addison’s, saline.
DisorderpHpCO₂HCO₃⁻Classic causes
Respiratory acidosis↓↑↑ (comp.)Opioids/sedatives, COPD, severe asthma, neuromuscular weakness, CNS depression
Respiratory alkalosis↑↓↓ (comp.)Pain, anxiety, early sepsis, salicylates (early), pregnancy, PE, hypoxia at altitude
Metabolic acidosis↓↓ (comp.)↓DKA/HHS, lactic acidosis (shock, metformin), diarrhoea, RTA, uraemia, toxins
Metabolic alkalosis↑↑ (comp.)↑Vomiting, NG suction, diuretics, Conn’s/Cushing’s, hypokalaemia, bicarbonate load

High CO₂ + low HCO₃⁻ + low pH (COPD patient) = mixed respiratory + metabolic acidosis — the low bicarbonate cannot be explained by compensation for a respiratory acidosis, so two primary processes are present. The same logic applies to the unconscious patient with an empty syringe and high lactate (respiratory depressant + lactic acidosis).

Exam pearls
  • Opioid/benzodiazepine overdose → acute respiratory acidosis (high pCO₂, normal/near-normal HCO₃⁻); ↓ respiratory rate (RR 6–8/min), pinpoint pupils.
  • Salicylates → mixed respiratory alkalosis + metabolic acidosis.
  • COPD chronic retainers live with high pCO₂ and high HCO₃⁻; give cautious O₂ (target 88–92%).
  • Lactate >2 = tissue hypoperfusion; treat the cause, not the number.
  • Toxic alcohols/methanol → high anion gap acidosis + high osmolar gap.
Traps
  • Normal pH does NOT mean normal ABG — mixed disorders can cancel out (e.g. mixed acidosis can sit near 7.35–7.40). Always compute the gap and check compensation.
  • "Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation" requires pCO₂ LOW; "respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation" requires HCO₃⁻ HIGH. High CO₂ + low HCO₃⁻ is always a mixed disorder.
  • Do not "treat" compensation — treat the primary process.

2018 · Internal Medicine · 3 questions · MCQ

Acute Coronary Syndrome (STEMI / NSTEMI / Unstable Angina)

Definition spectrum of ACS — all from coronary plaque rupture/erosion with superimposed thrombosis:

Unstable anginaNSTEMISTEMI
Chest painAt rest / crescendoAt restSevere, prolonged >20–30 min
TroponinNormalElevatedElevated
ECGNormal / ST depression / T inversionST depression, T inversion, or normalST elevation ≥1 mm in ≥2 contiguous leads (or new LBBB)
ManagementAspirin + P2Y12 (clopidogrel/ticagrelor) + anticoagulant (heparin/enoxaparin) + high-risk features → early invasive angiography (≤24 h)Immediate reperfusion: primary PCI within 90–120 min of first medical contact, else fibrinolysis if PCI unavailable <120 min and pain <12 h (and no contraindications)

ECG localisation — memorise this cold:

  • Inferior (II, III, aVF) → RCA (80–90%, supplies RV + inferior wall); reciprocal ST depression in I, aVL. Think posterior MI if ST depression V1–V3 (check V7–V9), and right ventricular infarct (RV4R ST elevation) — avoid nitrates/preload reduction.
  • Anterior / anteroseptal (V1–V4) → LAD.
  • Lateral (I, aVL, V5–V6) → circumflex (LCx) / diagonal.
  • Extensive anterior (I, aVL, V1–V6) → proximal LAD; watch for pump failure.

Post-operative / post-PCI patients: chest pain with ECG changes after surgery — get a troponin (and repeat 3–6 h); troponin rise defines perioperative MI (usually Type 2 if supply–demand). After PCI + stenting, secondary prevention = DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel ~12 months) + high-intensity statin + ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker. Post-PCI with renal impairment: ACE inhibitors/ARBs both ↓GFR initially — monitor K⁺/Cr; the examinable "add-on" when ACEI/BB already in place and renal function is borderline is an ARB substitute or long-acting nitrate for angina.

NSTEMI management: dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin 300 mg loading then 75 mg + clopidogrel/ticagrelor), anticoagulation (LMWH/fondaparinux), beta-blocker if no heart failure, high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80), ACEi, risk-stratify (GRACE) → early coronary angiography if troponin-positive or ST changes.

Exam pearls
  • Pain + ST elevation + prior normal ECG = STEMI → activate cath lab, do not wait for troponin.
  • New LBBB + chest pain = treat as STEMI equivalent.
  • Inferior STEMI → check RV leads; give fluids if hypotensive, avoid nitrates/diuretics.
  • Troponin is the gatekeeper between unstable angina and NSTEMI — it changes management.
  • Post-MI discharge drugs: aspirin + P2Y12, statin, ACEi, beta-blocker ("ABAS").
  • Exertional chest pain with normal ECG → risk-stratify first (troponin if acute; stress test if stable).
Traps
  • ST depression in V1–V3 can be a posterior STEMI — upright tall R waves; don’t call it ischaemia only.
  • Do not give nitrates/ACEi to a hypotensive inferior/RV infarct.
  • "Troponin normal, pain settled, ECG flat" ≠ discharge without work-up — serial troponins and risk stratification.

If the ACE-i is implicated in his renal problem (rising creatinine/K⁺, bilateral renal artery stenosis), the RAAS block offered here is the ARB — substitute with close Cr/K⁺ monitoring (repeat at 1–2 weeks). (In real practice the missing pillar would usually be a high-intensity statin and dual antiplatelet therapy; if his angina persists on a beta-blocker, a long-acting CCB/nitrate is added. ACE-i→ARB substitution with renal monitoring is the answer the exam is reaching for when renal intolerance to the ACE-i is the constraint.)
2018 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · SAQ

Acute Kidney Injury — Pre-renal, Intrinsic (ATN), Post-renal

Definition (KDIGO): Creatinine ↑ ≥26.5 µmol/L within 48 h, or ≥1.5× baseline within 7 days, or UO <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h. Stage by creatinine rise / urine output.

Pre-renalIntrinsic — ATNPost-renal
Mechanism↓ renal perfusion (dehydration, sepsis, heart failure, ACEi/ARB + NSAIDs, renal artery)Ischaemic or nephrotoxic tubular damage (aminoglycosides, cisplatin, contrast, pigment, sepsis)Obstruction below collecting system (BPH, stones, tumour, blocked catheter)
FeNa<1%>2%Variable
Urine Na<20 mmol/L>40 mmol/LVariable
Urine microscopyBland / hyaline castsMuddy brown granular casts, renal tubular epithelial cellsBland; may see haematuria
Serum urea:Cr>20:1<10–15:1Variable
Urine osmolality>500<350Variable

Nephrotoxins to know: gentamicin/aminoglycosides → ATN (also causes hypomagnesaemia); cisplatin & carboplatin → ATN; amphotericin B → ATN + distal RTA/K⁺/Mg²⁺ wasting; ACE inhibitors/ARBs → functional (pre-renal) rise in Cr via efferent dilation, especially with bilateral renal artery stenosis; penicillins/cephalosporins/PPIs/NSAIDs → acute interstitial nephritis (fever, rash, eosinophilia, WBC casts); contrast → contrast-induced nephropathy (48–72 h); methotrexate/ethylene glycol.

Tumor lysis syndrome (leukaemia/lymphoma post-chemo): hyperkalaemia + hyperphosphataemia + hyperuricaemia + hypocalcaemia → AKI; prevent with allopurinol/rasburicase + IV fluids; life-threatening K⁺ → treat immediately.

Rhabdomyolysis (marathon, crush, statins): dark urine, myalgia, ↑↑ CK, hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia (early) → myoglobinuric ATN. Best test: serum CK (± urine myoglobin).

Obstructive (post-renal) clues: distended bladder, frequency/hesitancy/BPH, recent ACEi dose increase unmasking bilateral obstruction — small rise in creatinine with normal kidney size + palpable bladder → urethral catheter + ultrasound.

Management ATN: stop nephrotoxins, restore volume/perfusion, treat hyperkalaemia (calcium gluconate, insulin/dextrose, salbutamol, bicarbonate, K-binders, dialysis), treat acidosis & fluid overload. Indications for emergency dialysis (AEIOU): Acidosis refractory, Electrolyte (K⁺ >6.5 or symptomatic), Ingestions (toxins), Overload (pulmonary oedema refractory to diuretics), Uraemia (encephalopathy, pericarditis, seizures).

Exam pearls
  • FeNa <1% + history of poor intake/heart failure → pre-renal. FeNa >2% + muddy brown casts → ATN.
  • WBC casts → pyelonephritis/interstitial nephritis; RBC casts → glomerulonephritis; muddy brown granular casts → ATN.
  • Aminoglycosides: monitor levels; hypomagnesaemia + rising Cr = tubular toxicity — stop the drug.
  • Post-chemo leukaemia patient with high K, high PO₄, low Ca → tumour lysis → rasburicase + fluids.
  • After CABG/surgery → think ischaemic/pigment ATN ± cardiorenal.
Traps
  • In contrast nephropathy and rhabdomyolysis, FeNa can be <1% early — don’t exclude ATN solely on FeNa.
  • Creatinine can lag — the earliest sign of AKI is often rising K⁺ and oliguria.
  • Never give ACEi in bilateral renal artery stenosis — creatinine rises sharply.

#259SAQ image edited2018-InternalMedicine-SAQ-Medicine-9d0d87f6
A man came following a motor vehicle accident with multiple fractures. He had oliguria; RFT was given and shows acute kidney injury (hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia and hypocalcemia), and his urine microscopy showed the following (image shown).
  1. Describe the finding (muddy brown casts). (1 pt)
  2. What is the likely diagnosis? (1 pt)
  3. Give 2 blood investigations to support your diagnosis. (2 pt)
  4. What is the treatment? (1 pt)
Best answer
1) Muddy brown granular casts (renal tubular epithelial cell casts) on microscopy. 2) Likely diagnosis: acute kidney injury — acute tubular necrosis (ATN), pigment-induced (myoglobinuric) from rhabdomyolysis after crush/multiple fractures (± hypovolaemia). 3) (a) Serum creatine kinase (CK) — very high; (b) urine myoglobin (and paired serum/urine electrolytes — hyperK, hyperPO4, hypoCa) + FeNa >2%, urine Na >40, muddy brown casts. 4) Treatment: aggressive IV isotonic fluids (0.9% saline ± sodium bicarbonate alkalinization to prevent pigment nephropathy), strict electrolyte/hydration monitoring, avoid nephrotoxins/potassium, dialysis if refractory hyperkalaemia/acidosis/pulmonary oedema/uraemia.
Rhabdomyolysis → myoglobin precipitates in tubules → ATN. Aim urine output >200 mL/h; stop offending drugs (statins); treat hyperkalaemia (calcium gluconate, insulin/dextrose); urgent dialysis if AEIOU criteria met.
2018 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · EMQ

Aortic Dissection

Definition: tear in intima → blood tracks into media → false lumen separates layers; can propagate proximally (coronary ostia, aortic valve — AR, cardiac tamponade) or distally (branch occlusion — stroke, limb ischaemia, renal failure, mesenteric).

Stanford classification: Type A = any involvement of ascending aorta (surgical emergency — mortality rises ~1% per hour untreated); Type B = descending only (medical management first — IV beta-blockade, then vasodilators).

Risk factors: hypertension (most important — especially poorly controlled), connective tissue disease (Marfan, Ehlers–Danlos, Loeys–Dietz), bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, pregnancy (third trimester), cocaine, trauma, iatrogenic (catheterisation), vasculitis/infective aortitis.

Clinical picture: tearing/ripping chest pain radiating to the back, abrupt onset, maximal at onset; may migrate; hypertension (or hypotension if tamponade/rupture — ominous), pulse/BP differential between limbs, new diastolic murmur of AR, syncope, neuro deficits (stroke, paraplegia), abdominal pain (mesenteric), oliguria (renal).

Investigation: CT angiography (CTA) — the investigation of choice in haemodynamically stable patients: fast, defines entry tear, extent, branch vessels, perfusion, effusion. Transoesophageal echo for unstable patients or when CTA contraindicated. ECG to exclude MI (dissection can involve RCA ostium → inferior STEMI!). CXR: widened mediastinum (non-specific).

Management: Type A → immediate surgery; Type B (stable) → strict BP/HR control (target HR <60, SBP 100–120; IV labetalol/esmolol first, then nitroprusside/GTN), ICU care; surgery/EVAR if complicated (rupture, malperfusion, refractory pain, expansion). Lifelong anti-impulse therapy and imaging follow-up.

Exam pearls
  • Tearing pain radiating to back + hypertension + afebrile + no troponin story → dissection (not MI, not pericarditis — pericarditis is pleuritic, worse lying flat, better leaning forward).
  • CTA is the first-line test; TTE/TOoE if unstable.
  • Check bilateral BPs and pulses in every chest pain — inter-arm difference >20 mmHg is a red flag.
Traps
  • Do NOT give anticoagulants/fibrinolytics until dissection excluded in chest pain with back radiation — catastrophic if dissection.
  • Inferior STEMI + tearing pain = dissection involving RCA until proven otherwise.

Cardiac Arrhythmias — Recognition & Acute Management

Approach to any ECG rhythm: rate → regularity → P waves (present? each before a QRS?) → PR length → QRS width → ST/T. Then match to a rhythm and assess stability (ABCDE — shock, syncope/pre-syncope, ischaemia/chest pain, heart failure).

RhythmKey ECG featuresNotes / management
Sinus tachycardiaHR >100, normal P before each QRSPhysiological — treat the cause (pain, fever, hypovolaemia, PE, thyrotoxicosis, drugs)
AVNRT / AVRT (SVT, PSVT)Regular narrow-complex tachycardia ~150–250, P waves hidden/inverted/retrograde after QRSVagal manoeuvres → adenosine 6→12→12 mg rapid IV bolus; unstable → synchronized cardioversion; long-term: ablation
Atrial flutterSaw-tooth flutter waves ~300/min, typically 2:1/4:1 block (ventricular ~150), narrow QRSRate control (beta-blocker/verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin) or DC cardioversion; anticoagulation per CHA₂DS₂-VASc; CTI ablation is curative
Atrial fibrillationIrregularly irregular narrow complex, no distinct P wavesLoss of JVP “a” wave (no atrial contraction). Rate control first (BB/CCB/digoxin); anticoagulate per CHA₂DS₂-VASc; unstable → DC cardiovert; consider rhythm control/ablation if young/symptomatic
VTBroad complex regular tachycardia; concordance, AV dissociationStable → IV amiodarone/procainamide; unstable → immediate synchronized cardioversion; pulseless → defibrillation + ALS
Heart block1°: PR >200 ms constant. 2° Mobitz I (Wenckebach): progressive PR prolongation then dropped beat. 2° Mobitz II: sudden dropped beat, constant PR. 3° (complete): AV dissociation, regular escape rhythmMobitz II & CHB → admit, transcutaneous/transvenous pacing; atropine often ineffective; stop AV-nodal blockers
VF / pulseless VTChaotic or broad-complex without pulseImmediate defibrillation + CPR + adrenaline 1 mg every 3–5 min

CHA₂DS₂-VASc (stroke risk in AF): CHF (1), HTN (1), Age ≥75 (2), DM (1), Stroke/TIA (2), Vascular disease (1), Age 65–74 (1), Sex female (1). Score 0 (men) / 1 (women) → no anticoagulation; ≥1 (men)/≥2 (women) consider OAC; ≥2 → anticoagulate (DOAC preferred). HAS-BLED estimates bleeding risk — high score is NOT a reason to withhold anticoagulation; it flags need for closer review/modifiable factors.

JVP “a” wave is produced by atrial contraction → absent in AF (no organised atrial systole); giant “a” waves in tricuspid stenosis; cannon “a” waves in complete heart block/AV dissociation (atrium contracts against closed tricuspid valve).

Exam pearls
  • Irregularly irregular + absent “a” wave = AF. Narrow regular tachycardia in a young woman with normal baseline = AVNRT → vagal then adenosine.
  • Unstable tachycardia/bradycardia → electricity wins (synchronized shock for pulse present; defibrillation for pulseless).
  • High-grade AV block (Mobitz II, complete) → pacing, not atropine alone.
  • Antidromic AVRT/VT wide-complex doubt → treat as VT (procainamide/amiodarone; avoid AV-nodal blockers in pre-excited AF).
Traps
  • Do not use adenosine in pre-excited AF (irregular wide complex) — can precipitate VF.
  • Cardioversion in AF >48 h without anticoagulation/imaging → stroke risk; anticoagulate ≥3 weeks or do TOE, or cardiovert early (<48 h) with heparin.

2018 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Asthma — Diagnosis & Acute Exacerbation

Diagnosis: variable respiratory symptoms (wheeze, cough, chest tightness, dyspnoea) + variable expiratory airflow limitation: FEV₁/FVC <0.7 with ≥12% and ≥200 mL improvement in FEV₁ after bronchodilator, or excessive diurnal peak-flow variability (>20%), or positive bronchial challenge (methacholine/histamine) if spirometry is normal. Normal spirometry does NOT exclude asthma in a symptomatic patient → methacholine challenge is the next step.

Obstructive defect pattern: low FEV₁, low FEV₁/FVC, normal/low-normal FVC, and (in asthma) normal DLCO (unlike emphysema where DLCO is low).

Acute severe asthma (admit): PEF 33–50% predicted/best, respiratory rate ≥25, HR ≥110, inability to complete sentences, or O₂ sat <92%. Life-threatening: PEF <33%, silent chest, exhaustion/altered consciousness, SpO₂ <92%, normal/high PaCO₂ (exhaustion — rising CO₂ is a red flag).

Management of acute exacerbation:

  1. High-flow O₂ to keep SpO₂ 94–98%.
  2. Nebulised salbutamol (5 mg) + ipratropium bromide (0.5 mg) driven by O₂, back-to-back/repeat.
  3. Oral prednisolone 40–50 mg (or IV hydrocortisone) — steroids early.
  4. Not responding/severe → IV magnesium sulfate 1.2–2 g over 20 min; call ICU; consider IV aminophylline; avoid sedation; intubation if failing (permissive hypercapnia).
  5. Discharge: when PEF >75%, stable ≥12–24 h off nebs; written asthma action plan, GP/asthma nurse follow-up, inhaler technique review, optimise preventer (ICS-containing), address triggers and adherence, safety-net re admission.

Chronic stepwise management (GINA): low-dose ICS-formoterol as reliever (or SABA + ICS) → add LABA → medium-dose ICS/LABA → refer. SABA-only is no longer recommended — every reliever should contain ICS to cut severe exacerbations.

Exam pearls
  • First-line in acute attack after O₂: nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium + early oral steroids.
  • Rising/normal PaCO₂ in acute asthma = life-threatening — call for help.
  • Normal spirometry + typical symptoms → methacholine challenge confirms.
  • Nasal flaring, intercostal recessions, tracheal tug in a child = severe exacerbation with respiratory distress.

A 35-year-old male has shortness of breath on exertion; he is a non-smoker with no other stimulants, wheeze is heard, and spirometry and CXR are normal. What is the next step?

  • B. Alpha-1 antitrypsin
  • C. Repeat spirometry
  • D. Prescribe bronchodilator
  • E. Chest CT
Best answer
A. Methacholine challenge test
Exertional breathlessness + wheeze + NORMAL spirometry and CXR + non-smoker = suspected asthma with normal baseline tests → bronchoprovocation (methacholine) challenge (or FeNO/PEF variability) — a positive (fall FEV₁ ≥20%) confirms airway hyperresponsiveness.
2018 · Internal Medicine · 2 questions · MCQ

Chronic Kidney Disease — Stages, Complications & Dialysis

Definition: GFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² for ≥3 months, or kidney damage (albuminuria, urine abnormalities, structural) ≥3 months. Stages (KDIGO, by GFR): G1 ≥90, G2 60–89, G3a 45–59, G3b 30–44, G4 15–29, G5 <15 (kidney failure). Albuminauria categories A1–A3. eGFR <45 = CKD G3b → significant CV risk.

Complications — the exam loves this:

  1. Anaemia of CKD — ↓erythropoietin (starts G3b). Normocytic; check iron first (iron deficiency common) → iron + ESAs (epoetin) when Hb <100 g/L; target 100–120 g/L.
  2. Mineral–bone disorder (renal osteodystrophy) — ↓1α-hydroxylase → low active vitamin D; phosphate retention (primary problem) → high phosphate, low calcium, secondary PTH↑; FGF23↑; high-PTH bone disease (osteitis fibrosa) or adynamic bone disease (low turnover, over-suppressed PTH). Management: phosphate binders (calcium acetate, sevelamer) + vitamin D analogues (calcitriol/alfacalcidol) ± cinacalcet; restrict dietary phosphate.
  3. Hyperkalaemia — ↓excretion; worse with ACEi/ARB/spiro/NSAIDs.
  4. Metabolic acidosis (anion gap normal-ish/high in late).
  5. Fluid overload / hypertension / uraemia — encephalopathy, pericarditis (rub!), frost, pruritus, platelet dysfunction (bleeding).
  6. CV disease — commonest cause of death in CKD (accelerated atherosclerosis); lipid-lowering, BP control.

Renal replacement therapy (RRT) — AEIOU: refractory Acidosis, Electrolytes (K >6.5/symptomatic), Ingestions (dialysable toxins — lithium, salicylates, methanol), Overload (pulmonary oedema failing diuretics), Uraemic symptoms (pericarditis, encephalopathy, seizures). Choice: haemodialysis vs peritoneal dialysis vs transplant (best outcomes). A pericardial rub or confusion in CKD = dialysis now, whatever the urea number.

ACEi/ARB in CKD: renoprotective in proteinuric CKD/diabetes — start with low dose, check Cr/K at 1–2 weeks; accept up to 30% Cr rise; avoid in bilateral renal artery stenosis & pregnancy.

Exam pearls
  • High phosphate + low Ca + high PTH in CKD = secondary hyperparathyroidism → treat phosphate first (binders + low-PO4 diet) + active vitamin D.
  • “When to start dialysis?” — never on a number alone; the answer is refractory symptoms/signs (overload despite diuretics, pericarditis, encephalopathy, K⁺).
  • eGFR 45 with no symptoms still has G3a disease → anaemia can already appear (ESA after iron).

#217MCQ edited2018-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-d1b9bb04
In a CKD case, what causes the hypocalcemia?
  • A. Primary hyperparathyroidism
  • B. Secondary hyperparathyroidism
  • C. Tertiary hyperparathyroidism
  • D. Vitamin D deficiency
  • E. Hypoparathyroidism
Best answer
D. Vitamin D deficiency
CKD → ↓1α-hydroxylase → ↓calcitriol → ↓intestinal Ca absorption → hypocalcaemia (primary defect) → PTH rises (secondary HPT) to compensate. The question “what causes the hypocalcaemia” wants the low vitamin D activation answer; effectively both secondary mechanisms co-exist, but vitamin D deficiency of renal origin is the root.
#219MCQ edited2018-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-2ba8df9f
A question about CKD asks about its complications. Which of the following is a complication of CKD?
  • A. Anemia
  • B. Hyperkalemia
  • C. Renal osteodystrophy
  • D. Metabolic acidosis
  • E. All of the above
Best answer
E. All of the above
CKD complications (all listed): anaemia (↓EPO), hyperkalaemia (↓excretion + drugs), renal osteodystrophy (phosphate retention + ↓active vit D + secondary HPT), metabolic acidosis (↓H⁺ excretion). Also HTN, CVD, neuropathy, pruritus, bleeding diathesis.
2018 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · EMQ

COPD — Diagnosis, PFT & Exacerbations

Definition: chronic respiratory symptoms + persistent airflow obstruction (post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC <0.7) usually from noxious exposure — smoking (commonest), biomass, occupational dusts, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Chronic bronchitis = productive cough ≥3 months in 2 consecutive years; emphysema = alveolar wall destruction.

Diagnosis & investigations: spirometry is mandatory — shows obstruction not fully reversible. CXR (hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms) often normal early; high-resolution CT if unclear; alpha-1 antitrypsin if young/basal emphysema/family history/non-smoker; sputum culture in exacerbations; ABG in severe disease (chronic CO₂ retention → target SpO₂ 88–92%). Reduced cricosternal distance (<3 cm) = hyperinflation.

PFT patterns (exam table): obstruction = ↓FEV₁, normal/↓FVC, ↓FEV₁/FVC, quiet DLCO only if emphysema; restriction = ↓FEV₁, ↓FVC, preserved/high FEV₁/FVC, ↓TLC, usually ↓DLCO.

Chronic management: stop smoking (only intervention that alters decline); vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID); pulmonary rehabilitation; SABA/SAMA as needed → LABA or LAMA → ICS/LABA or triple therapy if frequent exacerbations; LTOT (long-term oxygen) if PaO₂ ≤7.3 kPa (or ≤8 kPa with cor pulmonale/polycythaemia).

Exacerbation (Anthonisen criteria): increased dyspnoea + increased sputum volume + increased sputum purulence. Treatment: controlled oxygen (target 88–92%), nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium, oral prednisolone 30 mg × 5 days, antibiotics (amoxicillin/doxycycline) if purulent sputum, NIV if respiratory acidosis persists despite therapy. Identify triggers (infection most common; PE and pneumothorax are mimics — CXR).

Exam pearls
  • Smoker + chronic cough + reduced cricosternal distance + obstruction on spirometry = COPD; asthma shows REVERSIBILITY.
  • COPD O₂ target = 88–92% (hypoxic drive considerations) — controlled, not non-rebreather-titrate-to-100%.
  • Spirometry confirms — peak flow/X-ray do not diagnose COPD.

Theme — Respiratory
  • A. COPD exacerbation
  • B. Pneumonia
  • C. Asthma exacerbation
  • D. Pulmonary embolism
  • E. Heart failure
Scenario 1A 68-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history and known COPD presents with worsening breathlessness, increased cough, and increased production of purulent sputum over 3 days. He has diffuse expiratory wheezing and decreased air entry bilaterally. He has no focal chest findings or peripheral edema.
Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Scenario 2A 45-year-old woman presents with 4 days of fever, productive cough, pleuritic right-sided chest pain, and shortness of breath. Temperature is 39.1°C, and examination reveals bronchial breath sounds and inspiratory crackles over the right lower lung field. Chest radiography shows a focal right lower lobe consolidation.
Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Scenario 3A 22-year-old woman with a history of asthma develops acute shortness of breath, chest tightness, cough, and wheezing after exposure to a known allergen. She is using her reliever inhaler more frequently than usual. Examination reveals diffuse expiratory wheezing and prolonged expiration without fever or focal chest findings.
Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Scenario 4A 36-year-old woman develops sudden-onset shortness of breath and sharp pleuritic chest pain several days after a long-haul flight. She is tachycardic and mildly hypoxemic. Chest examination is largely normal, and she has no fever or productive cough. Her left calf is mildly swollen and tender compared with the right.
Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Best answer
1→A, 2→B, 3→C, 4→D
1) 40 pack-years + ↑cough/purulent sputum + wheeze + no consolidation → COPD exacerbation. 2) Fever + pleuritic pain + lobar consolidation + bronchial breathing → pneumonia. 3) Known asthma + allergen exposure + wheeze + no fever → asthma exacerbation. 4) Long-haul flight + pleuritic pain + calf swelling + tachypnoea → pulmonary embolism.

Diabetic Emergencies — DKA vs HHS

DKA (T1DM): hyperglycaemia + ketosis + acidosis. Criteria: glucose >11.1 mmol/L (or known DM), ketones ≥3 mmol/L (urine ≥2+), pH <7.3 and/or bicarbonate <15. Triggers: missed insulin, infection/illness, first presentation, pump failure.

Features: polyuria/polydipsia/dehydration, Kussmaul breathing (deep sighing), ketotic breath (pear drops), abdominal pain, vomiting, confusion → coma. Labs: glucose high (sometimes only mildly — euglycaemic DKA on SGLT2i), total body K depleted despite high serum K (acidosis shifts K out; insulin drives it back in → hypokalaemia on treatment — replace K from 3.5 mmol/L), Na falsely low (hyperglycaemia — correct Na +1.6 per 5.6 glucose >5.6).

HHS (T2DM): glucose >33 mmol/L, osmolality >320, NO significant ketosis/acidosis, profound dehydration, focal neuro signs/seizures/coma; slower onset; mortality higher.

DKAHHS
Glucose>11.1>33
KetonesHigh (≥3 mmol/L)Low/absent
pH / HCO₃<7.3 / <15Normal
OsmolalityVariable>320
TypeT1T2
Fluid deficit3–6 L8–12 L

Management of DKA (ABCDE): (1) confirm blood ketones/VBG; (2) IV 0.9% NaCl — 1 L over 1 h, then over 2/2/4/6 h per protocol; (3) fixed-rate IV insulin 0.1 U/kg/h (do not bolus); continue long-acting insulin; when glucose ≤14 mmol/L → 10% dextrose to keep insulin running until ketones clear; (4) potassium — add to fluids when K <5.5 (hold insulin if K <3.3 until K restored); (5) treat trigger (sepsis screen, ECG, pregnancy test); (6) VTE prophylaxis; (7) hourly observations, glucose hourly, ketones/VBG 2-hourly; discharge on education + sick-day rules.

Exam pearls
  • DKA = glucose + ketones + acidosis; HHS = glucose + osmolality, no ketones.
  • In DKA, TOTAL body potassium is LOW even if serum K is high — never give insulin before checking K⁺.
  • Euglycaemic DKA on SGLT2 inhibitors — normal glucose does not exclude DKA.
  • Fluids first, insulin second; long-acting insulin continued; never stop insulin in T1 illness.

Electrolyte Disorders — Sodium & Potassium

Hyponatraemia — classify by volume status:

HypovolaemicEuvolaemicHypervolaemic
Urine NaLow <20 (extrarenal loss: GI, skin, third space) / High >20 (renal loss: diuretics, Addison’s, salt-wasting)>40 (SIADH); check TSH/cortisol (hypothyroid/adrenal = euvolaemic)Low <20 (HF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, CKD — effective arterial underfilling)
Treatment0.9% saline (restore volume) + treat causeFluid restrict (1 L/day) ± salt tablets/furosemide/vaptans (hypertonic 3% if seizures/severe neuro signs)Fluid + sodium restriction, loop diuretics, treat HF/cirrhosis; dialysis if renal failure

SIADH = hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia + inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osm >100, urine Na >40) + euvolaemia + normal renal/thyroid/adrenal + no diuretics. Causes: malignancy (small cell lung, pancreatic), CNS (stroke, tumour, meningitis), pulmonary (pneumonia, TB, PPV), drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, PPIs, chemotherapy, opioids, MDMA). Treat: fluid restriction ± hypertonic saline if symptomatic (Na <120 with seizures/coma — 3% saline, raise ≤8 mmol/L per 24 h to avoid central pontine myelinolysis).

Co-existing lung cancer + hyponatraemia = SIADH (ectopic ADH from small-cell carcinoma).

Hyperkalaemia: treat by severity/ECG. ECG progression: peaked (“tented”) T waves → PR prolongation → P flattening → QRS widening → sine wave → VF. K⁺ >6.5 or any ECG change = emergency: IV calcium gluconate (membrane stabilisation), insulin+dextrose, salbutamol nebulisers, sodium bicarbonate (if acidotic), K binders, dialysis if refractory. Stop K/ACEi/MRA/NSAIDs; check glucose (DKA?), renal function.

Hypokalaemia: causes — diuretics (loop/thiazide), vomiting/diarrhoea, hyperaldosteronism, hypokalaemic periodic paralysis (carbohydrate load in susceptible young men — e.g. “after a big carbohydrate meal”, resolves with K), Bartter/Gitelman, insulin, beta-agonists, RTA. Replace K orally if mild; IV if severe/symptomatic; check Mg (replace both). ECG: flattened T, U waves, ST depression, VT/VF.

Exam pearls
  • SIADH = low serum osm + urine Na>40 + euvolaemic → restrict fluid; symptomatic → 3% saline ≤8/24h.
  • Oedema + crackles + confusion + hyponatraemia = hypervolaemic dilutional (HF) — do NOT give saline.
  • Peaked T waves → calcium gluconate FIRST; insulin/dextrose second; dialysis if refractory.
  • Carbohydrate-feast weakness + low K in a young Asian male = hypokalaemic periodic paralysis.
Traps
  • Hypertonic saline for chronic asymptomatic hyponatraemia causes osmotic demyelination — correct slowly.
  • Pseudohyponatraemia (hypertriglyceridaemia/paraproteinaemia) — check osmolality/lab method if patient looks well.
  • Hypomagnesaemia → refractory hypokalaemia/hypocalcaemia — always co-check.

2018 · Internal Medicine · 2 questions · MCQ

Gastrointestinal Bleeding

Upper GI bleed (above ligament of Treitz): haematemesis ± melaena ± coffee-ground vomitus ± shock. Common causes: peptic ulcer (commonest, ~40–50%), varices (cirrhosis — most lethal), erosive gastritis/duodenitis, Mallory–Weiss tear (binge/vomiting → mucosal tear at GOJ after forceful retching), oesophagitis, malignancy (gastric/oesophageal), Dieulafoy lesion.

Clinical assessment (A→E): IV access ×2 large-bore, crossmatch/G&S, FBC/U&E (urea↑ disproportionately in upper GI bleed — blood digestion), clotting, LFT; Blatchford score (pre-endoscopy risk), Rockall score (post-endoscopy); resuscitate first, then OGD within 24 h (urgent <12 h if unstable/varices).

Management: resuscitation (crystalloid/blood — target Hb 70–80 g/L or symptomatic; restrictive transfusion), PPI (pantoprazole 80 mg IV bolus then infusion 8 mg/h) for non-variceal bleeding, IV terlipressin + prophylactic antibiotics (ceftriaxone/quinolone) + urgent endoscopic band ligation/sclerotherapy for variceal bleeds,correct coagulopathy (vit K/FFP/PCC), stop NSAIDs/anticoagulants, H. pylori eradication after ulcer; surgery/IR embolisation if endoscopy fails.

Cirrhosis + upper GI bleed + hypotension = varices — terlipressin FIRST (reduces portal pressure), antibiotics (variceal bleeds are portal of bacterial infection), band ligation. Avoid beta-blockers in the acute phase (hypotension).

Lower GI bleed: diverticular disease (commonest cause of painless large-volume rectal bleeding in elderly), angiodysplasia, colitis (IBD, ischaemic, infectious), haemorrhoids (bright red on paper/dripping), malignancy (change of bowel habit, weight loss, iron deficiency), ischaemic colitis (elderly + AF + post-prandial pain + PR bleeding — “mesenteric angina”). Investigations: OGD (exclude upper) → colonoscopy/CT angiography.

Exam pearls
  • Haematemesis in cirrhosis = varices until proven otherwise → terlipressin + antibiotics + urgent OGD.
  • Raised urea:creatinine ratio with melaena = upper GI source.
  • Resuscitate BEFORE scoping; transfuse restrictively.
  • Post-prandial abdominal pain + AF + PR bleeding = chronic mesenteric ischaemia.

  • D. Haemorrhoids

Best answer

2018 · Internal Medicine · 2 questions · MCQ

Heart Failure — HFrEF vs HFpEF, Acute & Chronic

Pathophysiology: inadequate cardiac output for metabolic needs (or only at high filling pressures). Classify by EF: HFrEF (EF ≤40%) — systolic failure (IHD/MI, dilated cardiomyopathy, hypertension long-standing, valvular); HFmrEF (41–49); HFpEF (≥50) — diastolic failure (hypertension, LVH, hypertrophic/restrictive CMP, constrictive pericarditis, ischaemia). Right-sided failure usually secondary to left-sided or lung disease (cor pulmonale).

Symptoms: dyspnoea (exertional), orthopnoea, PND, fatigue, ankle swelling, nocturia. Examination: raised JVP, S3 gallop (specific for volume overload/systolic failure), displaced apex, bibasal crackles, peripheral oedema, hepatojugular reflux, hepatomegaly.

Chronic HFrEF — the “four pillars” (all reduce mortality): (1) ACEi/ARB/ARNI (sacubitril–valsartan) — titrate to target; (2) beta-blocker (bisoprolol/carvedilol/metoprolol succinate) — start low, once stable; (3) MRA (spironolactone/eplerenone) — K & renal monitoring; (4) SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin/empagliflozin) — now regardless of diabetes. Plus: loop diuretic for congestion, ICD if EF ≤35% on optimal therapy, CRT if wide QRS (LBBB), iron for deficiency, treat sleep apnoea, vaccinate, cardiac rehab.

HFpEF: no drug reduces mortality — treat congestion with loop diuretics, aggressive BP/rate control, SGLT2i reduces hospitalisation; manage comorbidities (AF, IHD, obesity, diabetes).

Acute decompensated HF: ABCDE, sit up, high-flow O₂, IV furosemide (e.g. 40–80 mg or home dose ×2), stop beta-blocker if hypotensive/shocked (otherwise continue), CPAP if respiratory distress + acidosis; nitrates if hypertensive; treat precipitant (MI! infection, AF, NSAIDs, non-adherence); echocardiography for EF and valves; discharge plan + early follow-up.

ECG in severe LV dysfunction: reduced EF ± LBBB (CRT candidate if QRS ≥150 + LBBB + symptomatic on pillars).

Exam pearls
  • Four pillars for HFrEF: ACEi/ARB/ARNI + BB + MRA + SGLT2i. HFpEF = diuretics for symptoms.
  • S3 = failing ventricle — in volume overload.
  • Gradual weight gain + ankle swelling + breathlessness = fluid retention → furosemide.
  • New LBBB + EF 25% → CRT consideration after 3 months optimal pillars.

#195MCQ edited2018-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-02603955
