2018 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Immunisation — Live Vaccines, Household Contacts & Contraindications

Live (attenuated) vaccines: BCG, MMR, varicella, oral polio (OPV), rotavirus, live intranasal influenza, live zoster (Zostavax), yellow fever, oral typhoid, Japanese encephalitis (live SA14). These are replication-competent — dangerous in severe immunosuppression (chemotherapy, transplant, high-dose steroids, biologics, primary immunodeficiency, HIV with low CD4) and can infect household contacts (OPV shed in stool).

Inactivated/killed/subunit/toxoid: hepatitis B, HiB, pneumococcal (conjugate/polysaccharide), DTP/Tdap, injectable polio (IPV), hepatitis A, HPV, injectable influenza, meningococcal — safe in immunosuppression.

Absolute contraindications: anaphylaxis to a previous dose or vaccine component; live vaccines in severe immunosuppression/pregnancy (MMR, varicella, BCG, OPV, yellow fever). NOT contraindications: mild febrile illness, recent exposure, prematurity (vaccinate by chronological age), breastfeeding, family history of seizures/adverse events, stable neurological conditions, antibiotic therapy, recovery from recent illness, local reaction/low-grade fever after dose.

Household contact rule (tested twice here): a severely immunocompromised child (chemotherapy for leukaemia) living with a sibling — the sibling must NOT receive live vaccines, especially OPV (viral shedding can paralyse the immunocompromised child) and BCG/varicella/MMR where applicable; use inactivated alternatives (IPV instead of OPV). Close contacts of transplant patients: avoid live vaccines except MMR/VZV per guidance (risk-benefit).

Tetanus prophylaxis for wounds: fully immunised + booster within 5 years → nothing; booster 5–10 y (clean wound) / any high-risk wound with booster >5 y → booster; incomplete/uncertain + high-risk wound → tetanus toxoid + tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG); dirty wounds: check.

Special situations: egg allergy → influenza/MMR/yellow fever generally safe with observation (severe egg anaphylaxis → specialist); HIV (CD4 >200): give MMR/varicella; pregnancy: no live vaccines (give MMR postpartum; Tdap from 16 weeks each pregnancy for pertussis; influenza any trimester); premature infants: vaccinate by chronological age.

Exam pearls
  • Chemo child at home → sibling gets IPV, NOT OPV; no live vaccines.
  • Immunosuppressed transplant patient → no live vaccines, ever (varicella!).
  • Only true general contraindication = anaphylaxis to prior dose. Mild illness ≠ contraindication.

Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Crohn’s vs Ulcerative Colitis

Crohn’s disease — transmural, discontinuous (“skip”) inflammation anywhere from mouth to anus (terminal ileum commonest). Features: crampy abdominal pain (often RLQ), weight loss, chronic diarrhoea (may be non-bloody), fever, oral ulcers, perianal disease (fistulae, fissures, abscesses), extra-intestinal (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, uveitis, iritis, episcleritis, arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, gallstones (↓bile salt absorption), renal stones (oxalate), B₁₂ deficiency). Histology: transmural lymphoid aggregates, non-caseating granulomas. Complications: strictures, fistulae, abscess, malabsorption/anaemia.

Ulcerative colitis — mucosal, continuous inflammation starting at the rectum extending proximally (always involves rectum). Features: bloody diarrhoea with mucus, urgency, tenesmus, lower abdominal pain, fever in flares; extra-intestinal (primary sclerosing cholangitis!, uveitis, arthritis, erythema nodosum); colon cancer risk (surveillance colonoscopy from ~8–10 y). Histology: continuous cryptitis, crypt abscesses, goblet cell depletion, no granulomas.

Crohn’sUlcerative colitis
DistributionMouth→anus, skip lesions, terminal ileumRectum→ proximally, continuous, colon only
DepthTransmuralMucosa/submucosa
Blood in stoolVariableAlways (hallmark)
PerianalCommon (fistulae)Rare
GranulomasNon-caseating (30–50%)Absent
SurgeryNot curative (recurs)Curative (proctocolectomy)
Cancer riskModestSignificant (esp. PSC overlap)

Diagnosis: colonoscopy + biopsy (gold standard), faecal calprotectin (raised in IBD; normal in IBS — great separator), CRP/ESR, FBC (anaemia), albumin, iron/B₁₂, stool cultures (exclude infection), barium/MRI enterography for Crohn’s, ASCA+ (Crohn) vs p-ANCA+ (UC). IBD vs IBS: IBD = blood, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, raised CRP/calprotectin; IBS = normal tests, no blood, never nocturnal.

Management flares: UC mild–moderate → 5-ASA (mesalazine) oral/topical; moderate–severe → oral prednisolone → steroid-refractory/dependent → azathioprine/mercaptopurine, anti-TNF (infliximab/adalimumab), vedolizumab; acute severe colitis → IV hydrocortisone + DVT prophylaxis → rescue ciclosporin or colectomy if failing. Crohn’s: induction steroids; maintenance azathioprine/antimetabolite ± anti-TNF; surgery for strictures/fistulae/refractory disease (resection, not curative); nutritional therapy (exclusive enteral) in children; stop smoking (worsens Crohn’s).

Exam pearls
  • Oral ulcers + RLQ pain + weight loss + aphthous ulcers = Crohn’s. Bloody diarrhoea from rectum upward = UC.
  • Calprotectin separates IBD from IBS — cheap and non-invasive.
  • UC + PSC = highest colon cancer risk — colonoscopy surveillance.

A question about IBD versus IBS. Which feature is more suggestive of IBD?
  • A. IBD
  • B. IBS
  • C. Celiac disease
  • D. Infectious colitis
  • E. Microscopic colitis
Best answer
A. IBD
Features pointing to IBD rather than IBS: blood/mucus in stool, nocturnal diarrhoea, weight loss, fever, anaemia, raised CRP/faecal calprotectin, perianal disease, oral ulcers, family history. IBS = normal calprotectin/CRP, no nocturnal symptoms, no bleeding.
2018 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Irritable Bowel Syndrome

Definition (Rome IV): recurrent abdominal pain, on average ≥1 day/week for last 3 months, associated with ≥2 of: (1) related to defecation; (2) associated with change in frequency; (3) associated with change in stool form/appearance. Present for ≥6 months. Subtypes: IBS-C (constipation), IBS-D (diarrhoea), IBS-M (mixed). No organic disease — diagnosis of exclusion of red flags.

Red flags NOT IBS: age >50 new onset, weight loss, rectal bleeding, nocturnal diarrhoea, anaemia (iron deficiency), raised CRP/faecal calprotectin, family history of IBD/CRC, palpable mass, fever → investigate (calprotectin, colonoscopy).

Investigations (limited): FBC, CRP, coeliac serology, faecal calprotectin, TFT (if IBS-C — hypothyroidism), screen for lactose intolerance if suggested; colonoscopy only if red flags/age >50.

Management: explanation/reassurance, dietary advice (regular meals, fluids, fibre — soluble (ispaghula) for IBS-C; low-FODMAP diet), exercise, reduce caffeine/alcohol/sorbitol; probiotics; antispasmodics (mebeverine, hyoscine, peppermint oil); linaclotide for IBS-C; loperamide for IBS-D; tricyclic antidepressant (amitriptyline) or SSRI for pain-predominant/refractory; CBT/gut-directed hypnotherapy.

Exam pearls
  • Alternating diarrhoea/constipation + normal tests + no red flags = IBS.
  • Calprotectin normal = IBS almost certain; raised = IBD/infection — scope.
  • Treatment = reassurance + antispasmodic + diet; no steroids/antibiotics.

  • A. IBS
  • B. IBD
  • C. Celiac disease
  • D. Lactose intolerance
  • E. Diverticulitis
Best answer
A. IBS

2018 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Low Back Pain & Radiculopathy

Most low back pain is mechanical (non-specific) — improves with movement/rest patterns, no neurological signs, self-limiting 4–6 weeks. Distinguish:

  • Mechanical/disc: pain classically worse with flexion, sitting, standing from sitting (intradiscal pressure), improves lying; age 20–40; lumbar strain/sprain.
  • Lumbar disc herniation (L4/5 or L5/S1): sciatica — radicular pain radiating below the knee; dermatomal sensory loss, myotomal weakness, reflex loss (L4 — knee jerk; S1 — ankle jerk); positive straight-leg raise (pain <60°); crossed SLR (specific). Most improve conservatively (analgesia, activity, physio ×6–12 wks); urgent MRI if red flags (fever, weight loss, cancer history, trauma, steroid use, immunosuppression, age <20 or >50 with new severe pain, saddle anaesthesia, bilateral leg weakness, urinary retention/incontinence = cauda equina — emergency decompression).
  • Spinal stenosis: neurogenic claudication — pain/heaviness/weakness in legs on standing and walking, relieved by sitting/flexion (leaning forward/shopping cart sign) (unlike vascular claudication — relieved by standing still); MRI confirms.
  • Ankylosing spondylitis: inflammatory — insidious onset <40 y, morning stiffness >30–60 min, improves with EXERCISE (not rest), night pain, reduced lumbar flexion (Schober’s <5 cm), alternating buttock/SIJ pain, enthesitis, uveitis, HLA-B27, X-ray sacroiliitis/“bamboo spine” late; NSAIDs + exercise; TNF-inhibitors if refractory.
  • Osteoporotic vertebral fracture: elderly + minimal trauma (sneeze/lift); X-ray wedge fracture; analgesia, early mobilisation; assess/treat osteoporosis (DEXA + bisphosphonate).

Red flags needing urgent imaging/referral: cauda equina (saddle anaesthesia + urinary retention + bilateral weakness), progressive neurological deficit, tumour (age >50/<20, weight loss, night pain, cancer history), infection (fever, IVDU, diabetes, ESR high), fracture (trauma/steroids/osteoporosis).

Exam pearls
  • Pain on standing from sitting & flexion = mechanical; inflammatory = better with exercise, worse rest.
  • Saddle anaesthesia + retention = cauda equina — immediate MRI + surgery.
  • Radiculopathy below the knee + SLR+ = disc herniation.

  • B. Ankylosing spondylitis
  • C. Spinal stenosis
  • D. Osteoporotic fracture
  • E. Muscle strain
Best answer
B. Ankylosing spondylitis
Back pain worse at rest/early morning, better with activity = inflammatory (ankylosing spondylitis) — versus mechanical (worse with movement, better rest: disc, strain, stenosis). “Pain increases on standing from sitting” could be mechanical flexion pain, but “increases standing from sitting” with inflammatory hallmarks = AS. HLA-B27, sacroiliitis on X-ray/MRI; treat NSAIDs, exercise; TNF/IL-17 if refractory.
2018 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Mesenteric Ischaemia

Two syndromes:

1. Acute mesenteric ischaemia — emergency. Causes: (a) arterial embolus (50% — from AF/MI/valvular disease → SMA); (b) arterial thrombosis (25% — atherosclerosis at SMA ostium); (c) non-occlusive (20% — low-flow states, vasopressors, shock); (d) venous thrombosis (5% — hypercoagulable states, pancreatitis, portal HTN). Classic: sudden severe periumbilical pain “out of proportion” to examination findings (soft abdomen despite agonising pain) + AF + fresh PR bleeding/guarding, rapid progression to peritonitis/acidosis/sepsis. Diagnosis: CT mesenteric angiography (± lactate↑ late). Management: resuscitation, broad antibiotics, urgent laparotomy/embolectomy/revascularisation + bowel resection if necrosis; treat AF (anticoagulation) — high mortality (50%+).

2. Chronic (“mesenteric angina”) — atherosclerotic stenosis/occlusion of coeliac/SMA: post-prandial epigastric pain 20–60 min after meals, weight loss (“food fear”), abdominal bruit; often other atherosclerotic disease; AF hints at embolic events but chronic form = plaque. Diagnosis: CT/MR angiography or duplex US; treatment: risk-factor modification, antiplatelets/statins, revascularisation (angioplasty/stent or bypass) if symptomatic.

Examination answer: post-prandial pain + irregular pulse (AF) → CT angiography of the mesenteric vessels (shown on CT abdomen option); ECG/echo in parallel to document the embolic source.

Exam pearls
  • “Pain out of proportion” + AF = acute mesenteric ischaemia — CT angiogram, urgent surgery.
  • “Pain after eating” + weight loss + bruit = chronic — CT angiogram.
  • AF is the link — embolic source, so assess the heart too.

A 55-year-old man presents with abdominal pain worse after eating. On examination he has an irregularly irregular pulse. What is the appropriate step?
  • A. ECG
  • B. Echo
  • C. CT abdomen
  • D. X-ray abdomen
  • E. Cardiac enzymes
Best answer
C. CT abdomen
Post-prandial abdominal pain + AF = mesenteric ischaemia until proven otherwise (atherosclerotic SMA/celiac stenosis — “mesenteric angina” — with an embolic risk from AF). CT mesenteric angiography (CT abdomen) is the investigation of choice — it shows the stenosis/occluded vessel segment + bowel wall perfusion. ECG/echo should be done in parallel to document AF/embolic source, but imaging defines the lesion; if acute with peritonitis → straight to laparotomy/embolectomy and resuscitation.
2018 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Motor Neurone Disease (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis)

Definition: progressive neurodegeneration of UMN (corticospinal tract) + LMN (anterior horn cells/cranial motor nuclei) — NO sensory loss, NO eye movement involvement (usually), NO sphincter involvement (helps distinguish).

Clinical patterns: limb-onset (asymmetric weakness, wasting, fasciculations, cramps + hyperreflexia/extensor plantars), bulbar-onset (dysarthria, dysphagia, tongue atrophy/fasciculations — worse prognosis), respiratory-onset; cognitive change (up to 50% mild; frontotemporal dementia overlap 10–15%). LMN signs in the arms/hands + UMN signs in the legs (or vice versa) = ALS pattern.

Key differentials to exclude (no single test diagnoses): compressive myelopathy (MRI — cervical spondylosis, tumour), cervical myelopathy, multifocal motor neuropathy, MG, Kennedy’s disease, B₁₂ deficiency, copper deficiency, hyperthyroidism, lead poisoning, Kennedy, Kennedy. Diagnosis: clinical + EMG (denervation) + MRI (exclude structural) + blood tests (B₁₂, TFT, Ca, VDRL, autoimmune).

Management: riluzole (glutamine antagonist — modestly prolongs survival ~3 months); MDT (neurology, respiratory, palliative); non-invasive ventilation when FVC falls; PEG feeding if dysphagia; secretions (hyoscine/amitriptyline); spasticity (baclofen); VTE prophylaxis if immobile; psychological support; advanced care planning (NIV vs tracheostomy, end-of-life wishes). Survival ~2–5 years from diagnosis.

Exam pearls
  • Weakness + wasting + fasciculations + hyperreflexia, NO sensory loss = MND.
  • Mixed UMN+LMN in the same patient = ALS.
  • MRI to EXCLUDE compression/tumour before labelling MND.
  • Riluzole + NIV + PEG + early palliative care.

  • B. Multiple sclerosis
  • C. UMN lesion
  • D. LMN lesion

Best answer
A. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)
UMN (extensor plantars, hyperreflexia) + LMN (fasciculations, wasting) in the SAME region, no sensory loss, progressive = motor neuron disease (ALS). MS = episodic + sensory; pure UMN/LMN single lesion = stroke/neuropathy.
2018 · Internal Medicine · 2 questions · MCQ

Neuromuscular Disorders — Myasthenia, GBS, Botulism

Myasthenia gravis — postsynaptic anti-AChR (or anti-MuSK) antibodies → fatigable weakness. Features: fatigable weakness WORSE with use/at the END of the day, improves with rest; starts with ocular (ptosis, diplopia — painless); bulbar (dysarthria, dysphagia, weak smile/head drop); generalised (neck/proximal/resp); spares reflexes and sensation; no autonomic signs. Associated: thymic hyperplasia/thymoma (15%) (check CT chest). Investigations: anti-AChR antibodies, anti-MuSK (if AChR-negative), repetitive nerve stimulation (decrement), ice-pack test (improves ptosis), CT chest (thymoma). Treatment: pyridostigmine (symptomatic), immunosuppression (prednisolone/azathioprine/mycophenolate), IVIG or plasma exchange for crises, thymectomy if thymoma or generalised AChR+ <65 y; avoid triggers (aminoglycosides!). Crisis = respiratory failure → NIV/intubation.

Guillain–Barré syndrome — post-infectious (Campylobacter jejuni (~40%), CMV, EBV, Zika, Mycoplasma, vaccination rare) autoimmune demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. Features: symmetric ASCENDING weakness + areflexia/hyporeflexia over days, sensory symptoms, minimal sensory loss, back/limb pain, autonomic instability; check FVC/NIF (respiratory failure in 20–30%); CSF: albuminocytologic dissociation (high protein, normal cell count) after week 1; EMG: demyelination (prolonged F waves, conduction block). Treatment: IVIG or plasma exchange (equal efficacy) — start ASAP; NO steroids; monitor respiratory function; VTE prophylaxis; most recover ~80% (mortality 3–5%).

Botulism — Clostridium botulinum preformed toxin (canned/preserved/smoked/honey in infants <12 mo) → blocks presynaptic ACh release. Features: descendING flaccid paralysis (cranial nerves FIRST — diplopia, ptosis, dysarthria, dysphagia, fixed dilated pupils, dry mouth) → arms → respiratory; deep tendon reflexes preserved; afebrile, clear mentation; autonomic signs (constipation). Infant botulism = “floppy baby” + constipation + poor suck. Diagnosis: clinical + toxin in serum/stool + EMG (incremental response on repetitive stimulation). Treatment: botulinum antitoxin ASAP (horse-derived; human BIG-IV for infants), supportive care, NO antibiotics in infant botulism (worsen toxin release), wound botulism → debridement + penicillin/metronidazole; recovery weeks–months (nerve terminal regrowth).

Peripheral nerve injury patterns: common peroneal (foot drop, dorsum sensory loss — fibular head), ulnar (claw hand, medial 1½ fingers — elbow groove), median (thenar wasting, “ape hand”, carpal tunnel — night numbness, Tinel/Phalen), radial (wrist drop), tibial (plantarflexion).

Exam pearls
  • Fatigable + evening + eyes first = MG (pyridostigmine; CT chest). Post-Campylobacter ascending areflexia = GBS (IVIG; watch FVC). Canned food + descendING = botulism (antitoxin).
  • MG fatigues; GBS ascends; botulism descends; both MG/GBS spare the pupils/bladder usually.

2018 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Osteoarthritis

Definition: degenerative joint disease — cartilage loss + subchondral change + osteophytes; not primarily inflammatory (local inflammation secondary).

Risk factors: age, obesity (biggest modifiable — knees/hips/hands), previous trauma/meniscal/ligament injury, occupation (kneeling/heavy lifting), repetitive use, family history, dysplasia, female sex (post-menopause), inflammatory arthropathy (secondary OA).

Features: joint pain WORSE WITH USE, relieved by rest (early), morning stiffness BRIEF (<30 min) (vs RA >1 h); crepitus, bony enlargement, reduced range, mild effusion, deformity late; Heberden’s nodes (DIP), Bouchard’s nodes (PIP), square thumb (1st CMC) — the exam’s “square thumb + PIP/DIP swelling” picture; knee/hip OA → medial compartment loss → varus/valgus; no systemic features, normal ESR/CRP.

X-ray (LOSS): Loss of joint space (asymmetric — medial compartment knee), Osteophytes, Sclerosis (subchondral), Subchondral cysts.

Management: education + weight loss + exercise (strengthening/aerobic — the core; “exercise is the drug”), pacing, walking aids, shoe insoles; topical NSAIDs (first-line for hand/knee); oral NSAIDs (short courses + PPI); paracetamol (weak, short-term); duloxetine (chronic); IA corticosteroid injections (flare, large joints); avoid opioids; surgery — joint replacement (hip/knee) for refractory symptoms/loss of function — most successful operation in medicine. Complementary: physiotherapy, occupational therapy aids, weight loss programmes.

Exam pearls
  • Usage pain + brief morning stiffness + bony nodes (Heberden/Bouchard) + square CMC thumb = OA.
  • X-ray: LOSS — asymmetric space loss + osteophytes + sclerosis + cysts.
  • Exercise + weight loss + topical NSAIDs first; surgery last — but very effective.

2018 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · SAQ

Pituitary Disorders

Pituitary adenomas — benign; functioning (prolactinoma, GH — acromegaly, ACTH — Cushing’s, TSH rare) vs non-functioning. Mass effects (any macroadenoma >10 mm): bitemporal hemianopia (optic chiasm compression — starts superiorly, respects vertical meridian), headache, hypopituitarism (hormone deficits — order: GH → gonadotrophins → TSH → ACTH last), cavernous sinus invasion (CN III/IV/VI palsies).

Prolactinoma — commonest functioning adenoma. Women: oligomenorrhoea/amenorrhoea + galactorrhoea ± infertility; men: hypogonadism, low libido, erectile dysfunction, gynaecomastia (earlier macro), bitemporal hemianopia. Prolactin very high (>5000 mIU/L usually macroadenoma; >10,000 = macroprolactinoma likely); check TSH (primary hypothyroidism → TRH → prolactin↑ — “pseudoprolactinoma”) and drugs (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, SSRIs, verapamil, opiates). Treatment: dopamine agonists — cabergoline/bromocriptine (first-line — shrinks tumour & normalises PRL); surgery (trans-sphenoidal) if intolerant/failed.

Acromegaly — GH excess (usually pituitary somatotroph adenoma): frontal bossing, prognathism, macroglossia, interdental spacing, coarse facies, large spade-like hands/feet, thick skin, sweating, carpal tunnel, sleep apnoea, diabetes, hypertension, colonic polyps, cardiomyopathy. Diagnosis: IGF-1 ↑; OGTT — GH fails to suppress (<1 mU/L); pituitary MRI. Treatment: trans-sphenoidal surgery (first-line); octreotide/lanreotide (somatostatin analogues), pegvisomant (GH-receptor antagonist), cabergoline; radiotherapy if refractory. Screen: colonoscopy, echo, glucose, sleep study.

Cushing’s disease — ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma: central obesity, moon facies, striae, proximal myopathy, diabetes, osteoporosis; diagnose: 24-h urinary free cortisol / low-dose dexamethasone suppression test; IPSS for localization; TS surgery.

Sheehan’s syndrome — postpartum pituitary necrosis after severe postpartum haemorrhage → panhypopituitarism: failure of lactation (first sign) + amenorrhoea + fatigue + loss of pubic/axillary hair + hypothyroidism/hypoadrenalism; treat with hormone replacement (thyroxine, hydrocortisone, oestrogen/progesterone, GH, fertility — gonadotrophins).

Pituitary apoplexy — sudden haemorrhage/infarction (this exam): sudden severe headache + visual loss (bitemporal) + acute ophthalmoplegia (CN III palsy) + meningism ± shock — emergency: IV hydrocortisone, urgent MRI, neurosurgery/ophthalmology; treat as adrenal crisis.

Visual fields: bitemporal hemianopia (chiasmal), homonymous hemianopia (retro-chiasmal — optic tract/radiations), tunnel vision (psychogenic).

Exam pearls
  • High prolactin + menstrual/galactorrhoea → cabergoline — but FIRST exclude pregnancy (β-HCG) and hypothyroidism/drugs.
  • Postpartum haemorrhage + lactation failure + amenorrhoea = Sheehan.
  • Big hands + jaw + field defect = acromegaly → IGF-1 + OGTT.
  • Sudden headache + chiasmal signs = apoplexy — hydrocortisone + urgent imaging/surgery.

#262SAQ image edited2018-InternalMedicine-SAQ-Medicine-748e2bf7
Two pictures were given of the patient.
  1. What is the diagnosis? (1 pt)
  2. Describe the features present in the pictures. (1 pt)
  3. Give two tests to confirm the diagnosis. (2 pt)
Best answer
1) Diagnosis: acromegaly — GH-secreting pituitary macroadenoma. 2) Features in the pictures: coarse facies with frontal bossing, prognathism, enlarged nose/lips/tongue (macroglossia), widely spaced teeth, oily doughy skin, enlarged hands (spade-like) (± bitemporal visual-field defect). 3) Two confirmatory tests: (a) serum IGF-1 (elevated, age/sex-matched); (b) oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) — failure of GH suppression below 1 (0.4) mU/L after 75 g glucose; then pituitary MRI for the adenoma (and do visual fields + full pituitary panel).
Acromegaly: slow insidious onset — compare old photos. Complications: diabetes, hypertension, cardiomyopathy, colonic polyps, carpal tunnel, sleep apnoea. Trans-sphenoidal surgery is first-line; somatostatin analogues (octreotide/lanreotide) or pegvisomant if refractory; radiotherapy last.
2018 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Poisoning & Overdose — Toxidromes

This exam: homeless + unconscious + respiratory acidosis (high CO₂) + RR 30 (opioid typically depresses — note the inconsistency; some written stems pair “respiratory acidosis + RR 30” with salicylate overdose (mixed respiratory alkalosis → high anion gap metabolic acidosis with compensation — but the pH in chronic salicylate intoxication can be acidemia). Empty syringe + RR 6 = opioid intoxication (respiratory depression → low minute ventilation → CO₂ retention → respiratory acidosis) — the classic pairing.

ToxidromeKey featuresTreatment
Opioids (heroin, morphine)CNS + respiratory depression (low RR!), miosis (pinpoint pupils), comaNaloxone IV (0.4–2 mg, repeat), ventilation support
SalicylatesTinnitus, vomiting, hyperventilation (early respiratory alkalosis) → metabolic acidosis (mixed), sweating, fever, confusionABCs, activated charcoal (<1–2 h), urinary alkalisation (sodium bicarbonate), dialysis if severe (>700 mg/L / renal failure / altered conscious / refractory acidosis)
ParacetamolOften delayed: days 1–2 asymptomatic (± nausea), day 3–5 fulminant hepatic failure (AST/ALT in thousands, INR↑)N-acetylcysteine (best <8 h; effective up to 24 h); check level at 4 h & plot nomogram
Methanol/ethylene glycol (toxic alcohols)Visual loss (methanol) / flank pain & hypocalcaemia (ethylene glycol), high anion gap + osmolar gap + acidosisFomepizole (alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor) or ethanol; sodium bicarbonate; haemodialysis
BenzodiazepinesSedation, ataxia, respiratory depression (mild), normal pupilsSupportive; flumazenil rarely (seizure risk)
Stimulants (cocaine/amphetamine)Hypertension, tachycardia, mydriasis, hyperthermia, agitation, seizures; cocaine → chest pain (ACS)Benzodiazepines; avoid pure beta-blockers (unopposed α); cooling
Anticholinergic“Mad as a hatter, blind as a bat, red as a beet, dry as a bone, hot as a hare” — dilated pupils, tachycardia, urinary retention, hyperthermiaSupportive; physostigmine (rare, specialist)

General: ABCDE first; call poison control/National Poisons Information Service; activated charcoal within 1–2 h (protected airway only!); avoid inducing vomiting; check glucose, ECG (QRS/QTc), U&E/osmolality/lactate; whole-bowel irrigation (iron/lithium); MDAC (multiple-dose charcoal) for carbamazepine/theophylline; specific antidotes per above.

Exam pearls
  • Empty syringe + RR 6 = opioid → naloxone.
  • Tinnitus + acidosis + hyperventilation = salicylate → bicarbonate.
  • Paracetamol day 3–5 liver failure — N-acetylcysteine works even late.
  • Methanol (blind) / ethylene (renal) — both high anion gap: fomepizole.

Best answer
C. Opioid intoxication
Empty syringe + respiratory rate 6/min (bradypnoea/hypoventilation) = opioid intoxication — decreased consciousness + respiratory depression. Amphetamines = tachycardia/hypertension/mydriasis; benzodiazepines = usually milder, rarely fatal alone; cocaine = stimulant. Naloxone + ventilation.
2018 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Pulmonary Embolism

Virchow’s triad: stasis (immobility, surgery, travel, pregnancy) + endothelial injury (trauma/surgery/central line) + hypercoagulability (cancer, OCP/HRT, pregnancy, Factor V Leiden, protein C/S deficiency, antiphospholipid, prior VTE).

Presentation: sudden dyspnoea + pleuritic chest pain + tachycardia; ± haemoptysis, syncope (massive), low-grade fever, unilateral leg swelling. Massive PE: hypotension (SBP <90), obstructive shock, raised JVP, loud P2. ECG: sinus tachycardia (commonest), S1Q3T3, right bundle branch block, right axis deviation, T inversions V1–3 (right strain).

Risk scores & testing pathway: Wells score — PE likely (>4 points) → CTPA directly; unlikely → D-dimer (sensitive, not specific): negative excludes; positive → CTPA. PERC for very low risk (“rule-out”). Never CT every breathless patient — use the algorithm; D-dimer only if low/moderate pre-test probability.

Wells componentPoints
Clinical signs of DVT; PE most likely diagnosis (3 each)3 + 3
HR >100; immobilization/surgery <4 wks; previous DVT/PE1.5 each
Haemoptysis; malignancy (active or treated <6 mo)1 each
>4 = likely → CTPA; ≤4 = unlikely → D-dimer

Echocardiography = RV dilation/hypokinesis + McConnell’s sign — diagnostic and prognostic in UNSTABLE patients (> can’t go to CT) — do echo first if hypotensive; contraindication to CTPA is another reason. This exam: BP 90/60 + tachy → urgent CTPA if stable, echo if peri-arrest/unstable (and per exam style: echo is the answer for the unstable scenario, CTPA for stable).

Treatment: anticoagulate immediately when suspect and no contraindication (LMWH/fondaparinux/DOAC — rivaroxaban/apixaban) while awaiting imaging; haemodynamically unstable → thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg/2 h) or embolectomy/catheter-directed therapy; VTE prophylaxis post-op prevents the bulk. Duration: 3 months (provoked), ≥6 months/indefinite (unprovoked or cancer). Warfarin for antiphospholipid syndrome. Fat embolism (femur fracture + chest pain/petechiae/GCS change, 24–72 h) — supportive; post-op immobility (cholecystectomy 3 days ago) → PE most likely.

Exam pearls
  • Wells >4 → CTPA; ≤4 → D-dimer; unstable → echo + thrombolysis.
  • ECG: tachycardia first, then S1Q3T3; neither is specific.
  • Femur fracture + hypoxaemia = fat embolism. Post-op + pleuritic pain = PE.

A patient presents with shortness of breath and ECG shows sinus tachycardia; BP 90/60, HR 120. What is the next best step?
  • A. CTPA
  • B. Echocardiography
  • C. Repeat ECG
  • D. IV fluids
  • E. Chest X-ray
Best answer
B. Echocardiography
Suspected PE + hypotension (90/60) + tachycardia (120) = haemodynamically unstable (high-risk/massive) PE → bedside echocardiography NOW (RV dilation/hypokinesis/ McConnell sign supports PE → thrombolysis). CTPA if stable; if arrest → thrombolysis immediately.

Pulmonary Function Tests — Reading the Pattern

The 6-number framework:

FEV₁FVCFEV₁/FVCDLCOFRC/TLCPattern
Obstructive↓↓N or ↓<0.7N or ↓ (emphysema ↓)↑ (hyperinflation)Asthma (+reversibility ≥12%/200 mL), COPD, bronchiectasis
Restrictive↓↓↓↓N or ↑ (≥0.7)↓ (parenchymal) or N (chest wall/ neuromuscular)↓↓ILD/fibrosis, scoliosis, obesity hypoventilation, neuromuscular, pleural effusion
Mixed↓↓↓↓<0.7↓variableSevere COPD + restriction, cf bronchiectasis + effusion

Which numbers change (exam question): in restriction, FEV₁/FVC is NOT reduced (both fall proportionally); FEV₁, FVC, PEF, TLC, VC, FRC all fall; DLCO falls when the lung parenchyma is stiff (ILD, emphysema) and stays normal in extraparenchymal restriction (obesity, chest wall, diaphragmatic weakness).

RA lung involvement (this exam): progressive dyspnoea + RA → restrictive defect + LOW DLCO (RA-ILD — usual interstitial pneumonia pattern); check HRCT, PFTs; treat: stop smoking, steroids/immunosuppressants per MDT; pirfenidone/nintedanib for fibrotic ILD.

Exam pearls
  • Obstruction: FEV₁/FVC <0.7; restriction: ratio normal/high + ↓TLC; mixed: ratio low + ↓TLC.
  • DLCO low = ILD (or emphysema/pulmonary vascular disease).
  • Asthma = obstruction WITH reversibility.

#197MCQ edited2018-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-0a71472c
A patient with a history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with respiratory symptoms. What are the expected PFT results?
  • A. Restrictive pattern with reduced DLCO
  • B. Obstructive pattern with normal DLCO
  • C. Normal PFT
  • D. Restrictive pattern with increased DLCO
  • E. Mixed pattern
Best answer
A. Restrictive pattern with reduced DLCO
Rheumatoid arthritis–associated interstitial lung disease (commonest pulmonary complication of RA) → restrictive spirometry (↓FVC, ↓TLC) + reduced DLCO (parenchymal thickening impairs gas transfer). Obstruction is NOT typical of RA lung except in bronchiolitis obliterans (rare).
#198MCQ edited2018-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-48bce8ef
A question about FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC ratios to choose the pattern that matches the case. Which spirometry result matches an obstructive picture?
  • A. FEV1 reduced, FVC normal, FEV1/FVC < 70%
  • B. FEV1 and FVC both reduced, FEV1/FVC normal
  • C. Normal values
  • D. FEV1 reduced with reversibility after bronchodilator
  • E. Isolated DLCO reduction
Best answer
A. FEV1 reduced, FVC normal, FEV1/FVC < 70%
Obstructive = ↓FEV₁, preserved/near-normal FVC, FEV₁/FVC <0.7 (e.g., COPD/asthma). Restrictive = both ↓ with preserved ratio; normal values = neither.

Sarcoidosis

Definition: multisystem non-caseating granulomatous disease — unknown cause; bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (radiographic hallmark); slightly commoner in women/Black ethnicity/Scandinavians; young adults.

Features (systems): respiratory — often asymptomatic CXR finding, dry cough, exertional dyspnoea; acute presentation = Löfgren syndrome — BHL + erythema nodosum + fever + arthralgia/periarthritis (ankles) — benign, remits spontaneously; eyes — uveitis/iritis (photophobia, red eye, blurred vision — urgent slit-lamp); skin — erythema nodosum, lupus pernio (violaceous shiny nasal/cheek plaques); neuro — VII cranial nerve (Bell’s) palsy, peripheral neuropathy, meningitis, hypothalamic; cardiac — conduction blocks, VT, heart failure; renal — nephrocalcinosis (hypercalcaemia from granuloma 1-α hydroxylase), interstitial nephritis; hypercalcaemia/hypercalciuria (10–20%); liver, spleen, salivary glands; lymphadenopathy.

THIS exam (2018 SAQ — BHL image): bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on CXR → top 2 diagnoses: sarcoidosis and lymphoma (then TB, metastatic nodes, histoplasmosis); two confirming tests: (a) serum ACE level (non-specific, raised in 50–80%) + (b) tissue biopsy — fibre-optic bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy (or mediastinoscopy) showing non-caseating granulomas + exclusion of TB (AFB/culture); calcium, ESR, FBC, lung function, slit-lamp, ECG.

Diagnosis triad: (1) compatible clinical/radiological picture, (2) non-caseating granulomas on histology, (3) exclusion of other granulomatous disease (TB, fungal, berylliosis, malignancy).

Management: most (Löfgren) = NO treatment — observe; treatment if: symptomatic pulmonary, cardiac/neuro/ocular, hypercalcaemia, renal → systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone) first-line; steroid-sparing: methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate; anti-TNF (infliximab) refractory; regular follow-up: symptoms, CXR, calcium, PFTs, eyes, ECG; annual or per severity.

Exam pearls
  • BHL + erythema nodosum + ankle arthritis/fever = Löfgren — reassure, no steroids.
  • Sarcoid with neuro/heart/eye/Ca elevation = steroids + specialist.
  • Diagnosis = non-caseating granulomas + exclusion of TB.

#258SAQ image edited2018-InternalMedicine-SAQ-Medicine-71d87a24
A chest X-ray was shown.
  1. Describe the finding (bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy). (1 pt)
  2. Give two differential diagnoses. (2 pt)
  3. Give two tests to confirm the diagnosis. (2 pt)
Best answer
1) Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL) — symmetric hilar enlargement, “1-2-3 sign” if with paratracheal nodes. 2) Two differentials: sarcoidosis (most likely — BHL + erythema nodosum, young adult, ↑ACE, hypercalcaemia, non-caseating granulomas) and lymphoma (Hodgkin’s) or tuberculosis (unilateral/asymmetric + B symptoms). 3) Two confirmatory tests: (a) serum ACE level + corrected calcium (often raised); (b) histology — biopsy of accessible node/mediastinal lymph node showing non-caseating granulomas; plus high-resolution CT chest, PFTs, tuberculin/IGRA, biopsy-guided. Serum calcium + ACE + HRCT + biopsy are the work-up.
Sarcoidosis: young adult, BHL, erythema nodosum, uveitis, ↑ACE, hypercalcaemia, restrictive PFTs, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on CXR — treat with steroids if symptomatic (stage II/III or organ involvement); most resolve spontaneously; screen eyes/heart/calcium; check HRCT and PFTs.

Seizures & Epilepsy

Semiology first — type defines treatment:

TypeFeaturesDrug of choice
Absence (typical)Child 4–10 y; sudden staring/“in a daze”, eyelid flutter, 5–15 s, many per day, no post-ictal confusion; 3 Hz spike-waveEthosuximide (or valproate)
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME)Morning myoclonic jerks of limbs/shoulders + GTC seizures + absence; onset 12–18 y; sleep deprivation/alcohol trigger; 4–6 Hz polyspike-waveSodium valproate (females of childbearing age: levetiracetam/lamotrigine)
Temporal lobe (focal impaired awareness)Aura (epigastric rising / déjà vu / burning smell — “burning leather”), staring, lip-smacking/automatisms (chewing, picking), post-ictal confusionCarbamazepine / lamotrigine / levetiracetam
Generalized tonic-clonicSudden fall, tongue biting, incontinence, post-ictal drowsiness/confusionValproate / levetiracetam
Infantile spasms (West syndrome)3–12 months; salaam attacks — sudden flexion of head/trunk/limbs in clusters; hypsarrhythmia on EEG; developmental regression — treat with vigabatrin ± ACTH; think tuberous sclerosisVigabatrin ± steroids
Febrile seizure6 mo–5 y, fever, generalized, <15 min, single in 24 h = SIMPLE (benign, ~1% later epilepsy); complex: focal / >15 min / recurrence within 24 hReassurance + safety (side position, nothing in mouth); treat fever does NOT prevent recurrence; benzodiazepine if >5 min
Non-epileptic (psychogenic) seizureEyes closed, prolonged fluctuating jerks, pelvic thrusting, crying/emotional context (exam stress), NO incontinence/tongue bite/injury/post-ictal state; normal EEGCBT/psychology — NOT anti-epileptics

Management of acute seizure (this exam): ABCDE + position + O₂ → abortive drug if >5 min: midazolam (buccal/IM/IV) or lorazepam IV or diazepam IV/PR — repeat once → if still seizing (status): second-line levetiracetam / phenytoin / valproate (>15–20 min) → refractory (>40 min): phenobarbital or anaesthesia + ICU. Maintenance after abortion of prolonged convulsion: continue anti-seizure prophylaxis with sodium valproate (or leviteracetam), not single-agent benzodiazepines alone.

Risk factors for epilepsy after febrile convulsion: complex febrile seizure, family history of epilepsy, pre-existing neurodevelopmental delay, short interval from fever onset to seizure (<1 h). Simple febrile = near-population risk.

Exam pearls
  • “Smell burning leather + lip smacking + staring” = temporal lobe epilepsy. “Morning limb jerks” = JME. “Exam-time jerks, eyes closed, crying, no incontinence” = psychogenic.
  • Absence = ethosuximide. Status: midazolam → phenytoin/levetiracetam → phenobarbital.
  • Febrile seizure ≠ epilepsy; complex features are the risk.

Shock — Classification & Monitors

The four classes of shock:

TypeCauseExam pearls
1HypovolaemicHaemorrhage (trauma/GI bleed), dehydration, burns, third-spacingCold, clammy, tachycardia, low JVP, narrow pulse pressure — fluids first (blood products if haemorrhage)
2CardiogenicMassive MI, decompensated HF, severe valve disease, arrhythmiaRaised JVP, pulmonary oedema, cold extremities — inotropes/revascularisation; avoid aggressive fluids
3ObstructiveTension pneumothorax, massive PE, cardiac tamponadeRAISED JVP + no pulmonary oedema, muffled sounds / hyperresonance / pleuritic — decompress/drain/lytic
4DistributiveSeptic (warm → cold), anaphylactic, neurogenic, spinal (bradycardia!)Warm peripheries early (septic/anaphylaxis); neurogenic = brady + warm + hypotension (above T6) — fluids/adrenaline/norepinephrine

Shock assessment — the exam’s favourite: “What is the proper monitor to know if the shock state has improved?” → urine output (B). Why: renal perfusion is the last thing sacrificed and first thing restored; ≥0.5 mL/kg/h (adult) = adequate end-organ perfusion. Adjuncts: lactate (clearance >10–20% per 2–4 h), capillary refill (<2–3 s), mental status, base deficit, SCVO₂, MAP ≥65 — BP alone can be preserved by vasoconstriction while tissue is still ischaemic; CVP used for trends not absolute value (target 8–12 cm, higher in ventilation).

Management sequence: ABCDE + O₂ + 2 large-bore IV + cross-match + fluid bolus (250–500 mL) + frequent reassessment + early senior/ICU call; identify class; source control (surgery/drain/antibiotics/percutaneous); vasopressors (norepinephrine first in septic); catheterise, strict ins/outs; treat the cause always.

Exam pearls
  • Urine output is the best bedside monitor of shock resuscitation.
  • Raised JVP + shock = cardiogenic or obstructive (not hypovolaemic/distributive).
  • Neurogenic shock = hypotension + BRADYCARDIA — atropine/pace + fluids.

#220MCQ edited2018-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-d64af625
What is the proper monitor to know if the shock state has improved?
  • A. Increase in BP
  • B. Urine output
  • C. Serum lactate
  • D. Capillary refill
  • E. Central venous pressure
Best answer
B. Urine output
Best real-time bedside monitor that shock is resolving = urine output (goal ≥0.5 mL/kg/h) — reflects renal perfusion directly. Lactate is excellent but slower; BP can lag/normalise falsely; capillary refill subjective; CVP unreliable.

Stroke & Transient Ischaemic Attack — Localization

Hemisphere syndromes:

TerritoryDeficits
MCA (commonest)Contralateral face & arm > leg weakness, contralateral sensory loss, homonymous hemianopia, aphasia (dominant), neglect (non-dominant), gaze deviation toward lesion
ACAContralateral leg > arm weakness, urinary incontinence, grasp reflex, behavioural change
PCAContralateral homonymous hemianopia (macula-sparing), memory loss, Alexia without agraphia (dominant)

Brainstem/lacunar (cross findings = ipsilateral cranial nerve + contralateral body — the exam’s favourite):

SyndromeSiteFeatures
Weber’sParamedian midbrain (III fascicles + corticospinal)Ipsilateral CN III palsy (“down and out”, ptosis, dilated pupil) + contralateral UMN hemiparesis (face + limbs); ± altered sensorium if haemorrhage/large lesion
Millard–Gubler / FovillePons (VI + VII + corticospinal)Ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy (can’t look that way) + LMN facial palsy + contralateral hemiparesis
Wallenberg (lateral medullary)PICA (posterior inferior cerebellar a.)Ipsilateral: facial pain/temp loss (spinal trigeminal), Horner’s, limb ataxia, nystagmus, dysphagia/hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus), vertigo (vestibular nuclei); contralateral: body pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic); NO weakness — classic “crossed” sensory pattern
BenediktMidbrain (red nucleus + III)CN III palsy + contralateral involuntary movements/tremor
Lateral pontineAICALike Wallenberg + ipsilateral facial weakness & hearing loss (CN VII/VIII)

Pure sensory / pure motor / ataxic hemiparesis / clumsy-hand dysarthria = lacunar (thalamus = pure sensory; internal capsule/corona radiata = pure motor; base of pons = ataxic hemiparesis). Thalamus → isolated hemisensory loss (this exam).

Acute management: ABCDE, glucose, seizures controlled → non-contrast CT brain (exclude haemorrhage) → eligibility for thrombolysis (IV alteplase within 4.5 h) or thrombectomy (large vessel occlusion, up to 24 h in selected) → admit stroke unit; antiplatelet (aspirin 300 mg) if ischaemic and not thrombolysed; BP control (do NOT lower acutely unless >220/120 or thrombolysing); swallow assessment before feeding; DVT prophylaxis; secondary prevention (statin, antiplatelet/anticoagulant for AF, BP, diabetes, smoking); speech & language, PT/OT, MDT; carotid imaging/CT angiography for anterior circulation TIAs.

Exam pearls
  • Crossed signs (ipsilateral CN + contralateral body) = brainstem, NOT cortex.
  • Down-and-out eye + contralateral weakness = Weber’s (midbrain). Gaze palsy + facial weakness + weakness = Millard–Gubler (pons). PICA = Wallenberg.
  • Isolated hemisensory loss = thalamus.
  • Never sit on chest pain/stroke red flags — CT first, thrombolyse if eligible.

A 56-year-old male presents with sudden onset of dysphagia, dysarthria and weakness of the right upper and lower limbs with a left eye (down and out) appearance. Where is the affected site?
  • A. Right cerebellum
  • B. Medulla oblongata

Best answer
E. Left midbrain
Contralateral hemiparesis (right arm + leg) + ipsilateral CN III palsy (left eye “down and out”) = Weber’s syndrome — paramedian midbrain (PCA perforators / basilar tip). Dysphagia/dysarthria from corticobulbar involvement. Medulla = Wallenberg (X), pons = VI/VII (Millard-Gubler).
2018 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

Definition: multisystem autoimmune disease — antinuclear antibodies (ANA) + lupus-specific antibodies: anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith. Female >> male (9:1), childbearing age; HLA-DR2/DR3; complement-consuming immune-complex disease.

ACR-like criteria (≥4):

  • Malar “butterfly” rash — this exam (image): erythematous rash across cheeks & nasal bridge SPARING the nasolabial folds (photosensitive)
  • Discoid rash — raised, scaly, atrophic plaques (leaves scars)
  • Photosensitivity — rash after sun
  • Oral/nasal ulcers
  • Non-erosive arthritis (≥2 peripheral joints, tender/swollen)
  • Serositis — pleuritis/pericarditis ± effusion
  • Renal — persistent proteinuria or cellular casts (lupus nephritis) — 40% develop; check urine/PCR
  • Neuro — seizures or psychosis (other: headache, mood)
  • Haematological — haemolytic anaemia, leucopaenia, lymphopaenia, thrombocytopaenia
  • Immunological — anti-dsDNA or anti-Smith, ANA+, low complement (C3/C4 LOW), antiphospholipid (lupus anticoagulant/anticardiolipin/β2GPI → recurrent thrombosis + miscarriage + thrombocytopaenia)

Complications & overlap: ILD/pulmonary fibrosis (this exam: dry cough + exertional dyspnoea → SLE-ILD) — HRCT + PFTs; pulmonary hypertension; Libman–Sacks endocarditis (sterile vegetations); nephritis; premature atherosclerosis. Differentiating RA from SLE (this exam): SLE = non-erosive, reversible deformities (Jaccoud’s), malar rash, low complement, dsDNA+, multisystem (renal/CNS/haem), no nodules; RA = erosive symmetric small-joint arthritis with morning stiffness >1 h, RF/anti-CCP+, rheumatoid nodules, spares DIP.

Management: avoid sun/photoprotection; hydroxychloroquine (ALL patients — skin/joints, reduces flares/mortality); NSAIDs (arthralgia); corticosteroids (moderate–severe flares); immunosuppressants — mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide (nephritis/neuropsychiatric), azathioprine maintenance; biologics (belimumab, rituximab) refractory; ACEi/ARB (renal); aspirin/heparin for antiphospholipid (recurrent thrombosis → warfarin); vaccinate, monitor (BP, urine, FBC, complement, dsDNA).

Exam pearls
  • Malar rash spares nasolabial folds; discoid = scarring; both photosensitive.
  • dsDNA + low C3/C4 = active lupus; Smith = specific.
  • Hydroxychloroquine for everyone. Nephritis → mycophenolate; monitor urine.
  • Drug-induced lupus: hydralazine, isoniazid, procainamide, minocycline — anti-histone, milder, no renal.

Thyroid Disorders — Hyperthyroidism & Thyroiditis

Hyperthyroidism patterns:

Graves’Toxic multinodular goitre / solitary toxic noduleThyroiditis (subacute/postpartum)Factitious
MechanismTSH-receptor antibodies — diffuse stimulationAutonomous nodulesInflammatory leak of stored hormone (no excess production)Exogenous thyroxine
Age/demographics Young/middle-aged womenOlderPost-viral/postpartum women—
ExamDiffuse goitre, ophthalmopathy (proptosis/lid lag/diplopia), pretibial myxoedemaMultinodular or single nodulePainful (subacute — de Quervain) or painless goitre; initial thyrotoxic then hypothyroid—
Uptake scanDiffusely increasedFocal (hot) nodule(s), suppressed elsewhereLOW/absent uptakeLOW

Diagnosis steps (this exam): TFT — ↓TSH + ↑T4/T3 = primary hyperthyroidism; uptake scan: one nodule = solitary toxic (adenoma) nodule; “hyperthyroidism + 6-month amenorrhoea” → β-HCG first (pregnancy) — do this before TFT/scan/TPO in EVERY reproductive-age woman with symptoms; “hyperthyroid + tender goitre + nausea/amenorrhoea” → β-HCG first, then TFTs/work-up (exclude pregnancy before any radioactive iodine).

Hypothyroidism — tiredness, cold intolerance, constipation, weight gain, menorrhagia, depression, bradycardia + slow-relaxing reflexes, dry skin, hair loss; commonest cause Hashimoto’s (TPO+); check TSH (↑), free T4 (↓); treat levothyroxine (start low in elderly/ischaemic heart).

Exam pearls
  • Every woman with hyperthyroid symptoms + amenorrhoea → β-HCG FIRST.
  • One “hot” nodule = solitary toxic adenoma; diffuse uptake = Graves; low uptake = thyroiditis — treat with propranolol only.
  • Graves = TSH-R Ab + eye signs — carbimazole 12–18 months.

2018 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Tropical & Travel-Related Infections

Dengue (commonest exam travel fever): fever + retro-orbital pain + severe myalgia (“break-bone fever”) + maculopapular rash + headache + LOW PLATELETS ± bleeding (gums/petechiae) — travel to India/SE Asia/Caribbean/Latin America; leucopenia, thrombocytopenia, rising haematocrit (plasma leak — warning signs: abdominal pain, bleeding, shock — “dengue haemorrhagic fever”); diagnosed by NS1 antigen/dengue serology (IgM), PCR; treatment = supportive — fluids (ORAL rehydration/IV), paracetamol (NO aspirin/NSAIDs/ibuprofen — bleeding risk), rest; admit if warning signs.

Malaria: cyclical fevers (every 48 h — P. vivax/ovale; 72 h — P. malariae), headache, rigors, sweats, hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia after travel to sub-Saharan Africa; P. falciparum = severe (seizures, coma, hypoglycaemia, renal failure, jaundice, severe anaemia, high parasitaemia); diagnosis: thick & thin film ×3 (ring forms — “headphone”/banana gametocytes) or RDT (antigen); urgent: artesunate/ACT for falciparum; chloroquine + primaquine for vivax; notify notifiable disease.

Chikungunya: fever + severe polyarthralgia (debilitating, small joints) + rash; lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia; self-limiting weeks; serology; supportive.

Typhoid (S. Typhi/Paratyphi): prolonged stepwise fever, relative bradycardia, abdominal pain, constipation (or “pea soup” diarrhoea), rose spots (trunk), hepatosplenomegaly — India/SE Asia/ traveller; leucopaenia; blood cultures (1st week) / stool; ceftriaxone/azithromycin; 10–14 days.

Zika: mild fever + rash + conjunctivitis + arthralgia; congenital Zika syndrome — microcephaly if infection in pregnancy; avoid pregnancy 2 months after exposure.

Leptospirosis — water/rats; biphasic fever, conjunctival suffusion (no discharge!), myalgia, jaundice + renal failure (Weil’s disease).

Exam pearls
  • Travel + fever + retro-orbital pain/rash/low platelets = dengue. Africa + cyclical fever + film = malaria. India + rash + low platelets = dengue.
  • Never give aspirin/NSAIDs in dengue.
  • Malaria: treat falciparum urgently; thick/thin film ×3.

Viral Hepatitis & HBV Serology

Route of transmission & course:

VirusTransmissionChronic?Vaccine/Tx
HAVFaecal–oral (food/water, travellers, MSM, shellfish) — faeces: CONTACT precautionsNever (self-limiting)Vaccine + Ig for contacts; supportive
HBVBlood/body fluids — perinatal (mother→infant), IVDU, sex, needle-stick~5–10% adults, >90% neonates → chronic HBVVaccine (birth dose + 3); tenofovir/entecavir if chronic active
HCVBlood — IVDU, transfusion (pre-screen), tattoos~80% chronic → cirrhosis/HCCNo vaccine; direct-acting antivirals cure >95%
HDVOnly with HBV (needs HBsAg for envelope)Accelerates HBVHBV vaccine protects
HEVFaecal–oral — travellers, pork/shellfishUsually self-limiting; chronic in transplant/immunosuppressedNo vaccine (outside China); pregnant women → severe/fulminant (20% mortality)
EBVSaliva (mononucleosis) — fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, hepatitis (this exam!)Lifelong latencySupportive — avoid amoxicillin (rash); splenic rupture risk (no sport)

HBV serology table — memorise cold:

HBsAgAnti-HBcAnti-HBsMeaning
+IgM−Acute HBV
+IgG−Chronic HBV carrier/infection (or window)
−IgG+Cleared past infection (immune)
−−+Vaccinated (immune)
−−−Susceptible — offer vaccine
−IgM−Window period (HBsAg cleared, anti-HBs not yet up) — test HBV DNA

This exam: HBsAg−, anti-HBs+, anti-HBc IgG+ → cleared (past) hepatitis B infection. Traveller + others affected + jaundice → hepatitis A → contact precautions/hand hygiene + notify public health + vaccinate contacts. Returned with markedly raised transaminases → acute hepatitis A/E.

Exam pearls
  • anti-HBs+ alone = vaccine; anti-HBs+ AND anti-HBc IgG+ = past infection.
  • HAV/HEV = faecal-oral (jaundiced travellers); HBV/HCV = blood.
  • EBV in a young adult = fever + pharyngitis + hepatitis — Monospot/VCA-IgM.

#202MCQ2018-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-02dcf967
Viral serology was given asking for the diagnosis: HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive, anti-HBc IgG positive, anti-HBc IgM negative. What does this indicate?
  • A. Immunity from vaccination
  • B. Chronic infection with Hep B
  • C. Cleared (past) infection
  • D. Acute infection
  • E. Susceptible (no immunity)
Best answer
C. Cleared (past) infection
HBsAg negative + anti-HBs positive + anti-HBc IgG positive (IgM negative) = resolved past natural infection (immune). Vaccination = anti-HBs+ ONLY, anti-HBc negative. Chronic = HBsAg+ >6 mo. Susceptible = all negative. Acute = HBsAg+ anti-HBc IgM+.
2018 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Wilson Disease

Definition: autosomal recessive ATP7B mutation (13q14.3) → failure to excrete copper into bile → copper accumulates in liver, brain (basal ganglia) and cornea. Presents 5–40 y.

Features:

  • Hepatic (childhood/adolescents): asymptomatic ↑LFTs → hepatitis/cirrhosis/fulminant failure (with acute haemolysis — Coombs-negative!)
  • Neurological (20s): dysarthria, dysphagia, drooling, tremor (wing-beating), dystonia (risus sardonicus), Parkinsonism, gait/balance problems, psychiatric (depression, personality change)
  • Kayser–Fleischer rings — golden-brown copper deposits at the corneal limbus (Descemet membrane) on slit-lamp — present in >95% with neuro signs (image in many exams)
  • Others: haemolytic anaemia (Coombs negative), renal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi), osteoporosis, cardiomyopathy, low-normal ALP (relative!), haematuria, sunflower cataracts

This exam: image findings (KF rings/liver/neuro) → Wilson disease (A).

Diagnosis: slit-lamp (KF rings); low serum caeruloplasmin (<20 g/L); high 24-h urinary copper (>1.6 micromol/24 h — >40 microgram/h); high free serum copper, low total; low ALP; Coombs-negative haemolysis; MRI (hyperintensities in basal ganglia/thalamus/midbrain — “panda sign”); liver biopsy — hepatic copper >250 microgram/g dry weight (gold standard when unclear); genetic testing (ATP7B).

Treatment (lifelong): chelating agents — penicillamine or trientine (trientine tolerated better); zinc salts (block intestinal copper absorption — maintenance/presymptomatic); low-copper diet (avoid shellfish/nuts/chocolate/liver); liver transplant for fulminant failure/decompensated cirrhosis (curative — corrects the metabolic defect); screen siblings (genetic +/or caeruloplasmin + slit lamp); avoid copper cookware; monitoring (LFTs, urinary copper, neuro).

Exam pearls
  • Young + neuro (dysarthria/dystonia) ± hepatic + KF rings = Wilson’s.
  • Low caeruloplasmin + high 24-h urine copper; Coombs-negative haemolysis; low ALP clue.
  • Penicillamine/trientine early — transplant if fulminant; screen siblings.

Birthmarks & Vascular Lesions

Common “birthmarks” every paediatrician must distinguish:

LesionAppearanceCourse / management
Nevus simplex (salmon patch / “stork bite” / angel kiss)Flat, salmon-pink macule on nape, glabella/forehead/eyelids; blanches; present at birthFades spontaneously (usually by 1–2 y) — reassure
Port-wine stain (nevus flammeus)Flat pink→purple patch, unilateral, respects midline, present at birth, may darken/thicken with agePersists; pulsed-dye laser; if V1 (ophthalmic trigeminal) distribution → risk Sturge–Weber (leptomeningeal angiomatosis → seizures, glaucoma) → ophthalmology/neurology review
Infantile haemangiomaNot at birth (or pale precursor); appears in first weeks, proliferates to ~5–6 months then involutes over years; bright red, raisedMost regress (50% by 5 y, 90% by 9 y) — reassure; treat if ulcerating/obstructing (airway, vision, feeding): oral propranolol first-line
Café-au-lait maculesFlat light-brown well-circumscribed patches≥6 (>5 mm prepubertal/>15 mm post) + freckling/nodules → NF1 → genetics referral
Congenital melanocytic naevusPigmented, may be hairy, often largeLarge (>20 cm projected) → melanoma risk (~5%+) + neurocutaneous melanosis (CNS) → specialist review
Mongolian spot (dermal melanocytosis)Blue-grey patch over sacrum/buttocks of darker-skinned infantsBenign — fades by childhood; document (can be mistaken for bruising — important for safeguarding!)

Image recognition: a symmetric pink macule on the forehead/glabella of a newborn = nevus simplex; a unilateral dark purple patch respecting the midline = port-wine stain.

Exam pearls
  • Salmon patch = fades; port-wine stain = persists and darkens.
  • V1 port-wine → eye pressure check + MRI (Sturge–Weber).
  • Haemangioma proliferates early — propranolol if cosmetic/functional threat.
  • ≥6 café-au-lait spots → NF1 evaluation.

Bleeding Disorders — Platelets vs Coagulation vs vWD

Bleeding pattern points to the defect:

Platelet / primary haemostasisCoagulation factor / secondary haemostasis
PatternMucocutaneous: petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, bleeding immediately after cutsDeep bleeds: haemarthroses, muscle/retroperitoneal haematomas, delayed bleeding (hours after surgery/dental extraction)
Platelet countLow (or functionally defective)Normal
PT / aPTTNormalPT = extrinsic (factor VII); aPTT = intrinsic (VIII, IX, XI, XII); both = common pathway (X, V, II, I) or vitamin K/liver disease

Key inherited disorders:

  • Haemophilia A (factor VIII) / B (factor IX) — X-linked recessive. Boys; deep haematomas, haemarthroses, prolonged aPTT with normal PT, normal platelets. Treat: factor VIII/IX replacement (on demand ± prophylaxis), DDAVP for mild A, avoid aspirin/IM injections. Check inhibitors if poor response.
  • Von Willebrand disease — most common inherited bleeding disorder; autosomal dominant; mucocutaneous bleeding, menorrhagia in women, family history; normal/high aPTT (factor VIII protected by vWF), prolonged bleeding time; test: vWF antigen/activity (ristocetin cofactor), factor VIII. Treat: DDAVP (mild), tranexamic acid, vWF/factor VIII concentrate for surgery/major bleeds.
  • Vitamin K deficiency — neonates (no stores, sterile gut), malabsorption (coeliac, CF, cholestasis), antibiotics, warfarin → affects factors II, VII, IX, X → PT (and later aPTT) prolonged; newborn bleeding prevented by IM/oral vitamin K at birth. Treat with vitamin K; PCC/FFP if bleeding.
  • ITP — isolated thrombocytopenia post-viral illness, well child, petechiae/purpura, normal Hb/WBC; observe if mild; IVIG/steroids if significant bleeding/platelets very low; avoid sports.
  • Haemophilia + circumcision bleed in a boy with knee haematomas = haemophilia A (commonest) vs B.

Laboratory triage: normal aPTT + prolonged PT → factor VII deficiency or vitamin K/warfarin/liver. Prolonged aPTT + normal PT → VIII/IX/XI. Both prolonged → common pathway (X/V/II/fibrinogen) or vitamin K deficiency/liver/DIC/warfarin; mixing study separates factor deficiency (corrects) from inhibitor (fails to correct — e.g. lupus anticoagulant, factor VIII inhibitor). Prolonged both + thrombocytopenia + high D-dimer + low fibrinogen = DIC (oozing everywhere, multi-organ failure — treat cause + replace).

Exam pearls
  • Petechiae + isolated low platelets post-viral in a well child = ITP.
  • Circumcision bleed + haemarthrosis + boy + family history = haemophilia (aPTT↑, PT normal).
  • vWD = menorrhagia + mucocutaneous bleed + family history; DDAVP trial.
  • Both PT & aPTT prolonged in a newborn/anticoagulated/malabsorbed = vitamin K — give vitamin K, check liver.
  • DIC = consumption — replace what you use, treat the cause (sepsis!).
Traps
  • Normal PT/aPTT does NOT exclude vWD or mild factor deficiency — check vWF/factor levels and bleeding time.
  • Platelet transfusion only in active bleeding/prophylaxis before procedures, not automatically in ITP.

Childhood Exanthems — Rash + Fever Pattern Recognition

The classic differentials (highest-yield table in paediatrics):

DiseaseAgentFeverRash patternKey distinguishing features
Measles (rubeola)ParamyxovirusHigh, 3–4 d BEFORE rashMaculopapular starting hairline/behind ears → face → trunk (craniocaudal spread)3 Cs: cough, coryza, conjunctivitis + Koplik spots (buccal mucosa white grains)
Rubella (German measles)TogavirusLow-gradePinpoint/maculopapular, face→trunk, fades by day 3Tender occipital/postauricular lymphadenopathy; mild in children; congenital rubella = cataract, deafness, PDA
Roseola infantum (exanthem subitum, 6th disease)HHV-6 (±HHV-7)High fever 3–5 d, child wellRash appears as fever resolves — trunk→face/extremities3 mo–4 y; febrile seizures common; rash blanching macules
Erythema infectiosum (5th disease, slapped-cheek)Parvovirus B19Low/none“Slapped cheek” → lacy reticular rash on limbs/trunkArthropathy in adults; aplastic crisis in sickle cell/chronic haemolysis; hydrops fetalis in pregnancy
Scarlet feverStrep pyogenes (erythrogenic toxin)Fever, sore throatSandpaper rash (blanching, pinpoint, sandpaper), circumoral pallor, Pastia’s lines (flexural accentuation)Strawberry tongue, tonsillitis; treat penicillin (prevents RF/PSGN)
Varicella (chickenpox)VZVFeverCrops of vesicles on an erythematous base — all stages simultaneously, itchy, dew-drops-on-petals; centripetalComplications: secondary bacterial infection, pneumonitis, congenital; exclude from school until all crusted
Hand, foot & mouthCoxsackie A16/EV71LowVesicles palms/soles + mouth ulcersSelf-limiting; nail shedding; myocarditis (EV71, rare)
MeningococcaemiaN. meningitidisFever + toxicNON-BLANCHING, palpable purpura/petechiaeEmergency: IV ceftriaxone + fluids; watch for shock/DIC

Management: measles/rubella/roseola/fifth = supportive (antipyretics, fluids). Scarlet fever = penicillin V/amoxicillin ×10 d. Varicella = supportive, acyclovir if severe/immunocompromised. Meningococcaemia = emergency. Measles: isolate, notify public health, vitamin A in severe/developing-world cases.

Exam pearls
  • Fever first, rash after fever breaks = ROSEOLA (HHV-6).
  • Cough+coryza+conjunctivitis then craniocaudal rash = MEASLES (plus Koplik).
  • Slapped cheek + reticular rash = parvovirus B19 → aplastic crisis risk in haemolytics.
  • Sandpaper rash + Pastia lines + circumoral pallor = GAS scarlet fever → penicillin.
  • Any non-blanching purpuric rash with fever = meningococcaemia → ceftriaxone NOW.
Traps
  • Measles is contagious 4 days before → 4 days after rash.
  • Fifth disease in pregnancy causes hydrops — advise pregnant contacts.
  • Don’t confuse roseola rash with drug rash — history of fever trajectory decides.

Childhood Vasculitis — Kawasaki Disease & HSP (IgA Vasculitis)

Kawasaki disease (mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome) — medium-vessel vasculitis of children <5 y; the leading cause of acquired heart disease in developed countries (coronary artery aneurysms).

Diagnostic criteria: fever ≥5 days PLUS ≥4 of: (1) bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection; (2) oral changes — strawberry tongue, cracked red lips, diffuse erythema; (3) rash (polymorphous, not vesicular); (4) extremity changes — erythema/oedema of palms & soles (acute) → periungual desquamation (2–3 wks); (5) cervical lymphadenopathy (≥1.5 cm, usually unilateral). Labs: leucocytosis, thrombocytosis (week 2+), high ESR/CRP, sometimes aseptic meningitis, sterile pyuria, raised transaminases.

Treatment — IVIG 2 g/kg over 12 h ASAP (ideally within 10 days of fever) + aspirin (high-dose acute phase 80–100 mg/kg/d until afebrile 48–72 h, then low-dose 3–5 mg/kg/d ×6–8 weeks). Baseline echocardiography (repeat at 2 wks and 6–8 wks) for coronary aneurysms. Refractory → second IVIG dose ± infliximab/steroids. Delay in IVIG = aneurysm risk.

Complications: coronary artery aneurysm (20% untreated vs ~5% with IVIG) → MI/sudden death; myocarditis; pericarditis; valvulitis; rarely giant aneurysms → thrombosis → warfarin/abciximab.

Henoch–Schönlein purpura (HSP / IgA vasculitis) — the commonest childhood vasculitis; small-vessel IgA immune-complex disease, classically 2–11 y, post-URTI. Classic tetrad: palpable purpura (buttocks/extensor legs — NON-blanching), colicky abdominal pain (± GI bleed), arthritis/arthralgia, renal disease (haematuria/proteinuria — IgA nephropathy pattern, usually mild but can cause RPGN). Diagnosis clinical; check urine microscopy + BP + U&E in every HSP child, weekly then monthly urinalysis up to 6–12 months. Treatment: supportive (hydration, analgesia); severe abdominal pain → steroids; renal failure/nephritic syndrome → nephrology (may need steroids/immunosuppression ± dialysis).

HSP complication in this exam: abdominal pain + palpable mass = intussusception (ileo-ileal — lead point from bowel-wall haematoma).

Exam pearls
  • Fever ≥5 d + strawberry tongue + conjunctivitis + rash + desquamating hands/ feet → IVIG + aspirin NOW; echo the heart.
  • HSP = purpura on extensor surfaces + abdominal colic + arthritis + haematuria → urine dip all children at presentation and follow up.
  • HSP + abdominal mass → ultrasound for intussusception.
  • Kawasaki thrombocytosis appears in week 2 — do not be reassured by an early normal count.
Traps
  • Only PARTIAL criteria (e.g. fever + 2 features + coronary aneurysm or very high inflammatory markers) = incomplete Kawasaki — still treat.
  • Aspirin in HSP is NOT required; it’s the big antiplatelet role only in Kawasaki/thrombocytosis.
  • Excludes: meningococcaemia (toxic, petechial), scarlet fever (circumoral pallor/Pastia lines), measles (Koplik).

Congenital Heart Disease — Murmur Recognition & Cyanosis

Approach: (1) Cyanotic vs acyanotic? (2) Where/when murmur? (3) Splitting behaviour.

LesionMurmurKey signsNotes
VSD (commonest CHD)Harsh pansystolic at left lower sternal edgeFeeding difficulty/FTT, recurrent chest infections; large VSD → heart failure, loud P2; small (restrictive) = louderMany close spontaneously; Eisenmenger if long-standing large defect (reversal → cyanosis)
ASDSoft ejection systolic at left upper sternal edge (relative pulmonary flow)Fixed widely split S2 (pathognomonic); often asymptomatic; split doesn’t vary with respirationTypes: ostium secundum (commonest, 90%), primum (AVSD), sinus venosus; embolic stroke risk (paradoxical); closure if shunt significant
PDAContinuous “machinery” murmur below left clavicleBounding pulses, wide pulse pressure; common in prematurityIndomethacin/ibuprofen or device closure if symptomatic
Tetralogy of Fallot (commonest CYANOTIC)Ejection systolic (pulmonary stenosis); single S2Hypercyanotic “tet” spells (squatting/knee–chest ↑SVR), clubbing, squatting; RVH (boot-shaped heart)4 features: pulmonary stenosis + VSD + overriding aorta + RVH; spell: knee–chest, O₂, morphine, beta-blocker, call ICU
Transposition of great arteries (TGA)Usually no murmur; single S2Severe cyanosis in first hours of life (needs duct/foramen to survive)Egg-on-string CXR; prostaglandin E1 to keep duct open; arterial switch operation
Eisenmenger syndrome± pansystolic (shunt may reverse → murmur diminishes)Cyanosis + clubbing + polycythaemia lateIrreversible pulmonary hypertension — surgery contraindicated; heart-lung transplant
Pulmonary stenosisEjection systolic, left upper sternal edge, normal/soft splitting or single S2 (delayed A2–P2)Widely split FIXED = ASD; single S2/soft P2 = PSBalloon valvuloplasty if gradient high
Aortic stenosisEjection systolic at right upper sternal edge radiating to carotidsEjection click, thrillBicuspid → coarctation association
Innocent murmur (Still’s)Soft, vibratory/“twang” systolic, disappears lying flat/sitting upWell child, normal S1/S2, normal growthReassure — no investigation

Cyanosis work-up: hyperoxia test (FiO₂ 100% ×10 min — PaO₂ stays low if cardiac, rises if pulmonary); echocardiography is definitive. Acute cyanotic neonate → prostaglandin E1 immediately if duct-dependent lesion suspected.

Cyanotic murmurs vs cyanotic single S2: TOF (murmur + hypoxic spells), TGA (single S2, no murmur, first-day cyanosis), truncus, tricuspid atresia, Ebstein.

Exam pearls
  • Pansystolic LLSE = VSD; fixed split S2 + soft ESM = ASD; machinery = PDA; ESM + single S2 + cyanotic + squatting = TOF.
  • “Blueness after crying” in a child = TOF tet spell → echo; knee–chest position.
  • Continuous murmur disappears supine = innocent (Still’s).
  • Uncorrected left-to-right shunt → Eisenmenger → cyanosis with diminished murmur.

2018 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Developmental Delay & Learning Disability

Developmental domains: gross motor → fine motor/vision → speech/language → social/personal. Global developmental delay (GDD) = significant delay in ≥2 domains; becomes “intellectual disability” once IQ measurable (<70 + adaptive impairment).

Red flags requiring urgent assessment: not smiling at 8 weeks, not sitting at 9–12 months, not standing by 12, not walking by 18 months, no words by 2 years, loss of previously acquired skills (regression → think ASD, Rett, neurodegeneration), hand preference before 12 months (cerebral palsy).

Assessment: detailed history (antenatal/perinatal/neonatal course, family history, consanguinity, milestones, regression, social interaction, sleep, feeding), examination (dysmorphology, growth parameters incl. head circumference, skin stigmata — café-au-lait, neurocutaneous, neurology, hearing/vision), investigations: hearing test first in language delay (audiogram/OAE — a deaf child doesn’t speak), FBC, TFT, U&E/Ca, lead, metabolic screen if indicated, karyotype/chromosomal microarray (first-line genetic test), Fragile X, MRI brain (if focal signs/microcephaly/regression), EEG (if seizures).

Management: MDT — paediatrician, early-intervention/portage, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech & language therapy, audiology, educational psychology; treat cause (hypothyroidism, metabolic); parent support groups; statementing/EHCP for special educational needs.

Autism spectrum disorder vs ADHD vs learning disability: ASD = social-communication deficit + restricted/repetitive behaviour (M-CHAT screen 16–30 mo); ADHD = inattention + hyperactivity/impulsivity in ≥2 settings (Conners rating scales); LD = below-average intellect without adaptive impairment of ASD. Not “naughty” — neurodevelopmental.

Exam pearls
  • Language delay → hearing test first, always.
  • Regression of skills = metabolic/neurodegenerative/ASD — investigate urgently (MRI, metabolic, genetics).
  • Global delay + dysmorphology + consanguinity → karyotype/microarray + FraX.
  • Early intervention (EI) before investigations are complete — don’t wait.

Core milestones to memorise (age → expected):

AgeGross motorFine motor / visionSpeech / languageSocial / behaviour
NewbornFlexed posture, ventral suspension lifts head momentarilyFixes to faces brieflyCriesRegards face
6 wksRaises head proneFixes & follows to midlineCoosSocial smile
3 moHead control developing, supports on forearms (prone), holds head steadyHands opening, follows 180°Laughs, turns to voiceKnows mother
4–6 moRolls tummy→back (4–5 mo), sits with support/tripod (6 mo)Palmar grasp (6 mo), transfers hand-to-hand (6–7 mo), reachesBabbles (monosyllables 6 mo)Recognises strangers
7–9 moSits unsupported (7–8 mo), crawls/pivots-sit, stands with supportInferior pincer grasp (9 mo), finger feeds, bangs toys“Mama”, “dada” non-specific (9 mo), understands “no”Stranger anxiety, waves bye-bye-ish
12 moStands alone, walks with one hand held / alone (12–15 mo), cruisingPincer grasp perfected, casts toys1–2 words with meaningDrinks from cup, points, waves bye-bye
18 moRuns stifflyTower of 2–4 blocks, scribbles6–20 words, 2 body partsFeeds self with spoon, symbolic play, temper tantrums
2 yWalks up/down stairs 2 feet per step, kicks ballTower of 6–7 blocks, imitates vertical line, turns pages2-word phrases, ~200+ wordsRemoves garments partially, parallel play, follows 2-step commands
3 yRides tricycle, climbs stairs alternating feet, stands briefly one footTower of 9–10, copies circle, bridge 3 blocks3–4 word sentences, asks “what/who”Puts on garments, plays with others (group play), dry by day
4 yHops, skips, throws/catchesCopies cross/square, uses scissors, draws person ~3 parts4-word sentences, narrates, asks “why/how”Dresses/undresses fully, names 4 colours, interactive pretend play

Developmental quotient (DQ) = developmental age ÷ chronological age × 100. DQ 85–115 normal; 70–85 borderline; <70 significant delay (support needed). Example: 2-year-old with 12-month milestones → 12/24 × 100 = 50.

Warning signs: no social smile by 8 wks, hand preference <12 mo, not sitting by 12 mo, not walking by 18 mo, no words by 2 y, no interest in peers, regression. When in doubt → formal developmental assessment + hearing + vision + referral to portage/EI.

Exam pearls
  • Smile 6 wks • sit 6–8 mo • walk 12–15 mo • words 12–18 mo • 2-word phrases 2 y • tricycle 3 y • hop/skip 4–5 y.
  • DQ = DA/CA ×100 — always a percentage, comparable across domains.
  • Head lag + poor head control in a 3-month-old → reassess urgently (neurological exam, neuroimaging).

Electrolyte Disorders — Sodium & Potassium

Hyponatraemia — classify by volume status:

HypovolaemicEuvolaemicHypervolaemic
Urine NaLow <20 (extrarenal loss: GI, skin, third space) / High >20 (renal loss: diuretics, Addison’s, salt-wasting)>40 (SIADH); check TSH/cortisol (hypothyroid/adrenal = euvolaemic)Low <20 (HF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, CKD — effective arterial underfilling)
Treatment0.9% saline (restore volume) + treat causeFluid restrict (1 L/day) ± salt tablets/furosemide/vaptans (hypertonic 3% if seizures/severe neuro signs)Fluid + sodium restriction, loop diuretics, treat HF/cirrhosis; dialysis if renal failure

SIADH = hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia + inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osm >100, urine Na >40) + euvolaemia + normal renal/thyroid/adrenal + no diuretics. Causes: malignancy (small cell lung, pancreatic), CNS (stroke, tumour, meningitis), pulmonary (pneumonia, TB, PPV), drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, PPIs, chemotherapy, opioids, MDMA). Treat: fluid restriction ± hypertonic saline if symptomatic (Na <120 with seizures/coma — 3% saline, raise ≤8 mmol/L per 24 h to avoid central pontine myelinolysis).

Co-existing lung cancer + hyponatraemia = SIADH (ectopic ADH from small-cell carcinoma).

Hyperkalaemia: treat by severity/ECG. ECG progression: peaked (“tented”) T waves → PR prolongation → P flattening → QRS widening → sine wave → VF. K⁺ >6.5 or any ECG change = emergency: IV calcium gluconate (membrane stabilisation), insulin+dextrose, salbutamol nebulisers, sodium bicarbonate (if acidotic), K binders, dialysis if refractory. Stop K/ACEi/MRA/NSAIDs; check glucose (DKA?), renal function.

Hypokalaemia: causes — diuretics (loop/thiazide), vomiting/diarrhoea, hyperaldosteronism, hypokalaemic periodic paralysis (carbohydrate load in susceptible young men — e.g. “after a big carbohydrate meal”, resolves with K), Bartter/Gitelman, insulin, beta-agonists, RTA. Replace K orally if mild; IV if severe/symptomatic; check Mg (replace both). ECG: flattened T, U waves, ST depression, VT/VF.

Exam pearls
  • SIADH = low serum osm + urine Na>40 + euvolaemic → restrict fluid; symptomatic → 3% saline ≤8/24h.
  • Oedema + crackles + confusion + hyponatraemia = hypervolaemic dilutional (HF) — do NOT give saline.
  • Peaked T waves → calcium gluconate FIRST; insulin/dextrose second; dialysis if refractory.
  • Carbohydrate-feast weakness + low K in a young Asian male = hypokalaemic periodic paralysis.
Traps
  • Hypertonic saline for chronic asymptomatic hyponatraemia causes osmotic demyelination — correct slowly.
  • Pseudohyponatraemia (hypertriglyceridaemia/paraproteinaemia) — check osmolality/lab method if patient looks well.
  • Hypomagnesaemia → refractory hypokalaemia/hypocalcaemia — always co-check.

Glomerulonephritis & Haematuria (Children)

Glomerular haematuria vs non-glomerular: glomerular = dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, smoky/tea-coloured urine, proteinuria, hypertension, renal impairment. Non-glomerular = red/pink urine, isomorphic RBCs, clots, no casts.

Post-streptococcal GNIgA nephropathy (synpharyngitic)AlportHSP nephritis
Timing vs URTI2–3 weeks AFTER throat/skin infectionWithin 1–2 days (“synpharyngitic”)Persistent/familialWith purpura (simultaneous)
ComplementLOW C3 (normalises in 6–8 wks); C4 normalNormalNormalNormal
Other labsASO ↑ (anti-streptolysin O) / anti-DNase B; throat swab may be negativeNormalNormal; hearing loss + ocular (anterior lenticonus)Normal ± renal involvement
Age5–12 yAdolescents/young adultsChildren, X-linked (boys)2–11 y
HistologyDiffuse proliferative GNMesangial proliferation, IgA depositsBasketweave GBM (EM); Type IV collagenIgA deposition (same disease as IgA nephropathy)
OutcomeSelf-limiting (95%+ recover)Variable; 20–40% progress to CKD over decadesProgressive CKD + sensorineural deafnessUsually good; monitor urine/BP for 12–24 mo

Features of nephritic syndrome: haematuria (smoky), hypertension, mild–moderate proteinuria, oedema (periorbital), oliguria. Management PSGN: supportive (salt/water restriction, antihypertensives), no steroids/antibiotics needed for the kidney (antibiotics treat the strep carrier state and prevent spread, not the GN); follow-up to confirm C3 normalisation; persistent hypertension/renal impairment → biopsy.

Alport: persistent glomerular haematuria + family history of males with CKD + sensorineural hearing loss + anterior lenticonus — COL4A5 (X-linked, 80%); supportive; ACEi slows proteinuria; genetic counselling; transplant is not contraindicated (no anti-GBM in most).

Exam pearls
  • Haematuria 2–3 weeks AFTER sore throat + low C3 + high ASO = PSGN.
  • Haematuria DURING sore throat + normal C3 = IgA nephropathy.
  • Haematuria + deafness + family history of renal failure = Alport.
  • Hypertension + periorbital oedema + smoky urine in a child = nephritic — check ASO/C3 first.
