2018 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Growth — Assessment, Percentiles & Faltering Growth

Key measurements: weight-for-age, length/height-for-age, weight-for-height/BMI, head circumference (0–2 y). BMI (child) = weight(kg) / height(m)² — age & sex needed only to plot centiles.

Normal variant patterns:

  • Parent-determined (familial short stature): height follows parental target centile; normal growth velocity; bone age = chronological age.
  • Constitutional delay: short stature + delayed puberty; growth catches up later; bone age delayed; normal final height (just later). “Late bloomer.”
  • Pathological: endocrine (hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, Cushing’s), chronic disease (coeliac, CF, CKD, asthma on steroids), neglect, genetic syndromes.

Faltering growth (failure to thrive): weight crossing down ≥1–2 centile lines (or weight below 3rd centile), often weight before height; causes — inadequate intake (feeding problems, poverty, neglect), inadequate absorption (coeliac, CF, CMPA), excessive losses (vomiting, diarrhoea — coeliac/CF), increased requirements (chronic infection, malignancy, hyperthyroidism). First step: plot the chart accurately + dietary history + observe a feed (for infants). Investigations guided by history: urine dip/MC&S, coeliac serology, sweat test, FBC, U&E/LFT, TFT, lead, development.

Reading growth charts: plot with correct age/sex chart; centiles: 3rd–97th ≈ normal; below 3rd = short/underweight; above 97th = tall/overweight; height above 97th centile — think Marfan/overgrowth; weight <3rd with height 50th = acute undernutrition (wasting); both <3rd = chronic; height <3rd with normal weight = “failure to thrive with preserved weight” — hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, skeletal dysplasia, syndromes.

Velocity matters more than one point: falling off the centile line (even within the normal range) is abnormal; single readings need confirmation.

Head circumference: ~34–35 cm at birth; +2 cm/mo ×3, then +1 cm/mo; at 12 mo ≈ 46 cm; macrocephaly >98th (hydrocephalus — check fontanelle, developmental progress); microcephaly <2nd (congenital infections, TORCH, chromosomal, metabolic).

Exam pearls
  • BMI = weight ÷ height² — needs only weight & height for the value; age/sex for the centile plot.
  • Weight <3rd + height 50th = wasting (acute); height <3rd + weight normal = endocrine/skeletal.
  • Deceleration (crossing down lines) = the red flag — plot and re-measure.
  • Faltering growth + offensive stools + recurrent chest infections = CF/coeliac — sweat test + tTG.

Innocent Murmurs & Still’s Murmur

Innocent murmurs are harmless flow murmurs with NO structural heart disease — common (up to 50% of children at some point). Recognition is the skill: no symptoms, normal examination otherwise (normal growth, normal S1/S2/split, no clicks/thrills/rubs, normal pulses, no hepatomegaly).

This exam (Still’s murmur): soft (grade 1–3), vibratory/musical/“twangy” systolic ejection murmur at the left lower/mid sternal edge, age 3–7 y, DISAPPEARS when lying down (changes with position — louder supine/sitting up quieter), well child = innocent (Still’s) murmur. Also innocent: pulmonary flow murmur (soft ESM at LUSB, louder supine), venous hum (continuous, supraclavicular, louder sitting, disappears supine/ with head turn), peripheral pulmonary stenosis of the newborn (soft ESM, back/axilla, disappears by ~6 mo).

Red flags needing echo: any symptoms (breathlessness, syncope, chest pain, poor feeding/failure to thrive, cyanosis), abnormal S2 (fixed split, single S2, loud P2), diastolic murmur, thrill, click, pansystolic, louder with standing, abnormal pulses/BP, family history of sudden death/CHD, abnormal ECG, unequal sats.

Management: still’s → reassure, no investigation, no follow-up beyond routine. Record in notes; safety-net advice; reassure parents (“the heart is normal; the noise is just blood flowing”).

Exam pearls
  • Vibratory systolic murmur that VANISHES lying flat in a well child = innocent (Still’s).
  • Diastolic/continuous louder standing/abnormal S2 = NOT innocent → echo.
  • Innocent murmurs are systolic, soft, short, positional — never diastolic.

Intussusception

Definition: telescoping of one bowel segment into another (usually ileocolic) — commonest acute abdominal emergency in infants 3–36 months (peak 5–9 months).

Classic triad (present in only ~25%): (1) colicky abdominal pain (sudden, intermittent, infant draws knees to chest, screams, between episodes pale/lethargic); (2) “red-currant jelly stool” (bloody mucus — LATE sign); (3) sausage-shaped mass in right upper quadrant / right iliac fossa + emptiness in the right iliac fossa (Dance’s sign). Other signs: vomiting (bilious if obstructed), lethargy/pallor (may dominate — “infant just sleepy”), abdominal distension, shock (late), peritonitis if perforated.

Causes/associations: 95% idiopathic (lymphoid hyperplasia — post-viral/rotavirus vaccine historically); pathological lead points (~5%): Meckel’s diverticulum, HSP (IgA vasculitis), polyps, lymphoma, CF (inspissated stool), parasites — in children >2 y or recurrent, look for a lead point.

This exam: colicky pain + bleeding on rectal examination/red-currant jelly → intussusception; abdominal mass + no stool in a 1-y-old → intussusception; HSP + abdominal pain + mass → intussusception.

Diagnosis: ultrasound — target/doughnut/bull’s-eye sign (transverse) or pseudo-kidney (longitudinal); also shows free fluid. X-ray may show soft-tissue density/absence of caecal gas/ obstruction.

Management: resuscitation first (ABCDE, IV access, NG tube, fluids, correct electrolytes/shock) → air-contrast (or barium) enema reduction (diagnostic AND therapeutic; success 70–90%; contraindicated if peritonitis/perforation/shock) → surgery if enema fails, peritonitis, perforation, shock, or suspected lead point (pathological) → manual reduction ± resection. Observe 12–24 h for recurrence (~10%).

Exam pearls
  • Colicky pain + red-currant jelly + mass = intussusception → ultrasound → air enema.
  • Infant “just lethargic/pale” between pain episodes = think intussusception, not sedation.
  • >2 y or recurrence → find the lead point (Meckel’s/HSP/lymphoma).

2018 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Acute Leukaemia in Children

ALL (acute lymphoblastic leukaemia) — commonest childhood cancer (~80% of leukaemias), peak 2–5 years. Risk factors: Down syndrome (AML M7/ALL), prior chemotherapy/radiation, ionising radiation, Fanconi anaemia, Bloom syndrome, ataxia telangiectasia.

Presentation: bone marrow failure — anaemia (pallor, fatigue), thrombocytopenia (petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, bruising), neutropaenia (fever, infection); tissue infiltration — bone pain (limping, refusal to walk — “growing pains” red flag), hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, mediastinal mass (T-cell ALL —SVC syndrome, orthopnoea), CNS involvement (headache, cranial nerve palsies), testicular involvement, gum hypertrophy/skin nodules (AML monocytic), DIC (APL / AML M3).

Labs: FBC — anaemia, thrombocytopenia, WCC can be LOW, normal OR HIGH — never exclude by WCC; blasts on peripheral film; raised LDH/uric acid; bone marrow aspirate: >25% lymphoblasts (diagnostic) with flow cytometry/immunophenotyping (B- vs T-lineage), cytogenetics/karyotype (t(12;21) ETV6-RUNX1 good risk; t(9;22) BCR-ABL poor; hyperdiploidy good); CXR (mediastinal mass), LP (CNS disease), uric acid/renal function.

Treatment phases: induction → consolidation → CNS prophylaxis (intrathecal methotrexate) → maintenance (2–3 years); high-risk/relapsed → allogeneic stem cell transplant; good supportive care (transfusion, antimicrobials, growth factors). Cure rate >85% in ALL with modern therapy.

Exam pearls
  • Petechiae + pallor + bone pain + hepatosplenomegaly → FBC + film → marrow.
  • “Growing pains” red flags: night pain, unilateral, refusal to walk, systemic signs.
  • Never attribute petechiae to ITP before seeing a differential count and film — leukaemia hides behind “low platelets”.

Best answer
C. Acute leukemia
Petechiae/purpura + blasts (large cells with large nuclei) on film + cytopenias (or normal WBC with blasts) = acute leukaemia (ALL in children). ITP = isolated thrombocytopenia, normal WBC/film otherwise; TTP = schistocytes; HUS = haemolysis + renal.
2018 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Neonatal Jaundice

Approach by timing:

TimingThink of
<24 h (always pathological)Haemolysis — Rh incompatibility (Rh-neg mother + Rh-pos baby), ABO incompatibility (O mother + A/B baby), G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis, sepsis (congenital), polycythaemia; direct hyperbilirubinaemia (TORCH/sepsis — urgent)
24 h–2 wksPhysiological (peak day 3–4, unconjugated, well baby, resolves ≤2 wks), breast-milk jaundice (peaks week 2, feeding well — continue breastfeeding), breastfeeding failure jaundice (under-feeding, weight loss — feed more), haemolysis, infection, polycythaemia, cephalohaematoma bruising
>2 wks (prolonged)Conjugated (cholestatic): biliary atresia (pale stools + dark urine — Kasai portoenterostomy before 8–12 wks!), choledochal cyst, Alagille, inborn errors (galactosaemia, α1-AT), infection (UTI!), hypothyroidism, breast-milk jaundice, haemolysis persisting

This exam’s EMQ (2020 set): day 3, well, unconjugated, resolves → physiological; first 24 h, mother O/baby A, DAT+, mild anaemia → ABO incompatibility; first day, Rh-neg mother sensitised (previous Rh-pos baby, no anti-D) → Rh incompatibility (severe — exchange transfusion risk); day 5 boy, male relatives affected, haemolysis → G6PD deficiency.

ABO vs Rh: ABO — mother O, baby A/B; usually mild, 1st baby can be affected (naturally occurring anti-A/B IgG), DAT weak/negative, no prenatal prophylaxis works (no anti-D for ABO). Rh — mother Rh-neg, baby Rh-pos; usually NOT first baby (needs sensitisation, unless prior transfusion/miscarriage), DAT strongly positive, severe haemolysis (hydrops fetalis), prevented by anti-D Ig (at 28/34 wks + within 72 h of delivery/sensitising events).

G6PD deficiency — X-linked; males; episodic severe haemolysis with infection/fava beans/drugs (sulfonamides, primaquine, nitrofurantoin, methylene blue); Mediterranean/African/Asian; avoid precipitants; check level; Heinz bodies/bite cells.

Management: monitor bilirubin (TSB or transcutaneous); phototherapy per age-appropriate thresholds (chart); exchange transfusion if severe (or BIND scores — bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction: lethargy, poor feeding, arching, high-pitched cry, later kernicterus — athetoid CP, hearing loss, gaze palsy); IVIG if immune haemolysis failing phototherapy; treat cause; breastfeeding support; prolonged conjugated → urgent USS + hepatology (biliary atresia timing critical).

Exam pearls
  • Jaundice <24 h = pathological — find the haemolysis.
  • Mother O + baby A/B = ABO (DAT±). Mother Rh− + baby Rh+ + prior affected sibling = Rh — anti-D prevents.
  • Pale stools + dark urine at 2–3 weeks = biliary atresia — Kasai before 8–12 weeks, every week counts.
  • G6PD: check family history of male jaundice; avoid oxidants.

2018 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Neonatal Sepsis

Early-onset (<72 h — vertical transmission): Group B Streptococcus (GBS) and E. coli (± Listeria). Risk factors: maternal GBS colonisation, prolonged rupture of membranes (>18 h), PPROM, chorioamnionitis (maternal fever), prematurity, maternal UTI/fever, previous baby with GBS sepsis.

Late-onset (>72 h — nosocomial/community): coagulase-negative staphylococci, S. aureus, Gram-negatives (Klebsiella), Candida (NICU), GBS (late).

Presentation (non-specific — suspect in ANY unwell neonate): poor feeding, lethargy, temperature instability (hypothermia typical — not always fever), tachypnoea/grunting, apnoea, tachycardia/bradycardia, mottled skin, abdominal distension, hypoglycaemia/hyperglycaemia, jaundice, seizures, bulging fontanelle, “just looks unwell”.

This exam: 5-hour-old + elective LSCS + maternal GBS colonisation + prolonged ROM + lethargy/tachypnoea → early-onset GBS sepsis.

Management: do NOT wait for cultures if unwell — full septic screen + immediate IV antibiotics: IV benzylpenicillin (or ampicillin) + gentamicin (cover GBS + Listeria + Gram-negatives). Screen: FBC (± differential, platelets), CRP (baseline + 12–24 h — CRP lags), blood cultures (mandatory), lumbar puncture if stable (exclude meningitis — count/glucose/protein/culture), urine culture, ± CXR. Supportive: SCBU, thermoregulation, glucose, feeding (IV if unwell), ventilation if needed, DVT N/A. Escalate immediately; inform parents.

Exam pearls
  • GBS risk (maternal colonisation/prolonged ROM/PPROM) + unwell neonate = sepsis until proven otherwise — screen + antibiotics NOW.
  • Hypothermia is a neonatal sepsis sign.
  • Ampicillin/penicillin + gentamicin = GBS/Listeria/Gram-negative cover.

2018 · Pediatrics · 2 questions · MCQ

Nephrotic Syndrome & Proteinuria (Children)

Definition: (1) proteinuria — nephrotic range: urine PCR >200 mg/mmol (spot) or >40 mg/m²/h (24 h) or 3–4+ dipstick; (2) hypoalbuminaemia (<25 g/L typically); (3) oedema (periorbital, genital, dependent, ascites/pleural effusions); ± hyperlipidaemia.

Causes by age (critical age splits):

  • Congenital (<3 months): congenital nephrotic syndrome (Finnish type) — NPHS1 (nephrin) mutation; massive proteinuria from birth; needs albumin infusions + ACE-i + eventually bilateral nephrectomy + transplant. Also Denys–Drash, Pierson syndrome.
  • 1–12 years: MINIMAL CHANGE DISEASE (~90%) — steroid-SENSITIVE; insidious onset oedema over days; normal renal function, complement normal; NO haematuria (if present → biopsy). Diagnosis = clinical — empirical prednisolone 60 mg/m²/d (max 60–80 mg) ×4–6 weeks then taper; 85–90% respond (remission in 2–4 weeks). Biopsy ONLY if: age <1 or >12, steroid resistance (no response by 4–6 wks), haematuria, hypertension, low complement, renal impairment, atypical course.
  • Steroid-resistant/frequent relapsers/adults: FSGS, membranoproliferative GN, membranous nephropathy, IgA, lupus (renal biopsy to differentiate). FSGS commonest in steroid non-responders (and in older children).
  • Secondary: infections (post-strep, hepatitis B/C, HIV), SLE, HSP/IgA, drugs (NSAIDs — membranous), amyloid, malignancy.

Orthostatic (postural) proteinuria — benign; adolescent; proteinuria when upright, absent in first-morning urine; normal renal function/complement; confirm with split urine samples (early AM vs daytime) or first-void UPCR <20 mg/mmol; NO treatment, annual review.

Management of MCD: prednisolone course; relapses (proteinuria return) → re-treat; frequent relapsers → alternate-day low-dose steroids or second-line (levamisole, cyclophosphamide, cyclosporine, mycophenolate/tacrolimus; rituximab); oedema — salt restriction, fluid restriction if severe, loop diuretics (furosemide ± spironolactone) + IV albumin if severe symptomatic hypovolaemia (then furosemide); immunisations (pneumococcal + meningococcal + influenza — infection risk from immunosuppression + loss of complement/immunoglobulins); thrombosis risk (hypercoagulable — sparse activity restriction, avoid dehydration; consider aspirin/warfarin if albumin very low <20 g/L or thrombotic event); lipids — usually normalise with remission.

Investigations at presentation: urine dip/PCR, serum albumin, renal function, lipids, C3/C4, ASO (excludes PSGN), FBC (infection), urine microscopy; exclude secondary causes (ANA, HBV/HCV); biopsy only as above.

Exam pearls
  • Child >1 y + oedema + heavy proteinuria + normal renal function = MCD → steroids — biopsy only if atypical.
  • Proteinuria only when standing = orthostatic — split samples, benign.
  • <3 months onset = congenital (Finnish) — nephrin; very bad; genetic testing.
  • Steroid resistance → biopsy → FSGS.

#225MCQ2018-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-2aa9e57f
An 8-year-old boy presents with a one-week history of eye puffiness and generalized edema, and urine dipstick shows +++ protein that was foamy and frothy. The parents refused kidney biopsy; however, he was prescribed treatment and all of the symptoms resolved. What was he prescribed?
  • A. Oral prednisolone
  • B. IV antibiotics
  • C. Oral antibiotics
  • D. IV fluids
  • E. Diuretics only
Best answer
A. Oral prednisolone
New nephrotic syndrome in a child = minimal change disease until proven otherwise → empirical prednisolone (60 mg/m²/d ×4–6 wks then taper) — ~85–90% respond; NO biopsy needed initially; NO antibiotics/fluids/diuretics-only as primary therapy.

A child has proteinuria with no other symptoms. How do you confirm positional proteinuria?
  • A. Urine dipstick
  • B. Urine microscopy
  • C. Urinalysis
  • D. Early morning urine sample
  • E. 24-hour urine protein
Best answer
D. Early morning urine sample
Orthostatic (postural) proteinuria: proteinuria when upright, ABSENT in first-morning urine — confirm with split urine collections (early AM vs daytime) or first-void albumin:creatinine ratio. Benign in adolescents; no treatment.
2018 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Neurodevelopmental Disorders — ADHD & ASD

ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder): persistent (≥6 months), onset <12 y, in ≥2 settings (home + school): inattention (careless mistakes, can’t sustain attention, doesn’t listen, fails to finish tasks — “does he leave tasks uncompleted?”), hyperactivity (fidgets, leaves seat, “driven by a motor”, talks excessively), impulsivity (blurts out, can’t wait turn, interrupts). Prevalence ~5%; boys > girls; strong genetic component (74%); co-morbid: ASD, conduct disorder, learning difficulties, anxiety, tics.

Diagnosis: clinical — interview parents + child + teacher rating scales (Conners, SNAP-IV); exclude mimics (hearing/vision, sleep apnoea, thyroid, absence seizures, iron deficiency, lead, psychosocial); DSM-5/ICD-11 criteria (≥6 inattentive and/or ≥6 hyperactive-impulsive symptoms).

Management: psychoeducation (parents, child, school — seat front, chunked tasks, movement breaks, immediate rewards); environmental interventions first for preschoolers; medication for ≥6 y (or moderate–severe): methylphenidate (first-line — immediate/modified release), lisdexamfetamine, atomoxetine (non-stimulant — if stimulants contraindicated), guanfacine; monitor growth, appetite, BP/HR, sleep; review every 6 months.

Autism spectrum disorder: impaired social communication/interaction (poor eye contact, no joint attention, not pointing by 18 mo, not sharing enjoyment, no pretend play, difficulty reading social cues) + restricted, repetitive behaviours (hand-flapping, lining up toys, rigid routines, sensory hyper/hyposensitivity, intense narrow interests). Recognised by 12–24 months; red flags: not responding to name, no babble, no pointing, no words by 18 mo, regression of language/social skills.

Screening: M-CHAT-R/F at 16–30 months (universal at 18 months) → positive → referral for formal developmental assessment (ADOS, MDT).

Management: early intervention (EI) programmes, behavioural therapy (ABA/ESDM), speech & language therapy (PECS if non-verbal), occupational therapy (sensory/integration), educational support, family counselling; treat comorbidities (sleep, anxiety, GI); NO medication for core symptoms (only for associated ADHD/irritability — risperidone short-term for severe aggression).

Exam pearls
  • M-CHAT at 16–30 months. 18-month universal screen.
  • ADHD: methylphenidate first-line ≥6 y; psychoeducation + behavioural always.
  • Language delay → HEARING TEST first — then M-CHAT/ASD screen.
  • Regression = urgent evaluation (metabolic, neuroimaging, genetics).

2018 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Newborn Assessment — Apgar Score

Apgar score — assess at 1 and 5 minutes (repeat at 10 if low). 0–2 in each of 5 domains:

012
Appearance (colour)Blue/pale all overPink body, blue extremities (acrocyanosis)Completely pink
PulseAbsent<100 bpm≥100 bpm
Grimace (reflex irritability)No responseWeak grimace/facesCries/coughs/sneezes on stimulation
Activity (tone)LimpSome flexionActive motion/flexed
RespirationAbsentWeak, irregular, gaspingGood, strong cry

Interpretation: 7–10 normal, 4–6 moderately depressed (needs stimulation/O₂/PPV), 0–3 severely depressed (immediate full resuscitation).

Worked example (this exam): blue all over (0) + HR 80 (1) + vigorous cry (respiration 2) + weak grimace (1) + ? (activity not stated — assume some flexion = 1, or active = 2; the published key = 4, so activity counted 0 or the body remained blue with HR 80: 0+1+2+1+0 = 4) → Apgar = 4 → immediate resuscitation (warm/dry/stimulate → PPV), not waiting for the 5-minute score.

Limitations: Apgar is NOT used to determine the need for resuscitation — start resuscitation on assessment (breathing/HR/tone) immediately; the score is for documentation/prognosis. Also confounded by prematurity, drugs (magnesium, narcotics), congenital conditions — these babies score “low” despite normal physiology.

Normal newborn checks: weight (~3.5 kg), length (~50 cm), HC (~34–35 cm), head-to-toe exam within 72 h (NIPE), red reflex, hips (Barlow/Ortolani), testicles, heart (sats pre/post-ductal, murmur), hearing (OAE), vitamin K (IM/oral — prevents haemorrhagic disease), feeding & weight monitoring, cord care, safe sleep advice.

Exam pearls
  • Apgar 0–3 = immediate full resuscitation; never use the score to delay.
  • Memorise the 0/1/2 grid — especially acrocyanosis = 1 (normal in first hours), HR <100 = 1.
  • Vitamin K at birth for all newborns.

#241MCQ2018-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-bdb66ee2
A newborn immediately after birth was found to be blue all over his body; HR was 80, he was crying vigorously with a weak grimace. What is the Apgar score?
  • A. 5
  • B. 6
  • C. 7
  • D. 8
  • E. 4
Best answer
E. 4
Apgar: colour blue all over = 0 (body blue, extremities blue → 0; pink body + blue extremities → 1); HR 80 = 1 (HR <100); crying vigorously = 2 (respirations strong cry); grimace weak = 1. Total = 4. (0,1,2 for each of appearance, pulse, grimace, activity, respiration.)
2018 · Pediatrics · 1 question · SAQ

Otitis Media & Otitis Externa

Acute otitis media (AOM) — middle-ear infection, commonest in 6–24 months; usually follows URTI (eustachian tube dysfunction — short/horizontal in infants). Organisms: S. pneumoniae (commonest), non-typable H. influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis; in neonates/IC: Gram-negatives; GBS; post-influenza → S. aureus/GBS.

Presentation (this exam): rhinorrhoea prodrome → fever, earache (otalgia), irritability, pulling at ear, hearing loss, poor feeding; otoscopy: bulging, erythematous, immobile tympanic membrane, loss of light reflex, effusion (± pus behind TM) — image typically shows a bulging red TM with loss of landmarks/light reflex.

Diagnosis = clinical (pneumatic otoscopy — impaired mobility). Management: analgesia + antipyretic; most viral and self-limiting — watchful waiting 24–48 h if mild >2 y; antibiotics (oral amoxicillin 5–7 d) if: <2 y (esp. bilateral/otorrhoea), severe symptoms, high fever, otorrhoea, unwell, no improvement; alternatives — amoxicillin-clavulanate (recent antibiotics/treatment failure); allergy → macrolide. Complications: mastoiditis (post-auricular swelling/erythema, pinna pushed forward — urgent IV antibiotics + CT + mastoidectomy), facial nerve palsy, meningitis, intracranial abscess, persistent effusion (glue ear → hearing loss — grommets).

Otitis externa — canal inflammation (swimming, trauma): pain with tragal movement/pinna pull, itchy, discharge, canal swelling; organisms S. aureus/Pseudomonas; treat: topical ciprofloxacin/ofloxacin drops (± steroid), keep dry, aural toilet; avoid aminoglycoside drops if perforated TM.

Exam pearls
  • Bulging erythematous TM after URTI = AOM → amoxicillin if severe/<2 y/otorrhoea; analgesia always.
  • Mastoiditis (boggy swelling behind ear) = emergency.
  • Ear pain + tragal tenderness + swimming = otitis externa — drops, not oral antibiotics.

A 4-year-old child presented with a 4-day history of rhinorrhea, fever and cough, and complained of ear pain. Examination of the ear showed the following (image shown).
  1. What is the likely diagnosis? (1 pt)
  2. List two organisms most commonly associated with this condition. (2 pt)
  3. What is the first-line treatment? (1 pt)
Best answer
1) Acute otitis media — erythematous, bulging tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex (± effusion) after URTI, otalgia, fever. 2) Two commonest organisms: Streptococcus pneumoniae and non-typable Haemophilus influenzae (then Moraxella catarrhalis). 3) First-line: oral amoxicillin (5–7 days) (± analgesia/antipyretics; review in 48–72 h; if recurrent/perforation — ENT).
AOM: diagnose clinically (bulging TM is THE sign). Analgesia first; antibiotics if <2 y/bilateral/otorrhoea/severe. Recurrent AOM → check for risk factors (passive smoke, day-care); grommets if persistent effusion with hearing loss.

Brachial plexus (birth injuries): Erb’s (C5–6, waiter’s tip) vs Klumpke’s (C8–T1, claw hand + Horner’s) — see Birth injuries review.

Management: remove compression/splint (foot drop — ankle-foot orthosis), physiotherapy, treat cause (diabetes/B₁₂/thyroid), surgical decompression/repair if laceration or no recovery 3–6 months, analgesia (gabapentin/amitriptyline/carbamazepine for neuropathic).

  • Foot drop + dorsal foot sensory loss = common peroneal (fibular head).
  • Wrist drop = radial. Claw hand = ulnar. Ape hand/thenar wasting = median.
  • Always compare with the contra-lateral side and check reflexes.

2018 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Seronegative Spondyloarthropathies & HLA-B27

Shared features: RF-NEGATIVE inflammatory arthritis + HLA-B27 association + axial skeleton/SIJ and enthesitis + extra-articular (uveitis/iritis, IBD, psoriasis, cardiac aortitis) + asymmetric.

DiseaseHallmarks
Ankylosing spondylitisYoung males, inflammatory back pain (morning stiffness >30 min, improves with exercise NOT rest, night pain, onset <40), ↓lumbar flexion (Schober <5 cm), bamboo spine late on X-ray, sacroiliitis; uveitis, aortitis
Reactive arthritis (Reiter’s)Post-GI (Shigella/Salmonella/Campylobacter) or STI (Chlamydia) infection — “can’t see, can’t pee, can’t climb a tree” — conjunctivitis/uveitis + urethritis/circinate balanitis + asymmetric arthritis of large joints (knees/ankles) + enthesitis
Psoriatic arthritisPsoriasis/nail pitting/onycholysis + DIP involvement, dactylitis (“sausage digits”), pencil-in-cup deformity, ± spondylitis (5% of psoriasis)
Enteropathic arthritisIBD (Crohn’s/UC) — peripheral or axial arthritis tracks bowel activity

HLA-B27 is most strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis (90–95%) — this exam: HLA-B27 positivity + joint pain → ankylosing spondylitis (B). (Reactive arthritis also B27-associated 60–80%, but the highest-yield single answer is AS.)

Management: NSAIDs + regular exercise/physiotherapy (the cornerstone of AS); TNF-α inhibitors (etanercept/adalimumab) for refractory/axial disease; peripheral — methotrexate/sulfasalazine; treat extra-articular manifestations; stop smoking; monitor uveitis (urgent ophthalmology for red painful eye).

Exam pearls
  • HLA-B27 + young man + inflammatory back pain = ankylosing spondylitis.
  • Post-GI/STI + “can’t see/pee/climb” = reactive arthritis.
  • AS = better with exercise; RA = worse with rest.

2018 · Pediatrics · 1 question · SAQ

Thalassaemia

Pathophysiology: reduced/absent globin-chain synthesis — α (2 genes on each chromosome 16) or β (1 gene on each chromosome 11); unbalanced chain accumulation → ineffective erythropoiesis + haemolysis + intramedullary destruction; autosomal recessive.

α-thalassaemiaβ-thalassaemia
Genetics4 deleted genes = Hb Bart’s (hydrops fetalis — intrauterine death); 3 = HbH disease (haemolytic anaemia); 2 = trait (mild); 1 = silent carrier2 mutated genes = thalassaemia MAJOR (Cooley’s anaemia) — normal at birth (HbF) → symptoms from ~4–6 months (this exam); 1 mutated = trait (minor, asymptomatic microcytosis)
LabsMicrocytic, hypochromic, target cells, ↑RBC count (unlike iron deficiency), normal/high ferritin, HbH inclusion bodies (HbH)Microcytic + VERY high HbF, raised HbA2 on electrophoresis/HPLC, absent HbA (major), ineffective erythropoiesis, high reticulocytes (this exam 9.9%), high LDH/indirect bilirubin, sickling test NEGATIVE (this exam)
Features (major)—Severe anaemia + hepatosplenomegaly (extramedullary haematopoiesis) + frontal bossing/maxillary overgrowth (“chipmunk face”) + growth failure + pathological fractures + gallstones (pigment) + iron overload (cardiomyopathy/endocrine failure); death in childhood untreated

THIS exam (twice — 2017/2018 identical): 5–7-month-old, pallor, splenomegaly 7 cm, Hb 5.7 / MCV 51 / retic 9.9% / negative sickle test → β-thalassaemia major; confirm: haemoglobin electrophoresis/HPLC (HbF↑, HbA2↑, absent HbA) + β-globin genotyping; treatment: (a) regular blood transfusion program to keep Hb ≥95–105 g/L + (b) iron chelation therapy (desferrioxamine / deferasirox / deferiprone) with cardiac-liver MRI T2* monitoring — folic acid supplements; splenectomy only if hypersplenism; allo-HSCT is curative (matched sibling); genetic counselling/screening for parents & siblings (25% each child).

Not iron deficiency: thalassaemia trait = high RBC, normal ferritin, high HbA2; iron deficiency = low ferritin, high RDW, low RBC; confirm with electrophoresis/iron studies — NEVER give iron to a thalassaemic unless deficient (overload risk).

Exam pearls
  • Microcytosis + high RBC + normal ferritin = thalassaemia (not iron deficiency).
  • 6-month-old + splenomegaly + severe anaemia + negative sickle = β-thal major → HPLC, then transfusion + chelation.
  • Hb Bart’s = hydrops; HbH = golf-ball; trait = silent.

#260SAQ edited2018-Pediatrics-SAQ-Medicine-3fec5a45
A seven-month-old male infant presented with pallor and abdominal distension. Physical examination revealed severe pallor and splenomegaly of 7 cm below the costal margin. Full blood count showed Hb 5.7 g/dL, MCV 51 fL, MCH 21 pg/cell, retic 9.9%, sickling test negative.
  1. What is the most likely diagnosis? (1 pt)
  2. Mention the best diagnostic test. (1 pt)
  3. Mention two lines of management. (2 pt)
Best answer
1) Most likely diagnosis: β-thalassaemia major (Cooley’s anaemia) — 7-mo infant, pallor, hepatosplenomegaly, severe microcytic hypochromic anaemia (Hb 5.7, MCV 51), raised reticulocytes, sickling test negative. 2) Best diagnostic test: haemoglobin electrophoresis/HPLC — absent/reduced HbA (SS), markedly raised HbF (and HbA₂); confirm with β-globin gene analysis; check both parents (carrier state). 3) Management: (a) regular blood transfusion programme (every 3–4 weeks, keep Hb >90–100) + iron chelation (deferasirox/desferrioxamine) to prevent iron overload; (b) folic acid supplementation + splenectomy only if hypersplenism; definitive = allogeneic stem-cell transplant if matched sibling donor; plus vaccination (pneumococcal) and long-term complications surveillance (cardiac/liver MRI T2*).
Without transfusion, children die before 10 y from high-output failure/infection; with iron chelation, survival into adulthood. Hypochromic microcytosis + high reticulocytes distinguishes from iron deficiency; electrophoresis is diagnostic. Newborn screening + genetic counselling (AR) essential in at-risk populations.
2018 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Vesicoureteral Reflux

Definition: retrograde flow of urine from bladder to ureter/kidney — commonest urological abnormality in children; primary (short intramural ureter tunnel — hereditary) or secondary (posterior urethral valves, neurogenic bladder, high-pressure voiding).

Clinical: usually presents as febrile UTI/pyelonephritis in infancy (or hydronephrosis antenatally); often asymptomatic; bilateral in ~50%; siblings at risk (screen).

Grades (International Reflux Study): I (ureter only), II (ureter + pelvis, no dilatation), III (mild–moderate dilatation/blunting of calyces), IV (moderate dilatation, some tortuosity, loss of calyceal outline), V (severe dilatation/tortuosity, absent calyceal outlines).

This exam: after confirmed UTI in a child with suspected reflux → MICUR/VCUG (micturating cystourethrogram) — the gold-standard grading investigation; Renal ultrasound = first-line for anatomy/hydronephrosis; DMSA scan = cortical scarring (functional damage); MAG3 = drainage/function; urodynamics — only if bladder dysfunction.

Management: low grades (I–III): observation + prophylactic antibiotics (trimethoprim/nitrofurantoin — controversial) + aggressive treatment of constipation/voiding dysfunction — many resolve spontaneously by age 4–6; high grades (IV–V), recurrent febrile UTIs despite prophylaxis, scarring, renal impairment → surgical/endoscopic correction (subureteric Deflux injection or ureteric reimplantation); breakthrough infection → re-check; all need BP + urine follow-up, growth & renal function surveillance; DMSA to assess scarring.

Exam pearls
  • VUR → test = VCUG (micturating cystourethrogram).
  • USS = anatomy; DMSA = scarring; MAG3 = function/drainage.
  • Screen siblings of children with reflux.

Vesicoureteral reflux grading & diagnosis = micturating cystourethrogram (VCUG). US screens for structural abnormalities/hydronephrosis; DMSA assesses cortical scarring; MAG3 for drainage/function. VCUG is invasive (catheter + contrast) — done after UTI settles.

2017 · Genetics · 1 question · MCQ

Fragile X Syndrome & Associated (FMR1) Disorders

Genetics: X-linked CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in FMR1 (Xq27.3). Normal <45 repeats; premutation 55–200; full mutation >200 → hypermethylation → silencing of FMRP (RNA-binding protein for synaptic development). Anticipation (repeats expand through generations, especially via mothers). Full mutations from fathers are rare (only daughters get his X). Premutations expand to full mutation when transmitted by a mother (not usually by a father).

Clinical features (males): intellectual disability (most common inherited cause of ID after Down syndrome), long face, large protruding ears, prominent jaw/forehead, macro-orchidism (post-puberty), large head circumference, joint hypermobility, autistic behaviour/gaze avoidance, mitral valve prolapse, seizures (~10–20%), behavioural problems (hand flapping, ADHD). Females (carriers) have milder/subtler features (learning difficulty, anxiety).

Premutation-associated conditions: Fragile X-associated primary ovarian insufficiency (FXPOI) — ~20% of female premutation carriers (premature ovarian failure/ovarian dysfunction — hence the ovarian-dysfunction question); FXTAS (fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome) — adult-onset intention tremor, cerebellar ataxia, parkinsonism, cognitive decline (older males, mean onset 60s).

Diagnosis: FMR1 DNA analysis (PCR ± Southern blot for methylation/repeat sizing). NOT detectable by karyotype/array/exome. Karyotype may show “fragile site” historical oddity only.

Genetic counselling: mother of affected son is an obligate premutation carrier → test her sisters/daughters; each daughter of a carrier has 50% chance of inheriting premutation (which expands in her offspring); discuss prenatal diagnosis (CVS/amniocentesis) for at-risk pregnancies.

Exam pearls
  • Intellectual disability + long face + large ears + macro-orchidism = fragile X → FMR1 testing.
  • Woman with ovarian insufficiency + intellectually disabled brothers = premutation → test her FMR1.
  • Testing fathers of young children with ID — daughters of an FMR1-premutation father are carriers too.

#276MCQ edited2017-Genetics-MCQ-Medicine-46f80279
In an older woman who is a carrier of fragile X (premutation), which of the following may occur?
  • A. Ovarian insufficiency (POF)
  • B. Hyperlaxity of joints
  • C. Seizures
  • D. Severe intellectual disability
  • E. Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome
Best answer
E. Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome
Premutation carriers (55–200 CGG) in OLDER adults develop FXTAS — late-onset intention tremor, cerebellar ataxia, parkinsonism, cognitive decline (usually males, but also women). Female premutation carriers of reproductive age get FXPOI (premature ovarian insufficiency) — option A — both occur in premutation; with “older woman”, FXTAS is the intended late-life presentation.
2017 · Genetics · 3 questions · MCQ

Patterns of Inheritance & Risk Calculation

Pedigree logic — the six patterns:

PatternHallmarksExamplesRisk to offspring
Autosomal dominantEvery generation; male-to-male; ~50% of children of affected parent; both sexesMarfan, HOCM, Huntington’s, neurofibromatosis, familial hypercholesterolaemia, achondroplasia50%
Autosomal recessiveSiblings only (one generation); consanguinity raises risk; 25% recurrence; silent carriers (2/3 of unaffected siblings are carriers)Cystic fibrosis, sickle cell, thalassaemia, PKU, congenital adrenal hyperplasia25% if both parents carriers
X-linked recessiveMales affected; female carriers usually unaffected (some manifesting); NO male-to-male; 50% sons of carrier mother affected; 50% daughters carriers; affected father → ALL daughters carriers, no sons affectedDMD, haemophilia A/B, G6PD, fragile X (X-linked with anticipation — CGG)Sons of carrier mother: 50%; daughters: 50% carriers (rarely symptomatic)
X-linked dominantBoth sexes; affected fathers → ALL daughters affected, no sons; 50% children of affected motherVitamin D–resistant rickets (XLH), Rett syndrome (female), Fragile X sometimes classified separately50%
MitochondrialMother → ALL children (both sexes) can inherit; father → NONE; highly variable (heteroplasmy); high energy tissues affected (MELAS, MERRF, LHON)MELAS, MERRF, Leber optic neuropathy, Kearns–SayreAll children of affected mother at risk (variable expression)
Y-linked (holandric)Only males; father → ALL sonsHairy ears (debated), some infertility (AZF deletions)100% of sons

Worked answers (this exam):

  • DMD in boy + 2 maternal uncles affected → mother obligate carrier → his sister: 50% carrier, 0% symptomatic.
  • HOCM: father, brother, paternal uncle — male-to-male = autosomal dominant.
  • Mitochondrial → maternal inheritance (all children of affected mother).
  • Marfan (father died suddenly, tall + pectus) = autosomal dominant.
  • DMD in family → daughter of affected? No — daughter of a carrier: 50% chance carrier; her sons: 50% affected. “Chance the daughters’ sons will be affected” = 50%.
Exam pearls
  • Father→son transmission = autosomal dominant (never X-linked).
  • Consanguinity = recessive; only one generation = recessive.
  • Mitochondrial = mothers transmit to all children; fathers transmit none.
  • DMD: sisters of affected boys — 50% carriers, ~0% symptomatic.

#350MCQ edited2017-Genetics-MCQ-Medicine-f04df659
A question about calculation of risk in mitochondrial disease. What is the pattern of inheritance?
  • A. Maternal inheritance (children of an affected mother are at risk)
  • B. Paternal inheritance
  • C. 50% from an affected father
  • D. 25% autosomal recessive
  • E. X-linked recessive
Best answer
A. Maternal inheritance (children of an affected mother are at risk)
Mitochondrial inheritance: mother → ALL children (both sexes) inherit her mitochondria (heteroplasmic — variable expression); father → NO children. Classic clues: matrilineal transmission, high-energy tissues (CNS, heart, muscle), variable severity (MELAS, MERRF, LHON).

  • B. Autosomal recessive
  • C. X-linked recessive
  • D. X-linked dominant

#352MCQ edited2017-Genetics-MCQ-Medicine-6b2a5b6c
There is a history of Duchenne muscular dystrophy in the family. What is the chance that the daughters' sons will be affected?
  • A. 50%
  • B. 25%
  • C. 0%
  • D. 100%
  • E. 75%
Best answer
A. 50%
DMD family: an affected boy’s sister (daughter of an obligate carrier mother) has 50% chance of being a carrier; each son of a carrier daughter has 50% chance of being affected → the chance the grandsons/daughters’ sons are affected = 50%. (Daughters of the affected male himself are obligate carriers — their sons 50%.)

NIPT (this exam)≥10 wksCell-free fetal DNA in maternal blood — ~99% sensitivity for trisomy 21/18/13; SCREENING (needs confirmatory test if positive)None
Quadruple test15–20 wksAFP, β-hCG, uE3, inhibin-A → risk (NTDs/T21)None
Amniocentesis (this exam)≥15 wksKaryotype/microarray — DIAGNOSTIC (definitive) — miscarriage risk ~1/200 (0.5%)Small (0.5%)
CVS11–14 wksPlacental biopsy — diagnostic earlier; risk ~1–2%; mosaicism (1–2%)Small (1–2%)
Cordocentesis (PUBS)>18 wksFetal blood — severe anaemia (Rh), thrombocytopaenia, rapid karyotypeHigher (2%)

18-week question: at 18 weeks CVS window has closed — options were ultrasound (soft markers only), amniocentesis (diagnostic — definitive) and NIPT (first-line screen). How Arena-bank keyed it: NIPT (E) — the modern pathway when the goal is “determine the status with no risk”; if it were “diagnostic certainty”, amniocentesis (C). Both are now used: NIPT → if positive or high suspicion → confirmation by amniocentesis.

Who gets offered invasive testing: previous affected child (like this case), known parental balanced translocation, screening result >1 in 150/300, advanced maternal age (historically), abnormal scan (soft markers), previous miscarriage with fetal karyotype.

Exam pearls
  • 10+ weeks → NIPT; 11–14 → CVS; ≥15–18 → amniocentesis; >18 cordocentesis.
  • NIPT is screening, amniocentesis is diagnostic — always confirm NIPT positives.
  • Never offer amniocentesis as “risk-free” — quote the ~0.5% miscarriage figure.

#322MCQ edited2017-Genetics-MCQ-Medicine-6bb842ee
An 18-week pregnant woman came to the clinic concerned about the current pregnancy as her previous child has trisomy 21. What test will you perform to determine the status of the current pregnancy?
  • A. Fetal ultrasound
  • B. CVS
  • C. Amniocentesis
  • D. Cordocentesis
  • E. NIPT
Best answer
E. NIPT
At 18 weeks the CVS window (11–14 wks) has passed. The modern first-line step for a couple with a previous trisomy-21 child is NIPT (cell-free fetal DNA from maternal blood) — ~99% sensitive for trisomy 21, no procedure risk. Caveat worth knowing: NIPT is a screening test — a positive result (or any raised suspicion) MUST be confirmed with amniocentesis (karyotype), which at 18 weeks is the definitive diagnostic test. If the examiner means “definitive answer for this fetus”, they want amniocentesis; in current practice you will still do NIPT first.

Treatment of Genetic Disorders — Levels of Intervention

The 2019/2017 exam questions test ONE concept — is this treatment acting at the level of the DNA/gene, the protein, or the phenotype/cell/organ?

LevelExamples
Gene/DNA levelCorrecting the mutation — gene therapy (viral vector with normal gene), CRISPR genome editing, spliced-oligo antisense (exon skipping — eteplirsen for DMD), transplantation IS NOT gene therapy per se but delivers normal cells
RNA levelmRNA therapy, antisense oligonucleotides, RNA interference (inclisiran for familial hypercholesterolaemia)
Protein level (this exam — TWICE)Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) — Pompe disease: recombinant acid α-glucosidase; ERT in Gaucher/Fabry/MPS; factor VIII/IX for haemophilia; insulin; growth hormone
Cellular level (this exam — TWICE)Stem cell (haematopoietic) transplantation — curative for SCID/thalassaemia major (matched sibling); bone-marrow transplant for lysosomal some; organ transplantation (liver for α1-antitrypsin)
Phenotype/organ levelSymptomatic: diet (low-Phe for PKU; galactose-free), drugs acting on pathways (sodium phenylbutyrate for urea cycle), surgery (appendicular... — e.g., coarctation repair), physiotherapy, chelation (iron overload in thalassaemia)

Worked answers: “Disease cured by giving a stem cell” → cellular level (D); “Pompe treated with ERT” → protein level (A/D depending on option letter in each year).

Family/familial level (prenatal): genetic counselling, PND (CVS/amniocentesis), NIPT, preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD for IVF — avoids transmission of cystic fibrosis etc.).

Exam pearls
  • ERT replaces the missing PROTEIN — answer “protein level”.
  • Stem cell transplant = cellular level (replaces the cell factory).
  • Gene therapy/CRISPR = gene/DNA level.

  • B. Translation level

2017 · Internal Medicine · 2 questions · MCQ

Acid–Base Disorders

Every ABG question in this exam is solved the same way — do it mechanically, never by pattern-guessing:

  1. Look at pH. <7.35 = acidaemia, >7.45 = alkalaemia (7.35–7.45 can still hide a mixed disorder).
  2. Look at pCO₂ and HCO₃⁻. Whichever moves in the same direction as the pH is the primary process: pCO₂↑ → respiratory acidosis; HCO₃⁻↓ → metabolic acidosis; pCO₂↓ → respiratory alkalosis; HCO₃⁻↑ → metabolic alkalosis.
  3. Check compensation. Acute respiratory acidosis: HCO₃⁻ rises 1 per 10 mmHg pCO₂; chronic: rises 3.5–4 per 10 (max ~31). Metabolic acidosis: expected pCO₂ = (1.5 × HCO₃⁻) + 8 ± 2 (Winter’s formula). If compensation is not as expected → mixed disorder.
  4. Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO₃); normal 8–12 (without K). High gap → MUDPILES (methanol, uraemia, DKA, propylene glycol/paraldehyde, iron/isoniazid, lactic acidosis, ethylene glycol, salicylates). Normal gap (hyperchloraemic) → diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis, Addison’s, saline.
DisorderpHpCO₂HCO₃⁻Classic causes
Respiratory acidosis↓↑↑ (comp.)Opioids/sedatives, COPD, severe asthma, neuromuscular weakness, CNS depression
Respiratory alkalosis↑↓↓ (comp.)Pain, anxiety, early sepsis, salicylates (early), pregnancy, PE, hypoxia at altitude
Metabolic acidosis↓↓ (comp.)↓DKA/HHS, lactic acidosis (shock, metformin), diarrhoea, RTA, uraemia, toxins
Metabolic alkalosis↑↑ (comp.)↑Vomiting, NG suction, diuretics, Conn’s/Cushing’s, hypokalaemia, bicarbonate load

High CO₂ + low HCO₃⁻ + low pH (COPD patient) = mixed respiratory + metabolic acidosis — the low bicarbonate cannot be explained by compensation for a respiratory acidosis, so two primary processes are present. The same logic applies to the unconscious patient with an empty syringe and high lactate (respiratory depressant + lactic acidosis).

Exam pearls
  • Opioid/benzodiazepine overdose → acute respiratory acidosis (high pCO₂, normal/near-normal HCO₃⁻); ↓ respiratory rate (RR 6–8/min), pinpoint pupils.
  • Salicylates → mixed respiratory alkalosis + metabolic acidosis.
  • COPD chronic retainers live with high pCO₂ and high HCO₃⁻; give cautious O₂ (target 88–92%).
  • Lactate >2 = tissue hypoperfusion; treat the cause, not the number.
  • Toxic alcohols/methanol → high anion gap acidosis + high osmolar gap.
Traps
  • Normal pH does NOT mean normal ABG — mixed disorders can cancel out (e.g. mixed acidosis can sit near 7.35–7.40). Always compute the gap and check compensation.
  • "Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation" requires pCO₂ LOW; "respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation" requires HCO₃⁻ HIGH. High CO₂ + low HCO₃⁻ is always a mixed disorder.
  • Do not "treat" compensation — treat the primary process.

#338MCQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-0af5d736
A young male was found unconscious with an empty syringe bottle and needle. Based on the ABG test below, what kind of imbalance does he have?
  • A. Respiratory acidosis
  • B. Metabolic acidosis
  • C. Mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis
  • D. Respiratory alkalosis
  • E. Metabolic alkalosis
Best answer
A. Respiratory acidosis
Young male + empty syringe + hypoventilation → acute respiratory acidosis (opioid overdose — high CO₂, low pH). If the full panel shows HCO₃⁻ also low, it is mixed metabolic + respiratory acidosis — but the classic teaching pattern for this vignette is acute respiratory acidosis; give naloxone + ventilation.
#339MCQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-541392aa
A COPD patient has low O2, high CO2, high HCO3- and low pH. What kind of imbalance does he have?
  • A. Respiratory acidosis
  • B. Metabolic alkalosis
  • C. Mixed respiratory acidosis and metabolic acidosis
  • D. Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
  • E. Respiratory alkalosis
Best answer
A. Respiratory acidosis
COPD (chronic CO₂ retention) + low O₂ + high CO₂ + HIGH HCO₃⁻ + low pH = respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation — in a chronic retainer, high HCO₃⁻ is the compensation; the pH remains low if compensation is incomplete or in acute-on-chronic decompensation. Controlled O₂ 88–92%, treat exacerbation.
2017 · Internal Medicine · 2 questions · MCQ/SAQ

Acute Coronary Syndrome (STEMI / NSTEMI / Unstable Angina)

Definition spectrum of ACS — all from coronary plaque rupture/erosion with superimposed thrombosis:

Unstable anginaNSTEMISTEMI
Chest painAt rest / crescendoAt restSevere, prolonged >20–30 min
TroponinNormalElevatedElevated
ECGNormal / ST depression / T inversionST depression, T inversion, or normalST elevation ≥1 mm in ≥2 contiguous leads (or new LBBB)
ManagementAspirin + P2Y12 (clopidogrel/ticagrelor) + anticoagulant (heparin/enoxaparin) + high-risk features → early invasive angiography (≤24 h)Immediate reperfusion: primary PCI within 90–120 min of first medical contact, else fibrinolysis if PCI unavailable <120 min and pain <12 h (and no contraindications)

ECG localisation — memorise this cold:

  • Inferior (II, III, aVF) → RCA (80–90%, supplies RV + inferior wall); reciprocal ST depression in I, aVL. Think posterior MI if ST depression V1–V3 (check V7–V9), and right ventricular infarct (RV4R ST elevation) — avoid nitrates/preload reduction.
  • Anterior / anteroseptal (V1–V4) → LAD.
  • Lateral (I, aVL, V5–V6) → circumflex (LCx) / diagonal.
  • Extensive anterior (I, aVL, V1–V6) → proximal LAD; watch for pump failure.

Post-operative / post-PCI patients: chest pain with ECG changes after surgery — get a troponin (and repeat 3–6 h); troponin rise defines perioperative MI (usually Type 2 if supply–demand). After PCI + stenting, secondary prevention = DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel ~12 months) + high-intensity statin + ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker. Post-PCI with renal impairment: ACE inhibitors/ARBs both ↓GFR initially — monitor K⁺/Cr; the examinable "add-on" when ACEI/BB already in place and renal function is borderline is an ARB substitute or long-acting nitrate for angina.

NSTEMI management: dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin 300 mg loading then 75 mg + clopidogrel/ticagrelor), anticoagulation (LMWH/fondaparinux), beta-blocker if no heart failure, high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80), ACEi, risk-stratify (GRACE) → early coronary angiography if troponin-positive or ST changes.

Exam pearls
  • Pain + ST elevation + prior normal ECG = STEMI → activate cath lab, do not wait for troponin.
  • New LBBB + chest pain = treat as STEMI equivalent.
  • Inferior STEMI → check RV leads; give fluids if hypotensive, avoid nitrates/diuretics.
  • Troponin is the gatekeeper between unstable angina and NSTEMI — it changes management.
  • Post-MI discharge drugs: aspirin + P2Y12, statin, ACEi, beta-blocker ("ABAS").
  • Exertional chest pain with normal ECG → risk-stratify first (troponin if acute; stress test if stable).
Traps
  • ST depression in V1–V3 can be a posterior STEMI — upright tall R waves; don’t call it ischaemia only.
  • Do not give nitrates/ACEi to a hypotensive inferior/RV infarct.
  • "Troponin normal, pain settled, ECG flat" ≠ discharge without work-up — serial troponins and risk stratification.

A patient has acute-onset chest pain on exertion; ECG is normal apart from subtle T wave changes. What is your next step?
  • A. Troponin
  • B. CK-MB
  • C. BNP
  • D. Exercise ECG stress test
  • E. Echocardiography
Best answer
A. Troponin
Exertional chest pain + normal/non-specific ECG (subtle T changes) — first exclude ACS: high-sensitivity troponin now (+ repeat 3 h). If negative and the patient is stable with exertional pattern only → risk-stratify with exercise ECG/stress imaging. Troponin is the gatekeeper.
#376SAQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-SAQ-Medicine-b260f297
A patient has shortness of breath and chest pain for one week. He was given oxygen, morphine and nasogastric GTN spray and improved. Troponin is normal. ECG is shown (ST-depression).
  1. What is the most likely diagnosis? (1 pt)
  2. List 3 medications to manage the patient. (3 pt)
  3. What further investigation will you do? (1 pt)
Best answer
1) Most likely diagnosis: unstable angina / NSTEMI (NSTE-ACS) — exertional/rest chest pain for a week, troponin currently normal, ECG: ST-depression (subendocardial ischaemia). (If troponin rises on repeat → NSTEMI; if stays normal → unstable angina.) 2) Three medications: (a) aspirin (300 mg loading then 75 mg) + (b) P2Y12 inhibitor (clopidogrel/ticagrelor) — dual antiplatelet therapy; (c) anticoagulation — LMWH or fondaparinux; PLUS (d) high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg) and (e) beta-blocker ± ACEi. 3) Further investigation: repeat/serial troponins + risk stratification (GRACE score) → early coronary angiography (invasive strategy); non-invasive stress imaging if low risk and diagnosis uncertain; echo for LV function and valves.
NSTE-ACS: DAPT + anticoagulant + admit CCU, continuous monitoring, nitrates/analgesia PRN, statin, beta-blocker if haemodynamically stable. Troponin-positive → angiography ≤24 h; never discharge troponin-negative pain without stress testing.
2017 · Internal Medicine · 2 questions · EMQ/MCQ

Acute Kidney Injury — Pre-renal, Intrinsic (ATN), Post-renal

Definition (KDIGO): Creatinine ↑ ≥26.5 µmol/L within 48 h, or ≥1.5× baseline within 7 days, or UO <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h. Stage by creatinine rise / urine output.

Pre-renalIntrinsic — ATNPost-renal
Mechanism↓ renal perfusion (dehydration, sepsis, heart failure, ACEi/ARB + NSAIDs, renal artery)Ischaemic or nephrotoxic tubular damage (aminoglycosides, cisplatin, contrast, pigment, sepsis)Obstruction below collecting system (BPH, stones, tumour, blocked catheter)
FeNa<1%>2%Variable
Urine Na<20 mmol/L>40 mmol/LVariable
Urine microscopyBland / hyaline castsMuddy brown granular casts, renal tubular epithelial cellsBland; may see haematuria
Serum urea:Cr>20:1<10–15:1Variable
Urine osmolality>500<350Variable

Nephrotoxins to know: gentamicin/aminoglycosides → ATN (also causes hypomagnesaemia); cisplatin & carboplatin → ATN; amphotericin B → ATN + distal RTA/K⁺/Mg²⁺ wasting; ACE inhibitors/ARBs → functional (pre-renal) rise in Cr via efferent dilation, especially with bilateral renal artery stenosis; penicillins/cephalosporins/PPIs/NSAIDs → acute interstitial nephritis (fever, rash, eosinophilia, WBC casts); contrast → contrast-induced nephropathy (48–72 h); methotrexate/ethylene glycol.

Tumor lysis syndrome (leukaemia/lymphoma post-chemo): hyperkalaemia + hyperphosphataemia + hyperuricaemia + hypocalcaemia → AKI; prevent with allopurinol/rasburicase + IV fluids; life-threatening K⁺ → treat immediately.

Rhabdomyolysis (marathon, crush, statins): dark urine, myalgia, ↑↑ CK, hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia (early) → myoglobinuric ATN. Best test: serum CK (± urine myoglobin).

Obstructive (post-renal) clues: distended bladder, frequency/hesitancy/BPH, recent ACEi dose increase unmasking bilateral obstruction — small rise in creatinine with normal kidney size + palpable bladder → urethral catheter + ultrasound.

Management ATN: stop nephrotoxins, restore volume/perfusion, treat hyperkalaemia (calcium gluconate, insulin/dextrose, salbutamol, bicarbonate, K-binders, dialysis), treat acidosis & fluid overload. Indications for emergency dialysis (AEIOU): Acidosis refractory, Electrolyte (K⁺ >6.5 or symptomatic), Ingestions (toxins), Overload (pulmonary oedema refractory to diuretics), Uraemia (encephalopathy, pericarditis, seizures).

Exam pearls
  • FeNa <1% + history of poor intake/heart failure → pre-renal. FeNa >2% + muddy brown casts → ATN.
  • WBC casts → pyelonephritis/interstitial nephritis; RBC casts → glomerulonephritis; muddy brown granular casts → ATN.
  • Aminoglycosides: monitor levels; hypomagnesaemia + rising Cr = tubular toxicity — stop the drug.
  • Post-chemo leukaemia patient with high K, high PO₄, low Ca → tumour lysis → rasburicase + fluids.
  • After CABG/surgery → think ischaemic/pigment ATN ± cardiorenal.
Traps
  • In contrast nephropathy and rhabdomyolysis, FeNa can be <1% early — don’t exclude ATN solely on FeNa.
  • Creatinine can lag — the earliest sign of AKI is often rising K⁺ and oliguria.
  • Never give ACEi in bilateral renal artery stenosis — creatinine rises sharply.

A male on a known ACE inhibitor (hypertensive) with BPH had his dose increased by his doctor. He developed low urine output, a sudden increase in creatinine and hyperkalemia. Ultrasound shows normal-sized kidneys but a distended bladder. What is the most probable cause?

  • C. Interstitial nephritis
  • D. Acute tubular necrosis

Best answer
A. Obstructive uropathy
BPH + ACEi dose increased + low urine output + sudden Cr rise + hyperkalaemia + distended bladder + normal-sized kidneys = post-renal obstruction (obstructive uropathy). Relieve it — insert urinary catheter + renal USS; stop/hold ACEi temporarily; reassess renal function after relief.

2017 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · SAQ

Acute Pancreatitis

Diagnosis = 2 of 3: (1) epigastric pain radiating to the back, (2) amylase or lipase >3× upper limit, (3) imaging consistent with pancreatitis. Amylase is the classic exam number (e.g. 1000 IU/L); lipase is more sensitive/specific and stays elevated longer.

Causes (GET SMASHED): Gallstones (commonest, ~40%), Ethanol, Trauma, Steroids, Mumps/viruses, Autoimmune, Scorpion sting, Hyperlipidaemia/Hypercalcaemia, ERCP, Drugs (azathioprine, valproate, diuretics, OCP/HRT, HAART). Also hereditary (PRSS1/CFTR).

Severity (Glasgow/Ranson/BISAP): age >55, WBC >15, glucose >10, urea >16, LDH >600, albumin low, calcium low, PaO₂ low, rising Cr. Local complications: peripancreatic fluid collections, pancreatic necrosis (sterile vs infected), pseudocyst (>4 weeks), haemorrhagic pancreatitis.

Imaging: Ultrasound abdomen (RUQ) first to find gallstones and duct dilatation (this patient has gallstones); contrast-enhanced CT if diagnosis uncertain, no improvement, or necrosis/severe disease suspected (ideally after 72 h). MRCP for stones in the duct.

Management (supportive — no specific drug): aggressive IV fluids (crystalloid, ~250–500 mL/h initially), analgesia (opioids), antiemetics, bowel rest/early enteral feeding as tolerated, oxygen, monitor vitals/urine output, treat cause (cholecystectomy during same admission for gallstone pancreatitis; ERCP for cholangitis/impacted CBD stone). Antibiotics only if infected necrosis/cholangitis. Alcohol cessation, stop culprit drugs.

Exam pearls
  • Pain radiating to the back + vomiting + elevated amylase + gallstones = gallstone pancreatitis — diagnosis is clinical/biochemical; CT is for severity, not diagnosis.
  • Cullen’s sign (periumbilical bruising) / Grey Turner’s sign (flank bruising) = haemorrhagic pancreatitis — severe.
  • A falling calcium is a bad prognostic sign.
Traps
  • Amylase can be normal if presentation is late or amylase-free (triglyceride-induced — check lipids).
  • Do NOT send straight to CT before ultrasound for the gallstone search.
  • Prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated in sterile necrosis.

#370SAQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-SAQ-Medicine-300273cd
A patient, known case of gallstones, presents with abdominal pain radiating to the back, N/V, and amylase increased (1000).
  1. What is the diagnosis? (1 pt)
  2. What is the best diagnostic imaging? (1 pt)
  3. Mention two medical treatments. (2 pt)
Best answer
1) Acute pancreatitis (gallstone pancreatitis) — epigastric pain radiating to the back + nausea/vomiting + amylase 1000 U/L (>3× ULN). 2) Best imaging: RUQ abdominal ultrasound FIRST to confirm gallstones/duct dilatation; contrast-enhanced CT abdomen at 72–96 h (or immediately if diagnosis uncertain/severe) to assess severity/necrosis. 3) Two medical treatments: (a) aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (0.9% saline) + early enteral (oral) feeding as tolerated; (b) analgesia (opioids) + antiemetics; plus oxygen; stop culprit drugs/alcohol; early cholecystectomy once settled.
Diagnosis 2 of 3 (pain, enzymes, imaging). Ranson/Glasgow severity scoring; look for complications (necrosis, pseudocyst); ERCP only for cholangitis/impacted duct stone; surgery for infected necrosis; cholecystectomy same admission.
2017 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Adrenal Disorders — Adrenal Crisis & Adrenal Insufficiency

Acute adrenal (Addisonian) crisis — a medical emergency, suspect it in any patient with glucocorticoid deficiency who becomes unwell: hypotension/shock unresponsive to fluids, abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia. Triggers: intercurrent illness, surgery, abrupt steroid withdrawal. Here the patient also has type 1 diabetes → think autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2 (autoimmune adrenalitis + T1DM ± thyroid disease).

Diagnosis: ACTH (cosyntropin) stimulation test — 250 µg synthetic ACTH IV/IM, cortisol measured at 0/30/60 min; failure of cortisol to rise (>500 nmol/L or incremental rise <170–200 nmol/L) confirms adrenal insufficiency. In crisis: treat FIRST (IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat, then 200 mg/24 h + 0.9% saline with dextrose), do not wait for the test. Basal 9 am cortisol <100 nmol/L is strongly suggestive; >500 makes it unlikely.

Distinguish primary vs secondary:

Primary (Addison’s)Secondary/tertiary
ACTHHighLow/inappropriately normal
Aldosterone–reninLow aldosterone, HIGH renin (salt wasting, hyperkalaemia)Normal (RAAS intact → no hyperkalaemia)
PigmentationHyperpigmentation (ACTH↑ → MSH)Absent
CausesAutoimmune (most common in developed world), TB, adrenal haemorrhage (Waterhouse–Friderichsen), infiltrative, congenital adrenal hyperplasiaChronic steroid therapy (commonest), pituitary/hypothalamic disease

Chronic management: hydrocortisone (e.g. 15–25 mg/day in divided doses, more in the morning) + fludrocortisone for primary AI; sick-day rules (double dose during illness); emergency hydrocortisone injection; medic-alert bracelet; bone/glucose monitoring.

Exam pearls
  • Hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia + hypotension in an autoimmune-disease patient → adrenal crisis → IV hydrocortisone NOW.
  • Do not wait for cortisol in crisis; measure random cortisol/ACTH if possible before the first dose, but treat immediately.
  • Adrenal crisis can mimic sepsis/gastroenteritis — clue is disproportionate electrolytes + poor response to fluids.

#285MCQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-c662672b
A type 1 DM patient presents with abdominal pain, fever, nausea and vomiting, low BP, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. What is the best test to reach the diagnosis?
  • A. ACTH level
  • B. Catecholamines
  • C. Serum cortisol
  • D. Serum aldosterone

Best answer
E. ACTH stimulation test
T1DM + fatigue + abdominal pain + hypotension + hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia = adrenal insufficiency (autoimmune Addison’s — polyglandular syndrome type 2). Short Synacthen (ACTH) stimulation test = confirmatory test (cortisol fails to rise). In crisis: treat first (IV hydrocortisone 100 mg) — never delay.
2017 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Alcoholic Liver Disease

Spectrum: steatosis → alcoholic hepatitis → fibrosis → cirrhosis → hepatocellular carcinoma.

Clinical clues: chronic heavy alcohol use; tender hepatomegaly, parotid enlargement (sialadenosis), bilateral Dupuytren’s contracture, palmar erythema, spider naevi, gynaecomastia, peripheral oedema/ascites, asterixis, encephalopathy (chronic); fever/leucocytosis/jaundice in alcoholic hepatitis.

Labs — classic exam pattern: AST:ALT ratio >2 with AST usually <300–400 IU/L (if AST >400 or ALT >500, think ischaemia/paracetamol/viral); raised GGT, macrocytosis (MCV↑ from direct marrow toxicity and B₁₂/folate deficiency), thrombocytopenia, low albumin in advanced disease, ↑IgA. Maddrey discriminant function guides steroid use in severe alcoholic hepatitis (DF ≥32 → prednisolone 40 mg if no infection/GI bleed).

Diagnosis is clinical + exclusion: exclude viral hepatitis, drugs (paracetamol), biliary obstruction (USS), autoimmune. Liver biopsy for uncertain cases.

Exam pearls
  • AST:ALT >2 + parotid swelling + alcohol history = alcoholic liver disease.
  • GGT tracks alcohol use but is non-specific (also rises with cholestasis and enzyme inducers).
  • Severe alcoholic hepatitis: stop alcohol absolutely, nutrition (thiamine/pabrinex to prevent Wernicke’s — give BEFORE glucose), treat infection, prednisolone if DF ≥32 and no contraindication.
  • Wernicke’s triad: confusion + ataxia + ophthalmoplegia → IV thiamine before dextrose.
Traps
  • Very high transaminases (>1000) argue AGAINST alcoholic hepatitis.
  • Macrocytosis + liver disease is not automatically alcohol — check B₁₂/folate/TSH.

Anaemia — Macrocytic & Haemolytic Patterns

Classify by MCV — every anaemia question starts there:

Microcytic (<80 fL)Normocytic (80–100)Macrocytic (>100)
Iron deficiency (bleeding GI/menstrual, malabsorption, dietary), thalassaemia trait, chronic disease (usually normo-), sideroblastic, leadAcute blood loss, chronic disease/inflammation (↑hepcidin), CKD (↓EPO), haemolysis, aplastic anaemia, mixed deficiencyMegaloblastic: B₁₂ or folate deficiency. Non-megaloblastic: alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis, myelodysplasia, drugs (azathioprine, hydroxyurea)

Folate vs B₁₂: both megaloblastic (hypersegmented neutrophils, macro-ovalocytes, ↓ reticulocytes, mild ↑bilirubin/LDH). Folate deficiency — poor diet, alcohol, pregnancy/increased demand, malabsorption, drugs (methotrexate, trimethoprim, phenytoin). B₁₂ deficiency — pernicious anaemia (anti-intrinsic factor/parietal cell antibodies, neurological signs: subacute combined degeneration — dorsal columns + corticospinal, i.e. ↓vibration/proprioception + spastic weakness), terminal ileum disease, vegan diet, metformin. After multiple pregnancies with jaundice + macrocytosis, folate deficiency is the classic answer (high folate demand + mild haemolysis jaundice).

Jaundice + anaemia = haemolysis until proven otherwise: check reticulocytes (high), LDH↑, unconjugated bilirubin↑, haptoglobin↓, blood film (schistocytes/spherocytes/sickle cells), direct Coombs (autoimmune) vs intravascular vs extravascular patterns.

Exam pearls
  • Macrocytosis + neurological deficit → B₁₂; macrocytosis + pregnancy/alcohol/poor diet → folate.
  • Giving folate alone in B₁₂ deficiency can precipitate/worsen subacute combined degeneration — replace B₁₂ first.
  • Reticulocyte count separates decreased production (low retics: deficiency/CKD/marrow failure) from destruction/loss (high retics: haemolysis/bleeding).

A 45-year-old female has had several pregnancies. On a normal check-up she is found to have jaundice and macrocytic anemia. What is the cause responsible for the anemia?
  • A. Folate deficiency
  • B. B12 deficiency
  • C. Iron deficiency
  • D. Pernicious anemia
  • E. Hemolysis
Best answer
A. Folate deficiency
Multiparous woman (multiple pregnancies) + jaundice + MACROCYTIC anaemia = folate deficiency (pregnancy increases folate demand; also poor dietary folate) — check red-cell folate/B₁₂; treat folic acid (always exclude/replace B₁₂ first to protect against subacute combined degeneration).

Antidiabetic Drugs & Hypoglycaemia

Sulfonylureas (gliclazide, glibenclamide/glyburide, glimepiride) — the only oral class that stimulates insulin secretion (close K-ATP channels on β-cells) → the classic cause of drug-induced hypoglycaemia, especially with skipped meals, renal impairment, elderly, and long-acting agents (glibenclamide). Always ask "which oral agent and when did they last eat?"

ClassMechanismKey adverse effects
Metformin (biguanide)↓ hepatic gluconeogenesis, ↑peripheral sensitivityGI upset, B₁₂ deficiency, lactic acidosis (avoid eGFR<30, acute illness, contrast). No hypoglycaemia alone.
Sulfonylureas↑ insulin releaseHypoglycaemia, weight gain
Meglitinides (repaglinide)Brief insulin pulseHypoglycaemia (shorter), weight gain
DPP-4 inhibitors (sitagliptin)↑ incretin (GLP-1) levelsWell tolerated, rare pancreatitis, arthralgia
GLP-1 agonists (exenatide, liraglutide)Incretin mimetic — glucose-dependent insulin, ↓glucagon, satietyNausea, weight loss, pancreatitis (rare), no hypo alone
SGLT-2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin)Block renal glucose reabsorption → glycosuriaGenital mycotic infections, UTI, volume depletion, euglycaemic DKA, Fournier’s (rare); CV/renal benefit
Thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone)PPAR-γ agonistFluid retention, weight gain, HF, fractures, bladder cancer (?)
α-glucosidase inhibitors (acarbose)↓ gut carb absorptionFlatulence, diarrhoea
InsulinReplacementHypoglycaemia, weight gain, lipohypertrophy at injection sites

Management of hypoglycaemia: conscious → 15–20 g fast sugar (glucose tablets/juice), recheck at 15 min, then snack/complex carb; unconscious → buccal glucose gel or IM glucagon 1 mg (or IV dextrose 10%/50% if IV access); stop culprit drug, review renal function, counsel on eating regularly.

Exam pearls
  • Only sulfonylureas, meglitinides and insulin cause significant hypoglycaemia — metformin does not.
  • Recurrent/nocturnal hypoglycaemia on glibenclamide → switch class, educate, check renal function.
  • Metformin in renal failure or contrast → hold; lactic acidosis risk.

#279MCQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-a7963367
A patient on an oral hypoglycemic agent developed hypoglycemia. Which medication caused his hypoglycemia?
  • A. Sulfonylurea (glyburide)
  • B. Metformin
  • C. GLP-1 agonist
  • D. SGLT-2 inhibitor
  • E. DPP-4 inhibitor
Best answer
A. Sulfonylurea (glyburide)
Sulfonylureas (glibenclamide/glyburide, gliclazide) stimulate insulin secretion → the classic drug cause of hypoglycaemia — especially with missed meals/renal impairment/elderly. Metformin alone never causes hypoglycaemia. GLP-1/DPP-4/SGLT-2 = glucose-dependent/independent, minimal risk.

Cardiac Arrhythmias — Recognition & Acute Management

Approach to any ECG rhythm: rate → regularity → P waves (present? each before a QRS?) → PR length → QRS width → ST/T. Then match to a rhythm and assess stability (ABCDE — shock, syncope/pre-syncope, ischaemia/chest pain, heart failure).

RhythmKey ECG featuresNotes / management
Sinus tachycardiaHR >100, normal P before each QRSPhysiological — treat the cause (pain, fever, hypovolaemia, PE, thyrotoxicosis, drugs)
AVNRT / AVRT (SVT, PSVT)Regular narrow-complex tachycardia ~150–250, P waves hidden/inverted/retrograde after QRSVagal manoeuvres → adenosine 6→12→12 mg rapid IV bolus; unstable → synchronized cardioversion; long-term: ablation
Atrial flutterSaw-tooth flutter waves ~300/min, typically 2:1/4:1 block (ventricular ~150), narrow QRSRate control (beta-blocker/verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin) or DC cardioversion; anticoagulation per CHA₂DS₂-VASc; CTI ablation is curative
Atrial fibrillationIrregularly irregular narrow complex, no distinct P wavesLoss of JVP “a” wave (no atrial contraction). Rate control first (BB/CCB/digoxin); anticoagulate per CHA₂DS₂-VASc; unstable → DC cardiovert; consider rhythm control/ablation if young/symptomatic
VTBroad complex regular tachycardia; concordance, AV dissociationStable → IV amiodarone/procainamide; unstable → immediate synchronized cardioversion; pulseless → defibrillation + ALS
Heart block1°: PR >200 ms constant. 2° Mobitz I (Wenckebach): progressive PR prolongation then dropped beat. 2° Mobitz II: sudden dropped beat, constant PR. 3° (complete): AV dissociation, regular escape rhythmMobitz II & CHB → admit, transcutaneous/transvenous pacing; atropine often ineffective; stop AV-nodal blockers
VF / pulseless VTChaotic or broad-complex without pulseImmediate defibrillation + CPR + adrenaline 1 mg every 3–5 min

CHA₂DS₂-VASc (stroke risk in AF): CHF (1), HTN (1), Age ≥75 (2), DM (1), Stroke/TIA (2), Vascular disease (1), Age 65–74 (1), Sex female (1). Score 0 (men) / 1 (women) → no anticoagulation; ≥1 (men)/≥2 (women) consider OAC; ≥2 → anticoagulate (DOAC preferred). HAS-BLED estimates bleeding risk — high score is NOT a reason to withhold anticoagulation; it flags need for closer review/modifiable factors.

JVP “a” wave is produced by atrial contraction → absent in AF (no organised atrial systole); giant “a” waves in tricuspid stenosis; cannon “a” waves in complete heart block/AV dissociation (atrium contracts against closed tricuspid valve).

Exam pearls
  • Irregularly irregular + absent “a” wave = AF. Narrow regular tachycardia in a young woman with normal baseline = AVNRT → vagal then adenosine.
  • Unstable tachycardia/bradycardia → electricity wins (synchronized shock for pulse present; defibrillation for pulseless).
  • High-grade AV block (Mobitz II, complete) → pacing, not atropine alone.
  • Antidromic AVRT/VT wide-complex doubt → treat as VT (procainamide/amiodarone; avoid AV-nodal blockers in pre-excited AF).
Traps
  • Do not use adenosine in pre-excited AF (irregular wide complex) — can precipitate VF.
  • Cardioversion in AF >48 h without anticoagulation/imaging → stroke risk; anticoagulate ≥3 weeks or do TOE, or cardiovert early (<48 h) with heparin.

A woman with a history of palpitations and sweating has an ECG (shown). What does the ECG show?

A. Atrial flutter

Regular ventricular response ~75–150 bpm; treat: rate control (BB/verapamil ± digoxin), anticoagulate per CHA₂DS₂-VASc; DC cardioversion/CTI ablation if unstable/refractory.
2017 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Autoimmune Liver Disease — PBC vs PSC vs AIH

Three autoimmune cholestatic/hepatitic diseases — the exam loves the antibody table:

Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC)Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH)
WhoMiddle-aged womenYoung men, ulcerative colitis (70%)Young/middle-aged women
TargetSmall intrahepatic bile ductsIntra- and extrahepatic bile ducts (beading)Hepatocytes
AntibodyAnti-mitochondrial (AMA)p-ANCA (atypical); ANA/SMA sometimesType 1: ANA, anti-smooth muscle; Type 2: anti-LKM1
LFT patternCholestatic (↑ALP, ↑GGT), IgM↑Cholestatic (↑ALP/GGT), p-ANCA+Hepatocellular (↑↑ALT/AST), IgG↑
SymptomsFatigue, pruritus, dry eyes/mouth, xanthomata/osteoporosis (vitamin D malabsorption), progression to cirrhosisPruritus, fatigue, cholangitis; ↑ risk cholangiocarcinoma + colorectal cancerFatigue, jaundice, hepatomegaly, spider naevi; may be asymptomatic with high ALT
AssociationsSjögren’s, RA, thyroid disease, SSc, coeliacUC, cholangiocarcinomaOther autoimmune disease
TreatmentUrsodeoxycholic acid (slows progression); ± fibrates; later transplantUDCA (symptomatic), manage strictures (ERCP), surveill for cancers, liver transplant definitiveImmunosuppression: prednisolone ± azathioprine

Work-up in a cholestatic pattern: ultrasound first (exclude obstruction/dilated ducts) → if ducts not dilated → check AMA. PBC = AMA+ cholestasis with normal biliary imaging. PSC = AMA-negative cholestasis + MRCP showing biliary beading/stricturing. AIH = hepatitic pattern + autoantibodies + raised IgG ± biopsy. In a patient with SLE presenting with cholestasis and AMA positive, the answer is primary biliary cholangitis — despite SLE.

AMA (anti-mitochondrial antibody) is the characteristic — and most specific — antibody of PBC (present in ~95%). Anti-LKM1 = autoimmune hepatitis type 2 and chronic hepatitis C overlap; anti-smooth muscle + ANA = AIH type 1.

Exam pearls
  • Pruritus + fatigue + ↑ALP in a middle-aged woman + AMA → PBC → ursodeoxycholic acid.
  • PSC + UC → annual colonoscopy (CRC risk) and MRCP surveillance for cholangiocarcinoma.
  • Cholestatic picture with dilated ducts = obstruction — image before assuming autoimmune.

#330MCQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-09444e41
A 35-year-old lady, a known case of SLE, presents with jaundice and dark urine. Labs show markedly elevated ALP, negative anti-smooth muscle antibodies, positive ANA and positive AMA. What is the most likely cause?
  • A. Primary biliary cirrhosis
  • B. Primary sclerosing cholangitis
  • C. Autoimmune hepatitis
  • D. Drug-induced cholestasis
  • E. Gallstone disease
Best answer
A. Primary biliary cirrhosis
35F + SLE background + jaundice + dark urine + markedly raised ALP + positive AMA = primary biliary cholangitis (the SLE is incidental — AMA is the disease-defining antibody). Anti-smooth muscle usually negative here (it would suggest AIH); confirm with AMA titre + MRCP (exclude PSC) + USS; treat ursodeoxycholic acid.
2017 · Internal Medicine · 3 questions · MCQ

Bleeding Disorders — Platelets vs Coagulation vs vWD

Bleeding pattern points to the defect:

Platelet / primary haemostasisCoagulation factor / secondary haemostasis
PatternMucocutaneous: petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, bleeding immediately after cutsDeep bleeds: haemarthroses, muscle/retroperitoneal haematomas, delayed bleeding (hours after surgery/dental extraction)
Platelet countLow (or functionally defective)Normal
PT / aPTTNormalPT = extrinsic (factor VII); aPTT = intrinsic (VIII, IX, XI, XII); both = common pathway (X, V, II, I) or vitamin K/liver disease

Key inherited disorders:

  • Haemophilia A (factor VIII) / B (factor IX) — X-linked recessive. Boys; deep haematomas, haemarthroses, prolonged aPTT with normal PT, normal platelets. Treat: factor VIII/IX replacement (on demand ± prophylaxis), DDAVP for mild A, avoid aspirin/IM injections. Check inhibitors if poor response.
  • Von Willebrand disease — most common inherited bleeding disorder; autosomal dominant; mucocutaneous bleeding, menorrhagia in women, family history; normal/high aPTT (factor VIII protected by vWF), prolonged bleeding time; test: vWF antigen/activity (ristocetin cofactor), factor VIII. Treat: DDAVP (mild), tranexamic acid, vWF/factor VIII concentrate for surgery/major bleeds.
  • Vitamin K deficiency — neonates (no stores, sterile gut), malabsorption (coeliac, CF, cholestasis), antibiotics, warfarin → affects factors II, VII, IX, X → PT (and later aPTT) prolonged; newborn bleeding prevented by IM/oral vitamin K at birth. Treat with vitamin K; PCC/FFP if bleeding.
  • ITP — isolated thrombocytopenia post-viral illness, well child, petechiae/purpura, normal Hb/WBC; observe if mild; IVIG/steroids if significant bleeding/platelets very low; avoid sports.
  • Haemophilia + circumcision bleed in a boy with knee haematomas = haemophilia A (commonest) vs B.

Laboratory triage: normal aPTT + prolonged PT → factor VII deficiency or vitamin K/warfarin/liver. Prolonged aPTT + normal PT → VIII/IX/XI. Both prolonged → common pathway (X/V/II/fibrinogen) or vitamin K deficiency/liver/DIC/warfarin; mixing study separates factor deficiency (corrects) from inhibitor (fails to correct — e.g. lupus anticoagulant, factor VIII inhibitor). Prolonged both + thrombocytopenia + high D-dimer + low fibrinogen = DIC (oozing everywhere, multi-organ failure — treat cause + replace).

Exam pearls
  • Petechiae + isolated low platelets post-viral in a well child = ITP.
  • Circumcision bleed + haemarthrosis + boy + family history = haemophilia (aPTT↑, PT normal).
  • vWD = menorrhagia + mucocutaneous bleed + family history; DDAVP trial.
  • Both PT & aPTT prolonged in a newborn/anticoagulated/malabsorbed = vitamin K — give vitamin K, check liver.
  • DIC = consumption — replace what you use, treat the cause (sepsis!).
Traps
  • Normal PT/aPTT does NOT exclude vWD or mild factor deficiency — check vWF/factor levels and bleeding time.
  • Platelet transfusion only in active bleeding/prophylaxis before procedures, not automatically in ITP.
