#281MCQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-b3820597
A patient has low Hb, low platelets and low RBCs. What is the likely diagnosis?
  • A. Consumptive coagulopathy (DIC)
  • B. ITP
  • C. Hemolytic uremic syndrome
  • D. Aplastic anemia
  • E. Leukemia
Best answer
D. Aplastic anemia
Pancytopenia (low Hb + low platelets ± low WCC) without blasts = aplastic anaemia (marrow failure). Must be distinguished from acute leukaemia (blasts on film/marrow — check film) and DIC (clotting deranged, schistocytes). ITP/HUS are single/dual lineages only.
#316MCQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-9adf0a74
A patient has normal PT, INR and platelets but bleeding after tooth extraction (gingival bleeding). What is the likely diagnosis?
  • A. Von Willebrand disease
  • B. Factor V deficiency
  • C. Factor IX deficiency
  • D. Vitamin K deficiency
  • E. Factor VIII deficiency
Best answer
A. Von Willebrand disease
Normal PT/INR/platelets/aPTT + mucocutaneous bleeding (gingival after extraction) = von Willebrand disease — vWF carries/protects factor VIII and mediates platelet adhesion. Check vWF antigen + ristocetin cofactor activity + factor VIII; treat DDAVP (mild) / vWF concentrate (severe/surgery); tranexamic acid adjunct for mucosal bleeding.
#317MCQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-58de95c0
A patient has normal aPTT with an isolated prolonged PT. What is the likely cause?
  • A. ITP
  • B. TTP
  • C. Factor VII deficiency
  • D. Vitamin K deficiency
  • E. Liver disease
Best answer
C. Factor VII deficiency
Isolated prolonged PT with normal aPTT = factor VII deficiency (extrinsic pathway — shortest half-life, falls first in early vitamin K deficiency too). Vitamin K deficiency and liver disease eventually prolong BOTH PT and aPTT. Haemophilia/vWD = aPTT.
2017 · Internal Medicine · 2 questions · MCQ

Calcium & Parathyroid Disorders

First, correct calcium for albumin (or use ionised calcium): corrected Ca (mmol/L) = measured + 0.02 × (40 − albumin g/L). Phosphate, PTH, vitamin D complete the picture.

Ca²⁺PO₄³⁻PTHThink of
Primary hyperparathyroidism↑↓↑/inappropriately normalAdenoma (80%); “stones, bones, groans, psychiatric moans”; check for MEN1/2A; management: parathyroidectomy if symptomatic/young/complications/eGFR low/osteoporosis/high stones risk
Secondary hyperparathyroidism↓ or N↑↑CKD / vitamin D deficiency — PTH elevated to compensate
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism↑↑/N↑↑Long-standing secondary disease → autonomous glands (post-transplant CKD) → parathyroidectomy
Hypoparathyroidism↓↑↓Post-surgery (thyroidectomy — commonest), autoimmune, DiGeorge, autoimmune polyglandular; symptoms: perioral numbness, carpopedal spasm, Trousseau’s, Chvostek’s, seizures, prolonged QT
Malignancy hypercalcaemia↑↓/NsuppressedPTHrP (squamous lung, breast, renal), bone mets, myeloma (high ALP/renal failure/anaemia + high Ig), 1,25-vit D (lymphoma)
Vitamin D deficiency↓/N↓↑Rickets/osteomalacia — secondary HPT normalises Ca; low phosphate (renal wasting under PTH)

Hypocalcaemia work-up: check Mg (low Mg causes/worsens hypocalcaemia and PTH resistance — correct it), phosphate, PTH, vitamin D, renal function. Acute severe: IV calcium gluconate 10–20 mL of 10% (cardiac monitoring). Chronic: oral calcium + calcitriol (1,25-OH vit D).

Tertiary HPT “next step”: confirm autonomy — raised Ca + raised/inappropriately normal PTH on background of CKD; localise with sestamibi scan/neck ultrasound then subtotal parathyroidectomy. Calcimimetics (cinacalcet) for those unfit for surgery.

Exam pearls
  • High Ca + low PO₄ + high PTH = primary HPT; high Ca + LOW PTH = malignancy/vitamin D excess/granulomas.
  • New numbness around mouth + carpopedal spasm after surgery = hypoparathyroidism → IV calcium gluconate.
  • CKD + high phosphate + low Ca + high PTH = secondary HPT → phosphate binders, vitamin D analogues; tertiary = autonomously high PTH + HYPERcalcaemia → surgery.
  • Back pain + high Ca + low phosphate + anaemia, normal WBC → check protein electrophoresis (myeloma) — NOT primary HPT alone.

#268MCQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-6d2953e7
A 30-year-old woman presents with back pain, hypercalcemia, low phosphate and anemia; WBC and the rest of labs are normal. What is the best next investigation?
  • A. Serum PTH
  • B. Serum protein electrophoresis
  • C. Renal biopsy
  • D. Bone marrow biopsy
  • E. Repeat serum calcium
Best answer
B. Serum protein electrophoresis
Back pain + hypercalcaemia + low phosphate + anaemia (normal WBC) in a 30-year-old = multiple myeloma until proven otherwise — get serum protein electrophoresis (M-protein) + free light chains + urine Bence-Jones + bone marrow biopsy + skeletal survey/MRI. PTH would be suppressed (hypercalcaemia of malignancy), so checking PTH is less discriminating; SPEP is the specific test.
#341MCQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-f7f3f61b
A question about hypercalcemia — what is the most likely cause?
  • A. Primary hyperparathyroidism
  • B. Malignancy
  • C. Sarcoidosis
  • D. Vitamin D intoxication
  • E. Thiazide diuretics
Best answer
A. Primary hyperparathyroidism
Commonest cause of hypercalcaemia in ambulant patients = primary hyperparathyroidism (adenoma — check PTH: HIGH + low phosphate). Malignancy = commonest INPATIENT cause (PTH suppressed). Sarcoidosis/vitamin D excess = ↑calcitriol (both raise Ca with suppressed/low PTH).
2017 · Internal Medicine · 2 questions · MCQ

Chronic Kidney Disease — Stages, Complications & Dialysis

Definition: GFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² for ≥3 months, or kidney damage (albuminuria, urine abnormalities, structural) ≥3 months. Stages (KDIGO, by GFR): G1 ≥90, G2 60–89, G3a 45–59, G3b 30–44, G4 15–29, G5 <15 (kidney failure). Albuminauria categories A1–A3. eGFR <45 = CKD G3b → significant CV risk.

Complications — the exam loves this:

  1. Anaemia of CKD — ↓erythropoietin (starts G3b). Normocytic; check iron first (iron deficiency common) → iron + ESAs (epoetin) when Hb <100 g/L; target 100–120 g/L.
  2. Mineral–bone disorder (renal osteodystrophy) — ↓1α-hydroxylase → low active vitamin D; phosphate retention (primary problem) → high phosphate, low calcium, secondary PTH↑; FGF23↑; high-PTH bone disease (osteitis fibrosa) or adynamic bone disease (low turnover, over-suppressed PTH). Management: phosphate binders (calcium acetate, sevelamer) + vitamin D analogues (calcitriol/alfacalcidol) ± cinacalcet; restrict dietary phosphate.
  3. Hyperkalaemia — ↓excretion; worse with ACEi/ARB/spiro/NSAIDs.
  4. Metabolic acidosis (anion gap normal-ish/high in late).
  5. Fluid overload / hypertension / uraemia — encephalopathy, pericarditis (rub!), frost, pruritus, platelet dysfunction (bleeding).
  6. CV disease — commonest cause of death in CKD (accelerated atherosclerosis); lipid-lowering, BP control.

Renal replacement therapy (RRT) — AEIOU: refractory Acidosis, Electrolytes (K >6.5/symptomatic), Ingestions (dialysable toxins — lithium, salicylates, methanol), Overload (pulmonary oedema failing diuretics), Uraemic symptoms (pericarditis, encephalopathy, seizures). Choice: haemodialysis vs peritoneal dialysis vs transplant (best outcomes). A pericardial rub or confusion in CKD = dialysis now, whatever the urea number.

ACEi/ARB in CKD: renoprotective in proteinuric CKD/diabetes — start with low dose, check Cr/K at 1–2 weeks; accept up to 30% Cr rise; avoid in bilateral renal artery stenosis & pregnancy.

Exam pearls
  • High phosphate + low Ca + high PTH in CKD = secondary hyperparathyroidism → treat phosphate first (binders + low-PO4 diet) + active vitamin D.
  • “When to start dialysis?” — never on a number alone; the answer is refractory symptoms/signs (overload despite diuretics, pericarditis, encephalopathy, K⁺).
  • eGFR 45 with no symptoms still has G3a disease → anaemia can already appear (ESA after iron).

#294MCQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-5133e4ef
A patient has a GFR of 45. Which of the following is a feature of CKD?
  • A. Anemia
  • B. Hyperkalemia
  • C. Hyperparathyroidism
  • D. Hypophosphatemia
  • E. Hypomagnesemia
Best answer
A. Anemia

#325MCQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-9d8ba67c
A 65-year-old man known to have diabetes is evaluated and found to have an eGFR of 47 ml/min/1.73 m^2. The possible complication that he has at this stage of CKD is:
  • A. Renal anemia
  • B. Hyperkalemia
  • C. Hypocalcemia
  • D. Uremic pericarditis
  • E. Uremic encephalopathy
Best answer
A. Renal anemia
eGFR 47 (CKD G3a) — earliest/most likely complication = anaemia of CKD (↓EPO production). Hyperkalaemia/osteodystrophy usually appear G4–5; uraemic pericarditis/encephalopathy only in G5 (dialysis-level).
2017 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Clostridioides (Clostridium) difficile Infection

Context: antibiotic-associated colitis — clindamycin, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, broad-spectrum penicillins; also PPIs, age >65, hospitalisation, immunosuppression, IBD. Transmission: faecal–oral via spores (alcohol gel does NOT kill — use soap & water + gloves; contact precautions).

Presentation: diarrhoea (watery, may be bloody) 5–10 d into antibiotics → can progress to pseudomembranous colitis: abdominal pain/distension, fever, leucocytosis, and in severe cases toxic megacolon (X-ray: distended large bowel) with risk of perforation and shock.

Diagnosis: stool GDH antigen + toxin A/B (± NAAT for toxin genes) — toxins define active disease; GDH alone = colonisation. Severe: WBC >15 ×10⁹/L, rising creatinine, fever, lactate, toxic megacolon on imaging.

Management: STOP the culprit antibiotic; mild–moderate → oral vancomycin 125 mg QDS ×10 d (or fidaxomicin); recurrent → repeat course ± fidaxomicin or faecal microbiota transplant (after ≥2 recurrences). Severe/fulminant (ileus, toxic megacolon, shock): IV metronidazole + high-dose oral/NG vancomycin ± colectomy; do NOT give antimotility agents (loperamide — precipitates toxic megacolon).

Exam pearls
  • Antibiotics + diarrhoea + distended colon on X-ray = C. difficile → stop antibiotic, oral vancomycin, soap-and-water hand hygiene + contact isolation.
  • Loperamide is contraindicated.
  • Toxin (not just GDH) = disease.

COPD — Diagnosis, PFT & Exacerbations

Definition: chronic respiratory symptoms + persistent airflow obstruction (post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC <0.7) usually from noxious exposure — smoking (commonest), biomass, occupational dusts, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Chronic bronchitis = productive cough ≥3 months in 2 consecutive years; emphysema = alveolar wall destruction.

Diagnosis & investigations: spirometry is mandatory — shows obstruction not fully reversible. CXR (hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms) often normal early; high-resolution CT if unclear; alpha-1 antitrypsin if young/basal emphysema/family history/non-smoker; sputum culture in exacerbations; ABG in severe disease (chronic CO₂ retention → target SpO₂ 88–92%). Reduced cricosternal distance (<3 cm) = hyperinflation.

PFT patterns (exam table): obstruction = ↓FEV₁, normal/↓FVC, ↓FEV₁/FVC, quiet DLCO only if emphysema; restriction = ↓FEV₁, ↓FVC, preserved/high FEV₁/FVC, ↓TLC, usually ↓DLCO.

Chronic management: stop smoking (only intervention that alters decline); vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID); pulmonary rehabilitation; SABA/SAMA as needed → LABA or LAMA → ICS/LABA or triple therapy if frequent exacerbations; LTOT (long-term oxygen) if PaO₂ ≤7.3 kPa (or ≤8 kPa with cor pulmonale/polycythaemia).

Exacerbation (Anthonisen criteria): increased dyspnoea + increased sputum volume + increased sputum purulence. Treatment: controlled oxygen (target 88–92%), nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium, oral prednisolone 30 mg × 5 days, antibiotics (amoxicillin/doxycycline) if purulent sputum, NIV if respiratory acidosis persists despite therapy. Identify triggers (infection most common; PE and pneumothorax are mimics — CXR).

Exam pearls
  • Smoker + chronic cough + reduced cricosternal distance + obstruction on spirometry = COPD; asthma shows REVERSIBILITY.
  • COPD O₂ target = 88–92% (hypoxic drive considerations) — controlled, not non-rebreather-titrate-to-100%.
  • Spirometry confirms — peak flow/X-ray do not diagnose COPD.

2017 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Diabetes Insipidus & Polyuria Work-up

Definition: passing >3 L (or >40–50 mL/kg) of dilute urine per day (or nocturnal polyuria). First split by urine osmolality: if concentrated (>750 mOsm/kg) → osmotic diuresis (DM, mannitol); if dilute → DI vs primary polydipsia.

Central DINephrogenic DIPrimary polydipsia
Cause↓ADH secretion — pituitary/hypothalamic surgery or tumour, trauma, infection (TB/meningitis), infiltration, Sheehan’s, idiopathicRenal resistance to ADH — lithium, demeclocycline, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, CKD, congenital (AVPR2/AQP2)Psychogenic (schizophrenia, anxiety), dipsogenic
Serum Na↑ (unless drinking keeps up)↑↓ or low-normal
Water deprivation testUrine stays dilute, plasma osm rises (>300)Urine stays dilute, plasma osm risesUrine concentrates normally (>750)
Desmopressin (DDAVP) responseConcentrates urine (+>50% osm)No responseConcentrates (normal)

Key exam scenario: post–pituitary/sellar surgery + hypernatraemia + normal other electrolytes + high-normal glucose → central DI (damaged posterior pituitary/stalk). Treat: desmopressin (DDAVP — intranasal/oral/IV), free water access; monitor Na.

Lithium-induced NDI: stop/reduce lithium; amiloride or thiazide + salt restriction (induces mild volume depletion → ↑proximal Na/water reabsorption); NSAID (indomethacin) adjunct if needed.

Always rule out: hyperglycaemia (DM), hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, diuretics before the water-deprivation test (only after stopping confounders, under supervision — stop when >3% body weight lost or plasma osm >305/Na >150).

Exam pearls
  • Polyuria + hypernatraemia after pituitary surgery = central DI → DDAVP.
  • Lithium + polyuria + normal glucose = nephrogenic DI → stop lithium ± amiloride/thiazide.
  • Hypernatraemia post-op also = lost insensible losses without replacement — check.

A 60-year-old man presents with polyuria. Past medical history includes hypertension and bipolar disorder; current medications include lisinopril, amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide and lithium. He smokes 20 cigarettes/day and drinks heavily. Symptoms have been present for around two months and getting worse. What is the likely diagnosis?
  • A. Central diabetes insipidus
  • B. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
  • C. Psychogenic polydipsia
  • D. Diabetes mellitus
  • E. SIADH
Best answer
B. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Polyuria + on lithium (bipolar) + salt-wasting diuretic also present — lithium causes ADH resistance (downregulates aquaporin-2) → nephrogenic DI. Central DI follows pituitary surgery/trauma; psychogenic polydipsia gives LOW sodium; DM gives high glucose. Stop lithium; amiloride/thiazide + salt restriction; check Ca/K.
2017 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Electrolyte Disorders — Sodium & Potassium

Hyponatraemia — classify by volume status:

HypovolaemicEuvolaemicHypervolaemic
Urine NaLow <20 (extrarenal loss: GI, skin, third space) / High >20 (renal loss: diuretics, Addison’s, salt-wasting)>40 (SIADH); check TSH/cortisol (hypothyroid/adrenal = euvolaemic)Low <20 (HF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, CKD — effective arterial underfilling)
Treatment0.9% saline (restore volume) + treat causeFluid restrict (1 L/day) ± salt tablets/furosemide/vaptans (hypertonic 3% if seizures/severe neuro signs)Fluid + sodium restriction, loop diuretics, treat HF/cirrhosis; dialysis if renal failure

SIADH = hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia + inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osm >100, urine Na >40) + euvolaemia + normal renal/thyroid/adrenal + no diuretics. Causes: malignancy (small cell lung, pancreatic), CNS (stroke, tumour, meningitis), pulmonary (pneumonia, TB, PPV), drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, PPIs, chemotherapy, opioids, MDMA). Treat: fluid restriction ± hypertonic saline if symptomatic (Na <120 with seizures/coma — 3% saline, raise ≤8 mmol/L per 24 h to avoid central pontine myelinolysis).

Co-existing lung cancer + hyponatraemia = SIADH (ectopic ADH from small-cell carcinoma).

Hyperkalaemia: treat by severity/ECG. ECG progression: peaked (“tented”) T waves → PR prolongation → P flattening → QRS widening → sine wave → VF. K⁺ >6.5 or any ECG change = emergency: IV calcium gluconate (membrane stabilisation), insulin+dextrose, salbutamol nebulisers, sodium bicarbonate (if acidotic), K binders, dialysis if refractory. Stop K/ACEi/MRA/NSAIDs; check glucose (DKA?), renal function.

Hypokalaemia: causes — diuretics (loop/thiazide), vomiting/diarrhoea, hyperaldosteronism, hypokalaemic periodic paralysis (carbohydrate load in susceptible young men — e.g. “after a big carbohydrate meal”, resolves with K), Bartter/Gitelman, insulin, beta-agonists, RTA. Replace K orally if mild; IV if severe/symptomatic; check Mg (replace both). ECG: flattened T, U waves, ST depression, VT/VF.

Exam pearls
  • SIADH = low serum osm + urine Na>40 + euvolaemic → restrict fluid; symptomatic → 3% saline ≤8/24h.
  • Oedema + crackles + confusion + hyponatraemia = hypervolaemic dilutional (HF) — do NOT give saline.
  • Peaked T waves → calcium gluconate FIRST; insulin/dextrose second; dialysis if refractory.
  • Carbohydrate-feast weakness + low K in a young Asian male = hypokalaemic periodic paralysis.
Traps
  • Hypertonic saline for chronic asymptomatic hyponatraemia causes osmotic demyelination — correct slowly.
  • Pseudohyponatraemia (hypertriglyceridaemia/paraproteinaemia) — check osmolality/lab method if patient looks well.
  • Hypomagnesaemia → refractory hypokalaemia/hypocalcaemia — always co-check.

A 17-year-old male's mother noticed that after eating a large amount of carbohydrates he shows lethargy and generalized weakness. Blood tests showed hypokalemia. What is the likely diagnosis?
  • A. Bartter syndrome
  • B. Fanconi syndrome
  • C. Hypokalemic periodic paralysis
  • D. Gitelman syndrome
  • E. Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis
Best answer
C. Hypokalemic periodic paralysis
Young male + flaccid weakness/paralysis after a LARGE CARBOHYDRATE meal + hypokalaemia = hypokalaemic periodic paralysis (channelopathy — often triggered by insulin-driven K⁺ shift into cells; Asian/Hispanic males; thyrotoxic variant if hyperthyroid — check TFT). Attacks last hours; K⁺ normal between attacks; treat acutely with KCl; prevent with low-carb diet ± acetazolamide; avoid carbohydrate binges.
2017 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Heart Failure — HFrEF vs HFpEF, Acute & Chronic

Pathophysiology: inadequate cardiac output for metabolic needs (or only at high filling pressures). Classify by EF: HFrEF (EF ≤40%) — systolic failure (IHD/MI, dilated cardiomyopathy, hypertension long-standing, valvular); HFmrEF (41–49); HFpEF (≥50) — diastolic failure (hypertension, LVH, hypertrophic/restrictive CMP, constrictive pericarditis, ischaemia). Right-sided failure usually secondary to left-sided or lung disease (cor pulmonale).

Symptoms: dyspnoea (exertional), orthopnoea, PND, fatigue, ankle swelling, nocturia. Examination: raised JVP, S3 gallop (specific for volume overload/systolic failure), displaced apex, bibasal crackles, peripheral oedema, hepatojugular reflux, hepatomegaly.

Chronic HFrEF — the “four pillars” (all reduce mortality): (1) ACEi/ARB/ARNI (sacubitril–valsartan) — titrate to target; (2) beta-blocker (bisoprolol/carvedilol/metoprolol succinate) — start low, once stable; (3) MRA (spironolactone/eplerenone) — K & renal monitoring; (4) SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin/empagliflozin) — now regardless of diabetes. Plus: loop diuretic for congestion, ICD if EF ≤35% on optimal therapy, CRT if wide QRS (LBBB), iron for deficiency, treat sleep apnoea, vaccinate, cardiac rehab.

HFpEF: no drug reduces mortality — treat congestion with loop diuretics, aggressive BP/rate control, SGLT2i reduces hospitalisation; manage comorbidities (AF, IHD, obesity, diabetes).

Acute decompensated HF: ABCDE, sit up, high-flow O₂, IV furosemide (e.g. 40–80 mg or home dose ×2), stop beta-blocker if hypotensive/shocked (otherwise continue), CPAP if respiratory distress + acidosis; nitrates if hypertensive; treat precipitant (MI! infection, AF, NSAIDs, non-adherence); echocardiography for EF and valves; discharge plan + early follow-up.

ECG in severe LV dysfunction: reduced EF ± LBBB (CRT candidate if QRS ≥150 + LBBB + symptomatic on pillars).

Exam pearls
  • Four pillars for HFrEF: ACEi/ARB/ARNI + BB + MRA + SGLT2i. HFpEF = diuretics for symptoms.
  • S3 = failing ventricle — in volume overload.
  • Gradual weight gain + ankle swelling + breathlessness = fluid retention → furosemide.
  • New LBBB + EF 25% → CRT consideration after 3 months optimal pillars.

Haemolytic Anaemia — Intravascular vs Extravascular

Haemolysis = premature RBC destruction (lifespan <120 d). Both types: ↑reticulocytes, ↑LDH, ↑unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin, ↓haptoglobin.

IntravascularExtravascular
SiteInside vesselsSpleen/liver macrophages
PlasmaHaemoglobinaemia → haemoglobinuria (dark/red urine), methaemalbuminaemiaBilirubin↑ (gallstones), haptoglobin↓ (mild)
LDH/haptoglobin↑↑ / ↓↓↑ / ↓
CausesG6PD deficiency (oxidant stress — fava beans, sulfa drugs, antimalarials, infection), mechanical (prosthetic valve, microangiopathic — DIC/TTP/HUS/HELLP/malignant HTN, “march” haemoglobinuria), transfusion reactions (ABO incompatibility), PNH, cold agglutinin (occasionally)Hereditary spherocytosis, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (warm — IgG; cold — IgM/EBV/Mycoplasma), sickle cell disease, thalassaemia, hypersplenism, clostridial sepsis

G6PD deficiency (X-linked): episodic haemolysis triggered by oxidant stress — fava beans, drugs (primaquine, sulfa, nitrofurantoin), infections; severe intravascular episodes with haemoglobinuria (classically asked: “what type of haemolysis?” → intravascular — many exams key it so; there is also an extravascular component via splenic removal of Heinz-body cells); neonatal jaundice risk; Heinz bodies and bite cells on film during crisis; enzyme level may be falsely normal during acute haemolysis (young RBCs) — retest later. Management: avoid triggers; transfusion if severe.

Hereditary spherocytosis: autosomal dominant; spherocytes, ↑MCHC, osmotic fragility/EMA binding, splenomegaly, gallstones (pigment) — splenectomy if symptomatic/severe (lifelong infection risk — vaccinate).

Exam pearls
  • Dark urine + jaundice + recent fava/sulfa/infection in a Mediterranean/African male = G6PD → intravascular haemolysis.
  • Fragmented cells (schistocytes) = mechanical/MAHA — check platelets/coagulation/BP.
  • Spherocytes + Coombs+ = autoimmune (warm IgG); Coombs− = hereditary spherocytosis.
  • Before splenectomy: vaccines (pneumo, HiB, meningococcal).

2017 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Infective Endocarditis

Definition: microbial infection of the endocardial surface (valves, congenital lesions, prosthetic material, device leads) with vegetations (platelet-fibrin-microbe). Modified Duke criteria: 2 major (typical organism in ≥2 sets of blood cultures; echo positive — vegetation/abscess/new regurgitation) OR 1 major + 3 minor OR 5 minor (fever, predisposition, vascular phenomena — emboli/Janeway/conjunctival haemorrhage, immunological — Osler nodes/Roth spots/RF, positive culture not typical, positive echo not major).

Organisms by setting:

SettingLikely organism
Native valve, dental diseaseViridans streptococci
Native valve, skin/soft-tissue, IVDUStaphylococcus aureus (commonest overall; tricuspid in IVDU)
Prosthetic valve (early <60 d)Coagulase-negative staphylococci
Prosthetic valve (late) / healthcareCoagulase-negative staphylococci, S. aureus, enterococci
GU/GI instrumentation, catheter (this exam!)Enterococcus faecalis
Dental + colon cancerStreptococcus gallolyticus (bovis) — check colonoscopy
Q fever settingCoxiella burnetii
HACEK group (culture-negative)Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella

Clinical: fever + malaise + new/changing murmur + emboli (stroke, limb ischaemia, splenic/renal infarcts, mycotic aneurysm) + peripheral stigmata: Osler’s nodes (tender, finger pulps — immune), Janeway lesions (painless palmar macules — septic emboli), splinter haemorrhages, Roth spots (retinal haemorrhages with pale centres), clubbing, splenomegaly.

Diagnosis steps: ≥3 blood culture sets from separate sites BEFORE antibiotics → echocardiography (TTE first; TOE if prosthetic/high suspicion/TTE negative — vegetation, abscess, perforation, new dehiscence).

Treatment: prolonged IV antibiotics (4–6 weeks; native valve Viridans → benzylpenicillin ± gentamicin; S. aureus → nafcillin/flucloxacillin ± gentamicin; MRSA → vancomycin; enterococcal → ampicillin + gentamicin/ceftriaxone); surgery (urgent) for heart failure, valve abscess/fistula, uncontrolled infection, large >10 mm vegetations with emboli, prosthetic dehiscence. Prophylaxis (high-risk: prosthetic valves, previous IE, cyanotic congenital): amoxicillin before dental procedures.

Exam pearls
  • Fever + new murmur + embolic/immune stigmata → blood cultures ×3 then echo.
  • Catheter/UTI → enterococci; IVDU → S. aureus tricuspid; dental → viridans; prosthetic early → coag-neg staph; colon cancer → S. bovis.
  • Osler = ow (painful); Janeway = just a mark (painless).

2017 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Crohn’s vs Ulcerative Colitis

Crohn’s disease — transmural, discontinuous (“skip”) inflammation anywhere from mouth to anus (terminal ileum commonest). Features: crampy abdominal pain (often RLQ), weight loss, chronic diarrhoea (may be non-bloody), fever, oral ulcers, perianal disease (fistulae, fissures, abscesses), extra-intestinal (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, uveitis, iritis, episcleritis, arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, gallstones (↓bile salt absorption), renal stones (oxalate), B₁₂ deficiency). Histology: transmural lymphoid aggregates, non-caseating granulomas. Complications: strictures, fistulae, abscess, malabsorption/anaemia.

Ulcerative colitis — mucosal, continuous inflammation starting at the rectum extending proximally (always involves rectum). Features: bloody diarrhoea with mucus, urgency, tenesmus, lower abdominal pain, fever in flares; extra-intestinal (primary sclerosing cholangitis!, uveitis, arthritis, erythema nodosum); colon cancer risk (surveillance colonoscopy from ~8–10 y). Histology: continuous cryptitis, crypt abscesses, goblet cell depletion, no granulomas.

Crohn’sUlcerative colitis
DistributionMouth→anus, skip lesions, terminal ileumRectum→ proximally, continuous, colon only
DepthTransmuralMucosa/submucosa
Blood in stoolVariableAlways (hallmark)
PerianalCommon (fistulae)Rare
GranulomasNon-caseating (30–50%)Absent
SurgeryNot curative (recurs)Curative (proctocolectomy)
Cancer riskModestSignificant (esp. PSC overlap)

Diagnosis: colonoscopy + biopsy (gold standard), faecal calprotectin (raised in IBD; normal in IBS — great separator), CRP/ESR, FBC (anaemia), albumin, iron/B₁₂, stool cultures (exclude infection), barium/MRI enterography for Crohn’s, ASCA+ (Crohn) vs p-ANCA+ (UC). IBD vs IBS: IBD = blood, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, raised CRP/calprotectin; IBS = normal tests, no blood, never nocturnal.

Management flares: UC mild–moderate → 5-ASA (mesalazine) oral/topical; moderate–severe → oral prednisolone → steroid-refractory/dependent → azathioprine/mercaptopurine, anti-TNF (infliximab/adalimumab), vedolizumab; acute severe colitis → IV hydrocortisone + DVT prophylaxis → rescue ciclosporin or colectomy if failing. Crohn’s: induction steroids; maintenance azathioprine/antimetabolite ± anti-TNF; surgery for strictures/fistulae/refractory disease (resection, not curative); nutritional therapy (exclusive enteral) in children; stop smoking (worsens Crohn’s).

Exam pearls
  • Oral ulcers + RLQ pain + weight loss + aphthous ulcers = Crohn’s. Bloody diarrhoea from rectum upward = UC.
  • Calprotectin separates IBD from IBS — cheap and non-invasive.
  • UC + PSC = highest colon cancer risk — colonoscopy surveillance.

2017 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · MCQ

Meningitis — CSF, Causative Organisms & Meningococcaemia

CSF interpretation — the exam table:

NeutrophilsGlucoseProteinPressureClassic
Bacterial↑↑ (pleocytosis, often >1000)LOW (<½ plasma)↑↑Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae b (unimmunised), neonates Group B strep / E. coli / Listeria (add amoxicillin for listeria cover!)
Viral (aseptic)Lymphocytes (early can be neutrophils)NormalNormal–mild↑Normal–mild↑Enterovirus, HSV-2, VZV, mumps — self-limiting; treat supportive
TuberculousLymphocytesVERY LOW (<2.2 mmol/L)VERY HIGH (1–5 g/L)↑↑Insidious; cranial nerve palsies (VI), basal exudates, hydrocephalus (dilated ventricles); “cobweb” clot; ADA >10; AFB rare — treat with RHZE + dexamethasone
Fungal (Cryptococcus, TB-like)LymphocytesLowHigh↑↑Immunocompromised (HIV) — India ink/CR antigens; amphotericin + flucytosine
GBS (neonatal)AnyAnyAny↑E. coli, GBS — ampicillin + gentamicin

Clinical features: fever, headache, neck stiffness (meningism), photophobia, vomiting, altered consciousness, seizures, non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash (meningococcaemia), Kernig’s (pain on knee extension with hip flexed), Brudzinski’s (neck flexion → hip flexion), bulging fontanelle (infants). Meningococcaemia → septic shock, DIC, Waterhouse–Friderichsen (bilateral adrenal haemorrhage).

Management: do NOT delay antibiotics for imaging/LP if unwell — immediate IV ceftriaxone/cefotaxime (add amoxicillin if <3 months or listeria risk), dexamethasone with first dose (↓hearing loss in pneumococcal; continue if confirmed), ABCDE + fluids/vasopressors (shock), isolate (droplet), notify public health, contact prophylaxis (ciprofloxacin/rifampicin) for household contacts, hearing test after recovery, treat complications (seizures, hydrocephalus — neurosurgery/VP shunt, SIADH).

Neurological exam findings asked (this SAQ): neck stiffness, Kernig’s/Brudzinski’s signs positive, photophobia, altered GCS, focal deficits, bulging fontanelle; complications — sensorineural deafness, seizures, hydrocephalus, subdural effusion, learning difficulty, shock/amputation (meningococcaemia).

Exam pearls
  • LP first only if NO contraindication & child stable; otherwise antibiotics first — never delay.
  • Low glucose + high protein + lymphocytes = TB; high PMN + low glucose = bacteria.
  • Non-blanching purpuric rash + fever = ceftriaxone STAT + public health notification.

#278MCQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-04f87b32
LP results show high WBC (high PMN), low glucose and high protein. What type of meningitis is this?
  • A. Bacterial meningitis
  • B. Fungal meningitis
  • C. TB meningitis
  • D. Viral meningitis
  • E. Aseptic meningitis
Best answer
A. Bacterial meningitis
High neutrophil (PMN) CSF + low glucose + high protein = bacterial meningitis (Gram-negative intracellular organisms likely). Viral = lymphocytes + normal glucose/protein; TB = lymphocytes + very low glucose + very high protein (1–5 g/L); fungal = similar but HIV context.
2017 · Internal Medicine · 2 questions · MCQ/SAQ

Neuromuscular Disorders — Myasthenia, GBS, Botulism

Myasthenia gravis — postsynaptic anti-AChR (or anti-MuSK) antibodies → fatigable weakness. Features: fatigable weakness WORSE with use/at the END of the day, improves with rest; starts with ocular (ptosis, diplopia — painless); bulbar (dysarthria, dysphagia, weak smile/head drop); generalised (neck/proximal/resp); spares reflexes and sensation; no autonomic signs. Associated: thymic hyperplasia/thymoma (15%) (check CT chest). Investigations: anti-AChR antibodies, anti-MuSK (if AChR-negative), repetitive nerve stimulation (decrement), ice-pack test (improves ptosis), CT chest (thymoma). Treatment: pyridostigmine (symptomatic), immunosuppression (prednisolone/azathioprine/mycophenolate), IVIG or plasma exchange for crises, thymectomy if thymoma or generalised AChR+ <65 y; avoid triggers (aminoglycosides!). Crisis = respiratory failure → NIV/intubation.

Guillain–Barré syndrome — post-infectious (Campylobacter jejuni (~40%), CMV, EBV, Zika, Mycoplasma, vaccination rare) autoimmune demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. Features: symmetric ASCENDING weakness + areflexia/hyporeflexia over days, sensory symptoms, minimal sensory loss, back/limb pain, autonomic instability; check FVC/NIF (respiratory failure in 20–30%); CSF: albuminocytologic dissociation (high protein, normal cell count) after week 1; EMG: demyelination (prolonged F waves, conduction block). Treatment: IVIG or plasma exchange (equal efficacy) — start ASAP; NO steroids; monitor respiratory function; VTE prophylaxis; most recover ~80% (mortality 3–5%).

Botulism — Clostridium botulinum preformed toxin (canned/preserved/smoked/honey in infants <12 mo) → blocks presynaptic ACh release. Features: descendING flaccid paralysis (cranial nerves FIRST — diplopia, ptosis, dysarthria, dysphagia, fixed dilated pupils, dry mouth) → arms → respiratory; deep tendon reflexes preserved; afebrile, clear mentation; autonomic signs (constipation). Infant botulism = “floppy baby” + constipation + poor suck. Diagnosis: clinical + toxin in serum/stool + EMG (incremental response on repetitive stimulation). Treatment: botulinum antitoxin ASAP (horse-derived; human BIG-IV for infants), supportive care, NO antibiotics in infant botulism (worsen toxin release), wound botulism → debridement + penicillin/metronidazole; recovery weeks–months (nerve terminal regrowth).

Peripheral nerve injury patterns: common peroneal (foot drop, dorsum sensory loss — fibular head), ulnar (claw hand, medial 1½ fingers — elbow groove), median (thenar wasting, “ape hand”, carpal tunnel — night numbness, Tinel/Phalen), radial (wrist drop), tibial (plantarflexion).

Exam pearls
  • Fatigable + evening + eyes first = MG (pyridostigmine; CT chest). Post-Campylobacter ascending areflexia = GBS (IVIG; watch FVC). Canned food + descendING = botulism (antitoxin).
  • MG fatigues; GBS ascends; botulism descends; both MG/GBS spare the pupils/bladder usually.

#284MCQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-4749240c
A patient post-gastroenteritis has ascending paralysis symptoms (GBS). What is the expected CSF finding?
  • A. Normal WBC, normal glucose, high protein (albuminocytologic dissociation)
  • B. High WBC, high protein, low glucose
  • C. High WBC, low glucose, low protein
  • D. Completely normal CSF
  • E. High WBC with high protein and normal glucose
Best answer
A. Normal WBC, normal glucose, high protein (albuminocytologic dissociation)
GBS — CSF albuminocytologic dissociation: high protein with a normal cell count (usually <10 cells/µL) and normal glucose; raised after week 1. Diagnostic hallmark with clinical ascending weakness + areflexia; also check EMG/FVC.
#374SAQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-SAQ-Medicine-98ddac4c
A woman has weakness in the lower limbs (3/5) and upper limbs (4/5) with difficulty walking, total sensory loss, muscle wasting below the knee level, areflexia and equivocal plantars.
  1. What type of lesion is this? (1 pt)
  2. Mention two other motor signs you may elicit. (2 pt)
  3. Give two possible localizations for this. (2 pt)
Best answer
1) Lower motor neurone lesion — length-dependent polyneuropathy (sensorimotor) (weakness distal > proximal, wasting, areflexia, sensory loss, no UMN/sphincter signs) — likely axonal peripheral polyneuropathy (e.g., GBS-spectrum, or metabolic/toxic). 2) Two other motor signs you may elicit: (a) fasciculations; (b) muscle wasting/hypotonia and absent/reduced reflexes (already present) — also foot drop/steppage gait. 3) Two localisations: (a) peripheral nerves (polyneuropathy — GBS/AIDP); (b) lumbosacral nerve roots/plexus or conus medullaris cauda equina region; (NOT spinal cord proper — which would give UMN signs + sphincter loss; NOT anterior horn — that spares sensation).
GBS = post-infectious ascending demyelinating polyneuropathy — CHECK FVC (respiratory failure); LP albuminocytologic dissociation; IVIG/plasma exchange; NO steroids. If the sensory level or sphincter loss is present → MRI urgently (myelopathy).
2017 · Internal Medicine · 2 questions · EMQ/MCQ

Peptic Ulcer Disease & Dyspepsia

Definition: mucosal defect penetrating the muscularis mucosae in stomach or duodenum (eroded by acid/pepsin) — vs gastritis/duodenitis (superficial).

Causes: Helicobacter pylori (~60–90% duodenal, ~50–70% gastric) and NSAIDs/aspirin (top two always); others — steroid + NSAIDs, smoking, alcohol, severe illness (stress ulcers), Zollinger–Ellison (gastrinoma — recurrent/multiple/distal ulcers + diarrhoea), malignancy (must exclude in gastric ulcer), Crohn’s (duodenal).

Symptoms: epigastric pain — duodenal ulcer: classically 2–3 h AFTER food/at night, relieved by food/antacids, weight gain (food buffers acid); gastric ulcer: pain SOON after eating (or with food), fear of food, weight loss; bloating, nausea, early satiety, melaena/haematemesis if bleeding; complications: bleeding (commonest), perforation (sudden severe pain + peritonitis — free air under diaphragm on erect CXR — emergency surgery), GOO (gastric outlet obstruction — projectile vomiting, succession splash, electrolyte loss), malignancy (gastric).

This exam: epigastric pain relieved by food = peptic (duodenal) ulcer disease.

Diagnosis: H. pylori testing — ¹³C urea breath test or stool antigen (stop PPIs/antibiotics first — false negative); endoscopy (OGD) if alarm features (age >55, weight loss, dysphagia, GI bleeding, anaemia, persistent vomiting, family history gastric cancer) or refractory to PPI — gastric ulcer → biopsy to exclude malignancy; FBC (anaemia).

Management: eradicate H. pylori — triple therapy: PPI (omeprazole 20 mg BD) + clarithromycin 500 mg BD + amoxicillin 1 g BD ×7–14 days (metronidazole if penicillin-allergic); confirm eradication if persistent symptoms (breath/stool test ≥4 weeks after). Stop NSAIDs (or switch to COX-2 + PPI); PPI 4–8 weeks; lifestyle (stop smoking, reduce alcohol, avoid spicy/caffeine/late meals); if bleeding ulcer → IV PPI + endoscopic therapy (adrenaline injection + clips); surgery rarely (refractory/complicated).

Exam pearls
  • Pain before meals relieved by food = duodenal; pain with meals + weight loss = gastric (biopsy!).
  • Test-and-treat H. pylori first in uncomplicated dyspepsia (young, no alarms).
  • NSAIDs + age = peptic ulcer — stop the NSAID.
  • Don’t test H. pylori on PPIs — false negative.

2017 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · SAQ

Pericardial Disease — Acute Pericarditis & Pericardial Effusion/Tamponade

Acute pericarditis — inflammation of the pericardium; commonest cause: viral (Coxsackie B, Echovirus, adenovirus); also post-MI (early peri-infarction/Dressler’s 2–6 wks), post-cardiac surgery, TB, uremia, autoimmune (SLE, RA), malignancy, radiotherapy, drugs, uraemia.

Features: central chest pain — sharp, pleuritic, WORSE LYING FLAT, BETTER SITTING FORWARD; pericardial friction rub (scratchy, best left sternal edge, leaning forward, breath held); fever, dyspnoea; ECG: widespread CONCAVE (“saddle-shaped”) ST elevation across multiple leads + PR depression (vs STEMI: regional, convex, reciprocal changes); raised troponin sometimes (myopericarditis); CRP/ESR↑.

Treatment: NSAIDs (ibuprofen/indomethacin) + colchicine (3 months) — first-line; avoid anticoagulants (haemorrhagic effusion risk); restrict exercise; steroids if refractory/contraindication (avoid in infective cases) or autoimmune; treat cause.

Pericardial effusion — fluid in pericardial sac; causes mirror pericarditis (+ uraemia, malignancy — lung/breast, hypothyroidism). Large/atypical (>3 cm) or any effusion → echocardiography (diagnostic). “Water-bottle” globular cardiac silhouette on CXR (this exam’s image).

Cardiac tamponade — life-threatening compression of the heart: Beck’s triad — hypotension + raised JVP + muffled heart sounds; pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg inspiratory SBP drop); tachycardia, dyspnoea, anxiety, cool periphery, electrical alternans (alternating QRS amplitude) on ECG, low-voltage QRS; echo = collapse of right atrium/ventricle, respiratory variation in flows. Emergency: urgent pericardiocentesis (echo-guided) — do NOT delay for imaging if obstructive shock.

Constrictive pericarditis (chronic) — RHF signs + Kussmaul’s sign (JVP rises with inspiration) + pericardial knock; TB commonest worldwide; treat: surgical pericardiectomy.

Exam pearls
  • Pain better sitting forward + friction rub + diffuse concave STE = pericarditis → NSAID + colchicine.
  • Globular water-bottle heart on CXR + SOB + raised JVP = pericardial effusion → echo.
  • Tamponade = Beck’s triad + pulsus paradoxus → urgent pericardiocentesis NOW.

A case of shortness of breath and chest pain with flu-like symptoms and raised JVP. A chest X-ray was shown below.

  2. What is the investigation to confirm the diagnosis? (1 pt)
  3. What is the complication? (1 pt)
Best answer
1) Most likely diagnosis: pericardial effusion (due to pericarditis with effusion) — SOB + pleuritic chest pain improving sitting forward + flu-like prodrome + raised JVP + globular “water-bottle” cardiac silhouette on CXR (image provided). 2) Investigation to confirm: transthoracic echocardiography (diagnostic — effusion size, tamponade physiology: RA/RV diastolic collapse, respiratory flow variation); add ECG (low-voltage, electrical alternans). 3) Complication: cardiac tamponade (hypotension + rising JVP + muffled sounds/Beck’s triad, pulsus paradoxus, obstructive shock) → urgent pericardiocentesis.
Viral/idiopathic pericarditis is commonest; treat NSAIDs + colchicine; drain if tamponade, diagnostic doubt, or large effusion; TB/malignancy/uraemia must be excluded if atypical features.
2017 · Internal Medicine · 3 questions · MCQ

Pituitary Disorders

Pituitary adenomas — benign; functioning (prolactinoma, GH — acromegaly, ACTH — Cushing’s, TSH rare) vs non-functioning. Mass effects (any macroadenoma >10 mm): bitemporal hemianopia (optic chiasm compression — starts superiorly, respects vertical meridian), headache, hypopituitarism (hormone deficits — order: GH → gonadotrophins → TSH → ACTH last), cavernous sinus invasion (CN III/IV/VI palsies).

Prolactinoma — commonest functioning adenoma. Women: oligomenorrhoea/amenorrhoea + galactorrhoea ± infertility; men: hypogonadism, low libido, erectile dysfunction, gynaecomastia (earlier macro), bitemporal hemianopia. Prolactin very high (>5000 mIU/L usually macroadenoma; >10,000 = macroprolactinoma likely); check TSH (primary hypothyroidism → TRH → prolactin↑ — “pseudoprolactinoma”) and drugs (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, SSRIs, verapamil, opiates). Treatment: dopamine agonists — cabergoline/bromocriptine (first-line — shrinks tumour & normalises PRL); surgery (trans-sphenoidal) if intolerant/failed.

Acromegaly — GH excess (usually pituitary somatotroph adenoma): frontal bossing, prognathism, macroglossia, interdental spacing, coarse facies, large spade-like hands/feet, thick skin, sweating, carpal tunnel, sleep apnoea, diabetes, hypertension, colonic polyps, cardiomyopathy. Diagnosis: IGF-1 ↑; OGTT — GH fails to suppress (<1 mU/L); pituitary MRI. Treatment: trans-sphenoidal surgery (first-line); octreotide/lanreotide (somatostatin analogues), pegvisomant (GH-receptor antagonist), cabergoline; radiotherapy if refractory. Screen: colonoscopy, echo, glucose, sleep study.

Cushing’s disease — ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma: central obesity, moon facies, striae, proximal myopathy, diabetes, osteoporosis; diagnose: 24-h urinary free cortisol / low-dose dexamethasone suppression test; IPSS for localization; TS surgery.

Sheehan’s syndrome — postpartum pituitary necrosis after severe postpartum haemorrhage → panhypopituitarism: failure of lactation (first sign) + amenorrhoea + fatigue + loss of pubic/axillary hair + hypothyroidism/hypoadrenalism; treat with hormone replacement (thyroxine, hydrocortisone, oestrogen/progesterone, GH, fertility — gonadotrophins).

Pituitary apoplexy — sudden haemorrhage/infarction (this exam): sudden severe headache + visual loss (bitemporal) + acute ophthalmoplegia (CN III palsy) + meningism ± shock — emergency: IV hydrocortisone, urgent MRI, neurosurgery/ophthalmology; treat as adrenal crisis.

Visual fields: bitemporal hemianopia (chiasmal), homonymous hemianopia (retro-chiasmal — optic tract/radiations), tunnel vision (psychogenic).

Exam pearls
  • High prolactin + menstrual/galactorrhoea → cabergoline — but FIRST exclude pregnancy (β-HCG) and hypothyroidism/drugs.
  • Postpartum haemorrhage + lactation failure + amenorrhoea = Sheehan.
  • Big hands + jaw + field defect = acromegaly → IGF-1 + OGTT.
  • Sudden headache + chiasmal signs = apoplexy — hydrocortisone + urgent imaging/surgery.

Pleural Effusion — Light’s Criteria & Causes

Light’s criteria (exudate if ANY one): (1) pleural fluid/serum protein > 0.5; (2) pleural fluid/serum LDH > 0.6; (3) pleural LDH > 2/3 upper normal serum LDH. Otherwise transudate.

TransudateExudate
Mechanism↑ hydrostatic / ↓ oncotic pressure↑ capillary permeability / ↓ lymphatic drainage
CausesHeart failure (commonest), cirrhosis (hepatic hydrothorax — right), nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminaemia, peritoneal dialysis, constrictive pericarditis, SVC obstructionParapneumonic/empyema, malignancy (lung, breast, mesothelioma — this exam), TB, PE, pancreatitis (left), RA/SLE, trauma/haemothorax, chylothorax, post-CABG
Fluid appearanceClear, strawCloudy/turbid/bloody/chylous

Approach: CXR (blunting of costophrenic angle; >200–300 mL visible; meniscus sign; massive → mediastinal shift away) + ultrasound-guided diagnostic aspiration (thoracentesis) — pH, protein, LDH, glucose, cell count (neutrophils = parapneumonic; lymphocytes = TB/malignancy), cytology, Gram stain/culture, AFB/ADA (TB), triglycerides (chylothorax >1.2 mmol/L), amylase (pancreatitis).

Parapneumonic effusion — uncomplicated: antibiotics; drain if: pH <7.2, glucose <3.3, LDH >1000, loculations on USS/CT, positive Gram stain, or large (>half hemithorax)/sepsis (chest drain ± fibrinolytics ± surgery/VATS).

Malignant effusion: cytology (sensitivity ~60%); repeat aspiration; indwelling pleural catheter or talc pleurodesis for symptom control.

This exam (2017 smoker, massive left effusion, weight loss, night sweats): X-ray findings: massive left pleural effusion with opacification of lower hemithorax, blunting costophrenic angle/obscured left hemidiaphragm, mediastinal shift to the right. Investigations: diagnostic thoracentesis (cytology, ADA/AFB/Gram/culture, Light’s), CT chest (mass, pleural thickening), bronchoscopy/biopsy, US. Top 2 diagnoses: malignant pleural effusion (bronchogenic carcinoma) and TB effusion.

Exam pearls
  • Light’s: protein >0.5, LDH >0.6, LDH >2/3 ULN — any ONE → exudate.
  • Fever + effusion + low pH/glucose = empyema — drain.
  • Lymphocytic exudate + high ADA = TB — treat as TB effusion (anti-TB + steroids sometimes).

Lymphocytic exudate + high ADA → TB; cytology/CT shows primary tumour → cancer; both need cause-directed treatment; consider pleurodesis/IPC for malignant effusion; anti-TB + steroids for TB effusion.
2017 · Internal Medicine · 1 question · EMQ

Pneumothorax & Tension Pneumothorax

Types: primary spontaneous (tall thin young men, subpleural blebs — rupture), secondary spontaneous (diseased lung — COPD/emphysema, asthma, TB, fibrosis — this exam: 20-year ex-smoker with COPD), traumatic/iatrogenic (rib fracture, central line, ventilation, biopsy), tension (one-way valve → rising intrapleural pressure → shift).

Tension pneumothorax — clinical diagnosis, never wait for imaging: sudden severe dyspnoea + ipsilateral pleuritic chest pain + hyperresonance + absent breath sounds + tracheal deviation AWAY + raised JVP + hypotension (obstructive shock) + tachypnoea/tachycardia. Management: immediate needle decompression (2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line, with a 14–16 G cannula) → chest drain (4th–5th ICS, anterior/mid-axillary line, > safe triangle) → O₂ → admit.

This exam: COPD patient + SOB + tracheal deviation = tension pneumothorax until proven otherwise.

Simple pneumothorax (stable): Observation if small (<2 cm rim) asymptomatic; needle aspiration if primary and larger/symptomatic; chest drain if secondary/large/symptomatic; smoking cessation; avoid flying (1 week after resolution) / diving (absolute bar until bled/pleurodesed).

Differentiation: vs pleural effusion (dull, shifted AWAY, reduced fremitus), vs acute asthma/COPD exacerbation (no deviation, wheeze), vs PE (pleuritic but normal CXR, no hyperresonance).

Exam pearls
  • Tension = deviation away + hypotension = NEEDLE DECOMPRESSION first, then drain.
  • Primary = young tall thin man; secondary = older smoker/lung disease.
  • Never CXR a suspected tension pneumothorax before treating.

Pulmonary Embolism

Virchow’s triad: stasis (immobility, surgery, travel, pregnancy) + endothelial injury (trauma/surgery/central line) + hypercoagulability (cancer, OCP/HRT, pregnancy, Factor V Leiden, protein C/S deficiency, antiphospholipid, prior VTE).

Presentation: sudden dyspnoea + pleuritic chest pain + tachycardia; ± haemoptysis, syncope (massive), low-grade fever, unilateral leg swelling. Massive PE: hypotension (SBP <90), obstructive shock, raised JVP, loud P2. ECG: sinus tachycardia (commonest), S1Q3T3, right bundle branch block, right axis deviation, T inversions V1–3 (right strain).

Risk scores & testing pathway: Wells score — PE likely (>4 points) → CTPA directly; unlikely → D-dimer (sensitive, not specific): negative excludes; positive → CTPA. PERC for very low risk (“rule-out”). Never CT every breathless patient — use the algorithm; D-dimer only if low/moderate pre-test probability.

Wells componentPoints
Clinical signs of DVT; PE most likely diagnosis (3 each)3 + 3
HR >100; immobilization/surgery <4 wks; previous DVT/PE1.5 each
Haemoptysis; malignancy (active or treated <6 mo)1 each
>4 = likely → CTPA; ≤4 = unlikely → D-dimer

Echocardiography = RV dilation/hypokinesis + McConnell’s sign — diagnostic and prognostic in UNSTABLE patients (> can’t go to CT) — do echo first if hypotensive; contraindication to CTPA is another reason. This exam: BP 90/60 + tachy → urgent CTPA if stable, echo if peri-arrest/unstable (and per exam style: echo is the answer for the unstable scenario, CTPA for stable).

Treatment: anticoagulate immediately when suspect and no contraindication (LMWH/fondaparinux/DOAC — rivaroxaban/apixaban) while awaiting imaging; haemodynamically unstable → thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg/2 h) or embolectomy/catheter-directed therapy; VTE prophylaxis post-op prevents the bulk. Duration: 3 months (provoked), ≥6 months/indefinite (unprovoked or cancer). Warfarin for antiphospholipid syndrome. Fat embolism (femur fracture + chest pain/petechiae/GCS change, 24–72 h) — supportive; post-op immobility (cholecystectomy 3 days ago) → PE most likely.

Exam pearls
  • Wells >4 → CTPA; ≤4 → D-dimer; unstable → echo + thrombolysis.
  • ECG: tachycardia first, then S1Q3T3; neither is specific.
  • Femur fracture + hypoxaemia = fat embolism. Post-op + pleuritic pain = PE.

Pulmonary Function Tests — Reading the Pattern

The 6-number framework:

FEV₁FVCFEV₁/FVCDLCOFRC/TLCPattern
Obstructive↓↓N or ↓<0.7N or ↓ (emphysema ↓)↑ (hyperinflation)Asthma (+reversibility ≥12%/200 mL), COPD, bronchiectasis
Restrictive↓↓↓↓N or ↑ (≥0.7)↓ (parenchymal) or N (chest wall/ neuromuscular)↓↓ILD/fibrosis, scoliosis, obesity hypoventilation, neuromuscular, pleural effusion
Mixed↓↓↓↓<0.7↓variableSevere COPD + restriction, cf bronchiectasis + effusion

Which numbers change (exam question): in restriction, FEV₁/FVC is NOT reduced (both fall proportionally); FEV₁, FVC, PEF, TLC, VC, FRC all fall; DLCO falls when the lung parenchyma is stiff (ILD, emphysema) and stays normal in extraparenchymal restriction (obesity, chest wall, diaphragmatic weakness).

RA lung involvement (this exam): progressive dyspnoea + RA → restrictive defect + LOW DLCO (RA-ILD — usual interstitial pneumonia pattern); check HRCT, PFTs; treat: stop smoking, steroids/immunosuppressants per MDT; pirfenidone/nintedanib for fibrotic ILD.

Exam pearls
  • Obstruction: FEV₁/FVC <0.7; restriction: ratio normal/high + ↓TLC; mixed: ratio low + ↓TLC.
  • DLCO low = ILD (or emphysema/pulmonary vascular disease).
  • Asthma = obstruction WITH reversibility.

A patient has a history of chronic productive cough; auscultation revealed bilateral crackles (restrictive disease history). Which spirometry result is for the patient?

Best answer
B. FEV1 low, FVC low, FEV1/FVC 83, DLCO low

Pulmonary Hypertension & Cor Pulmonale

Definition: cor pulmonale = right ventricular hypertrophy/dilation (± failure) secondary to lung disease/pulmonary hypertension — not caused by left heart disease.

Causes: COPD (commonest), interstitial lung disease (this exam — dry cough + clubbing), bronchiectasis, massive/recurrent PE, sleep apnoea, obesity hypoventilation, kyphoscoliosis, pulmonary fibrosis, primary pulmonary arterial hypertension (rare — young women, BMPR2), CTEPH.

Features: dyspnoea on exertion → at rest; fatigue; syncope (advanced); signs of right heart failure: raised JVP (giant A waves — tricuspid), loud palpable P2 + parasternal heave, hepatomegaly (pulsatile), ascites, peripheral oedema, right-sided S4, Graham-Steele murmur (PR); ECG: P pulmonale (peaked P >0.25 mV in II/III/aVF), right axis deviation, dominant R in V1, S1S2S3; echo = RV dilated, pulmonary pressure elevated (TR velocity).

This exam: chronic dry cough + clubbing (ILD) + pedal oedema + hepatomegaly = cor pulmonale (A) — not CCF (left), not nephrotic, not cirrhosis (no ascites/stigmata mentioned).

Management: treat the lung disease (the single most important) — optimise COPD (inhalers, smoking cessation), ILD (antifibrotics/steroids); long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) ≥15–16 h/day improves survival; diuretics for oedema (cautious — don’t reduce RV preload too much — target congestion); treat sleep apnoea (CPAP); pulmonary rehabilitation; vaccination; advanced: pulmonary vasodilators (endothelin antagonists, PDE-5 inhibitors, prostanoids — only for PAH/CTEPH — specialist; avoid in ILD without specialist input); anticoagulation for CTEPH; venesection if polycythaemia (Hct >0.55); avoid diuretic over-use.

Exam pearls
  • Lung disease + oedema + raised JVP = cor pulmonale — LTOT is the survival drug.
  • Loud P2 + RV heave + hepatomegaly.
  • Treat the lungs first, then the right heart.

Best answer
A. Cor pulmonale

Secondary Hypertension

Think secondary when: resistant to 3 drugs, onset <30 y (or abrupt severe at previously controlled BP), <40–50 with no family history, hypokalaemia (aldosteronism), spells (phaeo), abdominal bruit, unequal kidneys, renal impairment, obstructive sleep apnoea, drug triggers (COCP, NSAID, steroids, liquorice, decongestants, cocaine), Cushingoid features, radio-femoral delay (coarctation).

CauseClueTestTreatment
Renal artery stenosis (atherosclerotic — older + IHD; or fibromuscular dysplasia — young women)Refractory HTN, abdominal bruit, Cr rise on ACEi/ARB, ONE SMALLER KIDNEYDuplex USS → CT/MR angiographyFMD → angioplasty; atherosclerotic → medical (ACEi if unilateral + monitoring ± statin)
PhaeochromocytomaLabile/paroxysmal HTN + episodic headache + sweating + palpitations ± tremor/pallor24-h urinary / plasma free metanephrines → MRI/CT adrenal (MIBG)Alpha-block FIRST (phenoxybenzamine), THEN beta-blocker; surgical resection
Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn’s)HTN + hypokalaemia (± metabolic alkalosis, muscle weakness) — stop diuretics firstAldosterone:renin ratio → saline suppression test → CT adrenals ± adrenal vein samplingSurgery if adenoma; spironolactone/eplerenone if bilateral hyperplasia
Cushing’s syndromeCentral obesity, striae, moon face, glucose intolerance + HTN24-h urinary free cortisol / low-dose dexamethasone suppression testTreat cause (usually pituitary/adrenal adenoma — surgery)
Coarctation of aortaRadio-femoral delay, BP higher in arms than legs, rib notching on CXR, systolic murmur between scapulaeEcho (confirmatory) / MRI / CTSurgical repair/angioplasty + lifelong follow-up (HTN/restenosis)
OSA; CKD; drugsSnoring + apnoea + daytime sleepiness; ↑Cr; new drugSleep study; U&E/eGFR; drug reviewCPAP; CKD management; stop culprit

This exam: older IHD patient, one small kidney = renal artery stenosis; young male with labile BP + sweating + palpitations = phaeochromocytoma; obese + hyperglycaemic + HTN = Cushing’s; young male resistant to medications = renal artery stenosis.

Exam pearls
  • Small kidney + resistant HTN = renal artery stenosis. Spells + sweating = phaeo (alpha-block first!). Hypokalaemia = Conn’s.
  • Resistant HTN: verify adherence, stop NSAIDs, check ABPM, screen for secondary causes.

Paediatric SAQ (this exam): fever + leg pain + red image in a child → cellulitis — Group A (or S. aureus); treatment beyond antibiotics/fluids: supportive — elevate the limb, analgesia/antipyretic, mark the border, admit if unwell/rapidly spreading (measure & monitor spread; escalate to surgery if necrotising).

Spinal Cord & Brainstem Crossings — Brown-Séquard & Others

Key anatomy: Corticospinal tract & dorsal columns (vibration/proprioception) decussate HIGH (medullary pyramids) → lesions below cause ipsilateral weakness/proprioception loss. Spinothalamic tract (pain/temperature) decussates 1–2 levels BELOW its entry → lesions cause contralateral pain/temperature loss below the lesion.

Brown-Séquard syndrome (cord hemisection): ipsilateral spastic weakness + ipsilateral proprioception/vibration loss + contralateral pain/temperature loss (starting ~2 levels below) + ipsilateral LMN signs at the level + Horner’s if cervical (sympathetics at T1). Causes: trauma (penetrating), tumour, transverse myelitis, MS, disc herniation, cervical spondylotic myelopathy.

Cervical myelopathy: progressive UMN signs (spastic paraparesis, hyperreflexia, upgoing plantars) + hand wasting/weakness (LMN at level) + gait change + neck pain/stiffness; MRI is diagnostic; decompression for progressive/symptomatic disease.

This exam’s SAQ (right-sided ptosis + miosis + arm/leg numbness over days): lesion = lower cervical cord (T1-level — intramedullary) with ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome (T1 sympathetic outflow) + bilateral sensory level + UMN legs. Causes: intramedullary tumour (glioma/ependymoma), transverse myelitis (inflammatory — idiopathic/MS/NMO/post-infectious), syrinx, metastasis/compression (extrinsic); (disc disease less typical with Brown-Séquard pattern at C7-T1). Investigations: MRI whole cervical cord with gadolinium (first-line) + CSF analysis (cells, protein, oligoclonal bands, IgG index, viral PCR) ± visual evoked potentials, neuro-immunology (AQP4, MOG), work-up for infection (TB).

Central cord syndrome (syringomyelia): cape-like loss of pain/temperature in arms with preserved touch; anterior spinal artery syndrome: bilateral motor + pain/temp loss, preserved proprioception; cauda equina: saddle anaesthesia + urinary retention + bilateral LMN leg weakness (emergency).

Exam pearls
  • Hemisection: ipsilateral weakness + proprioception loss, contralateral pain/temp loss.
  • Horner’s + cord signs = T1 level — look there (MRI).
  • Myelopathy = MRI first, always.
  • Sphincter/saddle loss = cauda equina = emergency surgery.

#343MCQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-904366c5
A man has right-sided weakness and loss of proprioception with contralateral loss of pain sensation. Where is the site of the lesion?
  • A. Left-side Brown-Sequard syndrome
  • B. Right-side Brown-Sequard syndrome
  • C. Left thalamus
  • D. Left hemisphere
  • E. Right internal capsule
Best answer
B. Right-side Brown-Sequard syndrome
Ipsilateral (right) weakness + ipsilateral proprioception/vibration loss + contralateral pain/temperature loss = RIGHT cord hemisection — Brown-Séquard syndrome (corticospinal + dorsal columns ipsilateral; spinothalamic decussates 1–2 segments below → contralateral body pain/T loss below the lesion).
#378SAQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-SAQ-Medicine-cb0d978b
A patient has numbness for 3 days in the lower limbs and the medial aspect of the arms and fingers, weakness in both lower limbs for 1 day, mild ptosis in the right eye, and the right pupil is smaller than the left.
  1. Where is the lesion located? (1 pt)
  2. List 2 causes for this lesion. (2 pt)
  3. List 2 investigations to diagnose. (2 pt)
Best answer
1) Lesion location: lower cervical cord (C8–T1 segments) — intramedullary cervical cord process with ipsilateral (right) Horner’s syndrome (ptosis + miosis — T1 sympathetic involvement at that level) + bilateral leg numbness/weakness + arm/hand sensory loss — pattern = transverse cervical myelopathy with Horner’s. 2) Two causes: (a) cervical space-occupying lesion — cord tumour (glioma/ependymoma) or metastasis; (b) transverse myelitis (inflammatory/demyelinating — MS/NMO) or cervical disc prolapse/spondylotic myelopathy (compressive). 3) Two investigations: (a) MRI whole cervical spine WITH gadolinium (first-line — defines compression/inflammation); (b) CSF analysis (cell count, protein, oligoclonal bands, viral/AQP4) ± VEP/MRI brain.
Horner’s + cord signs localises below T1; always image urgently (myelopathy is time-critical). Cauda equina = saddle anaesthesia + urinary retention + LMN only (no Horner’s, no pyramidal signs) — different.

Stroke & Transient Ischaemic Attack — Localization

Hemisphere syndromes:

TerritoryDeficits
MCA (commonest)Contralateral face & arm > leg weakness, contralateral sensory loss, homonymous hemianopia, aphasia (dominant), neglect (non-dominant), gaze deviation toward lesion
ACAContralateral leg > arm weakness, urinary incontinence, grasp reflex, behavioural change
PCAContralateral homonymous hemianopia (macula-sparing), memory loss, Alexia without agraphia (dominant)

Brainstem/lacunar (cross findings = ipsilateral cranial nerve + contralateral body — the exam’s favourite):

SyndromeSiteFeatures
Weber’sParamedian midbrain (III fascicles + corticospinal)Ipsilateral CN III palsy (“down and out”, ptosis, dilated pupil) + contralateral UMN hemiparesis (face + limbs); ± altered sensorium if haemorrhage/large lesion
Millard–Gubler / FovillePons (VI + VII + corticospinal)Ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy (can’t look that way) + LMN facial palsy + contralateral hemiparesis
Wallenberg (lateral medullary)PICA (posterior inferior cerebellar a.)Ipsilateral: facial pain/temp loss (spinal trigeminal), Horner’s, limb ataxia, nystagmus, dysphagia/hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus), vertigo (vestibular nuclei); contralateral: body pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic); NO weakness — classic “crossed” sensory pattern
BenediktMidbrain (red nucleus + III)CN III palsy + contralateral involuntary movements/tremor
Lateral pontineAICALike Wallenberg + ipsilateral facial weakness & hearing loss (CN VII/VIII)

Pure sensory / pure motor / ataxic hemiparesis / clumsy-hand dysarthria = lacunar (thalamus = pure sensory; internal capsule/corona radiata = pure motor; base of pons = ataxic hemiparesis). Thalamus → isolated hemisensory loss (this exam).

Acute management: ABCDE, glucose, seizures controlled → non-contrast CT brain (exclude haemorrhage) → eligibility for thrombolysis (IV alteplase within 4.5 h) or thrombectomy (large vessel occlusion, up to 24 h in selected) → admit stroke unit; antiplatelet (aspirin 300 mg) if ischaemic and not thrombolysed; BP control (do NOT lower acutely unless >220/120 or thrombolysing); swallow assessment before feeding; DVT prophylaxis; secondary prevention (statin, antiplatelet/anticoagulant for AF, BP, diabetes, smoking); speech & language, PT/OT, MDT; carotid imaging/CT angiography for anterior circulation TIAs.

Exam pearls
  • Crossed signs (ipsilateral CN + contralateral body) = brainstem, NOT cortex.
  • Down-and-out eye + contralateral weakness = Weber’s (midbrain). Gaze palsy + facial weakness + weakness = Millard–Gubler (pons). PICA = Wallenberg.
  • Isolated hemisensory loss = thalamus.
  • Never sit on chest pain/stroke red flags — CT first, thrombolyse if eligible.

#269MCQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-8b4a93fa
A patient has acute left-sided facial weakness, right hemianopia and dysarthria. Where is the lesion?
  • A. Left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) territory
  • B. Left MCA territory
  • C. Left ACA territory
  • D. Right MCA territory
  • E. Left vertebral artery
Best answer
A. Left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) territory
Crossed brainstem signs — ipsilateral (left) facial involvement + contralateral (right) hemianopia/weakness + dysphagia/dysarthria = lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome — PICA occlusion: left facial pain/temperature loss (spinal trigeminal nucleus), left Horner’s, right body pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic), left limb ataxia, dysphagia/hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus). Left MCA would give right face/arm weakness + right homonymous hemianopia (same side, not crossed).
#300MCQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-1b883dc5
A patient presents with acute inability to look to the left side (squint), left facial paralysis and right-sided weakness. Where is the lesion?
  • A. Left medulla
  • B. Left pons
  • C. Left midbrain
  • D. Right cerebellum
  • E. Left internal capsule
Best answer
B. Left pons
Left lateral rectus palsy (cannot look left) + left facial palsy (LMN) + right hemiparesis = Millard–Gubler syndrome — paramedian pons (VI + VII + corticospinal). Midbrain = III nerve (Weber); medulla = IX/X (Wallenberg); internal capsule = pure motor.

Tropical & Travel-Related Infections

Dengue (commonest exam travel fever): fever + retro-orbital pain + severe myalgia (“break-bone fever”) + maculopapular rash + headache + LOW PLATELETS ± bleeding (gums/petechiae) — travel to India/SE Asia/Caribbean/Latin America; leucopenia, thrombocytopenia, rising haematocrit (plasma leak — warning signs: abdominal pain, bleeding, shock — “dengue haemorrhagic fever”); diagnosed by NS1 antigen/dengue serology (IgM), PCR; treatment = supportive — fluids (ORAL rehydration/IV), paracetamol (NO aspirin/NSAIDs/ibuprofen — bleeding risk), rest; admit if warning signs.

Malaria: cyclical fevers (every 48 h — P. vivax/ovale; 72 h — P. malariae), headache, rigors, sweats, hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia after travel to sub-Saharan Africa; P. falciparum = severe (seizures, coma, hypoglycaemia, renal failure, jaundice, severe anaemia, high parasitaemia); diagnosis: thick & thin film ×3 (ring forms — “headphone”/banana gametocytes) or RDT (antigen); urgent: artesunate/ACT for falciparum; chloroquine + primaquine for vivax; notify notifiable disease.

Chikungunya: fever + severe polyarthralgia (debilitating, small joints) + rash; lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia; self-limiting weeks; serology; supportive.

Typhoid (S. Typhi/Paratyphi): prolonged stepwise fever, relative bradycardia, abdominal pain, constipation (or “pea soup” diarrhoea), rose spots (trunk), hepatosplenomegaly — India/SE Asia/ traveller; leucopaenia; blood cultures (1st week) / stool; ceftriaxone/azithromycin; 10–14 days.

Zika: mild fever + rash + conjunctivitis + arthralgia; congenital Zika syndrome — microcephaly if infection in pregnancy; avoid pregnancy 2 months after exposure.

Leptospirosis — water/rats; biphasic fever, conjunctival suffusion (no discharge!), myalgia, jaundice + renal failure (Weil’s disease).

Exam pearls
  • Travel + fever + retro-orbital pain/rash/low platelets = dengue. Africa + cyclical fever + film = malaria. India + rash + low platelets = dengue.
  • Never give aspirin/NSAIDs in dengue.
  • Malaria: treat falciparum urgently; thick/thin film ×3.

Urinalysis — Casts & What They Mean

The cast table (this exam: WBC casts):

CastMeaning
WBC castsAcute pyelonephritis or acute interstitial nephritis (drug-induced — fever/rash/eosinophilia — PPI/NSAIDs/antibiotics); upper tract infection
RBC casts (dysmorphic RBCs + casts)Glomerulonephritis (IgA, PSGN, lupus nephritis) — upper urinary tract/parenchymal

No casts, bacteria + nitrites: lower UTI (cystitis) — ascending infection without parenchymal involvement.

Urinalysis work-up: dipstick (blood/protein/nitrite/leucocyte esterase/glucose/pH/SG) → mid-stream microscopy & culture → 24-h collections only when needed; urine PCR for nephrotic range quantification; always correlate with renal function, BUN, complement, serology.

Exam pearls
  • WBC cast = kidney infection/interstitial nephritis (not cystitis). Pure cystitis = no casts.
  • RBC cast = glomerulonephritis.
  • Muddy-brown cast = ATN.

Viral Arthritis — Parvovirus B19

Parvovirus B19 — small non-enveloped ssDNA virus; “slapped cheek” (fifth disease/erythema infectiosum) in children; acute polyarthritis in adults (symmetrical small joints — hands/wrists/knees/ankles) — especially women, nursery/school workers (this exam!) and healthcare staff — faecal-oral/respiratory spread.

Features: abrupt onset symmetric polyarthritis (can mimic RA!), RF negative, ANA negative, normal-to-mildly raised inflammatory markers; self-limiting (resolves 2–4 weeks, sometimes months); ± low-grade fever, rash; in pregnancy: severe anaemia in fetus → hydrops fetalis (fetal monitoring — serial MCA Doppler for anaemia); in SCD/immunosuppressed → aplastic crisis.

Diagnosis: parvovirus B19 IgM (acute) or PCR (especially in immunocompromised — IgM may be absent); FBC (drop in Hb/platelets/reticulocytes).

TREATMENT (this exam): NSAIDs — symptom control; no antiviral available; no steroids (unless chronic synovitis — rarely); no IVIG except in aplasia/immunocompromised; no antibiotics.

Other viral arthritis: hepatitis B (prodrome — polyarthritis + urticaria + HBsAg+), hepatitis C (mixed cryoglobulinaemia), chikungunya/alphavirus (severe symmetric — post-travel), rubella (post-vaccine/rubella — women), HIV (reactive-like), mumps.

Exam pearls
  • Nursery worker + symmetric small-joint polyarthritis + RF negative = parvovirus — NSAIDs; self-limiting.
  • Pregnant contacts of slapped cheek → notify/serology — fetal risk.
  • SCD + parvovirus = aplastic crisis (low retics).

Route of transmission & course:

VirusTransmissionChronic?Vaccine/Tx

HBV serology table — memorise cold:

HBsAgAnti-HBcAnti-HBsMeaning
+IgM−Acute HBV
+IgG−Chronic HBV carrier/infection (or window)
−IgG+Cleared past infection (immune)
−−+Vaccinated (immune)
−−−Susceptible — offer vaccine
−IgM−Window period (HBsAg cleared, anti-HBs not yet up) — test HBV DNA

This exam: HBsAg−, anti-HBs+, anti-HBc IgG+ → cleared (past) hepatitis B infection. Traveller + others affected + jaundice → hepatitis A → contact precautions/hand hygiene + notify public health + vaccinate contacts. Returned with markedly raised transaminases → acute hepatitis A/E.

  • EBV in a young adult = fever + pharyngitis + hepatitis — Monospot/VCA-IgM.

#326MCQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-ca32b121
A patient returned from travel with jaundice and hepatomegaly; other people with him were also affected. What type of precaution would you recommend?
  • A. Standard precautions
  • B. Droplet precautions
  • C. Hand hygiene
  • D. Airborne precautions
  • E. Contact precautions
Best answer
E. Contact precautions
Returning traveller + jaundice + hepatomegaly + others who travelled with him affected = hepatitis A (faecal-oral) — CONTACT precautions + meticulous hand hygiene (single room, gown/gloves, food handling) — not airborne/droplet. Notify public health; household contacts — vaccine/immunoglobulin.
#329MCQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-57f52656
Two questions about hepatitis B serology: what does each serological pattern indicate?
  • A. Active infection
  • B. Previous (cleared) infection
  • C. Immunized (vaccination)
  • D. Chronic carrier
  • E. Susceptible (no immunity)
Best answer
Depends on the two panels — see below.
Hepatitis B serology patterns: HBsAg+ + anti-HBc IgM+ = acute infection; HBsAg+ ≥6 mo + anti-HBc IgG+ = chronic infection/carrier; HBsAg− + anti-HBc IgG+ + anti-HBs+ = cleared past infection (immune); HBsAg− + anti-HBc− + anti-HBs+ = vaccine-induced immunity; all negative = susceptible; anti-HBc IgG+ only (isolated) = past infection, window/occult — look for HBV DNA. (Immunoglobulin levels against the core separate vaccine-from-natural immunity.)
#331MCQ edited2017-InternalMedicine-MCQ-Medicine-247c5637
A gentleman presents with jaundice and hepatomegaly with fever and high LFTs. What is the likely diagnosis?
  • A. Hepatitis A
  • B. Hepatitis C
  • C. Hepatitis E
  • D. Hepatitis B
  • E. EBV hepatitis
Best answer
E. EBV hepatitis
Young “gentleman” + fever + hepatomegaly + jaundice + high transaminases — EBV (infectious mononucleosis) hepatitis is the classic non-A–E viral hepatitis in young adults: fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, malaise. Also check: CMV, hepatitis A–E, drug-induced (paracetamol). Monospot/EBV-VCA-IgM confirm.

Viral Skin Infections — Herpes Zoster & Others

Herpes zoster (shingles) — this exam: reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in a dorsal root ganglion — unilateral dermatomal, grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, does NOT cross the midline, burning/stabbing neuropathic pain; typically thoracic/lumbar; risk factors: age >50, immunosuppression (HIV — suspect if young/severe/multidermatomal/recurrent), diabetes (this exam), malignancy, stress.

Management: oral aciclovir/valaciclovir/famciclovir within 72 h of rash (limits severity/duration — benefit if >72 h only if new lesions/complications); analgesia — paracetamol/NSAIDs + neuropathic agents (amitriptyline, gabapentin, pregabalin); keep rash clean/dry, non-adherent dressings; avoid contact with non-immune pregnant women/immunocompromised (infectious until crusted — only to those who never had chickenpox).

Complications: post-herpetic neuralgia (>90 days pain — 10–15%; risk ↑ with age), Ramsay Hunt syndrome (geniculate ganglion — facial palsy + ear vesicles + deafness — treat aciclovir + steroids), ophthalmic shingles (V1) — HUTCHINSON’S SIGN (lesion on tip/side of nose) → ocular involvement → urgent ophthalmology; disseminated in immunosuppressed; motor (paresis), encephalitis.

Prevention: shingles vaccine (Zostavax live — >60 y; Shingrix recombinant — even better, immunosuppressed OK) — reduces incidence/PHN.

Other viral skin infections: herpes simplex (lips/genital — aciclovir), molluscum contagiosum (poxvirus — self-limiting; very numerous in HIV), warts (HPV — cryotherapy/salicylic acid), chickenpox (generalised vesicles — supportive; acyclovir if severe/pregnant/immunocompromised/neonatal).

Exam pearls
  • Unilateral grouped vesicles, one dermatome, midline respected + older diabetic = shingles — aciclovir ≤72 h.
  • Tip-of-nose lesion = Hutchinson — eye involvement risk — urgent ophtho.
  • Vaccinate >60 y.

Asthma — Diagnosis & Acute Exacerbation

Diagnosis: variable respiratory symptoms (wheeze, cough, chest tightness, dyspnoea) + variable expiratory airflow limitation: FEV₁/FVC <0.7 with ≥12% and ≥200 mL improvement in FEV₁ after bronchodilator, or excessive diurnal peak-flow variability (>20%), or positive bronchial challenge (methacholine/histamine) if spirometry is normal. Normal spirometry does NOT exclude asthma in a symptomatic patient → methacholine challenge is the next step.

Obstructive defect pattern: low FEV₁, low FEV₁/FVC, normal/low-normal FVC, and (in asthma) normal DLCO (unlike emphysema where DLCO is low).

Acute severe asthma (admit): PEF 33–50% predicted/best, respiratory rate ≥25, HR ≥110, inability to complete sentences, or O₂ sat <92%. Life-threatening: PEF <33%, silent chest, exhaustion/altered consciousness, SpO₂ <92%, normal/high PaCO₂ (exhaustion — rising CO₂ is a red flag).

Management of acute exacerbation:

  1. High-flow O₂ to keep SpO₂ 94–98%.
  2. Nebulised salbutamol (5 mg) + ipratropium bromide (0.5 mg) driven by O₂, back-to-back/repeat.
  3. Oral prednisolone 40–50 mg (or IV hydrocortisone) — steroids early.
  4. Not responding/severe → IV magnesium sulfate 1.2–2 g over 20 min; call ICU; consider IV aminophylline; avoid sedation; intubation if failing (permissive hypercapnia).
  5. Discharge: when PEF >75%, stable ≥12–24 h off nebs; written asthma action plan, GP/asthma nurse follow-up, inhaler technique review, optimise preventer (ICS-containing), address triggers and adherence, safety-net re admission.

Chronic stepwise management (GINA): low-dose ICS-formoterol as reliever (or SABA + ICS) → add LABA → medium-dose ICS/LABA → refer. SABA-only is no longer recommended — every reliever should contain ICS to cut severe exacerbations.

Exam pearls
  • First-line in acute attack after O₂: nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium + early oral steroids.
  • Rising/normal PaCO₂ in acute asthma = life-threatening — call for help.
  • Normal spirometry + typical symptoms → methacholine challenge confirms.
  • Nasal flaring, intercostal recessions, tracheal tug in a child = severe exacerbation with respiratory distress.

Birth Injuries — Clavicle, Erb’s Palsy & Caput/Cephalohaematoma

Clavicle fracture — the commonest birth fracture (shoulder dystocia, macrosomia, vacuum). Findings: crepitus and a “step” over the clavicle, reduced arm movement/pseudoparalysis of one arm with normal Moro on the other side. X-ray confirms; management is conservative (analgesia, gentle handling, heals with callus in 2–3 weeks).

Brachial plexus injuries:

Erb’s palsy (C5–C6)Klumpke’s palsy (C8–T1)
MechanismTraction on the extended neck/shoulder during delivery (head pulled away from shoulder)Overstretching of the abducted arm (breech with arm above head)
Posture“Waiter’s tip” — arm adducted and internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated, wrist flexed; grasp reflex INTACTClaw hand (intrinsic hand weakness); grasp reflex ABSENT; Horner’s syndrome if T1 sympathetic fibres involved (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis)
ReflexesAbsent biceps/Moro on that side; grasp presentGrasp absent

Most brachial plexus injuries recover spontaneously by 3–6 months. Refer to paediatric physiotherapy; after ~3 months without recovery → detailed MRI/CT myelography, specialist (brachial plexus surgeon) review; delayed surgery (nerve graft/transfer) only for persistent deficits.

Head injuries: caput succedaneum — oedematous swelling crossing suture lines, present at birth, resolves in days. Cephalohaematoma — subperiosteal blood collection, does NOT cross suture lines, appears hours after birth, resolves over weeks (risk: jaundice from haemolysis, calcification). Facial nerve palsy (forceps): lower motor neurone pattern — forehead included; most recover in days–weeks; protect the eye if incomplete closure.

Exam pearls
  • One still arm + intact grasp reflex + difficult/instrumental delivery → Erb’s palsy (waiter’s tip).
  • Facial droop involving the forehead in a newborn = LMN (Bell’s-type) — forceps trauma; eye care; usually recovers.
  • Cephalohaematoma can unmask/worsen jaundice via extravascular haemolysis — track bilirubin.
