#265MCQ edited2017-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-14435814
A child had a complicated long delivery; Apgar was 3 then 9 then improved. He was found with caput succedanum, facial bruising and a left arm deformity (picture below); his other 3 limbs were normal. What is the most likely cause?
  • A. Hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy
  • B. Brachial plexus injury (Erb's palsy)
  • C. Clavicle fracture
  • D. Shoulder dislocation
  • E. Humeral fracture
Best answer
B. Brachial plexus injury (Erb's palsy)
Complicated long delivery + caput/facial bruising + one arm deformity with the other 3 limbs normal = brachial plexus birth injury — Erb’s palsy (C5–6, “waiter’s tip”) — shoulder dystocia/traction stretches the upper trunk. Klumpke’s (C8–T1) would give a claw hand ± Horner’s. Most recover spontaneously; refer to physio; MRI/neurosurgery review if no recovery by 3–6 months.

Bleeding Disorders — Platelets vs Coagulation vs vWD

Bleeding pattern points to the defect:

Platelet / primary haemostasisCoagulation factor / secondary haemostasis
PatternMucocutaneous: petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, bleeding immediately after cutsDeep bleeds: haemarthroses, muscle/retroperitoneal haematomas, delayed bleeding (hours after surgery/dental extraction)
Platelet countLow (or functionally defective)Normal
PT / aPTTNormalPT = extrinsic (factor VII); aPTT = intrinsic (VIII, IX, XI, XII); both = common pathway (X, V, II, I) or vitamin K/liver disease

Key inherited disorders:

  • Haemophilia A (factor VIII) / B (factor IX) — X-linked recessive. Boys; deep haematomas, haemarthroses, prolonged aPTT with normal PT, normal platelets. Treat: factor VIII/IX replacement (on demand ± prophylaxis), DDAVP for mild A, avoid aspirin/IM injections. Check inhibitors if poor response.
  • Von Willebrand disease — most common inherited bleeding disorder; autosomal dominant; mucocutaneous bleeding, menorrhagia in women, family history; normal/high aPTT (factor VIII protected by vWF), prolonged bleeding time; test: vWF antigen/activity (ristocetin cofactor), factor VIII. Treat: DDAVP (mild), tranexamic acid, vWF/factor VIII concentrate for surgery/major bleeds.
  • Vitamin K deficiency — neonates (no stores, sterile gut), malabsorption (coeliac, CF, cholestasis), antibiotics, warfarin → affects factors II, VII, IX, X → PT (and later aPTT) prolonged; newborn bleeding prevented by IM/oral vitamin K at birth. Treat with vitamin K; PCC/FFP if bleeding.
  • ITP — isolated thrombocytopenia post-viral illness, well child, petechiae/purpura, normal Hb/WBC; observe if mild; IVIG/steroids if significant bleeding/platelets very low; avoid sports.
  • Haemophilia + circumcision bleed in a boy with knee haematomas = haemophilia A (commonest) vs B.

Laboratory triage: normal aPTT + prolonged PT → factor VII deficiency or vitamin K/warfarin/liver. Prolonged aPTT + normal PT → VIII/IX/XI. Both prolonged → common pathway (X/V/II/fibrinogen) or vitamin K deficiency/liver/DIC/warfarin; mixing study separates factor deficiency (corrects) from inhibitor (fails to correct — e.g. lupus anticoagulant, factor VIII inhibitor). Prolonged both + thrombocytopenia + high D-dimer + low fibrinogen = DIC (oozing everywhere, multi-organ failure — treat cause + replace).

Exam pearls
  • Petechiae + isolated low platelets post-viral in a well child = ITP.
  • Circumcision bleed + haemarthrosis + boy + family history = haemophilia (aPTT↑, PT normal).
  • vWD = menorrhagia + mucocutaneous bleed + family history; DDAVP trial.
  • Both PT & aPTT prolonged in a newborn/anticoagulated/malabsorbed = vitamin K — give vitamin K, check liver.
  • DIC = consumption — replace what you use, treat the cause (sepsis!).
Traps
  • Normal PT/aPTT does NOT exclude vWD or mild factor deficiency — check vWF/factor levels and bleeding time.
  • Platelet transfusion only in active bleeding/prophylaxis before procedures, not automatically in ITP.

#266MCQ edited2017-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-66981776
A 6-month-old child has bleeding after circumcision with increased aPTT and PT but a normal INR. What is the likely diagnosis?
  • A. Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency)
  • B. Hemophilia B (factor IX deficiency)
  • C. Vitamin K deficiency
  • D. Von Willebrand disease
  • E. Platelet function disorder
Best answer
C. Vitamin K deficiency
Circumcision bleeding + BOTH aPTT and PT prolonged (even with normal INR reporting — inconsistency noted in the stem) → vitamin K deficiency (factors II, VII, IX, X) — think of neonates not given vitamin K at birth or malabsorption/antibiotics. Haemophilia prolongs aPTT only; vWD also aPTT; platelet disorders give normal PT/aPTT.

Bronchiolitis

Viral lower respiratory infection in infants <2 years (peak 2–6 months), usually RSV (also human metapneumovirus, adenovirus, parainfluenza). Presentation: coryza prodrome → dry cough, tachypnoea, wheeze, subcostal/intercostal recession, feeding difficulty, low-grade fever, crackles. Commonest cause of infant admission in winter.

Diagnosis is clinical — no routine tests. Oxygen saturation guides severity/admission (admit if SpO₂ persistently <92–94%, poor feeding <50–75% of normal, apnoea, severe recessions, or social concerns). Grunting = auto-PEEP — a sign of worsening respiratory distress. CXR only if atypical/deteriorating (hyperinflation ± focal atelectasis).

Management = SUPPORTIVE only: oxygen (if hypoxic), nasogastric/IV fluids (if poor feeding), nasal suctioning (especially before feeds; upper-airway secretions obstruct). NOT recommended: bronchodilators (salbutamol — no benefit), steroids, antibiotics (unless secondary bacterial infection), routine chest physiotherapy, hypertonic saline (debated; not routine in US; sometimes used in some protocols).

Prevention: palivizumab (monoclonal anti-RSV) for high-risk infants in season (ex-prems, chronic lung disease, congenital heart disease); hand hygiene; avoid sick contacts; smoke-free homes.

Exam pearls
  • Bronchiolitis ≠ asthma — salbutamol doesn’t work; supportive care is everything.
  • Severe: apnoea, SpO₂ <92%, poor feeding → admit + O₂ + NG/IV fluids.
  • Grunting = working hard — support the airway, don’t dismiss.
  • RSV is diagnosed clinically; family “cold” symptoms in a winter infant = bronchiolitis.

2017 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Child Maltreatment & Safeguarding

Recognise abuse patterns: injuries in non-mobile children; patterned bruises (hand prints, belts, ligatures); bruises in “sentinel” areas — ears, neck, upper arms, chest, abdomen, buttocks, inner thighs; bruising over soft tissue vs bony prominences; bruises of different ages and stages of healing; unexplained retinal haemorrhages (shaken baby); fractures in different stages, rib fractures in infants, spiral fractures, metaphyseal (“corner”) fractures; delay in seeking care; explanations inconsistent with injuries, developmental stage or mechanism ("fell off the sofa" in a non-mobile baby); behaviours (fearful, withdrawn).

“Sentinel injuries” precede serious abuse — ANY unexplained bruising/injury in a pre-mobile infant is a red flag. The AAP/NICE view: bruising in a baby who is not yet cruising = abuse until proven otherwise.

Your duty (UK/international standard): safeguarding overrides confidentiality. Always: document objectively (quote the caregiver verbatim), body-map/photo with consent, full history & exam including genital review when indicated, contact/refer to child protection services / social care immediately, admit the child if unsafe to discharge, involve the hospital safeguarding lead and paediatrics, consider skeletal survey + CT head (for infants with any suspected abuse) + coagulation/VWD screen (to exclude organic bleeding), notify police if crime suspected. Never accuse; never investigate beyond your role — refer.

Differential to exclude organic causes: bleeding disorder (bruising), osteogenesis imperfecta (fractures), dermal melanocytosis (sacral “bruising”), cultural practice (coining). But absence of a medical diagnosis does NOT clear the child — consult safeguarding regardless.

Management answer in this exam: bruises of different ages in non-mobile/various sites + inconsistent explanation → refer to child protection services immediately (do not discharge with reassurance, do not just scan/observe).

Exam pearls
  • Bruises at different healing stages + odd sites (buttocks, deltoid) + implausible story in a child = contact child protection NOW — that is the answer whenever offered.
  • Neglect: failure to thrive + poor hygiene + missed appointments; report/refer.
  • Document verbatim; never confront; safety of the child comes first.

Childhood Exanthems — Rash + Fever Pattern Recognition

The classic differentials (highest-yield table in paediatrics):

DiseaseAgentFeverRash patternKey distinguishing features
Measles (rubeola)ParamyxovirusHigh, 3–4 d BEFORE rashMaculopapular starting hairline/behind ears → face → trunk (craniocaudal spread)3 Cs: cough, coryza, conjunctivitis + Koplik spots (buccal mucosa white grains)
Rubella (German measles)TogavirusLow-gradePinpoint/maculopapular, face→trunk, fades by day 3Tender occipital/postauricular lymphadenopathy; mild in children; congenital rubella = cataract, deafness, PDA
Roseola infantum (exanthem subitum, 6th disease)HHV-6 (±HHV-7)High fever 3–5 d, child wellRash appears as fever resolves — trunk→face/extremities3 mo–4 y; febrile seizures common; rash blanching macules
Erythema infectiosum (5th disease, slapped-cheek)Parvovirus B19Low/none“Slapped cheek” → lacy reticular rash on limbs/trunkArthropathy in adults; aplastic crisis in sickle cell/chronic haemolysis; hydrops fetalis in pregnancy
Scarlet feverStrep pyogenes (erythrogenic toxin)Fever, sore throatSandpaper rash (blanching, pinpoint, sandpaper), circumoral pallor, Pastia’s lines (flexural accentuation)Strawberry tongue, tonsillitis; treat penicillin (prevents RF/PSGN)
Varicella (chickenpox)VZVFeverCrops of vesicles on an erythematous base — all stages simultaneously, itchy, dew-drops-on-petals; centripetalComplications: secondary bacterial infection, pneumonitis, congenital; exclude from school until all crusted
Hand, foot & mouthCoxsackie A16/EV71LowVesicles palms/soles + mouth ulcersSelf-limiting; nail shedding; myocarditis (EV71, rare)
MeningococcaemiaN. meningitidisFever + toxicNON-BLANCHING, palpable purpura/petechiaeEmergency: IV ceftriaxone + fluids; watch for shock/DIC

Management: measles/rubella/roseola/fifth = supportive (antipyretics, fluids). Scarlet fever = penicillin V/amoxicillin ×10 d. Varicella = supportive, acyclovir if severe/immunocompromised. Meningococcaemia = emergency. Measles: isolate, notify public health, vitamin A in severe/developing-world cases.

Exam pearls
  • Fever first, rash after fever breaks = ROSEOLA (HHV-6).
  • Cough+coryza+conjunctivitis then craniocaudal rash = MEASLES (plus Koplik).
  • Slapped cheek + reticular rash = parvovirus B19 → aplastic crisis risk in haemolytics.
  • Sandpaper rash + Pastia lines + circumoral pallor = GAS scarlet fever → penicillin.
  • Any non-blanching purpuric rash with fever = meningococcaemia → ceftriaxone NOW.
Traps
  • Measles is contagious 4 days before → 4 days after rash.
  • Fifth disease in pregnancy causes hydrops — advise pregnant contacts.
  • Don’t confuse roseola rash with drug rash — history of fever trajectory decides.

Congenital Heart Disease — Murmur Recognition & Cyanosis

Approach: (1) Cyanotic vs acyanotic? (2) Where/when murmur? (3) Splitting behaviour.

LesionMurmurKey signsNotes
VSD (commonest CHD)Harsh pansystolic at left lower sternal edgeFeeding difficulty/FTT, recurrent chest infections; large VSD → heart failure, loud P2; small (restrictive) = louderMany close spontaneously; Eisenmenger if long-standing large defect (reversal → cyanosis)
ASDSoft ejection systolic at left upper sternal edge (relative pulmonary flow)Fixed widely split S2 (pathognomonic); often asymptomatic; split doesn’t vary with respirationTypes: ostium secundum (commonest, 90%), primum (AVSD), sinus venosus; embolic stroke risk (paradoxical); closure if shunt significant
PDAContinuous “machinery” murmur below left clavicleBounding pulses, wide pulse pressure; common in prematurityIndomethacin/ibuprofen or device closure if symptomatic
Tetralogy of Fallot (commonest CYANOTIC)Ejection systolic (pulmonary stenosis); single S2Hypercyanotic “tet” spells (squatting/knee–chest ↑SVR), clubbing, squatting; RVH (boot-shaped heart)4 features: pulmonary stenosis + VSD + overriding aorta + RVH; spell: knee–chest, O₂, morphine, beta-blocker, call ICU
Transposition of great arteries (TGA)Usually no murmur; single S2Severe cyanosis in first hours of life (needs duct/foramen to survive)Egg-on-string CXR; prostaglandin E1 to keep duct open; arterial switch operation
Eisenmenger syndrome± pansystolic (shunt may reverse → murmur diminishes)Cyanosis + clubbing + polycythaemia lateIrreversible pulmonary hypertension — surgery contraindicated; heart-lung transplant
Pulmonary stenosisEjection systolic, left upper sternal edge, normal/soft splitting or single S2 (delayed A2–P2)Widely split FIXED = ASD; single S2/soft P2 = PSBalloon valvuloplasty if gradient high
Aortic stenosisEjection systolic at right upper sternal edge radiating to carotidsEjection click, thrillBicuspid → coarctation association
Innocent murmur (Still’s)Soft, vibratory/“twang” systolic, disappears lying flat/sitting upWell child, normal S1/S2, normal growthReassure — no investigation

Cyanosis work-up: hyperoxia test (FiO₂ 100% ×10 min — PaO₂ stays low if cardiac, rises if pulmonary); echocardiography is definitive. Acute cyanotic neonate → prostaglandin E1 immediately if duct-dependent lesion suspected.

Cyanotic murmurs vs cyanotic single S2: TOF (murmur + hypoxic spells), TGA (single S2, no murmur, first-day cyanosis), truncus, tricuspid atresia, Ebstein.

Exam pearls
  • Pansystolic LLSE = VSD; fixed split S2 + soft ESM = ASD; machinery = PDA; ESM + single S2 + cyanotic + squatting = TOF.
  • “Blueness after crying” in a child = TOF tet spell → echo; knee–chest position.
  • Continuous murmur disappears supine = innocent (Still’s).
  • Uncorrected left-to-right shunt → Eisenmenger → cyanosis with diminished murmur.

  • A. Knee-chest position

#315MCQ edited2017-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-465e96b5
A child has a crescendo-decrescendo mid-systolic ejection murmur heard best at the right upper sternal border and transmitted to the carotid arteries. What is the diagnosis?
  • A. Aortic stenosis
  • B. Aortic regurgitation
  • C. Mitral regurgitation
  • D. Mitral stenosis
  • E. Tricuspid regurgitation
Best answer
A. Aortic stenosis
Crescendo-decrescendo (ejection) systolic murmur at the RIGHT upper sternal border radiating to the CAROTIDS = aortic stenosis (obstructive lesion of LVOT — congenital bicuspid or degenerative). Aortic regurgitation = early diastolic decrescendo; MR = pansystolic apex→axilla.

Best answer
B. VSD
Pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge + normal O₂ saturation (96% — acyanotic) = VSD (left-to-right shunt). MR usually radiates to the axilla and is apical; PDA = continuous machinery below clavicle.

A question about a heart murmur in a child — what is the likely diagnosis?
  • A. VSD
  • B. ASD
  • C. PDA
  • D. Tetralogy of Fallot
  • E. Innocent murmur
Best answer
A. VSD
Child with a haemodynamically significant pansystolic murmur at left lower sternal edge = VSD — commonest CHD; feeding difficulty/FTT, frequent chest infections; most small VSDs close spontaneously by 2–4 years.
2017 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Cystic Fibrosis

Inheritance: autosomal recessive; CFTR gene (7q31) — ΔF508 commonest in Caucasians; defective chloride/bicarbonate channel → thick, dehydrated secretions in lungs, pancreas, liver, gut, vas deferens.

Clinical: meconium ileus (newborn — pathognomonic-ish), failure to thrive, offensive steatorrhoea hard to flush, recurrent/chronic chest infections (S. aureus, H. influenzae, later Pseudomonas aeruginosa — mucoid), wheeze, bronchiectasis, clubbing, nasal polyps, distal intestinal obstruction, biliary fibrosis/cirrhosis, delayed puberty/male infertility (absent vas deferens), CF-related diabetes, osteoporosis, salty sweat.

Diagnosis: sweat chloride test (pilocarpine iontophoresis) — ≥60 mmol/L on two occasions is positive; 30–59 borderline → CFTR genetic testing. Newborn screening (immunoreactive trypsinogen) detects most in developed countries; confirm all with sweat test ± genotyping.

Management: MDT CF-centre care. Respiratory: airway clearance (chest physiotherapy — twice daily), inhaled hypertonic saline, dornase alfa (DNase), bronchodilators, azithromycin (anti-inflammatory), aggressive antibiotics for exacerbations (anti-pseudomonal: IV ceftazidime/tobramycin ± oral ciprofloxacin), inhaled tobramycin/colistimethate for chronic Pseudomonas, CFTR modulators (ivacaftor ± lumacaftor/tezacaftor/elexacaftor) for gating/F508del mutations — transform prognosis. GI/nutrition: high-energy high-fat diet, pancreatic enzyme replacement (Creon) with every meal/snack, fat-soluble vitamins ADEK, salt supplements. Monitoring: annual review — spirometry, sputum culture, USS abdomen, bone density, glucose tolerance; influenza vaccine; double lung transplant for end-stage disease.

Exam pearls
  • Meconium ileus + recurrent chest + steatorrhoea + FTT → sweat test.
  • Sweat ≥60 = CF; CFTR modulators now change the disease course.
  • Pseudomonas colonisation → worse prognosis.
  • Male infertility (CBAVD) is virtually universal.

  • A. Sweat chloride test
  • B. Stool elastase
  • C. Chest X-ray
  • D. CFTR genetic testing
  • E. Sputum culture
Best answer
A. Sweat chloride test
Male infant + meconium ileus (delayed passage) + offensive bulky steatorrhoeic stools + recurrent respiratory distress/wheeze = cystic fibrosis → sweat chloride test (pilocarpine iontophoresis) ≥60 mmol/L diagnostic (×2); confirm genetic (CFTR). Faecal elastase assesses pancreatic insufficiency; stool elastase not diagnostic of CF.
2017 · Pediatrics · 1 question · SAQ

Developmental Delay & Learning Disability

Developmental domains: gross motor → fine motor/vision → speech/language → social/personal. Global developmental delay (GDD) = significant delay in ≥2 domains; becomes “intellectual disability” once IQ measurable (<70 + adaptive impairment).

Red flags requiring urgent assessment: not smiling at 8 weeks, not sitting at 9–12 months, not standing by 12, not walking by 18 months, no words by 2 years, loss of previously acquired skills (regression → think ASD, Rett, neurodegeneration), hand preference before 12 months (cerebral palsy).

Assessment: detailed history (antenatal/perinatal/neonatal course, family history, consanguinity, milestones, regression, social interaction, sleep, feeding), examination (dysmorphology, growth parameters incl. head circumference, skin stigmata — café-au-lait, neurocutaneous, neurology, hearing/vision), investigations: hearing test first in language delay (audiogram/OAE — a deaf child doesn’t speak), FBC, TFT, U&E/Ca, lead, metabolic screen if indicated, karyotype/chromosomal microarray (first-line genetic test), Fragile X, MRI brain (if focal signs/microcephaly/regression), EEG (if seizures).

Management: MDT — paediatrician, early-intervention/portage, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech & language therapy, audiology, educational psychology; treat cause (hypothyroidism, metabolic); parent support groups; statementing/EHCP for special educational needs.

Autism spectrum disorder vs ADHD vs learning disability: ASD = social-communication deficit + restricted/repetitive behaviour (M-CHAT screen 16–30 mo); ADHD = inattention + hyperactivity/impulsivity in ≥2 settings (Conners rating scales); LD = below-average intellect without adaptive impairment of ASD. Not “naughty” — neurodevelopmental.

Exam pearls
  • Language delay → hearing test first, always.
  • Regression of skills = metabolic/neurodegenerative/ASD — investigate urgently (MRI, metabolic, genetics).
  • Global delay + dysmorphology + consanguinity → karyotype/microarray + FraX.
  • Early intervention (EI) before investigations are complete — don’t wait.

A 2-year-old child has a palmar grasp (at 6 months' level), gross motor delay, and says 5 words.
  1. What is the diagnosis? (1 pt)
  2. What investigations would you do? (1 pt)
  3. Referral to two subspecialties. (2 pt)
Best answer
1) Global developmental delay (gross motor + speech delay) with dysmorphism query — at 2 years, a “palmar grasp” (6-month skill) + 5 words + gross motor delay = significant global developmental delay. 2) Investigations: (a) hearing test (audiology) — mandatory for speech delay; (b) chromosomal studies (karyotype/microarray) + metabolic screen (TFTs, CK, lead, amino acids, ammonia), MRI brain, FBC/UE; also creatine kinase (Duchenne if motor delay in boys). 3) Referrals: (a) developmental/community paediatrician + early-intervention programme; (b) speech & language therapy + physiotherapy/occupational therapy.
GDD → find the cause and treat early — early intervention changes outcomes. Screen hearing first; genetic microarray is first-line genetic test; follow growth (head circumference) and regression signs; involve family support.

Developmental quotient (DQ) = developmental age ÷ chronological age × 100. DQ 85–115 normal; 70–85 borderline; <70 significant delay (support needed). Example: 2-year-old with 12-month milestones → 12/24 × 100 = 50.

Warning signs: no social smile by 8 wks, hand preference <12 mo, not sitting by 12 mo, not walking by 18 mo, no words by 2 y, no interest in peers, regression. When in doubt → formal developmental assessment + hearing + vision + referral to portage/EI.

Exam pearls

  • DQ = DA/CA ×100 — always a percentage, comparable across domains.
  • Head lag + poor head control in a 3-month-old → reassess urgently (neurological exam, neuroimaging).

Foreign Body Aspiration

Peak age: 1–3 years — everything goes in mouths. Commonest: nuts (peanuts), seeds, grapes, popcorn, coins, small toys, pins.

Presentation: sudden episode of choking, coughing, gagging, cyanosis while playing/eating (witnessed in ~50%), then — if not expelled — wheeze/unilateral reduced air entry (classic: right main bronchus — wider, shorter, more vertical), stridor if laryngeal/tracheal, or asymptomatic interval then persistent unilateral wheeze/recurrent pneumonia in one lobe.

Red flags: unilateral wheeze or decreased air entry, unilateral hyperinflation/consolidation on CXR, air trapping on expiratory films, radio-opaque object (coins, pins, batteries — disc battery = emergency, oesophageal necrosis in 2 h), stridor/apnoea.

CXR findings: radio-opaque density (nail seen in the 2017 SAQ case — “nail impacted + consolidation”), focal hyperinflation (obstructive ball-valve), atelectasis, pneumonia distal to the object. Inspiratory/expiratory or decubitus views reveal air trapping.

Management: conscious, choking & cannot cough effectively/in distress → back blows/chest thrusts (infant) or abdominal thrusts (child >1 y). Stable with suspected aspiration → rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia — BOTH diagnostic and therapeutic (definitive treatment); flexible bronchoscopy for diagnosis only. Do NOT do blind finger sweeps; do NOT give food/water; batteries/magnets in oesophagus = urgent endoscopy. Antibiotics only if established pneumonia.

Exam pearls
  • Sudden choking + unilateral wheeze + hyperinflation on CXR = inhaled foreign body → rigid bronchoscopy.
  • Radio-opaque object + overlying lung consolidation = retained object — retrieve it.
  • Battery in oesophagus = 2-hour emergency.
  • Always ask the choking history in recurrent/persistent “pneumonia” of one lobe in a toddler.

  2. What is your diagnosis? (1 pt)

Best answer
1) Two X-ray abnormalities: (a) radio-opaque foreign body (a nail) projected over the LEFT hemithorax/left lower zone; (b) focal left lower-lobe consolidation/atelectatic change (distal to the object). 2) Diagnosis: inhaled foreign body with retention and distal pneumonitis/obstruction. 3) Definitive treatment: rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia with removal of the nail (both diagnostic and therapeutic — this is the definitive treatment).
Any radio-opaque object in a child with respiratory symptoms is an aspiration until proven otherwise; batteries are a 2-hour emergency. Prevention counselling: no nuts/small objects <5 y.

Key differentiators: incubation period, vomiting vs diarrhoea predominance, watery vs bloody, food type, setting (outbreak).

Management of acute diarrhoea: oral rehydration (ORS) is the cornerstone — IV fluids only if severe dehydration/unable to tolerate. Antibiotics NOT indicated for most (NOT for EHEC — precipitates HUS). Test stool only if bloody/severe/prolonged/immunocompromised.

Exam pearls
  • Cruise ship + everyone vomiting = norovirus. Reheated rice = B. cereus. Custard/cream 2 h later = S. aureus.
  • Bloody diarrhoea after beef + HUS risk = EHEC — NO antibiotics.
  • Bloody diarrhoea + travel = Shigella/Campylobacter; persistent after travel = Giardia.
  • Fluids first; antibiotics rarely.

Glomerulonephritis & Haematuria (Children)

Glomerular haematuria vs non-glomerular: glomerular = dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, smoky/tea-coloured urine, proteinuria, hypertension, renal impairment. Non-glomerular = red/pink urine, isomorphic RBCs, clots, no casts.

Post-streptococcal GNIgA nephropathy (synpharyngitic)AlportHSP nephritis
Timing vs URTI2–3 weeks AFTER throat/skin infectionWithin 1–2 days (“synpharyngitic”)Persistent/familialWith purpura (simultaneous)
ComplementLOW C3 (normalises in 6–8 wks); C4 normalNormalNormalNormal
Other labsASO ↑ (anti-streptolysin O) / anti-DNase B; throat swab may be negativeNormalNormal; hearing loss + ocular (anterior lenticonus)Normal ± renal involvement
Age5–12 yAdolescents/young adultsChildren, X-linked (boys)2–11 y
HistologyDiffuse proliferative GNMesangial proliferation, IgA depositsBasketweave GBM (EM); Type IV collagenIgA deposition (same disease as IgA nephropathy)
OutcomeSelf-limiting (95%+ recover)Variable; 20–40% progress to CKD over decadesProgressive CKD + sensorineural deafnessUsually good; monitor urine/BP for 12–24 mo

Features of nephritic syndrome: haematuria (smoky), hypertension, mild–moderate proteinuria, oedema (periorbital), oliguria. Management PSGN: supportive (salt/water restriction, antihypertensives), no steroids/antibiotics needed for the kidney (antibiotics treat the strep carrier state and prevent spread, not the GN); follow-up to confirm C3 normalisation; persistent hypertension/renal impairment → biopsy.

Alport: persistent glomerular haematuria + family history of males with CKD + sensorineural hearing loss + anterior lenticonus — COL4A5 (X-linked, 80%); supportive; ACEi slows proteinuria; genetic counselling; transplant is not contraindicated (no anti-GBM in most).

Exam pearls
  • Haematuria 2–3 weeks AFTER sore throat + low C3 + high ASO = PSGN.
  • Haematuria DURING sore throat + normal C3 = IgA nephropathy.
  • Haematuria + deafness + family history of renal failure = Alport.
  • Hypertension + periorbital oedema + smoky urine in a child = nephritic — check ASO/C3 first.

Growth — Assessment, Percentiles & Faltering Growth

Key measurements: weight-for-age, length/height-for-age, weight-for-height/BMI, head circumference (0–2 y). BMI (child) = weight(kg) / height(m)² — age & sex needed only to plot centiles.

Normal variant patterns:

  • Parent-determined (familial short stature): height follows parental target centile; normal growth velocity; bone age = chronological age.
  • Constitutional delay: short stature + delayed puberty; growth catches up later; bone age delayed; normal final height (just later). “Late bloomer.”
  • Pathological: endocrine (hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, Cushing’s), chronic disease (coeliac, CF, CKD, asthma on steroids), neglect, genetic syndromes.

Faltering growth (failure to thrive): weight crossing down ≥1–2 centile lines (or weight below 3rd centile), often weight before height; causes — inadequate intake (feeding problems, poverty, neglect), inadequate absorption (coeliac, CF, CMPA), excessive losses (vomiting, diarrhoea — coeliac/CF), increased requirements (chronic infection, malignancy, hyperthyroidism). First step: plot the chart accurately + dietary history + observe a feed (for infants). Investigations guided by history: urine dip/MC&S, coeliac serology, sweat test, FBC, U&E/LFT, TFT, lead, development.

Reading growth charts: plot with correct age/sex chart; centiles: 3rd–97th ≈ normal; below 3rd = short/underweight; above 97th = tall/overweight; height above 97th centile — think Marfan/overgrowth; weight <3rd with height 50th = acute undernutrition (wasting); both <3rd = chronic; height <3rd with normal weight = “failure to thrive with preserved weight” — hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, skeletal dysplasia, syndromes.

Velocity matters more than one point: falling off the centile line (even within the normal range) is abnormal; single readings need confirmation.

Head circumference: ~34–35 cm at birth; +2 cm/mo ×3, then +1 cm/mo; at 12 mo ≈ 46 cm; macrocephaly >98th (hydrocephalus — check fontanelle, developmental progress); microcephaly <2nd (congenital infections, TORCH, chromosomal, metabolic).

Exam pearls
  • BMI = weight ÷ height² — needs only weight & height for the value; age/sex for the centile plot.
  • Weight <3rd + height 50th = wasting (acute); height <3rd + weight normal = endocrine/skeletal.
  • Deceleration (crossing down lines) = the red flag — plot and re-measure.
  • Faltering growth + offensive stools + recurrent chest infections = CF/coeliac — sweat test + tTG.

Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome (HUS)

Definition: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia + thrombocytopenia + acute kidney injury — classically in children after diarrhoeal illness.

Typical (D+) HUS — 90%: preceded (2–14 days) by bloody diarrhoea from Shiga toxin–producing E. coli (STEC/EHEC 0157:H7) or Shigella dysenteriae. Toxin damages glomerular endothelium → platelet-rich microthrombi → intravascular haemolysis with schistocytes, low platelets, renal failure (oliguria, haematuria, hypertension, uraemia). Antibiotics and antimotility agents INCREASE toxin release — avoid. Chicken/undercooked beef/unpasteurised milk are sources.

Atypical (D−) HUS — 10%: complement dysregulation (factor H/I/MCP mutations), Strep pneumoniae (neuraminidase exposure of Thomsen–Friedenreich antigen), drugs, pregnancy, malignancy — recurs, worse prognosis; treat with plasma exchange/eculizumab (anti-C5).

HUS vs TTP: TTP = adults, neuro symptoms (seizures, confusion) + fever + severe organ dysfunction, platelets very low, ADAMTS13 deficiency; neuro-dominant. HUS = children, renal-dominant, post-bloody diarrhoea. Both = schistocytes + thrombocytopenia + haemolysis.

Features asked in this exam: thrombocytopenia + haemolytic anaemia with schistocytes (± bloody diarrhoea, renal impairment, seizures). Seizures can occur — especially in severe HUS/TTP.

Management: SUPPORTIVE is the cornerstone — careful IV fluids/electrolytes, transfuse packed red cells (Hb <70/symptomatic), dialysis for renal failure indications, NO platelets (unless active bleeding), NO antibiotics in STEC, control hypertension; early nephrology; monitor for neurological involvement. Most children recover renal function (70–80%); ~5% mortality; ~25% develop some chronic renal impairment — long-term follow-up.

Exam pearls
  • Bloody diarrhoea (undercooked beef) → child + pallor + oliguria + petechiae → HUS.
  • Schistocytes + low platelets + AKI = MAHA triad.
  • NEVER antibiotics for STEC-0157 — triggers HUS.
  • HUS = kidney; TTP = brain. Support the kidney; don’t give platelets.

Immunisation — Live Vaccines, Household Contacts & Contraindications

Live (attenuated) vaccines: BCG, MMR, varicella, oral polio (OPV), rotavirus, live intranasal influenza, live zoster (Zostavax), yellow fever, oral typhoid, Japanese encephalitis (live SA14). These are replication-competent — dangerous in severe immunosuppression (chemotherapy, transplant, high-dose steroids, biologics, primary immunodeficiency, HIV with low CD4) and can infect household contacts (OPV shed in stool).

Inactivated/killed/subunit/toxoid: hepatitis B, HiB, pneumococcal (conjugate/polysaccharide), DTP/Tdap, injectable polio (IPV), hepatitis A, HPV, injectable influenza, meningococcal — safe in immunosuppression.

Absolute contraindications: anaphylaxis to a previous dose or vaccine component; live vaccines in severe immunosuppression/pregnancy (MMR, varicella, BCG, OPV, yellow fever). NOT contraindications: mild febrile illness, recent exposure, prematurity (vaccinate by chronological age), breastfeeding, family history of seizures/adverse events, stable neurological conditions, antibiotic therapy, recovery from recent illness, local reaction/low-grade fever after dose.

Household contact rule (tested twice here): a severely immunocompromised child (chemotherapy for leukaemia) living with a sibling — the sibling must NOT receive live vaccines, especially OPV (viral shedding can paralyse the immunocompromised child) and BCG/varicella/MMR where applicable; use inactivated alternatives (IPV instead of OPV). Close contacts of transplant patients: avoid live vaccines except MMR/VZV per guidance (risk-benefit).

Tetanus prophylaxis for wounds: fully immunised + booster within 5 years → nothing; booster 5–10 y (clean wound) / any high-risk wound with booster >5 y → booster; incomplete/uncertain + high-risk wound → tetanus toxoid + tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG); dirty wounds: check.

Special situations: egg allergy → influenza/MMR/yellow fever generally safe with observation (severe egg anaphylaxis → specialist); HIV (CD4 >200): give MMR/varicella; pregnancy: no live vaccines (give MMR postpartum; Tdap from 16 weeks each pregnancy for pertussis; influenza any trimester); premature infants: vaccinate by chronological age.

Exam pearls
  • Chemo child at home → sibling gets IPV, NOT OPV; no live vaccines.
  • Immunosuppressed transplant patient → no live vaccines, ever (varicella!).
  • Only true general contraindication = anaphylaxis to prior dose. Mild illness ≠ contraindication.

2017 · Pediatrics · 1 question · EMQ

Innocent Murmurs & Still’s Murmur

Innocent murmurs are harmless flow murmurs with NO structural heart disease — common (up to 50% of children at some point). Recognition is the skill: no symptoms, normal examination otherwise (normal growth, normal S1/S2/split, no clicks/thrills/rubs, normal pulses, no hepatomegaly).

This exam (Still’s murmur): soft (grade 1–3), vibratory/musical/“twangy” systolic ejection murmur at the left lower/mid sternal edge, age 3–7 y, DISAPPEARS when lying down (changes with position — louder supine/sitting up quieter), well child = innocent (Still’s) murmur. Also innocent: pulmonary flow murmur (soft ESM at LUSB, louder supine), venous hum (continuous, supraclavicular, louder sitting, disappears supine/ with head turn), peripheral pulmonary stenosis of the newborn (soft ESM, back/axilla, disappears by ~6 mo).

Red flags needing echo: any symptoms (breathlessness, syncope, chest pain, poor feeding/failure to thrive, cyanosis), abnormal S2 (fixed split, single S2, loud P2), diastolic murmur, thrill, click, pansystolic, louder with standing, abnormal pulses/BP, family history of sudden death/CHD, abnormal ECG, unequal sats.

Management: still’s → reassure, no investigation, no follow-up beyond routine. Record in notes; safety-net advice; reassure parents (“the heart is normal; the noise is just blood flowing”).

Exam pearls
  • Vibratory systolic murmur that VANISHES lying flat in a well child = innocent (Still’s).
  • Diastolic/continuous louder standing/abnormal S2 = NOT innocent → echo.
  • Innocent murmurs are systolic, soft, short, positional — never diastolic.

Meningitis — CSF, Causative Organisms & Meningococcaemia

CSF interpretation — the exam table:

NeutrophilsGlucoseProteinPressureClassic
Bacterial↑↑ (pleocytosis, often >1000)LOW (<½ plasma)↑↑Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae b (unimmunised), neonates Group B strep / E. coli / Listeria (add amoxicillin for listeria cover!)
Viral (aseptic)Lymphocytes (early can be neutrophils)NormalNormal–mild↑Normal–mild↑Enterovirus, HSV-2, VZV, mumps — self-limiting; treat supportive
TuberculousLymphocytesVERY LOW (<2.2 mmol/L)VERY HIGH (1–5 g/L)↑↑Insidious; cranial nerve palsies (VI), basal exudates, hydrocephalus (dilated ventricles); “cobweb” clot; ADA >10; AFB rare — treat with RHZE + dexamethasone
Fungal (Cryptococcus, TB-like)LymphocytesLowHigh↑↑Immunocompromised (HIV) — India ink/CR antigens; amphotericin + flucytosine
GBS (neonatal)AnyAnyAny↑E. coli, GBS — ampicillin + gentamicin

Clinical features: fever, headache, neck stiffness (meningism), photophobia, vomiting, altered consciousness, seizures, non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash (meningococcaemia), Kernig’s (pain on knee extension with hip flexed), Brudzinski’s (neck flexion → hip flexion), bulging fontanelle (infants). Meningococcaemia → septic shock, DIC, Waterhouse–Friderichsen (bilateral adrenal haemorrhage).

Management: do NOT delay antibiotics for imaging/LP if unwell — immediate IV ceftriaxone/cefotaxime (add amoxicillin if <3 months or listeria risk), dexamethasone with first dose (↓hearing loss in pneumococcal; continue if confirmed), ABCDE + fluids/vasopressors (shock), isolate (droplet), notify public health, contact prophylaxis (ciprofloxacin/rifampicin) for household contacts, hearing test after recovery, treat complications (seizures, hydrocephalus — neurosurgery/VP shunt, SIADH).

Neurological exam findings asked (this SAQ): neck stiffness, Kernig’s/Brudzinski’s signs positive, photophobia, altered GCS, focal deficits, bulging fontanelle; complications — sensorineural deafness, seizures, hydrocephalus, subdural effusion, learning difficulty, shock/amputation (meningococcaemia).

Exam pearls
  • LP first only if NO contraindication & child stable; otherwise antibiotics first — never delay.
  • Low glucose + high protein + lymphocytes = TB; high PMN + low glucose = bacteria.
  • Non-blanching purpuric rash + fever = ceftriaxone STAT + public health notification.

  2. What are the neurological findings on physical examination? (2 answers) (2 pt)
  3. What are the complications? (1 pt)

1) Most likely diagnosis: meningococcal meningitis/meningococcemia — fever + vomiting + generalised tonic-clonic seizure + non-blanching purpuric rash on lower limbs (image provided). 2) Neurological findings on examination: (a) signs of meningism — neck stiffness, Kernig’s and Brudzinski’s signs positive, photophobia; (b) bulging fontanelle/altered level of consciousness (± focal neurology, papilloedema). 3) Complications: sensorineural hearing loss, seizures/epilepsy, hydrocephalus (± VP shunt), subdural effusion/empyema, cerebral palsy/learning difficulties — and in meningococcaemia: septic shock, DIC, Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome (adrenal haemorrhage), limb gangrene/amputation, death.
TREAT FIRST: IV ceftriaxone STAT (do not wait for LP/imaging), ABCDE + fluids, dexamethasone with first dose; admit ICU if unwell; public-health notification + household prophylaxis (ciprofloxacin/rifampicin); hearing test post-recovery.
2017 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

Thresholds: operational definition used for management = plasma glucose <2.6 mmol/L (47 mg/dL) in the first days — treat below this; <1.5–2.0 at 24 h is an emergency. “Minimum safest glucose range” in this exam = ≥2.6 mmol/L.

At-risk groups: preterm, SGA/IUGR, LGA (esp. infants of diabetic mothers), perinatal stress/asphyxia, hypothermia, sepsis, IDM (hyperinsulinaemia), inborn errors (FAO defects, glycogen storage), hyperinsulinism (congenital — diffuse β-cell), maternal hypoglycaemic drugs (after delivery — e.g., sulfonylureas cross placenta).

Symptoms: jitteriness/tremors, lethargy/poor feeding, apnoea, hypotonia, seizures, high-pitched cry, sweating, pallor, temperature instability — or asymptomatic.

Monitoring & management: check glucose within 1–2 h of birth and before feeds until ≥2.6 twice; at-risk all. Asymptomatic & ≥1.5–2.0: feed immediately + recheck in 30–60 min. Symptomatic or <1.5–2.0: IV 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg bolus then maintenance 4–6 mg/kg/min; if persistent → glucagon (if sufficient stores), consider diazoxide for hyperinsulinism; investigate cause; never give plain water. Longer dextrose needs: check urine strip for ketones (+ in FAO defects → avoid prolonged fasting & give low-fat meals; IV glucose if needed).

Exam pearls
  • <2.6 mmol/L = treat (feed or dextrose). Asymptomatic + mild = feed first, recheck.
  • IDM = hyperinsulinaemia → early feeds + early checks.
  • Seizure in a newborn = glucose FIRST, always.

Neonatal Jaundice

Approach by timing:

TimingThink of
<24 h (always pathological)Haemolysis — Rh incompatibility (Rh-neg mother + Rh-pos baby), ABO incompatibility (O mother + A/B baby), G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis, sepsis (congenital), polycythaemia; direct hyperbilirubinaemia (TORCH/sepsis — urgent)
24 h–2 wksPhysiological (peak day 3–4, unconjugated, well baby, resolves ≤2 wks), breast-milk jaundice (peaks week 2, feeding well — continue breastfeeding), breastfeeding failure jaundice (under-feeding, weight loss — feed more), haemolysis, infection, polycythaemia, cephalohaematoma bruising
>2 wks (prolonged)Conjugated (cholestatic): biliary atresia (pale stools + dark urine — Kasai portoenterostomy before 8–12 wks!), choledochal cyst, Alagille, inborn errors (galactosaemia, α1-AT), infection (UTI!), hypothyroidism, breast-milk jaundice, haemolysis persisting

This exam’s EMQ (2020 set): day 3, well, unconjugated, resolves → physiological; first 24 h, mother O/baby A, DAT+, mild anaemia → ABO incompatibility; first day, Rh-neg mother sensitised (previous Rh-pos baby, no anti-D) → Rh incompatibility (severe — exchange transfusion risk); day 5 boy, male relatives affected, haemolysis → G6PD deficiency.

ABO vs Rh: ABO — mother O, baby A/B; usually mild, 1st baby can be affected (naturally occurring anti-A/B IgG), DAT weak/negative, no prenatal prophylaxis works (no anti-D for ABO). Rh — mother Rh-neg, baby Rh-pos; usually NOT first baby (needs sensitisation, unless prior transfusion/miscarriage), DAT strongly positive, severe haemolysis (hydrops fetalis), prevented by anti-D Ig (at 28/34 wks + within 72 h of delivery/sensitising events).

G6PD deficiency — X-linked; males; episodic severe haemolysis with infection/fava beans/drugs (sulfonamides, primaquine, nitrofurantoin, methylene blue); Mediterranean/African/Asian; avoid precipitants; check level; Heinz bodies/bite cells.

Management: monitor bilirubin (TSB or transcutaneous); phototherapy per age-appropriate thresholds (chart); exchange transfusion if severe (or BIND scores — bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction: lethargy, poor feeding, arching, high-pitched cry, later kernicterus — athetoid CP, hearing loss, gaze palsy); IVIG if immune haemolysis failing phototherapy; treat cause; breastfeeding support; prolonged conjugated → urgent USS + hepatology (biliary atresia timing critical).

Exam pearls
  • Jaundice <24 h = pathological — find the haemolysis.
  • Mother O + baby A/B = ABO (DAT±). Mother Rh− + baby Rh+ + prior affected sibling = Rh — anti-D prevents.
  • Pale stools + dark urine at 2–3 weeks = biliary atresia — Kasai before 8–12 weeks, every week counts.
  • G6PD: check family history of male jaundice; avoid oxidants.

#267MCQ edited2017-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-d8f4dff2
8 hours after delivery (G3P2), total bilirubin is 30 and direct bilirubin is 8. Mother is blood type A- and the son is O+. Her previous baby had jaundice. What is the reason for the baby's deterioration?
  • A. ABO incompatibility
  • B. Rh incompatibility
  • C. G6PD deficiency
  • D. Physiological jaundice
  • E. Hereditary spherocytosis
Best answer
B. Rh incompatibility
Mother A-negative (Rh−), baby O-positive (Rh+), previous baby with jaundice (prior sensitisation), jaundice at 8 h with total bilirubin 30 → severe haemolytic disease of the newborn from anti-D (Rh) antibodies crossing the placenta. ABO incompatibility cannot occur here (mother A, baby O — no A/B antigen in baby). Needs urgent phototherapy/exchange ± IVIG; mother should have received anti-D prophylaxis; give anti-D post-delivery.

Differential by timing, mode of delivery and X-ray:

OnsetAt/within minutes–hours of birthWithin hours (2–6 h), resolves 24–72 hWithin hoursHours–daysAny time; sudden desaturation
X-rayGround-glass reticulogranular + air bronchograms + low lung volumesPerihilar streaking + fluid in fissures, hyperinflated, normal volumesCoarse patchy infiltrates, hyperinflation, flattened diaphragm, ± air leaksVariable — focal infiltrate/effusion or normalVisceral pleural line + absent lung markings beyond it; mediastinal shift if tension

This exam’s questions: 34-weeker + ground-glass = surfactant deficiency (RDS); term C-section + 3 h of distress = TTN; pea-soup liquor = MAS; PPROM = neonatal sepsis; post-C-section tachypnoea = TTN.

Acute care principles: ABCDE; thermoregulation; O₂ sats monitoring; blood glucose; escalate to CPAP/ventilation, CXR, treat sepsis if suspected (don’t wait for cultures), transfer to NICU.

Exam pearls
  • Ground-glass + air bronchograms + preterm = RDS = surfactant.
  • Term + LSCS + tachypnea in first hours = TTN = supportive.
  • Pea-soup liquor = MAS. PPROM + maternal infection = sepsis work-up now.
  • Sudden desaturation + asymmetry = pneumothorax — transilluminate/CXR.

Neonatal Resuscitation (NRP/ILCOR)

The golden questions at birth: term? breathing/crying? good tone? If YES to all → skin-to-skin, routine care. If NO → warm, dry, stimulate → reassess (30 s) → if apnoeic/gasping or HR <100 → positive-pressure ventilation (PPV) at 40–60 breaths/min, monitor heart rate (stethoscope/cord pulse/ECG — the best resuscitation monitor), pulse oximetry pre-ductal (right hand).

Algorithm: PPV → HR <100 after 30 s effective ventilation → ensure airway open (MR SOPA: Mask, Reposition, Suction, Open mouth, Pressure increase, Alternate airway — LMA/ETT) → if HR <60 after 30 s ventilation + chest compressions (3:1 compression:breath, 90 compressions + 30 breaths/min) + 100% O₂ + ETT + IV/IO adrenaline 10–30 microgram/kg (0.1–0.3 mL/kg of 1:10,000) → if HR remains <60 → repeat adrenaline every 3–5 min + consider volume (10 mL/kg 0.9% saline/O-negative blood if blood loss) → if no response ≥20 min: discuss stopping (poor prognosis), involve parents.

Meconium-stained liquor (this exam): vigorous + breathing/crying + good tone → routine care (no suction); NOT breathing or poor tone → open airway, clear secretions under direct vision, then PPV; if PPV ineffective or thick meconium obstructing → intubate and suction the trachea (only if trained/appropriate — not routine intubation of all meconium babies); do NOT routinely suction below the cords of vigorous infants; chest compressions only if HR <60 despite ventilation.

Apgar score (1 & 5 min; again at 10 if low): Appearance (colour), Pulse, Grimace (reflex irritability), Activity (tone), Respiration — 0–2 each. NOT used to guide resuscitation decisions — act on HR/breathing, not the score. Apgar 4 (this exam) = severe depression → immediate resuscitation.

Aftercare: prevent hypothermia (skin-to-skin, warm), monitor glucose, feeding, watch for complications (PPHN, hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy — consider therapeutic hypothermia if ≥36 wks, moderate/severe HIE within 6 h).

Exam pearls
  • First step for apnoeic baby after stimulation fails = PPV (not chest compressions, not O₂ mask).
  • Heart rate is THE monitor. Compressions only after effective ventilation.
  • Meconium + apnoeic/poor = clear airway under direct vision → PPV → intubate only if obstructed/failing.

2017 · Pediatrics · 1 question · MCQ

Nephrotic Syndrome & Proteinuria (Children)

Definition: (1) proteinuria — nephrotic range: urine PCR >200 mg/mmol (spot) or >40 mg/m²/h (24 h) or 3–4+ dipstick; (2) hypoalbuminaemia (<25 g/L typically); (3) oedema (periorbital, genital, dependent, ascites/pleural effusions); ± hyperlipidaemia.

Causes by age (critical age splits):

  • Congenital (<3 months): congenital nephrotic syndrome (Finnish type) — NPHS1 (nephrin) mutation; massive proteinuria from birth; needs albumin infusions + ACE-i + eventually bilateral nephrectomy + transplant. Also Denys–Drash, Pierson syndrome.
  • 1–12 years: MINIMAL CHANGE DISEASE (~90%) — steroid-SENSITIVE; insidious onset oedema over days; normal renal function, complement normal; NO haematuria (if present → biopsy). Diagnosis = clinical — empirical prednisolone 60 mg/m²/d (max 60–80 mg) ×4–6 weeks then taper; 85–90% respond (remission in 2–4 weeks). Biopsy ONLY if: age <1 or >12, steroid resistance (no response by 4–6 wks), haematuria, hypertension, low complement, renal impairment, atypical course.
  • Steroid-resistant/frequent relapsers/adults: FSGS, membranoproliferative GN, membranous nephropathy, IgA, lupus (renal biopsy to differentiate). FSGS commonest in steroid non-responders (and in older children).
  • Secondary: infections (post-strep, hepatitis B/C, HIV), SLE, HSP/IgA, drugs (NSAIDs — membranous), amyloid, malignancy.

Orthostatic (postural) proteinuria — benign; adolescent; proteinuria when upright, absent in first-morning urine; normal renal function/complement; confirm with split urine samples (early AM vs daytime) or first-void UPCR <20 mg/mmol; NO treatment, annual review.

Management of MCD: prednisolone course; relapses (proteinuria return) → re-treat; frequent relapsers → alternate-day low-dose steroids or second-line (levamisole, cyclophosphamide, cyclosporine, mycophenolate/tacrolimus; rituximab); oedema — salt restriction, fluid restriction if severe, loop diuretics (furosemide ± spironolactone) + IV albumin if severe symptomatic hypovolaemia (then furosemide); immunisations (pneumococcal + meningococcal + influenza — infection risk from immunosuppression + loss of complement/immunoglobulins); thrombosis risk (hypercoagulable — sparse activity restriction, avoid dehydration; consider aspirin/warfarin if albumin very low <20 g/L or thrombotic event); lipids — usually normalise with remission.

Investigations at presentation: urine dip/PCR, serum albumin, renal function, lipids, C3/C4, ASO (excludes PSGN), FBC (infection), urine microscopy; exclude secondary causes (ANA, HBV/HCV); biopsy only as above.

Exam pearls
  • Child >1 y + oedema + heavy proteinuria + normal renal function = MCD → steroids — biopsy only if atypical.
  • Proteinuria only when standing = orthostatic — split samples, benign.
  • <3 months onset = congenital (Finnish) — nephrin; very bad; genetic testing.
  • Steroid resistance → biopsy → FSGS.

2017 · Pediatrics · 3 questions · MCQ

Neurodevelopmental Disorders — ADHD & ASD

ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder): persistent (≥6 months), onset <12 y, in ≥2 settings (home + school): inattention (careless mistakes, can’t sustain attention, doesn’t listen, fails to finish tasks — “does he leave tasks uncompleted?”), hyperactivity (fidgets, leaves seat, “driven by a motor”, talks excessively), impulsivity (blurts out, can’t wait turn, interrupts). Prevalence ~5%; boys > girls; strong genetic component (74%); co-morbid: ASD, conduct disorder, learning difficulties, anxiety, tics.

Diagnosis: clinical — interview parents + child + teacher rating scales (Conners, SNAP-IV); exclude mimics (hearing/vision, sleep apnoea, thyroid, absence seizures, iron deficiency, lead, psychosocial); DSM-5/ICD-11 criteria (≥6 inattentive and/or ≥6 hyperactive-impulsive symptoms).

Management: psychoeducation (parents, child, school — seat front, chunked tasks, movement breaks, immediate rewards); environmental interventions first for preschoolers; medication for ≥6 y (or moderate–severe): methylphenidate (first-line — immediate/modified release), lisdexamfetamine, atomoxetine (non-stimulant — if stimulants contraindicated), guanfacine; monitor growth, appetite, BP/HR, sleep; review every 6 months.

Autism spectrum disorder: impaired social communication/interaction (poor eye contact, no joint attention, not pointing by 18 mo, not sharing enjoyment, no pretend play, difficulty reading social cues) + restricted, repetitive behaviours (hand-flapping, lining up toys, rigid routines, sensory hyper/hyposensitivity, intense narrow interests). Recognised by 12–24 months; red flags: not responding to name, no babble, no pointing, no words by 18 mo, regression of language/social skills.

Screening: M-CHAT-R/F at 16–30 months (universal at 18 months) → positive → referral for formal developmental assessment (ADOS, MDT).

Management: early intervention (EI) programmes, behavioural therapy (ABA/ESDM), speech & language therapy (PECS if non-verbal), occupational therapy (sensory/integration), educational support, family counselling; treat comorbidities (sleep, anxiety, GI); NO medication for core symptoms (only for associated ADHD/irritability — risperidone short-term for severe aggression).

Exam pearls
  • M-CHAT at 16–30 months. 18-month universal screen.
  • ADHD: methylphenidate first-line ≥6 y; psychoeducation + behavioural always.
  • Language delay → HEARING TEST first — then M-CHAT/ASD screen.
  • Regression = urgent evaluation (metabolic, neuroimaging, genetics).

#280MCQ edited2017-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-31a5a7f3
A child is restless and impulsive with decreased school performance. What is the diagnosis?
  • A. ADHD
  • B. ASD
  • C. Anxiety disorder
  • D. Learning disability
  • E. Conduct disorder
Best answer
A. ADHD
Restless + impulsive + decreased school performance = ADHD — inattention/hyperactivity/impulsivity in ≥2 settings, early onset. Conduct disorder = aggression/rule-breaking; learning disability = isolated academic failure; ASD = social-communication deficit + RRB.
#286MCQ edited2017-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-f06b43b5
A child came to the clinic with his parents with a history of not socializing with other children; his hearing and vision were normal. What is the diagnosis?
  • A. ADHD
  • B. Autism spectrum disorder (ASD)
  • C. Language delay
  • D. Reactive attachment disorder
  • E. Intellectual disability
Best answer
B. Autism spectrum disorder (ASD)
Poor social interaction (not socialising with peers) with normal hearing and vision = autism spectrum disorder — also look for language delay, restricted/repetitive behaviour, poor eye contact. ADHD = hyperactive/impulsive; learning disability = cognitive; conduct = antisocial.
#304MCQ edited2017-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-c90fc947
A child came to the clinic with his parents with a history of not focusing in class, disruptive playing and inability to sit; his hearing and IQ were normal. What is the diagnosis?
  • A. ADHD
  • B. ASD
  • C. Anxiety disorder
  • D. Learning disorder
  • E. Conduct disorder
Best answer
A. ADHD
Distractible in class, disruptive, can’t sit still, normal hearing & IQ = ADHD — combined inattentive-hyperactive type. Learning disorder = isolated academic difficulty; conduct = rule-breaking/aggression; ASD = social communication.

Primary Immunodeficiency

The clinical rule: pattern of infection tells you the defect:

ArmTypical infectionsDiseases
B-cell (antibody)Recurrent bacterial — sinopulmonary (pneumonia, sinusitis, otitis), encapsulated organisms (S. pneumo, H. flu), enteroviruses, Giardia; present after 6 months (maternal IgG gone)X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (Bruton — BTK) — ABSENT TONSILS/LYMPH NODES (this exam), absent B cells/Ig; common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) — low IgG, later onset; IgA deficiency (commonest — recurrent sinopulmonary/GI, anaphylaxis to blood products)
T-cellViral, fungal, protozoal, mycobacteria, opportunisticSevere combined immunodeficiency (SCID) — absent T (± B/NK) cells — absent thymic shadow on CXR (this exam!), chronic diarrhoea, failure to thrive, opportunistic infections from birth; DiGeorge (22q11) — thymic hypoplasia + hypocalcaemia + cardiac + cleft
PhagocyteCatalase-positive organisms — S. aureus, Serratia, Burkholderia, Aspergillus; deep abscesses, osteomyelitis; granulomasChronic granulomatous disease (CGD) — NADPH oxidase defect; leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD) — delayed umbilical stump separation, no pus, neutrophilia — treat: HSCT
ComplementRecurrent Neisseria (C5–9 MAC deficiency), SLE-like picture (C1q/C4)Complement deficiencies

This exam: repeated infections from birth + absent thymus on CXR = DiGeorge syndrome (absent/hypoplastic thymus — T-cell deficiency); recurrent infections + no tonsils + maternal uncle = X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (Bruton’s) — haemoglobin and lymphocytes may be normal; immunoglobulins very low; check CD19 B cells absent; treatment = lifelong replacement immunoglobulin therapy (IVIG/SCIG) + antibiotics.

Exam pearls
  • Absent tonsils/nodes + boys + bacterial infections = XLA.
  • Absent thymus on CXR = DiGeorge (22q11) — check Ca, echo, FISH.
  • SCID = no T cells — urgent HSCT before infection/vaccination.

#264MCQ edited2017-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-39a481ab
A child presents with recurrent infections; his mother's brother died young of similar conditions. On examination you find no tonsils. What is the most likely diagnosis?
  • A. Common variable immunodeficiency
  • B. X-linked agammaglobulinemia
  • C. SCID
  • D. DiGeorge syndrome
  • E. Chronic granulomatous disease
Best answer
B. X-linked agammaglobulinemia
Recurrent bacterial infections + absent tonsils/lymph nodes + affected maternal uncle + onset in boys = X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (Bruton — BTK mutation) — absent B cells/immunoglobulins from ~6 months (maternal Ig gone). Confirm: immunoglobulin levels (very low/absent), absent CD19 B cells, BTK sequencing; treat: replacement IVIG/SCIG.

Grunting & Work of Breathing in Children

Grunting = premature closure of the glottis during EXHALATION → generates positive end-expiratory pressure (auto-PEEP) → keeps alveoli open, increases functional residual capacity (FRC) and improves gas exchange. It is a sign of significant respiratory distress (like nasal flaring, chest recession, tachypnoea, head-bobbing in infants) — not a “harmless noise”.

Seen in: bronchiolitis (this exam — RSV), neonatal RDS, pneumonia, asthma exacerbation, pulmonary oedema/ARDS, neonatal sepsis.

This exam (two identical questions across 2017/2020): “Grunting → increases end-expiratory pressure” (A) / “Grunting physiology → keeps alveoli open (auto-PEEP)” — answer is the same concept; it increases FRC (does NOT decrease it) and does NOT reduce oxygen demand.

Assessment of work of breathing: rate + recession (subcostal/intercostal/sternal) + nasal flaring + grunting + head-bobbing (infants) + tracheal tug; red flags: apnoea, exhaustion, SpO₂ <90–92% despite O₂, altered consciousness, silent chest, hypoxaemia — immediate senior review/ITU.

Exam pearls
  • Grunting = auto-PEEP, keeps alveoli open.
  • All these signs (nasal flare, recession, grunt, head bob) = get help now.
  • Bronchiolitis: supportive + oxygen — no salbutamol/steroids routinely.

#275MCQ edited2017-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-ae097b79
A child is grunting. Which of the following is true about grunting?
  • A. It increases end-expiratory pressure
  • B. It increases inspiratory pressure
  • C. It increases airway diameter
  • D. It reduces oxygen demand
  • E. It decreases functional residual capacity
Best answer
A. It increases end-expiratory pressure
Grunting = forced expiration against a closed/partially closed glottis → generates auto-PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) → keeps alveoli open, increases FRC, improves oxygenation in bronchiolitis/RDS. It is a sign of significant respiratory distress (like nasal flaring and recessions) — treat the cause, give O₂.

Acute Rheumatic Fever

Definition: systemic autoimmune disease after Group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes) pharyngitis (never skin); 2–4 weeks after infection; type II hypersensitivity (molecular mimicry) — antibodies cross-react with valve/joint/brain antigens. Peak 5–15 y.

Jones criteria (2015): need evidence of preceding GAS infection (↑ASO titre or anti-DNase B, positive throat swab, or recent scarlet fever) + 2 major OR 1 major + 2 minor:

MAJOR (JONES)MINOR
Joints — migratory polyarthritis (knees/ankles/wrists/elbows — “moves from joint to joint”)
O — carditis (new murmur — mitral regurgitation (apical pansystolic → axilla), tachycardia, pericarditis/pleuritic pain, or echo valve regurgitation)
N — subcutaneous nodules (extensor surfaces, painless)
E — erythema marginatum (pink, ringed, non-pruritic rash on trunk)
S — Sydenham’s chorea (involuntary movements, emotional lability — may appear months later)		Fever; arthralgia; raised ESR/CRP; prolonged PR interval; previous RF/rheumatic heart disease

This exam: migratory polyarthritis + ASO+ + ESR/CRP↑ + new apical pansystolic murmur radiating to axilla = rheumatic fever with carditis (mitral regurgitation).

Management: eradicate strep — penicillin V/benzathine penicillin IM (or erythromycin); NSAIDs (naproxen/ibuprofen) for arthritis (avoid aspirin in children — Reye’s); severe carditis → prednisolone; bed rest while active; SECONDARY PROPHYLAXIS (the most important): penicillin V 250 mg BD (or benzathine penicillin 1.2 MU IM every 3–4 weeks) for 10 years or until age 21–25 (longer — life / to 40 y — if carditis); echo/serial follow-up for valvular disease; echo every 1–5 years; dental prophylaxis if prosthetic valve; avoid NSAIDs if renal issues.

Exam pearls
  • Migratory polyarthritis + post-strep + new MR murmur = RF with carditis.
  • Jones: 2 major or 1 major + 2 minor + evidence of GAS (ASO).
  • MS mid-diastolic murmur comes years later — acute RF gives MR (pansystolic).
  • Secondary prophylaxis benzathine penicillin every 3–4 weeks ×10 years — stops progression to chronic rheumatic heart disease.

#369SAQ edited2017-Pediatrics-SAQ-Medicine-512f8231
A patient presents with fever, pain in a finger joint then the knee joint, with tenderness; ESR high, CRP high, ASO titer positive, and a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla.
  1. What is the diagnosis? (1 pt)
  2. List four criteria mentioned in the case. (4 pt)
Best answer
1) Rheumatic fever (acute rheumatic carditis + migratory polyarthritis post-streptococcal; ASO+; pansystolic murmur at apex radiating to axilla = mitral regurgitation). 2) Four criteria from the case: (a) migratory polyarthritis (major), (b) carditis — new apical pansystolic murmur of MR (major), (c) fever (minor), (d) elevated ESR and CRP + raised ASO titre (minor + evidence of preceding GAS infection; also arthralgia).
Jones criteria diagnose RF. Treat: eradicate strep (penicillin V), NSAIDs/aspirin for arthritis, steroids if severe carditis; secondary prophylaxis IM benzathine penicillin 3–4-weekly for 10 years/into adulthood (longer if carditis).

Seizures & Epilepsy

Semiology first — type defines treatment:

TypeFeaturesDrug of choice
Absence (typical)Child 4–10 y; sudden staring/“in a daze”, eyelid flutter, 5–15 s, many per day, no post-ictal confusion; 3 Hz spike-waveEthosuximide (or valproate)
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME)Morning myoclonic jerks of limbs/shoulders + GTC seizures + absence; onset 12–18 y; sleep deprivation/alcohol trigger; 4–6 Hz polyspike-waveSodium valproate (females of childbearing age: levetiracetam/lamotrigine)
Temporal lobe (focal impaired awareness)Aura (epigastric rising / déjà vu / burning smell — “burning leather”), staring, lip-smacking/automatisms (chewing, picking), post-ictal confusionCarbamazepine / lamotrigine / levetiracetam
Generalized tonic-clonicSudden fall, tongue biting, incontinence, post-ictal drowsiness/confusionValproate / levetiracetam
Infantile spasms (West syndrome)3–12 months; salaam attacks — sudden flexion of head/trunk/limbs in clusters; hypsarrhythmia on EEG; developmental regression — treat with vigabatrin ± ACTH; think tuberous sclerosisVigabatrin ± steroids
Febrile seizure6 mo–5 y, fever, generalized, <15 min, single in 24 h = SIMPLE (benign, ~1% later epilepsy); complex: focal / >15 min / recurrence within 24 hReassurance + safety (side position, nothing in mouth); treat fever does NOT prevent recurrence; benzodiazepine if >5 min
Non-epileptic (psychogenic) seizureEyes closed, prolonged fluctuating jerks, pelvic thrusting, crying/emotional context (exam stress), NO incontinence/tongue bite/injury/post-ictal state; normal EEGCBT/psychology — NOT anti-epileptics

Management of acute seizure (this exam): ABCDE + position + O₂ → abortive drug if >5 min: midazolam (buccal/IM/IV) or lorazepam IV or diazepam IV/PR — repeat once → if still seizing (status): second-line levetiracetam / phenytoin / valproate (>15–20 min) → refractory (>40 min): phenobarbital or anaesthesia + ICU. Maintenance after abortion of prolonged convulsion: continue anti-seizure prophylaxis with sodium valproate (or leviteracetam), not single-agent benzodiazepines alone.

Risk factors for epilepsy after febrile convulsion: complex febrile seizure, family history of epilepsy, pre-existing neurodevelopmental delay, short interval from fever onset to seizure (<1 h). Simple febrile = near-population risk.

Exam pearls
  • “Smell burning leather + lip smacking + staring” = temporal lobe epilepsy. “Morning limb jerks” = JME. “Exam-time jerks, eyes closed, crying, no incontinence” = psychogenic.
  • Absence = ethosuximide. Status: midazolam → phenytoin/levetiracetam → phenobarbital.
  • Febrile seizure ≠ epilepsy; complex features are the risk.

#314MCQ edited2017-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-d6d62c05
A child had an ongoing 15-minute episode of seizure and went to the ED; after being stabilized, what abortive medication will you give?
  • A. Sodium valproate
  • B. Carbamazepine
  • C. Diazepam
  • D. Phenobarbital
  • E. Midazolam
Best answer
E. Midazolam
Ongoing seizure 15 min in ED (prolonged convulsion) — after ABC/stabilisation, IM/buccal/IV midazolam (or IV lorazepam) aborts it; repeat once; if refractory → levetiracetam/phenytoin/valproate; then ICU + anaesthesia if status continues.
#357MCQ edited2017-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-7837ff04
A question about the risk of epilepsy after a febrile convulsion — which of the following is a risk factor?
  • A. Family history of epilepsy
  • B. Age less than 2 years
  • C. Low weight
  • D. Complex febrile seizure
  • E. Female gender
Best answer
D. Complex febrile seizure
Risk factors for epilepsy after a febrile convulsion: complex febrile seizure (focal, >15 min, recurrence in 24 h), family history of epilepsy, developmental delay, short fever duration before seizure. Simple febrile seizure in a normal child = ~1% (similar to population). (A—family history—is also an accepted risk factor; D is the strongest single “epilepsy-prediction” answer in this list.)

Sepsis — Recognition & First Steps

Definition: life-threatening organ dysfunction due to dysregulated host response to infection — SOFA score ↑≥2 with suspected infection (qSOFA for screening: RR ≥22, altered mentation, SBP ≤100 mmHg) — septic shock = vasopressors needed to keep MAP ≥65 despite fluids + lactate >2 mmol/L.

This exam’s item: child with fever + lethargy + hepatomegaly — FIRST step: blood culture (A) — take cultures before antibiotics; then give empirical antibiotics urgently, FBC/CRP, urine dip, monitor. Fever + unwell child = sepsis pathway until proven otherwise.

The Sepsis Six (to do within 1 hour): (1) O₂ (to sats 94–98%); (2) blood cultures (+ focal cultures: urine, sputum, CSF, wound); (3) empirical IV antibiotics (right drug, right stat); (4) IV fluid bolus (500 mL crystalloid, reassess — 30 mL/kg if lactate >4/hypotension); (5) lactate + FBC (haemoglobin, WBC, platelets for DIC) + renal/liver function/coagulation; (6) monitor urine output (catheter) + strict fluid balance.

Source-specific: neonate = Group B strep/E. coli (benzylpenicillin + gentamicin); adult chest = co-amoxiclav + clarithromycin; urine = ceftriaxone/gentamicin; skin = flucloxacillin; line sepsis = vancomycin; neutropenic = piperacillin-tazobactam ± gentamicin.

This exam: “proper monitor to know shock improved” → urine output (B) — ≥0.5 mL/kg/h adults is the most sensitive bedside marker of adequate resuscitation; also lactate clearance, cap refill, mental status — but urine output is the exam classic.

Complications: multi-organ failure, DIC (schistocytes, ↑PT/aPTT/D-dimer, fibrinogen↓), AKI, ARDS, adrenal insufficiency, death — escalate to senior/HDU/ICU early.

Exam pearls
  • Fever + lethargy = blood cultures now, antibiotics within 1 hour.
  • Lactate + urine output + cap refill = perfusion targets — urine output is the exam answer.
  • Never let antibiotics wait for the CT scan or the LP.

  • A. Blood culture
  • B. Chest X-ray
  • C. Lumbar puncture
  • D. Urine culture
  • E. CT abdomen
Best answer
A. Blood culture

Sickle Cell Disease — Parvovirus Aplastic Crisis

Pathophysiology: β6 Glu→Val point mutation → HbS polymerises when deoxygenated → RBC sickling → haemolysis (compensated-reticulocytosis normally) + vaso-occlusion (ischaemic pain, acute chest syndrome, stroke, splenic infarction/sequestration, priapism, osteonecrosis).

This exam’s key teaching set (two 2019/2017 items):

  • SCD + sudden fall in haemoglobin with LOW reticulocytes (and pancytopenia ±) → parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis — the virus infects erythroid precursors → marrow arrest — confirm with reticulocyte count (LOW — the answer, B) + parvovirus IgM/PCR. Management: supportive — transfusion if symptomatic; self-limiting ~1–2 weeks; isolate (teratogenic — pregnant contacts at risk of hydrops).
  • SCD + acute chest syndrome (fever, hypoxia, new infiltrate on CXR) + low Hb/platelets/WCC = parvovirus aplastic crisis (the answer A) — but in real life acute chest has an infectious trigger (Mycoplasma/chlamydia/virus/fat embolism) and needs: O₂, incentive spirometry, broad-spectrum antibiotics (cover atypicals), bronchodilators, analgesia, and urgent transfusion/exchange transfusion if severe (PaO₂ falling, multilobar).

SCD core: newborn screen; hydroxycarbamide (raises HbF — fewer crises); penicillin V + PCV vaccine (functional asplenia — S. pneumoniae/H. flu/Neisseria risk); folic acid; transcranial Doppler annually (stroke — transfuse if abnormal); avoid dehydration/cold/hypoxia/altitude; immunisations including meningococcal vaccine.

Exam pearls
  • SCD + low Hb + LOW reticulocytes = parvovirus aplastic crisis.
  • Sickle test distinguishes SCD from thalassaemia; Hb electrophoresis confirms.
  • Functional asplenia → pneumococcal/meningococcal vaccination + daily penicillin.

#288MCQ edited2017-Pediatrics-MCQ-Medicine-0a477dba
A patient with sickle cell disease presents with acute chest syndrome, low Hb, low platelets and low WBCs. What is the likely cause?
  • A. Parvovirus B19 (aplastic crisis)
  • B. Streptococcus pneumoniae
  • C. Mycoplasma
  • D. Salmonella
  • E. Influenza
Best answer
A. Parvovirus B19 (aplastic crisis)
SCD + acute chest syndrome + suddenly LOW Hb + low platelets + low WBCs = parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis (marrow arrest — reticulocytopenia!). Check reticulocyte count (LOW) + parvovirus serology; supportive ± transfusion. (Acute chest syndrome proper is a separate SCD complication — fever + hypoxia + new infiltrate — but the LAB picture here is aplastic crisis.)

Skin & Soft-Tissue Infections — Cellulitis, Abscess

IDSA classification:

TypeFeaturesOrganismTreatment
Non-purulent cellulitisDiffuse, spreading erythema, warmth, swelling, pain, poorly demarcated, ± fever/streaking (lymphangitis)β-haemolytic streptococci (Group A — S. pyogenes)Oral/IV flucloxacillin/penicillin (+ clindamycin if severe)
Purulent (abscess/furuncle)Localized, fluctuant, tender, indurated red area ± central point/“head”Staphylococcus aureus (incl. MRSA — commonest purulent cause)Incision & drainage (main treatment) ± antibiotics if surrounding cellulitis/fever/immunocompromised
ErysipelasSuperficial, sharply demarcated, raised, face/leg, rapid onsetGroup A streptococcusPenicillin/flucloxacillin

Paediatric SAQ (this exam): fever + leg pain + red image in a child → cellulitis — Group A (or S. aureus); treatment beyond antibiotics/fluids: supportive — elevate the limb, analgesia/antipyretic, mark the border, admit if unwell/rapidly spreading (measure & monitor spread; escalate to surgery if necrotising).

Exam pearls
  • Diffuse spreading (adults) = Group A strep → penicillin/flucloxacillin.
  • Localised fluctuant/child’s calf = S. aureus → drainage ± anti-staph antibiotics.
  • Pain out of proportion + dusky skin = necrotising fasciitis → operate NOW.

Thalassaemia

Pathophysiology: reduced/absent globin-chain synthesis — α (2 genes on each chromosome 16) or β (1 gene on each chromosome 11); unbalanced chain accumulation → ineffective erythropoiesis + haemolysis + intramedullary destruction; autosomal recessive.

α-thalassaemiaβ-thalassaemia
Genetics4 deleted genes = Hb Bart’s (hydrops fetalis — intrauterine death); 3 = HbH disease (haemolytic anaemia); 2 = trait (mild); 1 = silent carrier2 mutated genes = thalassaemia MAJOR (Cooley’s anaemia) — normal at birth (HbF) → symptoms from ~4–6 months (this exam); 1 mutated = trait (minor, asymptomatic microcytosis)
LabsMicrocytic, hypochromic, target cells, ↑RBC count (unlike iron deficiency), normal/high ferritin, HbH inclusion bodies (HbH)Microcytic + VERY high HbF, raised HbA2 on electrophoresis/HPLC, absent HbA (major), ineffective erythropoiesis, high reticulocytes (this exam 9.9%), high LDH/indirect bilirubin, sickling test NEGATIVE (this exam)
Features (major)—Severe anaemia + hepatosplenomegaly (extramedullary haematopoiesis) + frontal bossing/maxillary overgrowth (“chipmunk face”) + growth failure + pathological fractures + gallstones (pigment) + iron overload (cardiomyopathy/endocrine failure); death in childhood untreated

THIS exam (twice — 2017/2018 identical): 5–7-month-old, pallor, splenomegaly 7 cm, Hb 5.7 / MCV 51 / retic 9.9% / negative sickle test → β-thalassaemia major; confirm: haemoglobin electrophoresis/HPLC (HbF↑, HbA2↑, absent HbA) + β-globin genotyping; treatment: (a) regular blood transfusion program to keep Hb ≥95–105 g/L + (b) iron chelation therapy (desferrioxamine / deferasirox / deferiprone) with cardiac-liver MRI T2* monitoring — folic acid supplements; splenectomy only if hypersplenism; allo-HSCT is curative (matched sibling); genetic counselling/screening for parents & siblings (25% each child).

Not iron deficiency: thalassaemia trait = high RBC, normal ferritin, high HbA2; iron deficiency = low ferritin, high RDW, low RBC; confirm with electrophoresis/iron studies — NEVER give iron to a thalassaemic unless deficient (overload risk).

Exam pearls
  • Microcytosis + high RBC + normal ferritin = thalassaemia (not iron deficiency).
  • 6-month-old + splenomegaly + severe anaemia + negative sickle = β-thal major → HPLC, then transfusion + chelation.
  • Hb Bart’s = hydrops; HbH = golf-ball; trait = silent.

#377SAQ edited2017-Pediatrics-SAQ-Medicine-10e2ebb4
A 5-month-old patient presents with pallor and abdominal distension. Physical examination shows splenomegaly 7 cm below the costal margin. Labs show microcytic hypochromic anemia with reticulocytes 9.9% and a negative sickle test.
  1. What is the most likely diagnosis? (1 pt)
  2. What is the investigation to confirm the diagnosis? (1 pt)
  3. How do you treat this patient? (2 answers) (2 pt)
Best answer
1) Most likely diagnosis: β-thalassaemia major (Cooley’s anaemia) — 5-month-old, pallor, splenomegaly 7 cm, severe microcytic hypochromic anaemia (Hb 5.7, MCV 51), reticulocytes 9.9%, sickling test negative. 2) Best confirmatory investigation: haemoglobin electrophoresis/HPLC — markedly raised HbF, raised HbA₂, absent/reduced HbA; plus β-globin genotyping; parental testing. 3) Treatment (2 answers): (a) regular blood transfusion programme (every 3–4 weeks to Hb ≥90–105 g/L) + (b) iron chelation therapy (deferasirox/desferrioxamine — monitor cardiac/liver iron MRI T2*) — plus folic acid; splenectomy only for hypersplenism; curative: allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplant (matched sibling).
Without transfusion: high-output cardiac failure, growth failure, death in childhood. Chelation prevents iron-overload cardiomyopathy/endocrinopathy. Vaccinate (pneumococcal); annual echo/MRI T2*.
